Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 1:

Surat al-Nur (The Light) is Medinan, as Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu Hayyan reported the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) that it is Medinan, and he did not exempt any of its many verses. It is reported from al-Qurtubi that the verse ﴿O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess and those among you who have not reached puberty ask your permission...﴾ [al-Nur: 58] etc. is Meccan. The surah has sixty-two verses, and it is said to have sixty-four.

The connection between this surah and Surat al-Mu'minun is that when Allah, glorified is He, said in it, ﴿and those who guard their private parts﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5], He then mentioned in this surah the rulings concerning those who did not guard their private parts, namely the adulterous woman and the adulterer, and what is connected to that concerning slander, the story of the slander (al-ifk), the command to lower the gaze, which is the invitation to fornication, and the seeking of permission (isti'dhan), which was only prescribed because of looking. In it He commanded marriage as a means of guarding the private parts, commanded whoever cannot marry to seek chastity, and forbade compelling slave-girls to fornication.

Al-Tabarsi said concerning this: When He, exalted is He, mentioned earlier that He did not create creation in vain but for command and prohibition, He, majestic and exalted, here mentioned a body of commands and prohibitions. Perhaps the first connection is the better one.

It is reported from Mujahid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Teach your men Surat al-Ma'idah, and teach your women Surat al-Nur.'"

And it is reported from Harithah ibn Mudarrib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to us: Learn Surat al-Nisa', al-Ahzab, and al-Nur."

﴿Surah﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "this is a surah," and it is pointed to with "this" (hadhihi), treating it as though it were present and witnessed. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We have sent it down﴾ together with what is conjoined to it, are attributes of it that confirm what the indefiniteness (tankir) conveys of grandeur (fakhamah) in respect of its essence, by the grandeur in respect of its attributes, as Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) mentioned. As for the view that it may be for specification (takhsis), to exclude what subsists in His essence, glorified is He, it is nothing at all, as is not hidden.

It is permitted that ﴿surah﴾ be the subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, i.e., "what is recited to you, or in what We have revealed to you, is a surah that We have sent down," etc. Some have said that the purpose of this sentence is praise, commendation, and encouragement, not the benefit of an informative statement (khabar) nor its necessary implication, which is that the speaker knows the ruling, since he knows all that. The discussion concerns a case where such a sentence is intended as an performative utterance (insha'), according to what al-Kashshaf chose, and this is the apparent meaning of al-Imam al-Marzuqi's saying regarding "my people, they killed Umaym, my brother": this speech saddens and grieves, and is not an informative statement. Others chose that the sentence is informative, meant as an informative statement, but it was only uttered for a purpose other than conveying the ruling or its implication, and this is the view of al-Sakalkuti. Al-Murawwazi's first statement is that what is meant by informing (ikhbar) in it is notifying (i'lam). The verification of this is in its proper place. Shaykh al-Islam objected to this view with what he investigated.

Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that ﴿surah﴾ be the subject, with the predicate being His saying, ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer﴾ etc. There is in it what is in it of remoteness. The commendable view is the first. In my opinion, in such sentences the affirmation (ithbat) is directed at the restriction (qayd). 'Abd al-Qahir mentioned this, and here it is the sending down of it and its prescription, and the sending down of clear verses in it so that those addressed may remember, or so that their remembrance is hoped for. So reflect.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Mujahid, 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi al-Basri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Hamdani al-Kufi, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Haywa, Mahbub from Abu 'Amr, and Umm al-Darda' read ﴿surah﴾ in the accusative (surah), as the object of an omitted verb, i.e., "recite" (utlu). Some estimated it as "recite" (utlu) in the plural with a plural pronoun, since the addresses that come after it are like that. This is not necessary, because the verb includes the meaning of saying (qawl), so the sentence in that case is like His saying, ﴿Say: Obey Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 32]. There is no doubt that this is permissible.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative as an incitement (ighra', attention-drawing), i.e., "[take] the surah in front of you." Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that it is not permissible to omit the incitement particle, because its effect is weak, since its operation is by analogy to the verb. Ibn Malik's statement implies its permissibility, and he claimed that this is the school of Sibawayh, and there is discussion about it. More than one scholar permitted that this is of the type of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun), which is apparent according to the view of one who does not require, for the accusative in ishtighal, that the nominative be valid as a subject-initial (mubtada'). As for the view of one who requires that, it is not apparent, because ﴿surah﴾ is indefinite and has no justification (musawwigh) for it, so it is not permissible to make it nominative as a subject-initial. Perhaps one who requires this and says the accusative is by ishtighal here makes the indefinite noun qualified by what the tanwin indicates, as if it were said: "a surah, great," as it was said: "an evil, its fang is bared."

Al-Farra' said: The accusative of ﴿surah﴾ is as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun of the accusative in ﴿We have sent it down﴾, and a circumstantial state from a pronoun may precede it. End of quote. Perhaps the pronoun on this view refers to the rulings understood from the speech, so it is as if it were said: "We sent down the rulings as a surah," i.e., in the state of being a surah from the surahs of the Qur'an. This is the view taken in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's commentary). Perhaps it is said that the pronoun may refer to the surah existing in knowledge without considering its restriction by an attribute, and the mentioned ﴿surah﴾ is qualified by what its tanwin indicates, so it is as if it were said: "We sent down the surah in the state of being a great surah." It is not hidden that all of that is an artificial stretch for which there is no need, when the view that is beyond dispute exists.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We have made it obligatory﴾ is either with an omitted noun, i.e., "We made obligatory its rulings," or on the basis of metaphor in the attribution (majaz fi al-isnad), in which what belongs to the signified is attributed to the signifier because of a connection between them that resembles the adverbial relation (zarfiyyah). It is possible, though remotely, that the speech contains istikhdam (a rhetorical device in which one word is used with two meanings), such that by ﴿surah﴾ its literal meaning is intended, and by its pronoun its metaphorical meaning is intended, namely the rulings indicated by it. The root meaning of fard is cutting a hard thing and making an impression on it. What is meant here is obligation (ijab) in the most complete manner, so it is as if it were said: "We made obligatory what is in it of rulings with a definitive obligation." In mentioning that there is a fine opening (baraʿat al-istihlal), as has been said.

'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu 'Amr, and Ibn Kathir read ﴿wa-farradnaha﴾ with a doubled ra' (to emphasize the obligation). The indication is to an increase in its binding force, or to the multiplicity and abundance of the obligations, or to the large number of those upon whom it was obligated among the predecessors and successors. In the Shihabi marginal notes it says: "He explained farradnaha as fasalnaha (we distinguished it), and what was mentioned also applies to it." ﴿And We have sent down in it﴾, i.e., in this surah, ﴿clear verses﴾. It is possible that what is meant by them is the verses to which the obligatory rulings are attached, and the adverbial relation applies to them clearly. The meaning of their being clear is the clarity of their indication of their rulings, not of their meanings absolutely, because they are the model for most verses in that respect. The repetition of "We have sent down," together with the fact that sending down the surah implies sending down its verses, shows the utmost care for its matter. It is possible that what is meant by them is all the verses of the surah, and the adverbial relation in that case is in terms of the whole including each of its parts. The meaning of its being clear is that there is no difficulty in it that would require interpretation as in some verses. The repetition of "We have sent down," although it is evident that sending down all the verses is the same as sending down the surah, is because the surah is distinguished by an appealing title that calls for singling out its sending down by mention, to make its importance known and to raise its status, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We delivered them from a severe punishment﴾ [Hud: 58], after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We delivered Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾ [Hud: 58]. The first possibility is more apparent.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: He, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of the surah types of rulings and limits, and at its end proofs of monotheism. So His saying, ﴿We have made it obligatory﴾, is an indication to the rulings established at the beginning, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and We have sent down in it clear verses﴾, is an indication to the proofs of monotheism that were explained. It is supported by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿so that you may remember﴾, for the rulings were not known so that they would be remembered. End of quote. This, in my opinion, is a good view. Yes, it was said that there is an objection to what he mentioned as support, since whoever holds the first possibility can say: the intended remembrance is its ultimate purpose, which is avoiding what is forbidden by acting according to what those verses require. One may say: this requires resorting to metaphor in "remembrance," unlike what the Imam mentioned, since remembrance according to it is in its apparent meaning, and this degree is enough for it to be supported.

The original form of ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ is tatadhakkarun, with one of the two ta's omitted. It was also read with the second of the two assimilated into the dhal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 2 (part 1 of 3):

﴿The adulteress and the adulterer﴾ is the beginning of the detailed explanation of the rulings that were alluded to at first. The word "al-zaniyatu" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the speech is on the basis of an omitted modifier, with the modified noun put in its place. The original is: "[what is] recited to you" or "in the obligations," i.e., the ruling of the adulteress and the adulterer, which was alluded to in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We have ordained it﴾. The "fa'" in His words, exalted is He: ﴿flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ is causal (sababiyyah), and it was said it is the "fa'" of the orator's speech (sayf khatib). Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj held that the predicate is the clause "flog" etc. The "fa'" according to the well-known view is because the subject includes the meaning of a condition, since the "al-" in it and in what is conjoined to it is a relative pronoun, i.e., "the one who committed fornication" and "the one who committed fornication," so: flog etc. Some permit the entry of the "fa'" into the predicate when the subject carries a meaning that makes the predicate's consequence deserved, even if there is no relative pronoun, as in his words: "And the one who says 'Khawlan' – marry their young women," for this tribe is famous for nobility and goodness, like the fame of Hatim for generosity and 'Antara for bravery, and that is a meaning that makes the command to marry a deserved consequence. On this basis the case for the entry of the "fa'" here is strengthened, as is not hidden. The scholar al-Qutb said: The "fa'" was brought because the subject came after "amma" implicitly, i.e., "as for the adulteress and the adulterer, flog etc." It is reported from al-Akhfash that it is the "fa'" of the orator's speech. What led Sibawayh to his view is what is understood from the Book, as it is said that the customary method in Arabic speech, when one wishes to explain a meaning and detail it, out of concern for its matter, is to mention before it what is a heading and summary of it; and this is only possible if it is built on two clauses. So what he held regarding the verse is more fitting for this than what others held. Also, it is free from the occurrence of an imperative as a predicate and the awkwardness in it, and the matter of the "fa'" on it is clear and needs no strain. Abu Hayyan said: The cause of the disagreement is that Sibawayh and al-Khalil stipulate for the entry of the "fa'" in the predicate that the subject be a relative pronoun, not something that directly accepts a conditional particle; while others do not stipulate that.

ʿAbd Allah read "wa-l-zan" without the yā’, as a lightening (takhfif). ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, Yahya ibn Yaʿmur, ʿAmr ibn Qa'id, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu al-Sammal and Ruways read "al-zaniyata wa-l-zani" with both in the accusative, by supposing a verb that the apparent one explains, and the "fa'" – according to what Ibn Jinni said – because the meaning ultimately tends to the condition, and the imperative in the answer is conjoined with it. So it is permissible to say "Zayd, so strike him," but not "Zayd, so I struck him" with the "fa'," because it does not enter the answer of a condition when the verb is past. The intended meaning here, according to what is in some commentaries on the Kashshaf: "If you want to know the ruling of the adulteress and the adulterer, then flog etc." It was also said: "If you flog the adulteress and the adulterer, then flog etc.," and this does not indicate the intended obligation. It was said the "fa'" entered because the duty of the explainer is to mention after the explained, like the detail after the summary in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. It is also permissible that it be conjunctive, and the meaning is a lashing after a lashing; and that does not contradict its being an explanation of the preceding, because it is by consideration of specific unity. End of quotation.

You know that the conjunction with "fa'" is not attested where the word of the explainer and the explained are identical, and they have explicitly stated the impermissibility of "Zayd, so I struck him" by consensus. So if conjunction were valid in what was mentioned, this would be permissible in the sense of "a strike after a strike." Moreover, that the intended meaning here is "a lashing after a lashing" is something whose problems are not hidden. So what is apparent is what was transmitted from Ibn Jinni. The well-known view is that Sibawayh and al-Khalil prefer the reading of the accusative because of the imperative, while others among the Basrans and Kufans prefer the nominative, because it is like a consensus in recitation, and it is stronger in Arabic, since the meaning upon it is: "Whoever commits fornication, flog him." So said al-Zajjaj. Al-Khafaji, after quoting Sibawayh's words in this context, said: There is nothing in Sibawayh's words that indicates preference, as you have heard; rather it is understood from him that the nominative in such cases is more eloquent and more forceful than the accusative in terms of meaning, and more eloquent than the nominative in that the speech is one clause in both meaning and wording together. So let it be reviewed and considered.

"Al-jald" is the striking with the whip (jald). The pattern of the triliteral verb with a fatha on the middle radical has been applied to names of concrete things, so one says "ra's-uhu" (his head), "zahr-uhu" (his back), "batn-uhu" (his belly). Al-Raghib permitted that the meaning of "jaldihi" be striking him with the hide (jald), like "'asahu" meaning striking him with the staff. The intended meaning here is the first, for the reports have shown that the adulteress and the adulterer are struck with a whip that has no knot on it and no branch. It was said that the whip being of this kind was in the time of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, by consensus of the Companions; but before him, it was sometimes with the hand, sometimes with a sandal, sometimes with a fresh palm stalk, and sometimes with a staff. Then, the apparent sense of "darb al-jald" is more general, whether it is without an intermediary or with one. Some claimed – and it is nothing – that the apparent is that it is without an intermediary, and that it may perhaps be supported for what our companions held, and Malik said likewise: that the adulterer's garments are removed at the time of flogging, except the waist-wrapper, for he is not stripped since it covers his nakedness with it. From al-Shafi'i and Ahmad: that a shirt or two shirts are left on him. ʿAbd al-Razzaq transmitted with his chain from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, that a man was brought for a hadd punishment and he struck him while he wore a Qastalani cloak. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is not lawful in this community to strip or to stretch." As for the woman, her garments are not removed according to us except the fur and the padded garment, and this is a clear view.

Some reports indicate that man and woman are equal in not removing garments except the fur and the padded garment. It seems that whoever does not say that garments are removed says: the word "jald" in custom means striking in general, and is not specific to striking the skin without an intermediary. Yes, it may be said: in choosing it over "darb" there is an indication that what is meant is a striking that causes pain to the skin; and perhaps for this reason it was said the fur and the padded garment are removed, for striking mostly does not cause pain to the skin of one who wears either of them. And the striking should not be severe, since destruction is not desired. From here they said:

If the one who is liable to the hadd is weak in constitution and destruction is feared for him, he is flogged with a light striking that he can bear. Likewise they said: the striking is distributed over the limbs of the one punished, because gathering it in one limb may spoil it and perhaps lead to death. The face and the private parts should be avoided, because of what was narrated as a halted report from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, that a man was brought, drunk or in a hadd case, and he said: "Strike, and give every limb its due, and avoid the face and the private parts." Likewise the head, because it is the gathering place of the inner senses, so it may be spoiled, and that is destruction in meaning. Abu Yusuf used to say to avoid it, then he retracted and said he is struck one blow. It is also reported from him that he excepted the belly and the chest, and this is open to question, unless it is said that the striking in his time was like the striking that the oppressors of our time do, and in that case it should be said that the head is excluded definitively. From Malik: he restricted the striking to the back and what is adjacent to it, because of what is authentically established from the Prophet ﷺ to Hilal ibn Umayya: "The evidence, or else a hadd on your back." It is answered that the "back" here means the self, i.e., a hadd established upon you, by the evidence of what is established from the senior Companions ʿUmar, ʿAli and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them. And the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "When one of you strikes, let him avoid the face." This applies to the like of the hadd and what is other than it is included in striking; then the private parts were excluded from it by consensus. From Muhammad, in ta'zir (discretionary punishment) he strikes the back, and in hudud he strikes the limbs. Then this striking is done to a man standing, not stretched, and to a woman seated; and this is reported from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face. It seems the reason is that the basis of the hadd is publicity, as a deterrent to the common people from the like, and standing is more effective in it; and the woman's matter is based on concealment, so the publicizing of the hadd alone is sufficient without addition. If the man refuses and does not stand still, or does not endure, there is no harm in tying him to a pillar or having someone hold him.

The number prescribed in the striking of each of them, namely one hundred lashes, is what is called "one hundred lashes" in some way, even if the first, second and third are not individually specified, up to the completion of the hundred. So if a hundred men struck him with a hundred whips at once, it suffices for the hadd. Rather, they said: it is permissible for the whips to be gathered so that he is struck once in such a way that each of them reaches him.

It is reported from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, that in a hadd he struck forty blows with a whip that had two ends, so each blow counted as two.

The adulteress is mentioned before the adulterer, although custom is to mention the adulterer before her, because she is the origin, since the motive in her is stronger, and had she not allowed it, he would not have committed fornication. Their derivation is from "zina," which is a shortened (maqsur) form in the eloquent language, the language of the people of the Hijaz; it may be lengthened (mamdud) in the dialect of the people of Najd, and upon that al-Farazdaq said:

"O Abu Tahir, whoever commits fornication, his fornication will be known, and whoever drinks the khurtum will become intoxicated in the morning."

And "zina," in the customary usage of language and in the Sharia, according to what has been said, is a man's penetrating a woman in the vagina, outside of ownership and the semblance of ownership. In this there is an objection: it applies to the woman's fornication, for it is fornication and the definition does not apply to it. What was said in reply, that the act of intercourse is a matter shared between man and woman, so when it occurs between them each of them is described by it, and she is called "wati'ah" (one who has intercourse), and for this reason He, glory be to Him, named her "zaniyah," is not hidden in its problems; besides, the definition contains what this answer would not fix, even if it were correct. The truth is that her fornication, linguistically, is her enabling of a man's fornication with her; and that if one wishes to define the zina meant in the verse so as to include her zina, then the enabling must be added with respect to her, indeed added with respect to each of them. It may be said: it is the entry by a responsible, consenting person of a quantity of his glans before a desired (mushtahah) person, presently or in the past, without ownership or semblance of ownership, or the enabling of that, or her enabling it in the abode of Islam, so that it applies to the case where, if he were lying on his back, she sat upon his member and he left her until she made it enter; for they are both subject to the hadd in this case, though nothing from him existed except enabling. It is known from this definition that there is no hadd on a child, a madman, or one compelled by the ruler; nor on one who inserts into the anus, or into the vagina of a young girl not yet desirable, or of a dead woman, or of an animal; unlike one who inserts into the vagina of an old woman. Nor on one who commits fornication in the abode of war, nor on one who commits it under a semblance (shubha). In some of what was mentioned there is discussion that should be sought in books of jurisprudence. The ruling is general for one who commits fornication while muhsan (married) and for others, but it was abrogated definitively in the case of the muhsan, for the ruling for him is stoning. Sufficient for us in identifying the abrogator is the certainty of his command ﷺ to stone, and his doing it in his lifetime, peace be upon him, on several occasions; so it is abrogation of the Book by the definitive Sunnah.

The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and those before them among the early generations, and the scholars of the Ummah and the imams of the Muslims, have agreed that the muhsan is stoned with stones until he dies. The denial of this by the Kharijites is false, for if they deny the authority of the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them,

[Page 79, continued]

...Allah the Exalted about them, is a compound ignorance (*jahl murakkab*, a state of ignorance that is unaware of itself). Even if they deny that it occurred from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because they reject the authority of a solitary report (*khabar al-wahid*, a report transmitted by one or a few narrators), then that denial, after its invalidity has been established by evidence, is not what we are discussing. This is because the establishment of stoning from him, upon him be prayers and peace, is *mutawatir* in meaning (widely transmitted so that its substance is certain), like the bravery of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and the generosity of Hatim. The solitary reports concern its particular forms and specific details. They, like all Muslims, hold that acting upon what is *mutawatir* in meaning is obligatory, just as what is *mutawatir* in wording is. However, their deviation from the Companions and the Muslims, and their abandonment of consulting the scholars of the Muslims and the narrators, led them into many ignorances, because the reports were hidden from them and not widely known. For this reason, when they criticized Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz for holding to stoning on the ground that it is not in the Book of Allah the Exalted, he obligated them to [accept] the numbers of the units of prayer and the amounts of zakat. They said: "That was done by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims." He said to them: "And this too is so." Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was made aware of them and made them manifest when he said, as al-Bukhari narrated: "I feared that a time would pass over people until someone says: 'We do not find stoning in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic,' and so they would go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had revealed. Indeed, stoning is a right upon whoever commits adultery when he has been married (*ahsana*), if evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession." Abu Dawud narrated that he, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered a sermon and said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent Muhammad ﷺ with the truth and revealed to him a Book, and among what He revealed to him was the verse of stoning, by which is meant His saying, the Exalted: 'The shaykh and the shaykha, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.' We recited it and memorized it..." until he said:

"And I feared that a time would pass over people and someone would say: 'We do not find stoning'..." The hadith with its chains. And he said: "Were it not that it would be said that Umar added to the Book, I would have written it in the margin of the noble Mushaf." Some people went to the view that the abrogating (*nasikh*, the ruling that cancels an earlier one) was the verse whose recitation was abrogated (*mansukh al-tilawa*), which Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned.

Al-Allama Ibn al-Humam said: That the abrogating element is a definitive Sunnah is more preferable than that the abrogating element is the verse he mentioned, because its establishment as Qur'an, followed by the abrogation of its recitation, is not certain, even though Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned it and the people remained silent. This is because a silent consensus (*ijma' sukuti*, agreement inferred from silence) being a proof is disputed. And even if it is accepted as a proof, we cannot be certain that all the mujtahid Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were present at that time. Then there is no doubt that the path to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, is speculative (*zanni*). For this reason, and Allah knows best.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said when he flogged Shurahah and then stoned her: "I flogged her by the Book of Allah the Exalted, and I stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

He did not justify stoning by the Qur'an whose recitation was abrogated. It is known from his aforementioned saying, may Allah ennoble his face, that he holds that the general application of the verse was not abrogated. Thus his view is that stoning is an additional ruling regarding the married person (*muhsan*), established by the Sunnah. This is also the view of the people of the apparent meaning (*Ahl al-Zahir*) and is a narration from Ahmad. They based this on what Abu Dawud narrated from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The married (*thayyib*) for the married: a hundred lashes and stoning with stones." In another narration by others: "And stoning with stones."

According to the Hanafis, one does not combine stoning and flogging for the married person. This is also the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i and another narration from Ahmad, because flogging empties the punishment of its purpose, for which the prescribed penalty was legislated, which is deterrence (*al-intizar*), or its purpose is nullified when killing follows it. The strongest basis for their argument is that he ﷺ definitively did not combine them. For the routes of narration are consistent that: "He ﷺ, after asking Ma'iz about his marital status and prompting him to retract, did not add anything beyond the command to stone, and said: 'Take him and stone him.'" He ﷺ also said, upon him be prayers and peace: "Go out, O Unays, to this man's wife, and if she confesses, then stone her." He did not say: "Flog her, then stone her." The rest of the noble hadith contains: "She confessed, so he ordered her, and she was stoned." Stoning recurred in his time ﷺ, and no one narrated that he combined it with flogging. So we are certain that there was only stoning. Hence the earlier report must be considered abrogated, even if the specific abrogating element is not known.

As for what Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, did regarding combining them, it is answered that it was an opinion which does not stand against the definitive transmission from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, nor against the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It may be said that it is possible that the matter had not been established for him as an act of *ihsan* until after the flogging, but this is very far-fetched, as is evident from returning to the account.

The conditions of *ihsan* for stoning are realized by things which one of the scholars arranged in verse, saying:

"The conditions of *ihsan* have come as six: so take them from the text, asking for clarification.
Maturity, sanity, freedom, and the fourth of them is that he be Muslim.
A valid contract and lawful intercourse; whenever one condition is lacking, he will not be stoned."

Several scholars added that each of the two spouses must be equal to the other in the conditions of *ihsan* at the time of intercourse, by the ruling of the marriage. So if a free, Muslim, adult, sane man marries a slave woman, or a female child, or a mad woman, or a Scripturist woman, and consummates the marriage with her, he does not become *muhsan* by this consummation, such that if he commits adultery afterward he will not be stoned. Likewise, if a free, adult, sane, Muslim woman marries a slave, or a madman, or a boy, and he consummates the marriage with her, she does not become *muhsana*, so she is not stoned if she commits adultery afterward.

Ibn al-Kamal mentioned another condition, which is that their *ihsan* is not nullified by apostasy. So if one of them apostatized, we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted, and then both embraced Islam again, it does not return except by consummation after that. If it was nullified by madness or imbecility, it returns upon recovery, and it was said: it returns by intercourse after that.

Al-Shafi'i does not stipulate equality in the conditions of *ihsan* at the time of intercourse, so there is no stoning according to him in the two aforementioned cases. Likewise, he does not stipulate Islam. So if a free, married dhimmi commits adultery, he is flogged according to us and stoned according to him. This is a narration from Abu Yusuf, and Ahmad also held it. Malik's view is like ours.

The opponent argued with what is in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and mentioned to him that a woman and a man from among them had committed adultery. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'What do you find in the Torah concerning the matter of stoning?' They said: 'We expose them and they are flogged.' Abdullah ibn Salam said: 'You have lied in what you claim, that it contains stoning.' So they brought the Torah and unrolled it, and one of them, namely Abdullah ibn Suwar, placed his hand on the verse of stoning and read what came before it and after it. Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: 'Lift your hand.' He lifted his hand, and there was the verse of stoning. They said: 'Speak the truth, O Muhammad.' So the Prophet ﷺ ordered them both, and they were stoned."

Our evidence is what Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated in his *Musnad*. He said: Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad informed us, Ubayd Allah narrated to us from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not *muhsan*."

Ishaq raised this report once, as he said, and stopped it (as a statement of a Companion) another time. Al-Daraqutni narrated it in his *Sunan* and said: "No one raised it except Rahawayh ibn Rahawayh." It is said that he retracted from that. The correct view is that it is *mawquf* (attributed to a Companion, not the Prophet). End of quotation.

In *al-Inaya* it is stated: The wording of Ishaq, as you see, contains no retraction. Rather, it is mentioned about the narrator that once he raised it and once he delivered it as a fatwa without raising it. There is no doubt that such a report, after the soundness of the route to it is established, is judged as *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), according to what is preferred in the science of hadith: that when raising and stopping conflict, the ruling is for raising. And after that, if it has come through routes that contain weakness, it does no harm.

Some of our eminent companions answered: Stoning was legislated without the condition of Islam at the time the Prophet ﷺ stoned the Jewish man and woman, by what Allah the Exalted revealed to him, upon him be prayers and peace. His asking the Jews about what they find in the Torah concerning this matter was not because he needed to know its ruling from that. The claim that he, upon him be prayers and peace, when he first came to Medina, was commanded to judge by what is in the Torah is disputed. Rather, that was only to rebuke them for abandoning judgment by what Allah the Exalted had revealed to them. When the purpose was achieved, the Prophet ﷺ ruled to stone them according to his own law, which agrees with their law. And since it is known that stoning was established in our law at the time of their stoning, without the condition of Islam... and the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, which indicates the condition of Islam, is established. There is no known history by which it can be determined whether the condition of Islam came before its non-stipulation or after it. A conflict arises between his action of stoning the two Jews and his aforementioned saying, so it requires weighing. They have said: when a saying and an action conflict and it is not known which came first, the saying is given precedence over the action. There is also another aspect: giving precedence to this saying necessitates averting the punishment (*dar' al-hadd*), while giving precedence to that action necessitates caution in imposing the punishment. And in matters of *hudud* (fixed punishments), the preferable course when there is conflict is to prefer what removes the punishment.

It is not hidden that every view that is preferred is judged as later in its time by *ijtihad* (independent reasoning). Therefore, what is relied upon in the ruling is the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The opponent's statement that the intended meaning of *muhsan* in it is the one who may be retaliated against from a Muslim is contrary to the apparent meaning, because the most common usage of *ihsan* is for the *ihsan* of stoning. Some answered the proponents of the view that the punishment for the virgin's fornication with a virgin is a hundred lashes and a year of exile, namely Imam al-Shafi'i, Imam Ahmad, al-Thawri and al-Hasan ibn Salih, by the verse. The answer is that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ and so on, is the beginning of an explanation of what the ruling for fornication is. So what is mentioned is the complete ruling. Otherwise it would be ignorance rather than explanation and detail, since it would be understood from it that it is complete, while it is not complete in reality. So with the beginning of the explanation, it would be further from explanation, because it causes compound ignorance more, whereas before it the ignorance was simple. Thus by its implication one understands that the ruling for the fornicatress and the fornicator is nothing but flogging. More concisely: the context is one of explanation, so silence in it implies restriction (*hasr*). The opponent said: even if we concede the indication of restriction, and that what is mentioned is the complete ruling, so that the meaning is that the punishment for each is nothing but flogging, that is abrogated by what is authentically narrated from the transmission of Ubada ibn al-Samit from him ﷺ: "The virgin for the virgin: a hundred lashes and exile for a year."

It is answered that, even granting this, the claim of abrogation by what has been mentioned is not valid, because it is a solitary report (*khabar al-wahid*), and according to us it is not permissible to abrogate the Book by it. The claim that the aforementioned report has been received by the community with acceptance does not benefit, because if by receiving it with acceptance is meant their consensus on acting upon it, this is disputed. For it is authentically reported from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he did not hold to its exile for both of them, and he said: "It is enough for them of trial that they be banished." In another narration: "Banishment is enough of a trial." And if by their consensus on its authenticity is meant the soundness of its chain, then many solitary reports are of this kind, and they do not thereby leave being solitary reports. Moreover, there is in it no more than that exile is obligatory, and it does not indicate that it is obligatory as a *hadd* (fixed punishment). Rather, what is in the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari from the saying of Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled concerning one who committed fornication and was not *muhsan* with a year's exile and the establishing of the *hadd*," is clear that exile is not part of the *hadd*, because it is conjoined to it (by the conjunction "and"). That he used *hadd* for part of what it denotes and conjoined to another part is far-fetched. So it is permissible that it is a *ta'zir* (discretionary punishment) for a public interest. The Imam may banish for a public interest he sees in other than what was mentioned, as it is authentically reported that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, banished Nasr ibn Hajjaj to Basra, because some women were captivated by his beauty. He heard a woman say, it is said she was the mother of al-Hajjaj al-Thaqafi, and therefore Abd al-Malik said to him one day: "O son of the one desired, you say:

'Is there a way to wine so I may drink it,
or is there a way to Nasr ibn Hajjaj?'"

[82]

*To a youth of noble lineage, in the prime of his years, gentle of countenance, generous, not quarrelsome.*

The view that ta'zir (discretionary punishment, a penalty set by the judge rather than fixed by the revealed texts) cannot be combined with the hadd (the prescribed punishment) is untenable. Al-Faqih al-Marghinani claimed that the aforementioned report is abrogated (mansukh), since its second part, which indicates the combining of flogging and stoning, is abrogated, as you have learned. But there is a reply: there is no necessity that a report whose parts include both abrogated and non-abrogated statements cannot be transmitted. Yes, it may be that the abrogation of one part makes it easier for the possibility of abrogation to reach the other part. In that case this possibility remains present in our matter, and so it weakens the report below the level of the solitary reports (ahad) to which that possibility has not reached. It is therefore more appropriate that what the Book has established, namely that the hadd is flogging alone, should not be abrogated, as you have heard it explained. So reflect.

Then, the banishment (taghrib) is not restricted to men according to those imams. They have said: a woman is banished accompanied by a mahram (a male relative she may not marry), and her expenses are upon her according to one opinion, and from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) according to another. If he refuses, then according to one opinion the imam compels him, and according to another he does not. If the road is safe, then regarding her banishment without a mahram there are two opinions. According to Malik and al-Awza'i, only the man is banished and the woman is not banished,

because of his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "The virgin for the virgin..." etc. The others among those mentioned earlier said: the hadith must include her, for its beginning is: "Take from me; Allah, may He be exalted, has made a way for them: the virgin for the virgin..." etc., and this is a text that banishment and flogging are the way for women. The virgin is referred to as female. Do you not see his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "The virgin is asked for permission" (al-bikr tasta'dhin)?

Setting all that aside, it may be said that this is among the matters in which rulings are established for women by texts that indicate them for men, through tanqih al-manat (purification of the ground of analogy, i.e., isolating the effective cause from irrelevant features). Furthermore, it is not hidden that the apparent sense of "the adulteress and the adulterer" includes the slave and others, so the measure of the hadd would be one for all. However, the words of the Exalted: "Upon them is half of the punishment imposed upon the chaste women" [al-Nisa': 25], etc., excluded the female slaves, for the verse was revealed concerning them. Likewise it excluded the male slaves, since there is no difference between male and female through tanqih al-manat. So this is referred to the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), on the basis that the indication does not require that the unmentioned be more deserving of the ruling than the mentioned; equality suffices in it. It has been said that the male slaves are included by way of predominance (taghlib), contrary to the rule, which is the predominance of males.

The condition of ihsan (chastity, marriage) does not apply to slaves, because of what Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Establish the hadd upon what your right hands possess, whether they are chaste or not chaste.'"

In it is evidence that the condition, namely ihsan, in the verse indicating the halving of the hadd, has no mafhum (implied opposite meaning). It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Tawus that there is no hadd upon the female slave until she is married. In this there is acceptance of mafhum. Then, this ihsan is a condition for flogging, because stoning cannot be halved. As for al-Shafi'i, regarding the banishment of the slave he has several opinions: he is banished for a year; he is banished for half a year; he is not banished at all.

The address in the words of the Exalted, "Flog them" (fa-jlidu), is to the leaders of the Muslims and their deputies.

It is disputed whether a master may enforce the hadd upon his slave. According to us (the Hanafis), he may not enforce it except with the permission of the imam. Al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad hold that he may enforce it without permission. According to Malik, this is so except for a married female slave. Al-Shafi'i excepted from the master a dhimmi master, a mukatab (slave under a contract of manumission), and a woman. Likewise it is disputed whether a Kharijite who has seized power may enforce the hadd. It is said he may enforce it, and it is said he may not. The evidence for these opinions and the verification of what is correct among them belong in their proper place. The apparent meaning is that the enforcement of this hadd comes after the establishment of the fornication by one of the known means.

Ishaq said: "If a man and a woman are found under one garment, each of them is flogged one hundred lashes." This is reported from Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ata', al-Thawri, Malik and Ahmad said: "They are disciplined according to their respective schools in matters of discipline (adab)."

*"And let not pity for them take hold of you"* (wa la ta'khudhkum bihima ra'fa): tenderness, and dealing with gentleness and compassion.

*"In the religion of Allah"* (fi dini Allah): in His obedience and the enforcement of His hadd, which He, may He be glorified and exalted, has legislated. The intended meaning is the prohibition of leniency in the flogging, either by flogging them with a blow that does not cause pain, or by reducing the number below one hundred lashes.

Abu Mujlaz, Mujahid, Ikrimah and Ata' said: the intended meaning is the prohibition of dropping the hadd through intercession and the like, as if it were said: "Establish the hadd upon them both, without fail." The same sense is reported from Umar and Ibn Jubayr. In this there is evidence that intercession to drop the hadd is not permitted. The apparent meaning is that the prohibition applies after the hadd has been established before the judge. As for before reaching him and before establishment, intercession by the one who brings the matter to the judge on behalf of one who has committed a cause of the hadd, asking him to release him before it reaches the judge and before its establishment, is permitted. They did not restrict this to fornication, because it is established that he, peace and blessings be upon him, disapproved of his beloved Usama ibn Zayd when he interceded on behalf of Fatimah bint al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumiyya, who had stolen a garment (qatifa), and it is said jewelry (hulyan). He said to him: "Do you intercede concerning one of the hadd punishments of Allah, may He be exalted?" Then he stood and gave a sermon, saying: "O people, those before you were only destroyed because when a noble person among them stole, they left him, and when a weak person stole, they enforced the hadd upon him. By Allah, if Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, had stolen, and far be it from her, I would have cut off her hand."

Just as intercession is forbidden, so is accepting it. It is reported from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the hadd reaches the imam, may Allah not pardon him if he pardons."

*"With them both"* (wa bihima): it has been said that it is connected with a deleted element, by way of explanation, meaning "I mean with them both." It has also been said that it is connected with a deleted "pity" (ra'fa) and is taken as "and do not show pity to them both." The statement of Abu al-Baqa' appears to prefer that it be connected to "take" (ta'khudh), with the ba' being causal: "and let not pity take hold of you because of them both." He did not allow its connection to "pity" (ra'fa), giving as his reason that a verbal noun (masdar) does not have its complement precede it. In my view it is connected to the verbal noun, and latitude is permitted with an adverbial phrase that is not permitted with other things.

Al-Allama Sa'd al-Milla wa al-Din verified this at the beginning of his commentary on al-Talkhis with what leaves nothing to add.

*"In the religion"* (fi dini): it has been said that it is connected to "take" (ta'khudh), and Abu al-Baqa' held this. It has been said that it is connected to a deleted element that serves as an attribute of "pity" (ra'fa).

Ali, may Allah honour his face, al-Sulami, Ibn Muqsim, and Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Mujahid, read "wa la yakhudhkum" with the ya' (third person), because the feminization of "ra'fa" is metaphorical, and the separation made it good. Ibn Kathir read "ra'fatan" with a fatha on the hamza. Ibn Jurayj read "rafatan," with an alif after the hamza, on the pattern fa'alah. This is reported from Asim and Ibn Kathir. Abu al-Baqa' reported that he read "rafatan" with the hamza converted to an alif. All of these are attested verbal nouns, but the more famous usage is what agrees with the reading of the majority.

*"If you believe in Allah and the Last Day"* (in kuntum tu'minuna billahi wa al-yawm al-akhir): this is in the mode of stirring up and rousing, as one says: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," with no doubt about his manhood. Likewise, those addressed here are certainly believers. But the intention is to stir them and move their zeal, so that they strive in the obedience of Allah, may He be exalted, and make every effort to carry out His rulings in their proper form. He mentioned "the Last Day" to remind them of the punishment in it, in contrast to the pity for them both.

*"And let a group of the believers witness their punishment"* (wa liyashhad 'adhabahuma ta'ifatun min al-mu'minin): that is, let it be attended, as an increase in deterrence, for public disgrace may deter more than punishment does; or for that purpose and also for lesson and admonition. It is reported from Nasr ibn Alqama that this is to pray for them both for repentance and mercy, not for disgrace. But this is far removed from the context. The command here, according to what the words of the jurists indicate, is for recommendation (nadb).

The identity of this group has been disputed. Abd ibn Humayd and others reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The group is a man or more." This is the view of Ahmad. Ata', Ikrimah and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: two or more, and this is the well-known view of Malik. Qatada and al-Zuhri said: three or more. al-Hasan said: ten. It is reported from al-Shafi'i and Zayd: four, and this is one view of Malik.

Al-Khafaji said: The verification of the matter is that the word ta'ifa is originally the feminine active participle from al-tawaf, meaning circling or encompassing. It is either an attribute of a self, meaning "the self of a group," and so it applies to one person; or an attribute of a collective, meaning "a collective of a group," and so it applies to what is more than one. Thus it is like a homonym among these meanings, and in each context it is understood according to what suits it.

Al-Raghib mentioned that when it is intended for one, it may be a plural referred to in the singular, and it may be a singular, the ta' in it being as in the report. In the marginal notes of al-Adud by al-Harawi: it may be said of one person "ta'ifa," meaning the self of a group, and so it derives from al-tawaf in the sense of circling.

In the commentary on al-Bukhari, al-Shafi'i interpreted ta'ifa in several places of the Qur'an according to different senses, depending on the context. In the words of the Exalted, "Why should not a group from every division of them go forth?" [al-Tawba: 122], it means one or more, and he cited it as evidence for accepting the report of a single narrator. In "And let a group of them witness their punishment," it means four. In "Let a group of them stand with you" [al-Nisa': 102], it means three. They distinguished these contexts according to the surrounding indications. As for the first, it is because warning is achieved by it. As for the second, it is because the disgrace is greater in it. As for the third, it is because the plural pronoun in "and let them take their weapons" [al-Nisa': 102] makes it distant, and the minimum of the plural is three. That it derives from circling does not conflict with this, for it may mean circling, or circling may be the original sense, and after it became dominant it may no longer be considered. For this reason it has been said that its ta' is for transfer (naql). This is still open to discussion.

The truth is that what is meant by "ta'ifa" here is a group by which exposure and deterrence are achieved. It varies in number and fewness according to differences in places and persons. Some individuals have their exposure and deterrence achieved by three, while others do not have their exposure and deterrence achieved by ten. For the one who holds four here there is a sound reason, as is not hidden.

[p. 84 continues from the previous part]

**"The fornicator marries none but a fornicator or a polytheist"**: this is a severe condemnation of the fornicator's affair, by showing that, having been content with fornication, it is not fitting for him to marry a chaste believing woman. Between them is as between Suhayl and the Pleiades: when one of them rises it is a Syrian star, and when the other rises it is a Yemeni star. What is fitting for him is to marry a fornicatress who matches him, so that he suits his counterpart, as it is said, "the pitcher suits its lid," or a polytheist woman who is worse than him in condition and more vile in deeds. The phrase "فَلا يَنْكِحُ" ("he does not marry") is a statement meant as a prohibition: it is not fitting for him to marry, as you say, "The ruler does not lie," meaning it is not fitting for him to lie. The unfitness of the act is placed in the position of its non-existence, which is common in speech. Then, what is meant is fitness and unfitness with regard to fornication, so there is in it of the condemnation of fornication what there is.

There is no difficulty in the validity of a Muslim fornicator marrying a Muslim fornicatress, and likewise a chaste Muslim woman, and in the invalidity of his marrying the polytheist woman mentioned in the verse if it is interpreted as an idolatress, by the consensus of scholars (ijma', scholarly consensus), because that is not a matter of fitness or unfitness with regard to fornication, but from another aspect known to the Lawgiver, as is not hidden. In this same manner is His saying, exalted is He: **"The fornicatress, none marries her except a fornicator or a polytheist"**, meaning the fornicatress, after she has been content with fornication and a dog has lapped into her, the desire of the fornicator, it is not fitting that he marry her insofar as she is like that, except one who is like her, namely the fornicator, or one who is worse in condition than her, namely the polytheist. As for the chaste Muslim, his zeal refuses to approach her watering-place:

*He avoids approaching water when dogs are lapping in it.*

It is not problematic on this that the validity of his marrying her and the invalidity of a polytheist's marrying her are the same, whether "polytheist" is interpreted as an idolater or a People of the Book, so as to need an answer. This is clear. The reference in His saying, glorified is He: **"And that has been forbidden to the believers"** may be to the fornication understood from what preceded, and the prohibition upon it is in its apparent sense, and likewise "the believers." Perhaps this sentence and what precedes it contain the justification for what preceded of command and prohibition, and for this reason He did not conjoin His saying, glorified is He, "The fornicator does not marry," etc., to it, as He conjoined His saying, mighty and majestic, which comes later: **"And those who accuse chaste women,"** etc. The indication of the preceding being a prohibition is easy. Restricting the believers with the prohibition upon them is clear according to the view of those who say that disbelievers are not obligated to the subsidiary laws (furu'). As for the view of those who say they are obligated to them as they are to the fundamentals, though they are not valid from them except after faith, then singling them out by mention is for their nobility.

It may also be that the reference is to marrying the fornicatress, and in that case what is meant by the prohibition is prevention, and by "the believers" are the complete believers. The meaning of preventing them from marrying fornicatresses is that it makes their souls disdainful of inclining toward her, so that such a thing is not fitting for them. Nor does it preclude taking the verse according to what was established in it, what was narrated concerning its occasion of revelation, which Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as *hasan*), al-Hakim (who graded it as *sahih*), al-Bayhaqi, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:

"There was a man called Marthad who used to carry captives from Makkah until he brought them to Madinah. In Makkah there was a prostitute called 'Anaq, who was a friend of his. He promised a man from the captives of Makkah to carry him. He said: 'I came until I reached the shade of a wall of Makkah's walls on a moonlit night. 'Anaq came and saw the black shadow under the wall. When she reached my upper room she said: "Marthad?" I said: "Marthad." She said: "Welcome and well come, come, spend the night with us." I said: "O 'Anaq, Allah the Exalted has forbidden fornication." She said: "O people of the tents! This man is carrying off your captives!" He said: "Eight men followed me and took the road of Khandama. I reached a cave or a cavern, and she entered it. They came and stood over my head, and their urine dripped on my head, and Allah blinded them to me. Then they returned, and I returned to my companion, carried him, and came to Madinah. I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I marry 'Anaq?' He remained silent and did not answer me anything, until there was revealed: 'The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or a polytheist,' the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Marthad, "The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or a polytheist, and the fornicatress, none marries her except a fornicator or a polytheist, and that has been forbidden to the believers." So do not marry her.'"

Because the branching of the prohibition in it concerning marrying that prostitute is, without doubt, valid on the assumption that the verse from which it branches is for condemning the affair of the fornicator and fornicatress. So it is as if it were said: When you know the affair of the fornicatress, and that she has reached such ugliness that it is not fitting for anyone to marry her except one like her or one worse in condition, then do not marry her.

Yes, in this report there is what is more consistent with making the reference in what passed to marrying the fornicatress, and from it is known the reason for placing "the fornicator" first, and the predication about the fornicatress that none marries her except a fornicator or a polytheist, against what the parallelism would require. This is all. The scholars have much discussion on this glorious verse. There is no harm in transmitting what is easily available of it and presenting some of what has been said. Then consider it and what we have already presented, and choose for yourself what is sweet. I say: It has been transmitted from al-Dahhak and al-Qaffal. Al-Nisaburi said: The best of the views on the verse is that His saying, glorified is He, "The fornicator does not marry," etc., is a ruling founded on the usual case, brought to deter the believers from marrying fornicatresses after deterring them from fornication. That is because the corrupt, wicked person whose nature is fornication and wantonness generally does not desire to marry righteous women who are opposite to his description; he desires only a wicked fornicatress of his own kind, or a polytheist. And a wicked fornicatress who commits fornication in that manner is not desired in marriage by righteous men, who shun her; rather, only those of her kind desire her, from among the sinners and the polytheists. A similar statement is: "None does good except the pious," for it runs in the manner of the usual case. The meaning of the prohibition upon the believers according to this is said to be reprehension, and it was expressed by it for emphasis. The justification for this is that marrying fornicatresses includes imitating the wicked, exposing oneself to suspicion, causing ill talk, and impugning lineage, with many corruptions. It was also said: The prohibition is in its apparent sense, and that act includes prohibited matters, and the prohibition does not return to the contract itself, so that the contract would be void. On both views the verse is *muhkam* (not abrogated).

It is not hidden that taking "the fornicator" and "the fornicatress" to refer to those whose nature is fornication and wantonness is not free from remoteness, because in what preceded they were not in this sense, and the apparent meaning is consistency. Also, it is hardly accepted that the usual case is that one whose nature is fornication has no desire to marry chaste women and desires fornicatresses or polytheists. For we have often witnessed that many fornicators are more scrupulous in marriage than others, so that hardly any of them marries a woman among whose relatives there is a suspicion of fornication, let alone one who is herself involved; and we have rarely heard of a fornicator's desire to marry a fornicatress or a polytheist. Also, in taking the prohibition as reprehension there is a certain remoteness, and likewise taking it in its apparent sense together with the commitment that the prohibition does not return to the contract itself.

In *al-Bahr* it is transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and their companions that the verse concerns particular people who used to commit fornication in their pre-Islamic time with well-known prostitutes. When Islam came and they embraced it, they could no longer commit fornication, so out of poverty they wished to marry those women, since it was their custom to spend on whoever married them. So the verse was revealed for that. The reference by "the fornicator" is to one of those people, and the name of fornication, which was in the pre-Islamic period, is applied to him for reproach. The meaning of "does not marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist" is: he does not desire to marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist, i.e., his soul does not incline except toward these base types, because of their lack of restraint. The reference by "that" is to the marriage of those prostitutes, and the prohibition is in its apparent sense. It is objected to this interpretation that there is consensus that a fornicatress may not be married by a polytheist. End of quotation.

And you know that this objection does not arise after taking the negation of marriage as the negation of the desire to marry, for the meaning then becomes: "The fornicatress, none desires to marry her except a fornicator or a polytheist," and there is nothing in the consensus that rejects this. There is also in it a discussion that you will know shortly, if God the Exalted wills. Yes, that "the fornicator" refers to one of those people, who were among the emigrants, may God be pleased with them all, as came in many reports, and that they had embraced Islam and repented from fornication, is a matter of hesitation. For it is utterly remote that God, mighty and majestic, would name a Companion as a fornicator who had committed fornication before his Islam, then embraced Islam and repented, and so came out of his sins as on the day his mother bore him. And He, glorified is He, would apply to him this shameful description, which He, blessed and exalted is He, forgave him merely because he inclined toward marrying a fornicatress on account of the poverty he had before knowing the prohibition of that. Moreover, they were men who would separate from those they married when they found wealth from them.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil that he said: "When the emigrants came to Madinah, they came in hardship, except a few of them, and Madinah had high prices and severe hardship. In the market there were prostitutes, arrogant ones, from the People of the Book, and slave-women of some of the Ansar, and each of them had raised a sign over her door to make known that she was a fornicatress. They were among the most fertile and most bountiful people of Madinah. Some of the emigrant Muslims desired what they earned because of the hardship they had. Some of them advised others: 'If only we married some of these fornicatresses, so that we might benefit from the surplus of what they earn.' Some of them said: 'Let us ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' They came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, hardship has pressed upon us, and we do not find what to eat. In the market are the prostitutes from the women of the People of the Book, and their slave-girls, and the slave-girls of the Ansar, who earn for themselves. Is it lawful for us to marry from among them, so that we may benefit from the surplus of what they earn? When we find wealth from them, we will leave them.' So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse."

Also, applying the term "fornicator" to him in this sense does not agree with applying the term "fornicatress" to one of the women with banners, nor does it agree with applying the term "fornicator" to the one to whom it is applied in His saying, glorified is He: **"The fornicatress and the fornicator, lash each of them"**, etc.

Abu Muslim and Abu Hayyan said, and Abu Dawud transmitted it in his book on *naskh* (abrogation), and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah*, and a group, through Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, that *nikah* here means *wati'* (sexual intercourse), i.e., fornication, and "that" refers to it. The meaning: "The fornicator does not have intercourse, at the time of his fornication, except with a fornicatress from among the Muslims, or one lower than her, who is the polytheist. The fornicatress, at the time of her fornication, is not had except by a fornicator from among the Muslims, or one lower than him, who is the polytheist. And Allah the Exalted has forbidden fornication to the believers."

This has been criticized on two grounds: that *nikah* in the Book of God is known only in the sense of marrying, and that it leads to your saying: "The fornicator does not fornicate except with a fornicatress, and the fornicatress does not fornicate except with a fornicator," and this is not always the case, since a fornicator may fornicate with a non-fornicatress, one of them knowing of the fornication while the other is ignorant of it, thinking it lawful. And if it is claimed that this is in the sense of the usual case, then it is a report of obvious matters. Also, if the negation is taken as a prohibition, the meaning would be: "Prohibit the fornicator from fornicating except with a fornicatress, and vice versa," and this is clearly corrupt.

The first has been answered: most scholars hold that *nikah* in His saying, exalted is He, **"until she marries another husband"** (al-Baqarah 2:230) means intercourse and not the contract, and they refuted whoever interpreted it as the contract, claiming that a woman divorced three times becomes lawful to her former husband by the second husband's contract to her without intercourse. The second has been answered: it is a report that departs in the sense of the usual case, intended to make the affair of fornication appear shameful, and for this reason the polytheist was added. The objection based on obviousness is nothing.

Al-Fadil Siri al-Din al-Misri has a lengthy discussion on this. It has been said that, in that case, it would be like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The evil women are for the evil men﴾ [al-Nur: 26], etc., and so there would be repetition. You will know, God willing, that this does not hold except on one opinion.

It has also been said: "nikah" here means marriage (tazawwuj), and the negation is in the sense of a prohibition, and the expression was used for it for emphasis. This is supported by the reading of Amr ibn Ubayd, "la yankih" (with a jussive), and the prohibition is taken in its apparent sense.

Ibn al-Musayyib said: The ruling was general regarding fornicators, that none of them may marry except a fornicatress. Then a concession came, and that was abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32], and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. The view of abrogation is also reported from Mujahid, and al-Imam al-Shafi'i went to this view. He said in al-Umm: The people of tafsir differed regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress﴾, etc., with widely differing disagreement. It was said: it is general but it was abrogated. Sufyan informed us, from Yahya, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that he said: it is abrogated; the verse ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ abrogated it, so the fornicatress is among the single women of the Muslims, as Ibn al-Musayyib said, God willing. We have proofs from the Book and the Sunnah against the invalidity of any other view, and a full discussion. Al-Biqa'i reported this from al-Shafi'i, then said: Al-Shafi'i did not mean that this ruling was abrogated by the verse of the single women alone, but together with what was joined to it of consensus and other verses and hadiths, such that this made its indication of what it covers certain, like the indication of the specific (khass) over what it covers. Thus it cannot be said that he opposed his principle that the specific is not abrogated by the general; rather the later general is taken as restricted to the specific, because what the specific covers is certain and what the general covers is presumed. End.

Al-Jubba'i claims that abrogation is by consensus. Perhaps he meant that it reveals an abrogating text; otherwise consensus cannot itself abrogate, as is explained in the science of usul al-fiqh. Indeed, there is discussion about whether consensus is realized here. This view has been objected to on the ground that it entails the permissibility of a polytheist marrying a Muslim woman. I say: the marriage of a disbeliever to a Muslim woman was permitted before the Hijrah and after it until the sixth year, and in that year, after al-Hudaybiyah, the verse of prohibition was revealed, as al-Allamah Ibn Hajar al-Haytami and others have stated explicitly. It is sound that the Prophet (ﷺ) married his daughter Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her) to Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' before the mission, and after the mission he (ﷺ) sent... then he emigrated and she emigrated with him, while she was still in the marriage of Abu al-'As, who was not a believer at that time. The matter continued thus until the sixth year. When the verse of prohibition was revealed, he did not remain long before he came and openly declared his Islam (may Allah be pleased with him), and the Prophet (ﷺ) returned her to him with the first marriage.

So it is possible that the marriage mentioned was permitted at the time the verse was revealed, by its being revealed before the sixth year and then abrogated. In this surah there are verses which they stated were revealed before that: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander﴾ [al-Nur: 11], etc. He said: it was revealed in the year of the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, and that was in the fifth year, two nights after the beginning of Sha'ban. So perhaps this verse is of this kind. Indeed, in a report transmitted by Ibn Abi Shaybah from Ibn Jubayr, which al-Iraqi and Ibn Hajar also mentioned, there is what apparently indicates that this verse is Meccan. If this is combined with what was reported from Ibn al-Musayyib and what al-Shafi'i held, there would be two abrogations in it, but I have not seen anyone point this out. And if it is sound, this view would be less burdensome than the previous views, and I think you would not prefer any other over it.

Some people held that the prohibition of marrying a fornicatress, or marrying a fornicator, remains in force until now if repentance from fornication does not appear. According to them, if one of the spouses commits fornication, the marriage between them is invalidated. Some of them said: it is not annulled, but the man is commanded to divorce his wife if she commits fornication, and if he keeps her he sins. According to some scholars, fornication is among the defects by which the option (khiyar) is established. So if she marries a man and it becomes clear to her that he is one known for fornication, she has the option of remaining with him or separating from him. From al-Hasan: the prohibition of a fornicator marrying a chaste woman applies only when he has been flogged, and likewise the prohibition of a chaste man marrying a fornicatress applies only when she has been flogged. So for him, a flogged man marries only a flogged woman, and a flogged woman is married only by a flogged man. This agrees with some reports.

Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A flogged fornicator marries none but his like.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir reported that a man married a woman, then he committed fornication and the prescribed punishment was applied to him. They brought him to Ali, may Allah honor his face, and he separated him from his wife and said to him: "Marry none but a flogged woman like yourself." From Ibn Mas'ud and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: whoever commits fornication with a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her at all. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, and a group of the Successors and the imams held otherwise.

He argued for this with what al-Tabarani and al-Daraqutni reported from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a man who committed fornication with a woman and wanted to marry her, and he said: 'The unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful.'"

Here, among the weakest things said about the verse is that its meaning may be what is in the hadith, that whoever commits fornication, his wife commits fornication, and whoever she commits fornication with, her husband commits fornication. So reflect on all of that, and may Allah, Mighty and Majestic, guide your thread.

Abu al-Barhasam read "wa-harrama" with the active voice, its subject being Allah Exalted. Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read "wa-hurrima" with a fatha on the ha' and a damma on the ra'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 4 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ This begins the explanation of the ruling on one who attributes fornication (zina) to another, after the explanation of the ruling on one who commits it. According to what al-Allama al-Thani (al-Taftazani) chose in al-Talwih, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted and indicated by the imperative verb after it, meaning "flog those who." It may also be in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and its predicate is not hidden from you. The verse was revealed concerning the wife of 'Uwaymir, as in Sahih al-Bukhari. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was revealed because of the incident of the slander (al-ifk). The word "accuse" (ramy) here is used metaphorically for insult (shatm).

The wounding of the tongue is like the wounding of the hand. The intended meaning is accusing of fornication, as indicated by placing this ruling right after the mention of fornicators, together with the object being "chaste women" (al-muhsanat), which indicates freedom from fornication. This is almost explicit in that regard. It may be argued that requiring four witnesses who testify to the actual occurrence of what was imputed is a clue to the intended meaning, as His words indicate: ﴿Then they do not bring four witnesses, so flog them eighty lashes﴾. This is based on the knowledge that there is nothing whose establishment depends on the testimony of four witnesses except fornication. The apparent meaning is that the intended ones are chaste women. In that case, the obligation to flog one who accuses a chaste man is established by the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), since the distinguishing factor is definitively nullified, which is the attribute of femaleness, and the independent ability to remove the shame of what was attributed to him through influence, such that understanding it does not depend on establishing the qualification of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning). Likewise, the obligation to flog one who accuses a chaste man or a chaste woman is established by that same indication. Otherwise, the words ﴿those who accuse﴾ are in the masculine plural form, and the specification of males on the side of the accuser and females on the side of the accused is due to the particular circumstance of the event. It has been said that the intended meaning is "chaste private parts" (al-furuj al-muhsanat), but this is objected to, since attributing the accusing (ramy) to them is rejected by it, along with the description with "chaste," which contradicts the apparent meaning.

Ibn Hazm said, and al-Zahrawi related it: the intended meaning is "chaste persons" (al-anfus al-muhsanat). Abu Hayyan used as evidence His words: ﴿And married women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. He argued that if "chaste" (al-muhsanat) were not capable of generality, it would not have been restricted. This was objected to on the grounds that "among the women" there is a clue to generality, but there is no clue here. He made the fact that the ruling for men is similar a clue, but this is not free from difficulty. So what is preferred is relying on what was mentioned earlier.
