Ihsan (chastity, the state of being muhsan) here is not realized except by the realization of 'iffa (abstinence) from fornication, which is its well-known meaning, together with freedom, puberty, sanity, and Islam.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: "We do not know of any disagreement among the jurists on this." Perhaps someone else knew of one, as you will know, God willing. Its establishment is by the confession of the accuser, or the testimony of two men, or one man and two women, contrary to Zufar. The reason for requiring abstinence from fornication is clear. However, in the commentary of al-Tahawi, in discussing 'iffa, it is not limited to abstinence from fornication, for he said regarding it: that he has not had intercourse with a woman through fornication, nor through a doubtful union (shubha), nor through an invalid marriage during his lifetime. If he did that once, intending an invalid marriage, his uprightness (adala) falls away and there is no hadd (prescribed punishment) against one who accuses him. Likewise, if he had intercourse outside of ownership, as when he had intercourse with a slave-girl shared between him and another, his uprightness falls away. If he had intercourse within ownership but it was forbidden, then one considers: if the prohibition is temporary, his uprightness does not fall away, as when he has intercourse with his wife during menstruation, or with his Magian slave-girl. If the prohibition is permanent, his uprightness falls away, as when he has intercourse with his slave-girl who is his foster-sister.

If he touched a woman or looked at her private part with lust, and then married her daughter and consummated it, or her mother, his ihsan does not fall away according to Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him). According to the two disciples, it falls away. If he had intercourse with a woman through marriage and then married her, his ihsan falls away. End of quotation.

What is mentioned in several works is that Abu Hanifa requires, for the dropping of the hadd from the accuser of one who had intercourse in a permanent prohibition, that this prohibition be established by a well-known hadith, such as the prohibition of intercourse with a married woman without witnesses, which is established by His saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "There is no marriage except with witnesses." This is a well-known hadith. Or that it is established by consensus (ijma'), such as one whose father had intercourse with her through marriage or through right of ownership, if the son married her or bought her and had intercourse with her. Similar to this, according to him, is intercourse with one who was fornicated with by one's own (wife/slave): the disagreement is not considered when the prohibition is established by the text. Here, it has been established by it, based on His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. He only considers it when it is established by analogy (qiyas) or caution (ihtiyat), such as its establishment by looking at the private part and touching with lust. Its establishment in what was mentioned is to make the cause stand in place of the effect, out of caution. From this you can know the situation of many branch rulings, so memorize it.

As for what was mentioned about the falling of the ihsan of one who had intercourse with his slave-girl who is his foster-sister, there is a disagreement from al-Karkhi. He said: the ihsan does not fall away by intercourse with her. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, Malik, and Ahmad, because the ownership exists, so it is like intercourse with his Magian slave-girl. The reply is that the prohibition in intercourse with a Magian can be lifted, so it is temporary, whereas the prohibition by foster-nursing cannot be lifted, so the object was not at all capable of being made lawful. He also stipulated for ownership that its defect not be apparent through being entitled to recovery. So if he bought a slave-girl, had intercourse with her, and then she was claimed by a rightful owner, and someone accused him, he is not subject to hadd. In the Kafi of al-Hakim, al-Qahistani, and al-Fath, it is stated that intercourse in an invalid purchase makes the hadd fall away from the accuser. Some interpreted this as what we have mentioned.

Some eminent scholars said: just as chastity from fornication is required, freedom from suspicion of it is also required. He excluded from this the accusation against a woman who has a child but no known father, for they mentioned that one who accuses her is not subject to hadd because of the suspicion. This was mentioned by al-Haskafi in the chapter on li'an (mutual cursing) in the commentary of Tanwir al-Absar. Sodomy (liwat) is not analogized to fornication, so if one is accused of it, the accuser is not subject to hadd, contrary to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and they differed on many rulings which Zayn al-Din mentioned in his Bahr.

As for the requirement of freedom, it is because the term ihsan is applied to it. God Most High said: ﴿Upon them is half of what is upon the chaste women of punishment﴾, for the intended meaning of "chaste" there is free women. Thus a slave is not chaste in this sense. Being chaste in another sense, such as Islam or other, makes him chaste in one respect and not in another, and that is a doubt regarding his ihsan, so it is obligatory to avert the hadd from his accuser. So he is not flogged until he is chaste in all the senses to which the word ihsan applies, except what there is consensus is not to be considered in establishing ihsan, namely that the accused woman is a wife or that the accused man is a husband. For this meaning comes in His words: ﴿And married women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], meaning those who are married. This is not considered in the ihsan of accusation, but in the ihsan of stoning (rajm).

Then there is no doubt that ihsan has been applied with the meaning of freedom, as you have heard, and with the meaning of Islam in His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But when they are chaste (uhsinna)﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. Ibn Mas'ud said: "They became Muslim." This suffices to establish that Islam is considered in ihsan. It is narrated from Dawud that freedom is not required, and that one who accuses a slave is flogged. As for requiring sanity and puberty, there is consensus on it, except what is narrated from Ahmad (may God have mercy on him), that a boy who has intercourse with one like himself is chaste, so his accuser is flogged. The more correct view from him is agreement with the majority. Malik's view concerning a girl who has intercourse with one like herself is that one who accuses her is flogged, especially if she is an adolescent, since the reason for the hadd is the imposition of shame, and such a person can be shamed. Likewise is his view, and the view of al-Layth, that one who accuses a madman is flogged for that reason. But the majority deny that a boy or a madman is shamed by being attributed with fornication. Rather, one who relates such attribution to them may even be laughed at, either because their intention is not valid, or because they are not addressed with the prohibitions, and similar reasons. Even if we suppose that an adolescent is shamed, it is not to the full extent, so the hadd is averted. Similar to a boy and a madman in that the attribution of fornication to them may cause laughter is a barren woman (al-ratqa') and a eunuch (al-majbub). Indeed, they are more deserving of it, since it is inconceivable in their case. For this reason one is not flogged for accusing them. Except what is narrated from Sa'id and Ibn Abi Layla, that one is flogged for accusing a dhimmi woman if she has a Muslim child. Likewise what was said: one is flogged for accusing her if she is under a Muslim husband.

Furthermore, if Islam and freedom do not exist at the time of the fornication that is attributed, but existed at the time of the accusation, they are of no benefit. So if he accuses a Muslim woman who committed fornication while she was a Christian, or a Muslim man who committed fornication while he was a Christian, and says: "You committed fornication while you were an unbeliever," or "You committed fornication while you were an unbeliever," or if he accuses a freed person who committed fornication while he was a slave, or a freed woman who committed fornication while she was a slave-girl, and says: "You committed fornication" or "You committed fornication while you were a slave," or "You are a slave-girl," he is not flogged. Likewise a mukatab (contracted slave) man or woman, and a hostile non-Muslim who committed fornication in the territory of war and then became Muslim. It is understood from their words that puberty and sanity are like Islam and freedom in this respect. They explicitly stated that if one says, "You committed fornication while you were a child," or "You committed fornication while you were insane," he is not flogged. The basis for averting the hadd is truthfulness in all of that.

From here al-Mabsut said: if a woman was forced, her ihsan falls away and her accuser is not flogged, just as the ihsan of a forced man who had intercourse falls away and his accuser is not flogged, because coercion removes the sin but does not take the act out of being fornication. However, it was mentioned in it that whoever accuses a fornicator is not subject to hadd, whether he accused him of that very fornication, or of another fornication of the same kind, or was vague at the time of the accusation. The justification is that God Most High required the hadd against one who accuses a person characterized by ihsan, and with fornication no ihsan remains, so the hadd is not established. This is contrary to Ibrahim and Ibn Abi Layla. Yes, if the accusation was of a fornication from which the accused repented, the accuser is subject to ta'zir (discretionary punishment). This indicates that it is not necessary to restrict the falling away of the hadd in the previous cases, so reflect.

If a Magian married his mother or his daughter, then he became Muslim and the marriage was annulled, and a Muslim accused him while he was Muslim, the accuser is flogged according to Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), based on his view that Magian marriages have the status of validity. The two Imams said: he is not flogged, based on the view that they do not have the status of validity, and this is the view of the three Imams. There is no known disagreement, among those who consider freedom a requirement for ihsan, that one who accuses a mukatab who died leaving property is not subject to hadd, because the doubt is established regarding a condition of the hadd, namely ihsan, due to the disagreement of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, as to whether he died free or as a slave. That requires averting the hadd, and because it is averted by doubt. One who accuses a deaf-mute (akhras) is not flogged, because there is the possibility that he would confirm it if he spoke. His gesture is not relied upon here, even though they said it stands in place of his expression in some rulings, due to the existence of possibility in them.

They also stipulated that ihsan must exist at the time of the hadd, so if the accused apostatized, the hadd falls away, even if he later became Muslim. Likewise if he committed fornication or had intercourse in a prohibited manner, or became mentally incapacitated, or deaf-mute, and that condition remained, the accuser is not flogged, as in the Kafi of al-Hakim. They also stipulated that the accused must not die before the accuser is flogged, because the hadd is not inherited. And that the accused not be a child of the accuser or a child of his child, so one is not flogged for accusing either of them. As for the rest of what you will learn some of, God willing. Most jurists did not explicitly state the conditions of the accuser, but it is understood from their words that he must be: adult (baligh), so a child is not flogged if he accuses, but is subject to ta'zir; sane ('aqil), so a madman is not flogged, nor an intoxicated person unless he became intoxicated through something forbidden; speaking (natiq), so a deaf-mute is not flogged, since he did not explicitly state the fornication; this was stated by Ibn al-Shalabi from al-Nihaya; voluntary (ta'i), so a coerced person is not flogged; and an accuser (qadhif) in the land of justice. So the accuser is not flogged in the land of

...the war or rebellion. The verse contains an indication of some of this. It is possible that one of the conditions is that the one who makes the accusation knows the prohibition, either in reality or in legal effect, by being raised in the territory of Islam. However, in the view of al-Hakim al-Kafi, a non-Muslim combatant (harbi) who entered the territory of Islam under a safe-conduct and then slanders a Muslim is subject to the hadd punishment, according to his last opinion, which is the opinion of his two companions. Its apparent meaning is that he is subject to the hadd even if the slander occurred immediately upon his entry. Perhaps the reasoning is that fornication is prohibited in every religious community, so accusing someone of it is likewise prohibited, and therefore it is not accepted that he acted out of ignorance. It is required that the accusation be an explicit accusation of fornication, in whatever language it is made, as a number of jurists have stated explicitly. They also attached to it some expressions by which the hadd has been established through transmitted report and consensus. Thus one is subject to the hadd for saying: "You committed zina" (zanayta), or "zani" with a sukun on the ya'. Likewise "ya zani'" with a damma on the hamza, according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, in contrast to Muhammad, who holds that one is not subject to the hadd for that, because according to him it is literally used for "ascending" (climbing). It has been objected that this is understood only when it is mentioned together with a place of ascent. Moreover, the school's position should be that if it is said, together with mention of a place of ascent, in a state of anger and abuse, it constitutes slander. He has definitively ruled in al-Mabsut that one is subject to the hadd if he says, in a state of anger, "Zana'ta fi al-jabal" or "ala al-jabal" (she ascended the mountain). If he says to a woman, "Ya zani," he is subject to the hadd by unanimous agreement. In al-Jawhara he gave the reason that the basic form of speech is the masculine. If he says to a man, "Ya zaniyah," then according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf he is not subject to the hadd, because he has transferred his speech and described the man with the attribute of a woman. Muhammad said he is subject to the hadd, because the ta' marbuta enters for emphasis, as in "allama." It is answered that its being for emphasis is figurative; rather, it is for what is known of it as a feminine form. Even if it were literal in that respect, the hadd is not obligatory because of doubt. One is subject to the hadd for saying: "You are more adulterous than so-and-so," or "than me," according to what is in al-Zahiriyya, and this is the apparent view. However, al-Fath, quoting al-Mabsut, states that there is no hadd for "You are more adulterous than so-and-so" or "You are the most adulterous of people." In al-Jawhara he gave the reason that its meaning is "You are more capable of fornication." In al-Fath, the reason is that "af'al" in such a construction is used to express preference in knowledge, so it is as if he said: "You know more about fornication." It is not hidden that intending this in a state of abuse is far-fetched. In al-Khaniyya, for "You are the most adulterous of people" or "more adulterous than so-and-so," there is the hadd, but for "You are more adulterous than me" there is no hadd. It is not hidden that the distinction is not evident. It may be said that his saying "You are more adulterous than so-and-so" involves attributing fornication to so-and-so and including the addressee with him in that, unlike "You are more adulterous than me," because it involves attributing fornication to himself, which is not slander, and so it is not slander toward the addressee, since it is an inclusion of him in what is not slander. One is subject to the hadd for saying "Lasta li-abika" (You are not your father's son), because it involves attributing fornication to the mother, and because of what came in the report from Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no hadd except for slandering a chaste woman or denying a man's descent from his father." He restricted it to being said in a state of anger, since in a state of contentment it is meant as a rebuke by denying resemblance to him. He mentioned that analogy would indicate that there is no hadd for it at all, since descent may be denied from the father without the mother being fully an adulteress, such as when she was impregnated by mistaken intercourse and gave birth during the waiting period of the man who had intercourse with her. But leaving that aside is due to the report. There is no hadd for allusion (ta'rid), such as saying "I am not an adulterer" or "My mother is not an adulteress." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Shubruma, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and it is the well-known narration from Ahmad. Malik, and a narration from Ahmad, said: one is subject to the hadd for allusion, based on what al-Zuhri narrated from Salim from Ibn Umar, who said: "Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to inflict the hadd for allusion." And from Ali, may Allah honor his face, that he flogged a man for allusion. Also, when the intended meaning is known through its contextual evidence, it becomes like the explicit. The majority argue that the Lawgiver did not consider such (allusion) equivalent: he forbade the explicit proposal to a woman whose husband has died during her waiting period, and permitted allusion, saying: ﴿But do not promise them secretly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235], and He said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of proposal to women or conceal within yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235]. Since it is established from the Shari'a that their rulings are not unified in matters other than the hadd, it is not permissible to treat allusion as equivalent in a way that requires the hadd, which is to be averted through caution. This argument is preferable to the argument that the Prophet, peace be upon him, did not impose the hadd on the one who said: "O Messenger of Allah, my wife has borne a black boy," alluding to himself, because imposing the hadd for slander depends on a claim, and the wife did not make such a claim. There is no hadd for saying to someone: "You had intercourse with so-and-so unlawfully," or "He had unlawful intercourse with you," or "You fornicated with so-and-so," or "O unlawful one" (ya haram zadah), or "Go and say to so-and-so: You are an adulterer." The Messenger went and told him that on his behalf by saying: "So-and-so says you are an adulterer." But if he said to him directly, "You are an adulterer," then he is subject to the hadd at that point. The detailed treatment of what entails the hadd and what does not is in the books of jurisprudence. Our statement "in such-and-such there is the hadd" is meant when the condition understood from His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they do not bring﴾, etc., is fulfilled. He required four witnesses as a strictness upon the slanderer. It is required that they be men, because they have stated explicitly that testimony of women has no place in hudud. The feminine form of the number in the verse indicates that they must be so. It is not required that they be just (adl), so that the failure to bring four witnesses entails flogging the ones who are upright. This is because of what was stated in al-Multaqat: if four wicked people came and testified that the matter was as he said, the hadd is averted from the slanderer, the one slandered, and the witnesses. The reason is that there is a degree of deficiency in a wicked person, although he is competent for giving testimony and for bearing it. Therefore, if a judge ruled on his testimony, it takes effect according to us, so their testimony establishes a doubt of fornication, and the hadd falls from them and from the slanderer; likewise from the one slandered, because justice is required for establishment. If they were blind, or slaves, or previously punished for slander, they are flogged for the slander, not for the accused, because they lack the competence for testimony, as has been said. It is apparent that the slanderer is also flogged, because if the witnesses are flogged even though they spoke only in the form of testimony and not slander, then flogging the slanderer is more fitting. The apparent meaning is that "then they do not bring four witnesses" refers to witnesses who testify concerning the one accused of having committed zina, and it is evident that this is based on direct observation. However, al-Fath says: if two men, or one man and two women, testify to the one slandered's confession of fornication, the hadd is averted from the slanderer, and likewise from the three, namely the man and the two women, because what is established by evidence is like what is established in fact, as if we had heard his confession of fornication. End of quote.

You know that evidence for a confession is not considered with respect to the hadd of the one slandered, because if he denies it, he has retracted his confession by denial, which itself requires averting the hadd, so the evidence is void; and if he confirms it under its condition, it is not heard, since it is only heard alongside confession in seven

Ḥaqqan lahu ʿazza wa-jall. Ibn al-Humam mentioned that there is no disagreement that this punishment contains both the right of God Most High and the right of the servant (ḥaqq al-ʿabd), except that al-Shafiʿi inclined toward giving precedence to the right of the servant, in view of the servant's need and the self-sufficiency of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted. We, however, have gone to giving precedence to the right of God Most High, because the rights the servant holds are exercised by his Master (mawlā), so the right of the servant becomes a reason for giving precedence to the right of God Most High, not its nullification. The reverse is not the case: if the right of the servant were given precedence, it would follow that the right of God, ʿazza wa-jall, could only be exercised by vesting the authority to exercise it in the servant, and this is not permissible except by an established textual proof that the Law appoints for the servant to exercise it. No such proof has been established; rather, what is established is the appointment of the Imam (istinabat al-imam), so that it is he who exercises it, like all the ḥudud which are the right of God, glory be to Him and exalted.

It follows from this disagreement that whoever is proven to have slandered (qadhafa) and then died before the hadd was carried out on the slanderer does not pass on the carrying out of the hadd from him, according to our school, since inheritance applies to the rights of people only on condition that they are wealth, or connected to wealth, or that they turn into wealth and are inherited by him. According to our school, the hadd does not lapse once it has been established, except when the one slandered says: "He did not slander me," or "My witnesses lied." At that point it becomes evident that the slander did not occur as a cause for the hadd, not that it occurred and then lapsed by his saying that. This is like the case where the one slandered confirms it.

Zayn al-Din said: if the one slandered pardons (ʿafā), the Imam has no right to carry out the hadd, due to the absence of a demand (ṭalab). If he later returns and demands it, the Imam carries it out, and the pardon is void. According to al-Shafiʿi, the pardon is valid, and the same is reported from Abu Yusuf. It seems that the meaning is that if he pardons, the hadd falls, and returning to the demand does not benefit; and that it is not permissible to take a payment in exchange for it according to our school. This is also the view of Malik. According to him (al-Shafiʿi) it is permissible; this is the view of Ahmad. It also applies that overlapping (tadakhkhul) occurs according to our school but not according to him. Our view is held by Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, Tawus, Hammad, and Ahmad in one narration: so that if he is given the hadd except for one lash, and then another slanders him, the first is completed and there is nothing for the second.

Likewise, if he slanders one person several times, or a group with one phrase, such as "You are fornicators (zunat)," or with several phrases, such as "You, O Zayd, are an adulterer; and you, O ʿAmr, are an adulterer; and you, O Bishr, are an adulterer," on one day or several days, he receives one hadd, provided no hadd has intervened between the two slanders.

Al-Shafiʿi agreed with us regarding a single hadd for one who slanders a group with one phrase once. In al-Zahiriyya: whoever slanders a person, is given the hadd, and then slanders him a second time, is not given the hadd again. The basis for this is what is reported: when Abu Bakra testified against al-Mughira and the hadd was applied, he continued afterward to say in gatherings: "I bear witness that al-Mughira is indeed an adulterer." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, wished to give him the hadd a second time, but ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, prevented him, so he returned to his position, and the matter became a consensus (ijmaʿ), end of quote. The apparent meaning is that this applies when he slanders him a second time with the same first fornication, or uses an unrestricted phrase that is to be understood as referring to the first, because one who has been given the hadd for slander repeats his speech to show the truth of what he was punished for, as Abu Bakra did, for he did not mean by "al-Mughira is an adulterer" a fornication other than the first. However, if he slanders him after the hadd with a different fornication, he is given the hadd for that, as in al-Fath.

Sadr al-Islam Abu al-Yusr in his sound Mabsut mentioned that the predominant character of this hadd is the right of the servant, as al-Shafiʿi said, because most of the rulings indicate it, and reason supports it: the servant benefits from it specifically. Muhammad (al-Shaybani) stated explicitly in al-Asl that the hadd for slander is like retaliation (qisas), a right of the servant, and its delegation to the Imam is because not everyone can rightly carry it out, and because the one slandered may wish his death out of rage, so that it would result in destruction. It does not pass on by inheritance because it is merely a right, not wealth nor equivalent to wealth; it is like the option of stipulation (khiyar al-shart) and the right of pre-emption (shufʿa). This differs from retaliation, which turns into wealth. Also, it is in the sense of ownership of the body, because the one entitled to retaliation has the power to destroy the body, and the power to destroy is ownership of the body according to people; thus the one owed retaliation is like a possession of the one entitled to retaliation, so the heir holds it with respect to exercising retaliation. Its pardon is invalid only because he (the one pardoning) is being stubborn in it, since to accept the shame is to be content with shame, and shame is shameful. The debates on this are not hidden.

Al-Shafiʿi argues from the verse for non-overlap (ʿadam al-tadakhkhul), since its implication is that the ruling is attached to a descriptive attribute that indicates causation, so it is repeated with the repetition of that attribute. It is answered that since the consensus is based on averting hudud through doubts, it restricts what the verse implies regarding repetition upon repetition, to repetition that occurs after the first hadd. Indeed, this is necessary, since it is evident that those addressed with the command to carry it out in His saying, ﴿So lash them﴾, are the rulers, and this address does not apply to them except after proof (thubut) before them. The outcome of the verse is therefore the obligation of the hadd when the cause, which is the accusation (ramy), is established before them. The accusation is more general than being done with the attribute of multiplicity or singularity. So when it is established that it occurred from him many times, it obligates lashing eighty times only, and when that is carried out, compliance is achieved. Then, as for the Merciful One's (ʿalayhi al-rahma) abandonment of the implication of repetition upon repetition in the case where he slanders one person once and then slanders him again with the same fornication, he too does not give two hadds according to him, and likewise in the hadd for fornication and drinking: if he commits fornication a thousand times, or drinks similarly, he is given the hadd only once. Thus the truth is that his use of the verse as proof does not free him, since it compels him to abandon it by another verse, the verse of the hadd for fornication, and so it returns to the point that this is a right of the human being, unlike fornication. The matter then rests on establishing whether it is the right of God, ʿazza wa-jall, or the right of the servant. Careful examination requires that the predominant character here is the right of God, glory be to Him and exalted, so reflect upon this.

Then, the apparent meaning is that the accusation intended in the verse does not depend on the presence of the one accused or his address. Slandering a chaste person, whether present or absent, carries the stated ruling, as in al-Tatarkhaniyya quoting al-Mudmirat, and this is what al-Durar adopted. What shows that absence is like presence is that the Prophet ﷺ gave the hadd to the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk), though none of them spoke to him directly, while God cleared her of it. As for what is in Hawi al-Zahidi: one who heard from many people that so-and-so commits fornication with so-and-so, then spoke of what he had heard from them with another in the absence of so-and-so, is not liable to the hadd for slander, because it is backbiting (ghayba), not accusation (ramy) and slander of fornication, since accusation and slander with it are only by direct address, as in saying "O fornicator! O fornicatress!", is a weak opinion that is not relied upon.

It is also apparent that there is no difference between accusing the living and accusing the dead. If he says, "Your father is a fornicator," or "Your mother is a fornicatress," he is a slanderer and is liable to the hadd when the condition is fulfilled. But if he says, "Your grandfather is a fornicator," he is not liable to the hadd, because, as stated in al-Zahiriyya, he does not know which grandfather is meant, and in al-Fath because among his grandfathers there may be one who is a disbeliever, so he is not a slanderer unless he specifies a chaste person.

The demand for the hadd for slander on behalf of the dead is made by one whose lineage is impugned by the slander, namely the parent however high, and the child however low. Neither demands on behalf of an absent person, contrary to Ibn Abi Layla, because there is no despair of his demanding it himself, and because the slanderer may be believed to be truthful. The son of a daughter is like the son of a son in this matter, contrary to what is narrated from Muhammad. The demand is established for one who is barred from inheritance by killing, slavery, or disbelief. Yes, a slave may not demand from his master the hadd for slander against his free mother whom he slandered while she was dead. According to Zufar, if the child is a slave or a disbeliever, he has no right at all in it. The demand is established for the more remote when the closer is present, so a grandchild demands even though a child exists, contrary to Zufar. If some of them pardon, others may still demand, because it is for removing shame from oneself. A mother is like a father in demanding the hadd for slander against her child, but not her mother's mother or father. A son does not demand against his father or grandfather, however high, for slandering his mother. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and Ahmad, and one narration from Malik. The well-known view from Malik is that a son may demand that the father be given the hadd for slandering the mother, and this is the view of Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir, due to the generality or unrestricted wording of the verse, and because it is a hadd which is the right of God, ʿazza wa-jall, and the kinship of parenthood does not prevent its implementation.

It is answered that the generality of His saying, ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra' 23], prevents a child from implementing the hadd upon his father, and there is no benefit to the demand other than that, and the preventing factor takes precedence. It is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A father is not retaliated against for his child, nor a master for his slave." They agreed that one is not subjected to retaliation for killing his child. There is no doubt that nullifying his offense against the child's person entails nullifying it against his honor by a stronger reasoning, especially since retaliation has a certain cause, and what predominates in it is the right of the servant, unlike the hadd for slander in both respects. The brother, paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt of the deceased have no right to demand the hadd for slandering him.

According to al-Shafiʿi and Malik, may God have mercy on them both, the demand is established for every heir. This is a rare narration from Muhammad. For the Shafiʿis, regarding who inherits from him, there are three opinions: first, all the heirs; second, those not heirs by marriage; third, only the male agnatic heirs. The apparent meaning is that demanding the hadd by one who has the right to demand it is not obligatory upon him. Rather, in al-Tatarkhaniyya: it is commendable that the slanderer not bring the matter to the judge and that the claimant not demand the hadd, and the Imam commends that he say to the claimant, "Turn away from it and leave it," end of quote. It seems there is no difference in this between the claimant knowing the slanderer is truthful and knowing he is lying. As for what is related in al-Qunya, that the one slandered, if he was not chaste in private, has the right to demand from the slanderer in religious terms (diyanatan), there is an unclear point which is evident. The apparent meaning of the verse is that there is no difference between the accuser being free or a slave: each of them, if he slanders and the condition is fulfilled, is lashed eighty lashes. This is the view of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, al-Awza'i, and the majority of the imams, that a slave receives half the hadd, for what you know from the beginning of the surah. When the hadd for slander is to be carried out, the one slandering is not stripped of his clothes except in the view of Malik, because its cause is attributing fornication, which is a false and unestablished claim, since it is possible that he is truthful but unable to prove it.

Yes, his cloak (faru) and padded garment are removed, because these prevent the pain from reaching him. This is so in most books. Its implication is that if he wears a lined garment that is not padded, it is not removed. The apparent view, as in al-Fath, is that if this garment is over a shirt, it is removed, because together with the shirt it becomes like padding or close to it, and it prevents the pain from reaching him. And how could it not, since the beating here is lighter than the beating for fornication.

Furthermore, Abu Zur'a and Abdullah ibn Muslim read «bi-arba'atin» with tanwin, so that "shuhada'" is either an apposition (badal) or an attribute (sifa). It is also said to be a circumstantial (hal) or specifying (tamyiz) accusative, but this is not so. This is an eloquent reading, and Ibn Jinni preferred it over the reading of the majority, based on the general statement that when a numeral and an attribute come together, following (itba') is better than annexation (idafa).

This was challenged: that applies when the attribute does not function like nouns in directly taking governing particles. But when it does function in that way, its ruling is the same as the numeral and others, the only point being that substitution after the numeral is permissible, considering that it is not purely nominal. And "shuhada'" belongs to that category. So "arba'atu shuhada'" with annexation is more eloquent than "arba'atin shuhada'" with tanwin and following. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Sibawayh holds that tanwin of the numeral and omitting its annexation is permitted only in poetry, end of quote. It seems he intended to criticize this reading according to this view. But it is objected that Sibawayh holds this only for a numeral followed by a noun, such as "thalathatu rijal," and not for a numeral followed by an attribute, for in that case it follows the detail mentioned, as Abu Hayyan said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 4 (part 4 of 4):

His exalted saying: ﴿And do not accept their testimony ever after⦆, that is, for the duration of their lives, as is the apparent meaning. It is a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿flog them﴾, included within its ruling as a complement to it, as if it were said: "Flog them and reject their testimony," meaning: combine for them the flogging and the rejection. The rejection of their testimony, according to Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), is contingent upon the completion of the flogging. So if they testify before the flogging, or before its full execution is complete, their testimony is accepted. It has also been said: it is rejected once they are struck with a single lash; and it has been said: it is rejected once the majority of the punishment has been carried out. Among the strange reports is what Ibn al-Humam narrated from Malik that, together with his statement that a son may demand the hadd punishment for his father if he slanders his mother, he said: if the father receives the hadd punishment, the son's uprightness (ʿadalah) falls away, because he has directly participated in the cause of his father's punishment; that is, the father's uprightness likewise [falls away]. This is evident.

His exalted saying: ﴿And it is those who are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾ is a resumptive statement clarifying the bad condition they are in according to the ruling of Allah, mighty and majestic. The sense of distance in the demonstrative (ulaʾika) serves to indicate the remoteness of their rank in evil and corruption; that is, "those are the ones who are judged as defiantly disobedient, who depart from obedience and transgress the limits, who are perfect in it," as though they alone deserve to be called fasiq, not the other sinners. From what we have indicated, it is known that they are fasiq in the view of the Law, which judges by the outward, not that they are so in reality and before Allah, mighty and majestic, who knows the hidden matters, since their testimony may be true while they are unable to bring witnesses, as is not hidden. Some exegetes have stated this explicitly.

He permitted that the intended meaning is the report about their defiance before Allah the Exalted and in His knowledge. Its justification if they are lying is clear. As for its justification if they are truthful, it is that they have exposed the concealment of the believers and caused the hearer to fall into doubt without any religious benefit in doing so, and honour is among what Allah the Exalted has commanded to be protected when no benefit is tied to exposing it. Thus they were fasiq, not complying with His command, mighty and majestic. The fine appropriateness of reading the verse in this sense is not hidden, and it is more in line with what al-Haskafi stated in his commentary on al-Multaqa, quoting al-Najm al-Ghuzzi, that accusing someone of fornication is one of the major sins, even if the accuser is truthful and has no witnesses, even if it is from a father to his child, and even if he is not subjected to the hadd punishment for it; rather he is subjected to discretionary punishment (taʿzir), even if the victim is not muhsan. The jurists' condition of ihsan (chastity/free status) is only for the obligation of the hadd, not for it being a major sin.

Al-Tabarani narrated from Wathila, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever slanders a dhimmi, he will be given the hadd punishment on the Day of Resurrection with whips of fire."

This is a matter on which there is disagreement. In the commentary of Jam' al-Jawami' by the scholar al-Mahalli, al-Halimi said:

Slandering a young child, a slave, or a woman who openly flaunts her conduct is among the minor sins, because the harm in slandering them is less; whereas slandering a free, mature, and modest woman [is major]. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salam said: slandering a muhsan in private, such that none hears it except Allah the Exalted and the recording angels, is not a major sin entailing the hadd, because the mischief is absent. As for a man accusing his wife when she brings forth a child he knows is not his, that is permissible; likewise, impugning a narrator or a witness for fornication when he knows [its truth], rather it is obligatory. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of what was quoted from Ibn ʿAbd al-Salam is that it concerns the obligation of the hadd, not a denial that it is a major sin as well, since negation commonly attaches to the qualifier in such a case. If we say that here it negates both the qualifier and the qualified, then it is evident, as al-Zarkashi said, regarding the case where the accuser is truthful, not where he is lying, for his lying is audacity against Allah the Exalted, mighty is His majesty, and so it is a major sin even if done in private. Perhaps what he mentioned about the obligation to impugn a witness for fornication when one knows [it] is restricted to the case where one is able to bring witnesses. In my view, the better course, when the harm of accepting his testimony against him is slight, is not to impugn him on that basis, even if one is able to prove it. What he mentioned regarding impugning the narrator does not, in my view, hold according to the opinion of those who accept impugnment without stating its cause.

It is not far-fetched to say that among accusations some are unbelief (kufr), like the accusation against ʿA'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), whether it was openly or secretly made, and whether it concerned the one from whom Allah cleared her or someone else; and likewise the accusation against all the Mothers of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with them), and likewise the statement regarding Maryam (peace be upon her). Among them are those that are major sins short of unbelief, whose example is evident. Among them are those that are minor sins, like accusing a slave or a young girl. Among them are those that are obligatory, like accusing a witness, against a Muslim whose blood is protected, of something that would be the cause of his killing if his testimony were accepted and it were known to be false, and this is useful for rejecting his testimony and protecting that Muslim from being killed, even if the accusation, along with the establishment of proof against him for fornication, would entail his stoning. Among them are those that are recommended (sunnah), like an accusation that produces a benefit less than the benefit of the obligatory accusation.

His exalted saying:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 5 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Except for those who repent﴾, that is, who turn back from what they said and feel remorse for what they uttered, [p. 98] is an exception (istithna', exception) from "the defiantly disobedient" (al-fasiqun), as most of the companions (al-Ashab) have stated explicitly. Some of them said: "The thing excepted from in reality is (ulaika) ['those']." What relates to this will come, God willing. The place of the excepted term is in the accusative (nasb), because it is an exception from an obligation (mujib). His words, Exalted and Majestic is He, ﴿after that﴾, serve to magnify the sin repented of, that is: after they committed that great and terrible sin. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and make amends﴾, mean: and they amend their deeds by seeking pardon (istihlal) from those they accused. This is evident if the accused is still alive. If he has died, then perhaps asking forgiveness for him (al-istighfar lahu) takes the place of seeking his pardon, as has been said regarding a similar question. If they accused the dead, then it is apparent that they seek pardon from those who litigated against them and demanded the enforcement of the prescribed punishment (hadd) upon them. It is also possible that asking forgiveness for those who were accused suffices in its place. Combining the seeking of pardon from those litigants with asking forgiveness for the accused is better. I have not seen anyone address this.

That the exception applies to the last sentence (al-jumla al-akhira) is the position of the Hanafis (al-Hanafiyyah). According to them, the testimony of one who has been punished for slander (qadhf) is not accepted, even if he repents and makes amends. However, they said: if an unbeliever was punished (hudd) and then embraced Islam, his testimony is accepted, even though it was not accepted before, [i.e., from] the People of the Dhimma. They justified this by saying that the text requires the rejection of his testimony which arises from his legal capacity (ahliyya) established for him at the time of the slander. For this reason it was said: ﴿and do not accept testimony from them﴾, rather than "do not accept their testimony," meaning: do not accept from them any testimony of the testimonies, in the state in which it existed for them at the time of the accusation. The testimony that was in existence for the unbeliever at the time of the accusation is testimony against members of his own kind, so it falls under the rejection. As for the testimony which is considered after Islam, it is other than that testimony. For this reason it is accepted against the People of Islam and others, so it does not fall under the rejection. This differs from the case of a slave who was punished for slander and then was freed, for his testimony is not accepted, because he had no testimony before, due to his servitude. Therefore, the completion of his punishment requires the rejection of his testimony which has newly arisen for him. It has been asked what distinguishes this from one who committed fornication (zina) in the abode of war (dar al-harb) and then left for the abode of Islam (dar al-Islam). The latter is not punished (la yuhadd), since the ruling on the obligation (hukm al-mujib) for the slave was delayed until it became possible, while the obligation for fornication in the abode of war was not delayed until it became possible by leaving for the abode of Islam.

It is answered: fornication in the abode of war never came to be an obligation at all, due to the Imam's lack of capacity. Therefore the Imam was not addressed with its enforcement at all, because capacity is a condition of responsibility (taklif). So if he were punished after leaving, without another cause, it would be punishment without an obligation. Something that is not an obligation does not turn into one by itself, especially in a punishment whose averting is desired. As for the slave's slander, it is an obligation at the time it occurs for the punishment, except that its completion was not in the present, so its completion was delayed until this occurred after freedom. This is what has been said. In al-Mabsut, in distinguishing between the unbeliever who embraced Islam after the punishment and the slave who was freed after it, it says: the unbeliever gained through Islam a probity ('adala) which did not exist in him at the time the punishment was carried out, and this probity was not impaired, whereas the slave, by being freed, does not gain a probity that did not exist before, and his probity has been impaired by the carrying out of the punishment. Furthermore, there is no difference for the slave between being punished and then freed, and being freed and then punished, since his testimony is not accepted in both cases. As for the unbeliever, if he slandered a chaste person (muhsan), then embraced Islam, and then was punished, his testimony is not accepted. The implication of the verse is that every testimony of the one who has been punished is not accepted, whether it is recent or old, because ﴿testimony﴾ is indefinite (nakira), and it falls within the scope of a prohibition, so it conveys generality, like an indefinite term falling within the scope of a negation. This conflicts with what was mentioned earlier about accepting the testimony of the unbeliever who was punished when he embraces Islam. Ibn al-Humam (al-Allama Ibn al-Humam) answered that obligation is by what is within one's capacity, and that [the judges] were charged with rejecting his testimony. Compliance is only realized by rejecting an existing testimony. Therefore, when it was rejected, compliance was achieved and completed. Another [testimony] has since arisen, and if it were rejected, it would not be what is required, since the obligation is to take what is required. There is room for debate on this. The implication of generality is also the non-acceptance of the testimony of one who has been punished in matters of religion (diyanat), other than [testimony]. This is the report of al-Muntaqa. In another report, it is said that it is accepted in matters of religion. It seems they regarded it as a report and a narration (riwaya wa khabar), not a testimony, and a person whose testimony is rejected may have his narration accepted. [p. 99] An objection was raised against the generality: they relied on the testimony of those who had been punished in marriage (nikah).

It is answered: the testimony there means presence (al-hudur), and presence alone is sufficient for the conclusion of the marriage contract. They have stated explicitly that marriage has two rulings: the ruling of its conclusion (hukm al-in'iqad) and the ruling of its announcement (hukm al-izhar). In the second, only the testimony of one whose testimony is accepted in all other rulings is accepted, as in the commentary of al-Tahawi. The summary is: the verse indicates the obligation to reject the testimony of one who has been punished before the judges, in the sense that if he testifies before them on a ruling, they must reject his testimony. This includes his testimony in marriage, because he testifies before them when disputes arise. Therefore the requirement of his presence at the marriage session for the validity of its conclusion does not conflict with the generality, since that is a matter beyond what we are discussing. This is what has been said, so reflect on it.

Al-Shafi'i went to the acceptance of the testimony of one who has been punished when he repents. By his repentance is meant that he denies his slander of himself. The root of the disagreement lies in the well-known question of whether, when an exception comes after a series of sentences joined by "and" (wa), it applies to the last sentence, or to all of them, or whether there is a detailed distinction. What the companions of al-Shafi'i held is that it applies to all, and what the companions of Abu Hanifa held is that it applies to the last sentence. Al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and a group of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) said: if the beginning of the second sentence is a turning away (idrab) from the first, and nothing implied in the first is implied in it, then the exception is specific to the last sentence, because it is apparent that he did not move from the first sentence, although it is self-standing, to another unless its aim from it had been achieved. This has four categories. The first is that the two sentences differ in type, as when one says: "Honor the Banu Tamim, and the grammarians of Basra except the Baghdadis," since the first sentence is an imperative and the second is a declarative. The second is that they share a type but differ in subject and ruling, as when one says: "Honor the Banu Tamim, and strike Rabi'a except the tall ones," since both are imperatives. The third is that they share a type and agree in ruling but not in subject, as when one says: "Greet the Banu Tamim, and greet the Banu Rabi'a except the tall ones." The fourth is that they share a type and agree in subject but not in ruling, and the two rulings do not share any purpose, as when one says: "Greet the Banu Tamim, and hire the Banu Tamim except the tall ones." The strength of the implication that the exception is specific to the last sentence in these categories follows this order, even if the beginning of the second sentence is not a turning away from the first, but there is some connection between the two sentences. Then the exception applies to all. This has four categories. The first is that the two sentences share a type and subject but not a ruling, though the two rulings share one purpose, as when one says: "Honor the Banu Tamim, and greet the Banu Tamim except the tall ones," because they share the purpose of honoring. The second is that the two sentences share a type, differ in ruling, and the subject of the first is implied in the second, as when one says: "Honor the Banu Tamim, and hire them except the tall ones." The third is the reverse of the preceding, as when one says: "Honor the Banu Tamim and Rabi'a except the tall ones." The fourth is that the types of sentences differ, but the subject has been implied in the last one, or the purposes of the differing rulings are one. The verse of accusation which we are discussing is of this kind, since its sentences differ in type: the words of Exalted God ﴿whip them eighty lashes﴾ are an imperative; His words ﴿and never accept their testimony ever﴾ are a prohibition; and His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ are a declarative. It also falls under the first of these four categories, since the rulings of these sentences share the purpose of retribution and humiliation. It also falls under the second category, by implying the subject mentioned earlier in them.

Al-Sharif al-Murtada of the Shi'a went to the view of the exception being shared (al-ishtirak) among them all. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr and al-Ghazali and a group went to suspension (al-waqf), that is, withholding judgment. Al-Amidi said: the preferred view is that whenever it is apparent that the "and" (wa) is for beginning a new sentence, the exception is specific to the last sentence, as in the first category of the eight categories, because one of the two sentences is not connected to the other, which is evident. When it is possible for the "and" to be coordinating (li al-'atf) or for beginning (li al-ibtida'), as in the remaining seven categories, then suspension is obligatory. He mentioned the proofs of the schools with what is for and against them regarding the rulings. In al-Talwih and elsewhere, it says there is no disagreement about the permissibility of the exception returning to all [sentences], [p. 100] and the disagreement is only about which is more apparent. This is open to scrutiny, since some of the arguments of those who hold that it returns to the last sentence have themselves relied on something that indicates it cannot return to all. Al-Qalanisi said: the accusative (nasb) of what follows the exception in an affirmative sentence occurs only by the preceding verb, through the indirect implication (bi-i'ana), except according to what the leading Basran grammarians held. So if it were said that it returns to all, what follows "illa" would be governed by the verbs assumed in each sentence, and this would entail two governors acting upon one governed term. This is impermissible, because if one assumes that each of them opposes the other in governance, it would follow that one governed term is simultaneously nominative and accusative, which is impossible. Also, if each of them were independently governing, it would necessitate that neither is independent, since it is clear that for each to be independent means nothing but that the ruling was established by it and not by anything else. If neither were independent, this would contradict the premise. If only one were independent and not the other, this would necessitate preference without a preferring factor (tarjih bila murajjih). The indication of this, although debated, shows the impermissibility of its return to all [sentences]. Just as the principles scholars (al-usuliyyun) disagreed on this, the grammarians (al-nuhat) disagreed on it. In the commentary on al-Luma', it says that it is specific to the last [sentence], and that connecting it to all is an error, because it necessitates multiple governors acting on one governed term, unless one holds that the governor of illa is "or" or the completion of the sentence.

Abu Hayyan said: I have not seen anyone among the grammarians who discussed this question except al-Mahabadhi and Ibn Malik. Ibn Malik preferred that the exception return to all the sentences, like the conditional (al-shart). Al-Mahabadhi preferred that it return to the last sentence. Al-Wali ibn al-Iraqi said: Ibn Malik did not restrict its return to all sentences absolutely, but excepted from this what happens when the governor and the governed differ, as in your saying: "Clothe the poor, feed the wayfarers except whoever is an innovator," and he said in this case that it returns only to the last one. He related from Abu Ali al-Farisi the view that it returns to the last one absolutely, and this is like the view of the Hanafis, according to the well-known position. The truth is that they only say it returns to the last one alone when the speech is stripped of evidence that it returns to all. But when evidence is found, it is acted upon, as in His words, Exalted is He, concerning the highway robbers (al-muharibin): ﴿that they be killed, or crucified﴾ up to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿except for those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. The words of Exalted God ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 33, 34] require its return to all, for if it returned only to the last one, meaning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾, the restriction by that would serve no purpose, since repentance removes punishment. The purpose of "before" would only be the removal of the prescribed punishment (hadd). It is upon this kind of reasoning that the statement of the Shafi'is should be interpreted, by saying that they meant the return of the exception to all when there is no evidence requiring its return to the last one.

Some distinguished verifiers (muhaqqiqun) mentioned that the Hanafis only held that the exception (istithna') returns to the last clause here because the first two clauses came as a conditional consequence (jaza'), since they were addressed to the rulers (a'imma) in the form of a command, and the difference between them, one being a command and the other a prohibition, does no harm. The final clause is a new independent sentence (mustanfa'a) in the form of a report, to dispel the supposition that it is far-fetched for slander to be a cause for the obligation of a punishment that is averted by doubt (tandaree'u bil-shubha). That punishment is present here, because slander is a report that may be true and may perhaps be done for the sake of public duty (hisba). The way of dispelling this is that they have committed wickedness (fisq) by violating the veil of chastity without benefit, since they failed to produce proof, and therefore they deserve the punishment. And since it is a new independent sentence, the exception is directed toward it.

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that he made ﴿And do not accept﴾ a separate new sentence cut off from the preceding sentence, and refused that it be part of the hadd (legal punishment), because there is no connection between flogging and the non-acceptance of testimony. He directed the exception to it by making "except those who repent" an exception from the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And those are the wicked (fasiqun)﴾, would then be an interjected clause (i'tirad) functioning as the reason (ta'lil) for the non-acceptance of testimony, not cut off from what precedes it. For this reason it is permissible to place it between the exception and what is excepted from, and the exception is not attached to it. Ibn al-Hajib favoured this in his Amali, where he said: "The exception does not return to the whole. As for the flogging, it is by agreement. As for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And those are the wicked﴾,
Page 101
it was only brought to establish the prohibition of testimony, so only the second clause remains, and the exception returns to it." It was objected that the new sentence ﴿And do not accept﴾ etc. is far-fetched in the extreme, and that the meaning of non-acceptance of testimony is its rejection, and its connection to flogging is evident, because each of them is painful and deterrent from committing the crime of accusation, and many a person does not feel pain from beating as he feels pain from the rejection of his testimony. It may be said that rejecting testimony is, in meaning, a cutting of the treacherous instrument, which is the tongue, so it is like cutting off the hand in theft literally. Whoever is fair sees that its connection to flogging is more complete than the connection of exile (taghrib) to it, because exile may be a cause of increased fornication, since few people watch over and feel shame before one in a foreign land, and a woman who has gone abroad may be compelled, to sustain her life, to surrender herself in order to obtain that. Also, flogging is an act that the ruler is obliged to perform, and rejection, which is meant by non-acceptance, is likewise; and both imperative clauses, in wording and meaning, were addressed to the rulers. By this the strength of the connection is confirmed.

Al-Zayla'i objected to the claim that the clause ﴿And those are the wicked﴾ is a reason for the rejection of testimony, saying: "It is not permissible that the rejection of his testimony be because of his wickedness, because what is established by the text regarding the report of a wicked person is suspension (tawaqquf), by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿If a wicked person comes to you with news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6], not rejection, and the cause of rejection here is nothing but that it is a hadd, which has ended." This is open to examination. Al-Shafi'i, on this transmission, did not make the mentioned clause, although it functions as a reason for what precedes it, coordinated (ma'tufa) to it, because many have said that coordination with waw prevents intending it as a reason for the rejection of testimony due to wickedness, since a reason is not coordinated to a ruling with waw but is mentioned with fa'. Likewise it should not be coordinated to what was previously indicated, namely that it is a reason for the entitlement to punishment, since that is not explicitly stated. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, was defended in what he held, namely acceptance of his testimony when he repents, by the argument that if the clause is made a reason for the rejection, then this is complete; and even if one grants that the exception returns to the last clause of successive clauses joined by waw, it necessitates the removal of the ruling upon the removal of the cause. I do not think this can be answered except by committing to the view that it is not for causation.

Some of them said: "There is no cutting between clauses according to al-Shafi'i, and his well-known principle requires the exception to return to all of them, so the flogging would then fall by repentance. But he does not say this, because the verification of his school is that return to the whole may be departed from when there is evidence and an obstacle becomes evident, and the obstacle here against its return to the first clause, according to what is said, is the consensus that flogging does not fall by repentance because it involves the right of the servant. Even more preferable is what al-Qadi al-Baydawi hinted at, that submitting to the flogging is part of the repentance, so how could it return to it? It cannot be said that non-acceptance of testimony and labelling as wicked are also part of it, as is not hidden." It was said that the verse may come out according to his well-known principle, and there is no obstacle to the exception returning to the first clause as well, since the excepted is ( those who repented and reformed ), and from the components of reform is seeking pardon and making amends (istihlal) from the one slandered; and when that occurs, the flogging falls as well. But it is objected that seeking pardon not being part of reform is not beneficial, because flogging does not fall by seeking pardon; rather it is the pardon itself, and that is not among this reform, since pardon is an act of the slandered and this reform is an act of the slanderer, so it is not valid to direct the exception to the whole as is his well-known principle.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "What the apparent meaning and composition of the verse require is that the three clauses together are the consequence (jaza') of the condition, and the meaning is: whoever slanders, then combine for them all three penalties, except those among them who repent, so they return not flogged, not with rejected testimony, and not labelled as wicked." In al-Kashf he said: "This proceeds on al-Shafi'i's principle that the exception returns to the whole, and what joins it here is that the clauses have entered the scope of the condition, so they become like single terms." It was objected to his saying that the clause ﴿And those are the wicked﴾ entered the scope of the consequence: the proof of non-participation in the condition requires non-entry, for it is a declarative clause not addressed to the rulers, since the kaf in ( ulā'ika ) is singular; so it is either coordinated to the nominal clause, i.e., "those who accuse etc.," or a new sentence to narrate the state of the accusers in the sight of the Law. It was answered that coordinating a report to a command and the reverse are both common in speech because of differences in purposes, and that singular address with the kaf together with the demonstrative is permissible in addressing a group, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52]. Moreover, the verified view is that ( those who accuse ) is in the accusative by a deleted verb, i.e., "flog those who..." etc., so it is also a verbal imperative clause addressed to the rulers; hence the mentioned obstacle stands here, namely the additional deviation from the nearer to the farther. And even if one grants that ( those who ) is a subject, a imperative clause placed in the position of the predicate requires interpretation and turning away from the imperative according to most; then the coordination of ﴿And those are the wicked﴾ to it is valid. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning of ﴿And those are the wicked﴾ is that they have made them wicked (fasaquhum)." Fairness judges that it is not clearly apparent that the final clause enters the scope of the consequence, and everything they mentioned only establishes validity, not apparentness.

It seems apparent, however, that it is a concluding new sentence (istinaf tadhyili) explaining the bad state of the accusers in the judgment of God the Exalted; and then the return of the exception to it is evident. It cannot be said that this negates the benefit, because it is known by the Law that repentance removes wickedness apart from this verse; for we say: there is no doubt that knowledge of this is by way of revelation, and He mentioned the evidence for it from it, and making another verse to convey it does no harm, since it is certain that the way of the Qur'an is the repetition of indicators, especially when emphasis is desired. This is what has been said. As for the view of Abu Hanifa that the testimony of one punished for slander is not accepted if he repents, it was held by al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Sa'id ibn Jubayr; al-Jalal al-Suyuti narrated this from all of them in al-Durr al-Manthur. As for the view of al-Shafi'i that his testimony is accepted, it was held by Malik and Ahmad, and it is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Tawus, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, Muharib, Shurayh, Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, Ikrima and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, according to what al-Tibi mentioned; and Ibn Jubayr is counted among those who said as al-Shafi'i said, which contradicts what you have just heard. Ibn al-Humam counted Shurayh among those who said as Abu Hanifa said. From Ibn Abbas there are two narrations. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Umar, may God be pleased with him, flogged Abu Bakra, Shibl ibn Ma'bad and Nafi' for the accusation against al-Mughira, then he asked them to repent, and said: "Whoever repents, his testimony is accepted." Whoever examines thoroughly finds that most jurists agree with the saying of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and the claim of consensus of the jurists of the Successors upon it is not correct, as is not hidden. And God the Exalted knows best. The reason (ta'lil) derived from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is apparent on both views, but it has been said that it is more apparent on the view of Abu Hanifa. It is a reason for what the exception implies, and it has no place in the grammatical analysis (la mahalla min al-i'rab). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ( alladhina ) be a subject, and this sentence its predicate, with a deleted resumptive pronoun, i.e., "for them."

The majority chose the new sentence and the exception, and according to what our companions held, it is a disconnected exception (munqati'). Abu Zayd al-Dabbusi explained this in al-Taqwim with a summary meaning that the excepted, although it entered the opening statement, was not intended to be removed from its ruling in the manner of a connected exception, but rather a different ruling was intended for it, namely that the penitent does not remain wicked. Al-Allama al-Thani objected that this is complete only if the meaning of ﴿they are the wicked﴾ is not permanence and continuance; otherwise there is no obstacle to connection, so there is no basis for disconnection. Fakhr al-Islam explained that the excepted does not enter the opening statement, because the penitent is not wicked by necessity; it is an expression for one in whom wickedness subsists, and the penitent is not so, since wickedness is removed by repentance. This is based on the condition that the meaning of the verb must remain in the true sense of the active participle; but if that is not required, then the inclusion is realized, yet exclusion is not valid, because the penitent is not excluded from those who were wicked in past time.

It was objected that the excepted noun, on the assumption that the exception is connected, is not the wicked but those who were judged with that, namely those who accuse, referred to by the Exalted's saying ( and those ). There is no doubt that the penitents are included among them, excluded from their ruling,
Page 103
which is wickedness; as if it were said: all accusers are wicked except those among them who repent, as one says: "the people are departing, except Zayd," a connected exception, on the basis that Zayd is included among the people and excluded from the ruling of departing; so the connected exception is valid whether the excepted noun by wording is "the people" or the concealed pronoun in "departing," on the basis that it is closer, and that the operation of the attribute on the excepted is more evident. It is not meant that the excepted noun by wording is absolutely the word "the people." If the excepted noun is taken as the pronoun of "departing," the meaning of the sentence is: Zayd is included among the persons judged as departing and excluded from the ruling of departing, as in our saying: "the people departed except Zayd." Likewise the discussion in the verse.

And I answer: the *fasiqun* (transgressors) here may be understood in one of three ways. It may mean the one who is characterized by transgression in a continuous and enduring sense, or it may mean the one from whom transgression proceeded in the past, or it may mean the one in whom transgression exists in general, whether in the past or the present. If the first sense is intended, then the penitent is not a transgressor, by necessity, since the Lawgiver has ruled that the penitent is not a transgressor in reality. And among the conditions of a *istithna' muttasil* (connected exception) is that the ruling would include the excepted item if the exception were left unstated. This is what Fakhr al-Islam (al-Bazdawi) means by saying that the transgressors do not include the penitents, unlike the statement "*Muntaliqun* (they set out)," where Zayd would be included if there were no exception. If the second or third sense is intended, then there is no validity in excluding the penitent from the transgressors, because he is a transgressor in the sense that transgression has proceeded from him in general, since he is one who commits *qadhf* (false accusation), and *qadhf* is transgression.

It is not hidden that the denial that the penitents are included among the transgressors in the sense we have mentioned, and the denial that their exclusion from them is invalid in the other sense, are both not well-founded. The argument for their inclusion, namely that a judgment of transgression has been passed upon "*ulaika*" (those), referring to ﴿Those who accuse﴾, which is a general term, is not sound, because of the decisive consensus (*ijma'*) that there is no transgression with repentance. And that is sufficient as a specification (*takhsis*). End of quotation. In it, however, is the point that consensus cannot be a specifier in the matter under discussion, because it is later than the text, since there is no consensus except after the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). So the judgment of transgression upon "*ulaika*," referring to ﴿Those who accuse﴾, which is general, is complete, and the argument stands.

I answer this by saying that what is meant by specification here is restricting a general term to some of what the wording includes, not the technical specification (*takhsis mustalah*). This is as you see. And in his statement "among the conditions of the connected exception etc." there is a discussion that will become clear from what comes soon, God willing. The *'Allama* said: The apparent reading is that the exception is connected, meaning: "those who accuse" are judged to be transgressors, except the penitents among them, for they are not judged to be transgressors, because the penitent from sin is like one who has no sin. It seems that he meant that they are not judged to be transgressors in the enduring sense, which is what was ruled upon them at the beginning, by the indication of the nominal sentence.

Some of the eminent scholars, in explaining why it is connected, mentioned that the inclusion of the excepted item within the item excepted from occurs only with regard to the item excepted from having the wording include it and encompass it, not in terms of its actually being established for it in reality. How so? For if the ruling were established for it, its exception would be valid. So here, "those who accuse" includes the penitents among them, and therefore the fact that they are not transgressors does not harm the validity of the exception, and that repentance negates the establishment of transgression, just as when Zayd is not included in "went out," where his exception is valid on the basis of his being included among the people, as in "the people went out except Zayd."

The summary is that it suffices for an exception that the excepted item be included in the ruling of the item excepted from by the indication of the wording, even if it is not included by a separate proof outside it, as one says: "God the Exalted created everything except His Essence, glorified is He, and His exalted attributes." The *'Allama* said: It is possible to answer this by saying that there is no benefit to the connected exception on this reckoning, because the exclusion of the excepted item from the ruling of the item excepted from is already known, so it is taken to be a disconnected exception (*munqati'*) that yields a new benefit. And this is what Fakhr al-Islam meant by the non-inclusion of the penitents in the opening statement. But it was questioned on the ground that the non-application of the legal ruling is derived from the exception mentioned in the verse, and the hadith, namely "the penitent from sin is like one who has no sin," which explains it, so there is no basis for denying the existence of a benefit. Also, that the exclusion of the excepted item from the ruling of the item excepted from is known here is not known, because of the disagreement over whether the continuation of the act is a condition. And also, the new benefit in the disconnected exception, which the connected exception lacks, is not evident.

He also said: One may ask why it is not permissible for the item excepted from to be the transgressors, and the exception to serve to exclude the penitents from them in the ruling that is the attribution to those accusers and the establishment for them. For the exception is permissible from what is ruled upon as it is permissible from other than it, as one says: "The noble ones of the people of our town are their rich, except Zayd," meaning that Zayd, although he is rich, is nonetheless excluded from being counted among the noble. We reply: In that case it would follow that the penitents are among the transgressors but not among the accusers, and the matter is the reverse. It may also be said that the exception is disconnected, in the sense that they are transgressors in all states except the state of repentance. But it is not hidden that this requires an imposed supposition in the wording, namely: "except the state of repentance of those who..." or "except the repentance of the accusers," that is, the time of their repentance, on the condition that *alladhina* is taken as a verbal (infinitival) particle, not a relative noun, and the pronoun of "*tabu*" (they repented) refers back to "*ulaika*" (those). And after *illa alladhina* and *illa allati* the exception becomes truncated and connected, not disconnected. End. So reflect.

[p. 104]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 6:

﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾ [al-Nur: 6, 20] explains the ruling concerning those who accuse their wives specifically. It abrogates (naskh) the generality of "the chaste women" (al-muhsanat). Before the revelation of this verse, they understood from the verse ﴿And those who accuse﴾ etc. [al-Nur: 4] that the ruling for one who accuses a non-related woman and the ruling for one who accuses his wife were the same.

Abu Dawud and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "When the verse ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4] was revealed, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, who was the chief of the Ansar, said: 'Is it revealed in this way, O Messenger of Allah?'
