In light of this, ﴿Glory be to You﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it and a preface to His saying: ﴿This is a monstrous slander﴾, meaning a lie that stupefies and bewilders the hearer because of its enormity, ﴿great﴾, whose true magnitude cannot be measured, due to the greatness of the one slandered. The lowliness or greatness of sins is often determined by their objects. Apparently, the rebuke is directed at the listeners who engaged in the talk, not at all listeners in general.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that when Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard what was said about the matter of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, he said: "Glory be to You, this is a monstrous slander." And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "Two men among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever they heard something of that kind, would say what Usama ibn Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Ayyub said, may Allah be pleased with them both." Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the wife of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari said to him: "O Abu Ayyub, do you not hear what the people are talking about?" He said: "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You, this is a monstrous slander."

The basis of this certainty, according to what Imam al-Razi said, is the knowledge that the wife of the Messenger (ﷺ) cannot be an adulteress. He explained that this is because such a thing would repel people from following him, thereby undermining the wisdom of the mission (*hikmat al-ba'tha*), just as baseness of fathers and immorality of mothers would. The "second scholar" (al-'Allama al-Thani) explicitly stated that among the conditions of prophethood (*nubuwwa*) is freedom from this, and indeed from everything that repels people from following.

This raises a problem: if what was mentioned is a condition, how could those who heard it, and who said what they said, have known it? And the matter was hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he said, as in Sahih al-Bukhari and others: "O 'A'isha, it has reached me that such-and-such was said about you. If you are innocent, Allah will surely clear you. And if you have committed a sin, then seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him."

In some narrations it came: "O 'A'isha, if you have done this thing, then tell me, so that I may ask Allah's forgiveness for you."

Likewise, it was hidden from his companion Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Bazzar reported with a sound chain from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that when her innocence was revealed, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, kissed her head. She said: "Would that you had excused me." He said: "What heaven would shade me and what earth would bear me if I said what I do not know?"

It is answered that this is not among the rational conditions of prophethood, like trustworthiness and truthfulness. Rather, it is among the legal and customary conditions, as al-Laqani stated. Thus it is permissible to say that it was not known beforehand, but was known only after the verses of the exoneration of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, were revealed. Not knowing such a matter does not detract from the station of prophethood. As for the claim that those who were mentioned in this context knew it, there is no evidence for it. Their statement may have arisen from good opinion (*husn al-zann*) and not from knowledge that freedom from what repels people from following is a condition of prophethood. This is supported by considering some of those who spoke. Apparently, they were equal in this. What Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir reported from some of the Ansar supports this: that the wife of Abu Ayyub said to him when the People of the Slander (*ahl al-ifk*) said what they said: "Do you not hear what people say about 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her?" He said: "Yes, and that is a lie. Would you have done such a thing, O Umm Ayyub?" She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then 'A'isha, by Allah, is better and purer than you. This is merely a lie and a false fabrication." Al-Hakim and Ibn 'Asakir also narrated something similar from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, and perhaps he is the one meant by "some of the Ansar" in the preceding report. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not say anything like that, owing to good opinion, because of the intensity of his jealousy (*ghayra*) over his wife. A person who is jealous does not usually rely on good opinion in such a matter.

It is possible that their statement arose from knowledge that freedom from what repels people from following is a condition of prophethood, in that they perceived that the wisdom of the mission requires that freedom. A knowledgeable person may perceive what someone more knowledgeable than him does not perceive.

It is also permissible to claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that the wives of prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, cannot commit immorality, because of the repulsion this would cause, which would undermine the wisdom of the mission. However, he, upon him blessings and peace, wished to make manifest the exoneration of the Truthful One, may Allah be pleased with her, like the sun's appearance at mid-morning, so that no doubt would remain for any of the noble Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The distress that afflicted him was a natural matter that occurred because of the immersion of the hypocrites and those who followed them, and the spreading of falsehood with no basis among the people. It is also possible that he (ﷺ) knew that freedom from what repels people is a condition of prophethood, but he feared God, mighty and majestic, to whom nothing is obligatory, that He might make what the hypocrites and their followers were immersed in into something repellent, by not arranging that the aversion be created in hearts toward him so as to prevent people from following him, thereby undermining the wisdom of the mission. So the distress that befell him, upon him blessings and peace, befell him, and he began to investigate the matter in the most complete way. This was nothing but from abundance of knowledge and perfection of resolve. A parallel to this is his fear, upon him blessings and peace, of the Hour arriving when the wind grew strong, to the extent that he could not sleep as long as the matter was so, until the sky rained.

It has also been said that the immorality of a wife is not considered repellent unless she remains with the husband after knowing of it. So why should it not be permissible for it to occur, in which case her divorce would be obligatory? And if she is divorced, the repellent factor that undermines the wisdom would not arise. Yet you should not be unaware of what is in some of these possibilities of discussion, and indeed some of them are very far from being accepted. Perhaps the truth is that he, upon him blessings and peace, was not informed of the conditional matter until the innocence became clear and the verses concerning it were revealed, for the wisdom of trial and other reasons known only to God, exalted is He.

As for the statement of those Companions, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿Glory be to You, this is a monstrous slander﴾, it arose only from good opinion. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not adopt it, because it does not cut off gossip and talk, nor does it refute any falsehood. It is not fitting for one who believes in Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) that, after considering the verses and reports, any doubt should stir in his heart concerning the purity of the wives of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, from immorality during their husbands' lives and after their deaths.

It is attributed to the Shi'a that they slander 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, with what Allah has cleared her of. They deny this most strongly, and there is not a single trace of it in their trusted books, nor any report at all. Likewise they deny what is attributed to them regarding the claim that such a thing occurred with her after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and there is likewise no trace of it in their books.

Apparently, there is no Islamic sect in which anyone harbors such a thought in his heart, let alone the slander from which Allah, mighty and majestic, has cleared her.

﴿Allah admonishes you﴾, i.e., advises you, ﴿never to return to the like of it﴾, i.e., out of aversion to returning, or lest you return, or He magnifies the matter for you regarding returning, i.e., regarding its affair and the sin and harms in it, as one says: "I admonished him about wine and what is in it of disgrace." Or He restrains you from returning, by way of *tadmin* (the implicit inclusion of the meaning of one verb in another), so that *wa'z* (admonition) carries the meaning of *zajr* (restraint). It is said: *ʿadahu*, *ʿada ilayhi*, *ʿada lahu* and *ʿada fihi* all have the same meaning. By *abadan* ("never") is meant the duration of life.

﴿If you are believers﴾. This is of the type of the saying *in kunta aban laka, fa-lima la tahsunu (ilayya)* ("If you are a father to me, then why do you not treat me well?"). It includes a reminder to them of faith, which is the reason for abstaining and the incitement, and it is expressed in the form of doubt, and in it there is an element of reproach.

﴿And Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾. That is, He sends them down clear, with their meanings manifestly evident. What is meant by them are the verses that indicate the laws (*shara'i'*, the legal rulings) and the noble etiquettes of dealing with the Muslims. The explicit mention of the Exalted Name (*al-ism al-jalil*) in place of a pronoun serves to magnify the matter of clarification.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the conditions of all His creatures, the great and the small, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His acts. How, then, could what was said be true of one whom He has sanctified and chosen for His message, and sent to all of creation, so that He might guide them to the truth, purify them, and cleanse them thoroughly? The explicit mention of the Exalted Name here serves to emphasize the independence of the parenthetical concluding statement (*al-i'tirad al-tadhyili*) and to indicate that divinity is the cause of knowledge and wisdom.

﴿Indeed, those who love﴾ — that is, desire and intend — ﴿that indecency should spread﴾, that is, spread ( ﴿al-fāḥisha﴾ ), meaning the excessively ugly trait, which is slander and the accusation of fornication, or fornication itself, as narrated from Qatadah. What is meant by its spreading is the spreading of news of it ﴿among those who believe﴾. The phrase ﴿among those who believe﴾ is connected to "spreading," meaning spreading among people.

The believers are mentioned because they are the core of the community, or it is connected to an implied element that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "indecency," meaning existing with regard to the believers and concerning them. What is meant by them are the chaste men and the chaste women, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. ﴿For them﴾, because of that, ﴿is a painful punishment in this world﴾, of what befalls them of trials such as paralysis and blindness, ( and in the Hereafter ), of the punishment of the Fire and the like. That this punishment is consequent upon love is evident according to what is transmitted from al-Karmani, that evil deeds of the heart, such as rancor, envy, and love of the spread of indecency, bring the servant to account when he resolves himself upon them. From the verse it is known in the most complete manner how evil is the state of those concerning whom the verse was revealed, such as Ibn Ubayy and whoever agreed with him in heart and in conduct. And that they have the greater share of the two punishments, since they loved the spreading and spread it.

Some of them said: What is meant by love of spreading is the spreading itself, by the indication that the punishment is consequent upon it, for it is consequent only upon the spreading and not upon love, which lies outside choice. And even if it is granted that what is meant by it is a love that falls under choice, and that it is among the things that bring punishment, we say: that is the punishment of the Hereafter, not the punishment of this world, such as the legal penalty (ḥadd). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr explained the painful punishment in this world here as the legal penalty, and this does not follow from love in any absolute sense by consensus. From here it has also been said: mention of love is by way of ellipsis (iktifāʾ), in which the thing, which is spreading, is left unmentioned by mentioning what necessitates it, as an alert to the strength of what necessitates it. It has also been said: the statement is by way of implicit complementation (tadmīn), meaning they spread indecency while loving its spread, because both meanings, love and spreading, are intended.

It was objected that interpreting the painful punishment in this world as the legal penalty is problematic, since the punishment in the Hereafter is not added to it, because the prescribed penalties are expiatory. 

It is answered that the ruling of the verse is specific to whoever spread that concerning the Mother of the Believers. It has also been said: the legal penalty is for those among the Muslims who transmitted the slander, and the punishment of the Hereafter is for Abu ʿUdhrah, Ibn Ubayy, and the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is general to both of them. Moreover, regarding whether the prescribed penalties are expiatory in every case, there is disagreement: some said so except for apostasy (ridda), some denied it, and some suspended judgment on it,

according to the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet, may peace be upon him, said: "I do not know whether the prescribed penalties are expiation for their people or not."

Perhaps the most suitable reading with the course of the noble composition, which censures those who plunged into the slander and spread it, is what we mentioned first. What is meant by the relative pronoun is either those people, taking it as the external reference (al-ʿahd al-khārijī), as narrated from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, and the use of the present tense in the relative clause indicates the increase in their censure, in that their love for the spread of indecency has become a continuous habit. Or it refers to everyone, including them and others, from every person characterized by the content of the relative clause, taking it generically, and those spreaders enter it primarily, as has been said. ﴿And Allah knows﴾ all matters, of which is what is in their hearts of the aforementioned love, and likewise the wisdom in intensifying the threat ﴿while you do not know﴾ what Allah, glorified and exalted, knows.

The clause is a concluding parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī), brought in to confirm that the punishment is theirs and to give its reason. It has been said: the meaning is that Allah knows what is in their hearts, so He will punish them for it in the Hereafter, while you do not know that; rather you know only what appears to you of their words, so you punish them for it in this world.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 20:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy...﴾ The address is, according to what al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, directed to Mistah, Hassan and Hamnah, or to others besides them, namely Ibn Ubayy and his like among the hypocrites who engaged in the slander (al-khA'iDun). This is a repetition of the favour, by not hastening the punishment, in order to draw attention to the complete gravity of the offence. His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿the grace of Allah﴾. The mention of the noble Name is to cultivate awe and to indicate that the attribute of divinity entails kindness and mercy. The change of its composition and its opening with the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) is because the intended meaning is to express that He, exalted is He, is characterised in His essence by these two noble attributes permanently and continuously, not to express that their application to them has occurred. Likewise, the intended meaning of what is conjoined (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) and the response of (law la) is omitted, as has passed. This is similar to the verse that passed at the end of the hadith of li'an, except that the closing with "Most Kind, Most Merciful" in place of "Ever-Relenting, All-Wise" there indicates that the sin in this matter is greater, and that it seems it is not removed except by the sheer kindness of Allah, exalted is He, and it is too great to be removed by repentance, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: whoever engaged in the discourse of the slander and repented, his repentance will not be accepted. The purpose is severity, so do not be heedless.

[Al-Nur: 21. 28] That is, do not follow his ways in anything you do or leave undone.

[Page 124]

The phrase is a kinayah (an allusive expression) for following Satan and obeying his whisperings. It is as if it were said: Do not follow Satan in any of the deeds, among which is spreading indecency and loving it.

Nafi', al-Bazzi in the transmission of Ibn Rabi'ah from him, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Hamzah read *khuṭuwāt* with a sukun on the ta'. It was also read with a fatha. In all of these readings it is the plural of *khuṭwah*, with a damma on the kha' and a sukun on the ta', which is a noun for the distance between the two feet. As for *khaṭwah* with a fatha on the kha', it is a verbal noun from *khaṭā*. The general rule for a noun in the plural is that its middle vowel is moved, to distinguish it from an adjective, so it takes a damma to match the fa', or a fatha for lightness, and it may also take a sukun.

﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan﴾: the two nouns, *khuṭuwāt* and *al-shaṭān*, are used in full instead of pronouns referring to *khuṭuwāt* and *al-shaṭān*. He did not say "whoever follows them" or "whoever follows his steps," in order to add emphasis and intensity. ﴿Indeed he commands indecency﴾: this is what is extremely ugly, such as *fāḥishah*. ﴿And wrongdoing﴾: this is what the Law (al-shar') denounces. The pronoun in *innahu* refers to Satan, and it has been said that it refers to the matter (al-sha'n). The answer to the conditional is omitted, and what follows the fa' stands in its place. Originally, this is a justification of the conditional sentence and an explanation of the reason for the prohibition, as if it were said: Whoever follows Satan has committed indecency and wrongdoing, for he commands only these two, and one who is like this may not be followed or obeyed. Al-Nasafi and Ibn Hisham established this in the fifth chapter of *al-Mughni*. It has been objected that this is contradicted by what the grammarians have stated, that the answer may be omitted only when the condition is in the past tense, to the point that they counted as a poetic necessity the line:

*"If your houses have become too narrow for me, then let my Lord know that my house is wider."*

It is answered that the verse is not of the same kind as the line they cited, for in the line the answer is omitted entirely, whereas here something stands in its place which can be taken as the answer on the surface. Abu Hayyan said: the pronoun refers back to the one in the conditional *man*, and no omission is assumed in the sentence at all. The meaning on this basis is: whoever follows Satan, he becomes a leader in misguidance to the extent that he is one who commands indecency and wrongdoing. This is based on the requirement that a nominal answer to a conditional contain a pronoun referring back to the condition, and what is to be said about that will come, God willing.

﴿And were it not for the grace of God upon you and His mercy﴾: by what is among them, namely the sending down of these clear verses and the granting of success in repentance that purifies from sins. Likewise the legislation of the prescribed punishments (*ḥudūd*), which expiate what is other than apostasy, according to the view of a group of scholars. They answered the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned just above by saying that it was before he (ﷺ) was revealed this. ﴿Would not have purified﴾: that is, would not have cleansed from the defilement of sins.

[Page 125]

Rawh and al-A'mash read *mā zakkā* with tashdid and imalah. The word *zakiya* with a lightened form was written with a ya', although it is from the roots with waw, and its proper spelling would be with an alif. Abu Hayyan said: this is because it may be pronounced with imalah, or because it was analogized to the doubled form. The *min* in His saying ﴿from you﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah). In His saying ﴿anyone﴾ *min* is a sword of the preacher (an emphatic addition). *Aḥad* is in the position of the nominative as subject according to the first reading, and in the position of the accusative as object according to the second reading, and the subject in it is His pronoun, the Exalted, meaning: God, exalted is He, has never purified any one of you ﴿ever﴾, without limit of time. ﴿But God purifies﴾, that is, cleanses ﴿whom He wills﴾ of His servants, by bestowing upon him the effects of His grace and mercy, guiding him to repentance and accepting it from him, as He, glory be to Him, did with those who were spared the disease of hypocrisy from among those of you who fell into the snare of the slander.

﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾: intensive in His hearing of the sayings, among which is what they expressed of repentance. ﴿All-Knowing﴾: of all the things known, among which are their intentions. In this there is an exhortation for them to be sincere in repentance. The mention of the noble Name (Allah) is to indicate that divinity calls for hearing and knowledge, together with what it contains of the emphasis of independence in a concluding (tadhyil) manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 22:

﴿And let not those endowed with virtue and abundance among you swear﴾ — that is, let them not swear, from the form ifti'al of al-alyah (oath). Abu 'Ubayda said, and Abu Muslim preferred it: that is, let them not fall short, from al-alw (falling short), on the pattern of al-dalw (bucket), and al-alw on the pattern of al-utuw (transgression). It has been said: the first (meaning, oath) is more fitting given the occasion of revelation, for it is authentically related from 'A'isha and others that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, swore, when he saw the innocence of his daughter, that he would never spend anything on Mistah ever. Mistah was among the poor Muhajirun of the first generation who witnessed Badr, and he was the son of his maternal aunt; it is also said he was the son of his sister, may Allah be pleased with him. Then the verse "And let not those endowed with virtue..." was revealed, etc., and this is the well-known view.

It is related from Muhammad ibn Sirin that Abu Bakr swore not to spend on two men who were orphans in his care, since they had joined in the matter of 'A'isha, one of them being Mistah, and then the verse was revealed. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that a group of believers, among them Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, cut off their benefits from those who spoke concerning the slander, and they said: "By Allah, we will not maintain whoever spoke about her," and then the verse was revealed. 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas ibn Rabi'a, Abu Ja'far his freedman, and Zayd ibn Aslam read "yatal" (yatāl), the present tense of tala, meaning "swore," as the poet said:

"Ibn Aws swore an oath that he would return me to women of mine who look like camel-drivers' mounts."

This reading supports the first meaning of la yata'l. "Those endowed with virtue among you" — that is, increase in religion — "and abundance" — that is, in wealth — "that they give" — that is, not to give, or from aversion to giving, or not to fall short in giving.

Abu Haywa, Ibn Qatib and Abu al-Barhasim read "tu'tu" with the second-person address, by way of iltifat (shift of person).

"The needy and the emigrants in the way of Allah" are attributes of one referent, on the basis of what you have learned, that the verse was revealed, according to the sound view, on account of Abu Bakr's oath not to spend on Mistah, who has these attributes as you have heard. The conjunction serves to treat the difference of attributes as the difference of referents. The plural, although the occasion was specific, is for the sake of generality and of not confining the matter to one attribute, to emphasize the entitlement of Mistah and the like to the giving, for whoever is characterized by one of these attributes, if he deserves it, then whoever combines them all does so by the better way. It has also been said that these are for referents which were put in their place, and the second object is omitted for its clear evidence, i.e., that they give them something. "Let them pardon" what was neglected by them, "and let them overlook" it by turning away from it. 'Abdullah, al-Hasan, Sufyan ibn al-Husayn and Asma' bint Yazid read "wa-lta'fu wa-ltasfahu" with the second-person address, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: "Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?" — that is, in return for your pardon, your overlooking and your kindness to one who has wronged you. "And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful" — intensive in forgiveness and mercy, together with His perfect power, exalted is He, to take to account and the multitude of the sins of servants which call for it. In this is a great exhortation to pardon and a generous promise of its recompense, as if it were said: "Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?" — so this is one of its requirements.

It is sound that when Abu Bakr heard the verse he said: "Yes, by Allah, O our Lord, we indeed love that You forgive us," and he restored his spending to him. In another report, he began giving him twice what he had been giving him at first. This verse was revealed, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil, after Mistah came to Abu Bakr apologizing, and he said: "May Allah make me your ransom! By Allah who sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ, I did not slander her, and I did not speak any of what was said about her," that is, "O uncle." Abu Bakr said: "But you did laugh and were pleased by what was said about her." Mistah said: "Perhaps he had some part of it."

In the verse is incitement to noble character, and what it contains. It has been used as evidence for the virtue of the Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, for he is definitely among "those endowed with virtue," either alone or together with a group, being the cause of revelation. The general application of the ruling to all believers does not harm this, as is apparent, and there is no need for the claim that it is specific to him, and the plural is for glorification. That it is specific by the first-person pronoun is rejected, since in it there is what there is of departing from the apparent meaning. The Rafidah answered that the intended meaning of "virtue" is increase in wealth, and this is refuted, since then it would repeat with His saying, exalted is He, "and abundance." The Imam claimed that it indicates that the Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is the most excellent of all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and he established this by what is far from his virtue. He also mentioned its indication of aspects of praise of him, may Allah be pleased with him, most of which are open to discussion.

It was also used as evidence that what is not apostasy among sins does not nullify the deed, for otherwise Allah would not have named Mistah a Muhajir, although what proceeded from him proceeded. And that swearing to abandon an act of obedience is impermissible, for He forbade it by His saying, exalted is He, "let not...swear," and its meaning, according to what the occasion of revelation requires, is "let them not swear." The apparent sense of this is to take the prohibition as prohibition of unlawfulness. It has been said it is for disapproval. It has been said: the truth is that swearing to abandon obedience may be unlawful, and may be disapproved, so the prohibition here is for seeking abandonment absolutely, and in this there is discussion.

The majority of jurists mentioned that: "If one swears an oath and sees something other than it as better, let him do what is better and expiate his oath," as has come in the hadith. Some of them said: "If he swears, let him do what is better, and that is its expiation," as has come in another hadith.

It was objected that the expiation in that hadith means expiation of the sin, not the legal expiation which is by one of the modes of atonement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste women﴾ — their explanation has already passed. ﴿Heedless﴾ of what they are accused of, meaning that it never even occurred to them, because they are disposed to goodness and created from the substance of purity. So in this description there is an indication of perfect innocence that is not present in "chaste women" ﴿believing﴾, that is, those characterised by faith in everything that must be believed, of obligations and prohibitions and other matters, with true and detailed faith, as the delaying of "believing" after what precedes it indicates, although the attribute of faith is primary. This is because it signals that what is meant is the descriptive sense expressed by what was mentioned, not the nominal sense that validates the application of the name in general, as is the obvious reading on the assumption of the anteriority (of the attributes). So reported in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (of Abu al-Sa'ud).

And as a consequence of this, the meaning is that it refers to ʿAʾisha al-Siddiqa, may Allah be pleased with her. And there has been reported something whose apparent meaning is this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr. The plural in this case is by way of considering that her accusation is an accusation against all the Mothers of the Believers, because all of them share in purity and in being connected to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. A parallel to this is the plural "the messengers" in the words of the Exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. It has also been said that what is meant is the Mothers of the Believers, so ʿAʾisha enters among them by primary inclusion. There has been reported something supporting this from Abu al-Jawza' and al-Dahhak, and there has also come from Ibn ʿAbbas something that implies it. For Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh recorded that he, may Allah be pleased with him, recited Surat al-Nur and explained it, and when he reached this verse, ﴿Indeed, those who﴾ and so on, he said: "This is about ʿAʾisha and the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. He did not make repentance available for the one who does this, and he made repentance available for one who accuses a woman of the believing women other than the wives of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he recited ﴿And those who accuse chaste women, then do not produce four witnesses﴾ up to the words of the Exalted: ﴿except those who repent﴾ [al-Nur: 4-5]. The report ends. Its apparent meaning is that the repentance of one who slanders any of the pure wives, may Allah be pleased with them, is not accepted.

It has also come from him in some reports an explicit statement that the repentance of one who engaged in the matter of ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, is not accepted. Perhaps this came from him as an exaggeration in magnifying the matter of the slander, as we mentioned earlier. Otherwise the apparent meaning of the verses is that his repentance is accepted, and those among the slanderers who repented did so, such as Mistah, Hassan and Hamna. Had they known that their repentance would not be accepted, they would not have repented. Yes, the apparent meaning of this verse, according to what you have heard of its intended referents from those described by these attributes, is that it declares as disbelievers those who slander the Mothers of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with them, because the Mighty and Majestic God has attached to their accusation punishments specific to the disbelievers and hypocrites. So the Glorified said: ﴿They are cursed﴾, that is, because of their accusing them, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, where cursers and the angels curse them in both abodes. ﴿And for them﴾, in addition to the curse mentioned, ﴿is a great punishment﴾, terrible, whose extent cannot be measured, due to the extreme enormity of the crime they committed.

Likewise the Glorified mentioned conditions specific to those people, so the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿يَوْمَ تَشْهَدُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ etc. The evidence for the restriction is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered together﴾ [Fussilat: 19], up to the end of the three verses. From here it has been said that it is not permissible to mean by "the chaste women" (al-muhsanat), etc., those characterized by the described qualities, the Mothers of the Believers and other women of the Community, because there is no doubt that slandering women other than the Mothers of the Believers is not disbelief. What should be relied upon for the ruling is that whoever slanders one of the Mothers of the Believers after the revelation of these verses, and it becomes clear that they are pure, is a disbeliever, whether he considers the slander permissible, intends to disparage the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or neither considers it permissible nor intends it. As for whoever slandered before (the revelation), the ruling that he is a disbeliever without qualification is not evident.

It is apparent that he is ruled a disbeliever if he considers it permissible or intends to disparage the Messenger (ﷺ) through it, like Ibn Ubayy, may Allah curse him, for this is what his persistence in enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) requires. He is not ruled a disbeliever if he is not like that, such as Hassan, Mistah and Hamnah, for it is apparent that they did not consider it permissible, nor did they intend to disparage the master of the Messengers, may Allah the Exalted bless him and his family, all together. They only said what they said by imitation, and so they were severely rebuked for it. Among what clearly indicates that those who slandered before were not disbelievers is that the Messenger (ﷺ) did not treat them as apostates, by ijma' (scholarly consensus). Rather, he enforced upon them the prescribed punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf), as is reported in some narrations. So the verse, on the view of the restriction to the chaste women, which most narrations support, if it was to explain the ruling on whoever slanders ʿĀʾishah or one of the Mothers of the Believers in general after that incident, as is apparent from the present-tense verb in the relative clause, then the threat mentioned in it, on the view that it is specific to the disbelievers and hypocrites, is evident, because of what you have heard of the view that the one who slanders one of the Mothers of the Believers afterwards is a disbeliever without qualification. If, however, it was to explain the ruling on whoever slandered before, the threat requires the view that the relative pronoun refers to specific people who slandered ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, considering her honor permissible and intending to disparage the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), like Ibn Ubayy and his hypocrite brethren, upon whom be the curse. On this view, the use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind, as it is one of the strangest of strange things, or, as has been said, to indicate that their habit is slander and that it is renewed from them moment by moment. On this basis, it can be said that the purpose is to explain the ruling on whoever does not repent of slander, for one who repents of an action is rarely described as having that action as his habit. Thus the threat is specific to those who do not repent.

What the reports indicate is that all who fell into that sin repented, except the accursed Ibn Ubayy and his followers among the hypocrites. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed specifically concerning him, and the way of reconciling this with it is not hidden. It has also been said that the purpose is to explain the ruling on whoever slandered, and the threat is conditional upon not repenting, but this was not mentioned because it is known from the established principles, since sin, however it occurs, is forgiven by repentance. So there is no need to say: the meaning is that those whose habit is slander (are threatened), so as to imply non-repentance. The apparent meaning is that whoever does not repent after the revelation of these verses is a disbeliever, and that is none other than the accursed one and his hypocrite followers.

A group chose this view, and al-Nahhas said: "It is the best of what has been said, that the ruling is general concerning whoever slanders the women described by the mentioned qualities from among the women of the Community. If the slander is accompanied by considering it permissible, then it is disbelief, and its doer deserves the threat mentioned, even if he does not repent, according to what is known from the principles. If it is without considering it permissible, then it is a major sin and not disbelief." It requires either preventing the restriction of those punishments and states to the disbelievers and hypocrites, or committing to the view that this applies to the category (genus), and it suffices for its establishment that it applies to some of its members. There is no doubt that among them are those who die as disbelievers.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), it fits that this verse, as has been said, was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca: when a woman went out to Medina as an emigrant, they would slander her and say, "She went out to commit fornication." This was said by Abu Hamzah al-Yamani, and the words of the Exalted, ﴿on the Day when﴾ etc., support it. End of quotation.

You know that what is more in accord with the context and the immediately preceding verses is what most scholars hold: that it was revealed concerning the Mother of the Believers ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and that the ruling on slandering the rest of their mothers is the ruling on slandering her. Likewise, the ruling on slandering the wives of the other Prophets, peace be upon them, and likewise their mothers. In my view, the ruling on slandering the daughters of the Prophet (ﷺ) is also the same, especially his pure and noble branch, Fatimah al-Zahra, may Allah the Exalted bless her, her father and her. I have not seen anyone address this, so reflect upon it.

Know that there is no disagreement about the permissibility of cursing a specific disbeliever whose death in disbelief has been confirmed, provided that it does not involve harming a Muslim or a dhimmi, if we hold that the dhimmi is equal to the Muslim in the sanctity of not being harmed. If it involves that, it is prohibited.

Among what is forbidden is cursing Abu Talib, on the view that he died a disbeliever. Indeed, this is among the greatest of things that involve harming one whose harming is prohibited. Furthermore, I do not consider cursing one who may be cursed to be an act of worship unless it involves a legitimate religious benefit. As for cursing a specific living disbeliever, the well-known view is that it is prohibited. The implication of the words of Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali is that such a person becomes a disbeliever, because it involves asking that he be kept firm in the disbelief which is the cause of the curse, and asking for that is disbelief. Al-Zarkashi explicitly endorsed this, saying: "Aqabah said: So be mindful of this issue, for it is unusual, its ruling is clear, and a group has erred regarding it." Al-ʿAllamah Ibn Hajar said regarding this: "It should be said: if by cursing him he intends invoking a hardening of the matter against him, or he says it without qualification, he does not become a disbeliever. If he intends asking that he remain in disbelief, or is content with his remaining in it, then it is disbelief." Then he said: "So reflect upon this with the utmost reflection, for it is a clear and correct distinction, which their statements support." End of quotation.

Just as cursing a living specific disbeliever is prohibited, so too is cursing a specific sinner. Al-Siraj al-Balqini said: it is permissible to curse a specific disobedient person, and he argued for this with the hadith in the two Sahihs: "When a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses to come, and he spends the night angry with her, the angels curse her until morning." It is clearly evident for what he claims. But the statement of his son, Jalal al-Balqini, in his discussion with him, that it is possible that the angels' cursing of her is not specific but general, namely that they say: "May Allah curse whoever his wife calls to her bed and she refuses, so that he spends the night angry," is very far-fetched. What supports al-Siraj's view is the report of Muslim that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a donkey with a brand on its face, and he said: "May Allah curse whoever did this." This is further from the possibility mentioned by his son.

It is also authentically established that the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed specific tribes of the Arabs by name, saying: "O Allah, curse Ra'l, Dhakwan and ʿUsayyah, who disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." This also provides some support for that. Yet it has been said that it is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that they, or most of them, died in disbelief, and so he cursed only those whom he knew had died in it. The safer course in this matter is not hidden from you.

For it is authentically established: "Whoever curses something that is not worthy of it, the curse returns upon him."

I consider invoking blessing and righteousness upon a specific sinner to be more beloved than cursing him, on the view that cursing is permissible. I consider cursing those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, by description or by name, to be an act of worship, insofar as it involves following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Likewise, cursing whom Allah the Exalted has cursed, in the manner in which He cursed him.

This is what I say. As for His, Glorified and Exalted, saying: ﴿on the Day when﴾ etc., it is either connected to what precedes it, serving to establish the great punishment by specifying the time of its arrival and magnifying it by showing the manifestation of the crime of the slanderers, which entails their punishments in a terrifying manner and an appearance that breaks customary norms. Thus "the Day" (yawm) is an adverbial complement for what is implied in "for them" (lahum) of the sense of settledness, not for "punishment," as al-Hawfi held, because of the disagreement over the operation of a described verbal noun. It has been said that this would disrupt the eloquence of the meaning, but there is room for discussion on this. Or it is disconnected from what precedes it, with it being an adverbial complement that is either omitted from mention, or governed by the later "will pay them in full" (yuwaffihim), as has been said in both ways. It has been chosen that it is an adverbial complement of a verb that is postponed, and the mention of that verb has been deliberately omitted, to signal that expression can hardly encompass the details of the great matters that will occur on it. The discourse is directed toward magnifying the Day by magnifying what it contains, as if it were said: ﴿on the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾, there will become apparent of states and terrors what the scope of speech cannot encompass. Furthermore, the relative pronoun mentioned refers to the collection of their evil deeds and abominable crimes, not only to their specific known crimes.

The meaning of the testimony of the mentioned limbs is that He, Glorified and Exalted, will make them speak by His power, so that each limb informs about what proceeded from it of its owner's deeds, not that each of them informs only about their known crime. The omitted relative pronoun refers to these and to all the varieties of punishments that result from them, not to any one of them in particular. Thus it contains every kind of magnification, in general and in detail, beyond which there is nothing more. This was stated by Shaykh al-Islam. Then he said: "Making the mentioned relative pronoun refer to their habitual crimes and restricting the testimony of the limbs to their merely informing about them is a restriction of what is broad and a diminishing of the deterrent matter." The combination of the two forms, past and future, indicates their persistence in those deeds in this world and their renewal from them moment by moment. Placing "against them" (ʿalayhim) before the subject is for the haste toward the testimony being harmful to them, along with the anticipation for what is delayed. End of quotation, and it is not without beauty.

It is also permitted that the testimony with what has been mentioned be a metaphor for the manifestation of its traces upon those limbs, such that whoever sees them knows what they did, in a manner known to Allah the Exalted. It was objected that this conflicts with His saying: ﴿Allah, who made everything speak, has made us speak﴾ [Fussilat: 21].

It is answered that the one who permits what was mentioned makes speech a metaphor for clear indication, as has been said in the expression "the situation spoke," or he says: this is in one state and that in another state, or each of them is for a different people.

It is not hidden that the apparent meaning is that the testimony remains upon its literal reality. However, this has raised a difficulty, that it would then entail a contradiction between what is here and His saying in Surat Ya Sin: ﴿Today We shall seal upon their mouths﴾ [Ya Sin: 65], because sealing upon the mouths contradicts the testimony of the tongues.

It is answered that what is meant by sealing upon the mouths is preventing them from speaking with the tongues within them, and that does not contradict the tongues themselves, which is what is meant by testimony, as we indicated. For the tongues in the first are instruments of action, and in the second are agents of it. Thus sealing upon the mouths and the testimony of the tongues can be combined, by preventing them from speaking with the tongues while making the tongues themselves speak and talk, just as the Exalted made the poisoned foreleg speak and talk, until it informed the Prophet (ﷺ) that it was poisoned. The Mu'tazilah have a discourse about this. It has also been said in reconciliation that each of the sealing and the testimony may occur in a different place and state, and that the testimony applies to the slanderers and the sealing applies to the disbelievers. It seems that since this verse concerned the one who slanders with his tongue, and he is required to produce four witnesses, it mentions five here, and explicitly names the tongue with which his act was done, in order to disgrace him, as a recompense of the same kind as his action. This was said by al-Khafaji, who said: "It is a secret subtlety, and Allah the Exalted knows best the secrets of His Book, so reflect upon it."

Al-Akhawan, al-Zaʿfaranī, Ibn Muqsim and Ibn Saʿdan read "yashhadu" with the yāʾ at the beginning of the verb, and its basis is evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 25:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On that day﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) of His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Allah will pay them in full their due recompense (dinahum al-haqq)﴾. The tanwin (nunation) in "yawma'idhin" is a substitute (iwad) for the sentence to which it is added. Tawfiyah (paying in full) means giving a thing in complete measure. Here al-din (the recompense) means the requital, as in the saying "as you do, so shall it be done to you" (kama tadin tudan). Al-haqq means the one who brings things into being in accordance with what wisdom requires. Close to this is its interpretation as "the established one, whose establishment for them is necessarily due," meaning: on that day their limbs, mentioned above, will bear witness against them for their evil deeds, and Allah Exalted will give them their requital, which corresponds to what wisdom requires, in full and complete measure. The statement is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that serves to explain the order of the ruling on the testimony, and it includes an explanation of that vague, elided element mentioned earlier in summary form. It is also permitted that ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿yawma tashhadu﴾, according to those who permit that the former be linked to yuwafihim.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "yuwfihim" with a lightened form. Abdullah, Mujahid, Abu Rawq and Abu Haywah read "al-haqqu" in the nominative, making it an attribute of the Majestic Name. It is permissible to separate the attribute from the qualified noun by the object (al-maf'ul). According to al-Raghib, the meaning of al-haqq in this reading is the one who brings a thing into being in accordance with what wisdom requires. Some interpreted it as "the just one," but most explained it as "the one who is necessary in Himself" (al-wajib li-dhatih). The same applies to His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And they will know that Allah is the manifest truth (al-haqq al-mubin)﴾. Al-mubin is either from abana (intransitive), meaning the manifest one in His truthfulness, if it is taken as an attribute of al-haqq; or the manifest one in His divinity, Mighty and Majestic, if it is taken as a second predicate; or from abana (transitive), meaning the one who makes things clear as they are in themselves.

The clause ﴿yaʿlamuna﴾ (they will know) is conjoined to the clause ﴿Allah will pay them﴾. If it is restricted by what the first was restricted by, the meaning is: on the day when their limbs, mentioned above, will bear witness against them for their evil deeds, they will know that Allah is... etc. If it is not restricted by that, it is permissible that the meaning be: and they will know, upon witnessing the terrors and calamities, that Allah is... etc. The apparent view is that the testimony in the first case, and the witnessing in the second, both enter into the attainment of knowledge of the content of what falls within the scope of "they will know." So reflect, so that you may understand how the inference for this is made, for there is obscurity in it, especially when the restriction derived from the definition of the two terms and the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) are taken into account.

It has been said that the knowledge of creation of His attributes, Exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection is necessary (daruri), and although they differ in this in some respects, they will know what was mentioned without either of the two matters having a bearing. Perhaps the benefit of this knowledge is their despair of anyone rescuing them from what they are in, or the closing of the door of objection, which would otherwise ease the heart to some extent, against them, or the clarification of their error in their slander of the sanctity (haram) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with falsehood. For His truthfulness precludes His being, Mighty and Majestic, al-haqq, that is, one who brings things into being in accordance with what wisdom requires, because of what we have previously set forth: that the immorality of the wives of the prophets, peace be upon them, undermines the wisdom of the mission. Likewise, it precludes His being, Mighty and Majestic, al-haqq, that is, necessary in Himself, on the basis that necessity in Himself entails being characterized by wisdom, indeed by all perfect attributes. This sentence is very clear that the verse concerns Ibn Ubayy and his like among the hypocrites who slandered the sanctity of the Messenger ﷺ, because the believer knows that Allah Exalted is the manifest truth from the time he is in this world, not that this knowledge comes to him on the Day of Resurrection. As for those who held that it concerns the believers who slandered, or both them and others among the hypocrites, he said: It is possible that the intended meaning of knowledge of this is the mind's turning its attention toward it, and that this does not preclude its having been attained before. Sayyid al-Sanad, may Allah sanctify his secret, in the margins of al-Matali', took "knowledge" in their definition of indication (dalalah) as the state of a thing whereby knowledge of it necessitates knowledge of something else, lest it be objected that on the apparent reading there would be no indication for a word upon repetition, since knowing what is already known is impossible. It is also possible that their knowledge that had already been attained is treated as if it were unattained, since what it requires of ceasing from slander does not follow from it. Such a treatment is common in the Mighty Book. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: they will know by direct witnessing the requirement that Allah is the manifest truth, namely, the retribution against the wrongdoer on behalf of the wronged. Other meanings are also possible.

And you know that all of this is contrary to the apparent sense, so reflect.

The Almighty's words, ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and the wicked men are for wicked women; the good women are for good men, and the good men are for good women﴾, and so on, form a resumptive sentence (istinaf) founded on the custom prevailing among people, in keeping with the principle that God, exalted is He, has an angel who drives families to families. And the saying of the one who said, "Birds of a feather flock together," means: wicked women are for wicked men, that is, they are specific to them and do not go beyond them to others, on the reading that the lam denotes exclusivity (ikhtisas). ﴿And wicked men are likewise for wicked women﴾, because similarity of kind is a cause of union. ﴿And good women are for good men﴾, ﴿and good men are likewise for good women﴾, such that they do not pass beyond them to anyone else. Since the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the best of the good and the choicest of the first and the last, it becomes clear that the Truthful One (al-Siddiqah), may God be pleased with her, is necessarily among the best of the good women, and the falsehood of the fabrications that were said about her becomes evident, as expressed in His, glorified is He, words: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾. This is on the basis that the reference is to the People of the Prophet's House, men and women, and the Truthful One, may God be pleased with her, enters into this primarily. It was also said that the reference is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the Truthful One, and Safwan. Al-Farra' said: it is a reference to the Truthful One and Safwan, and the plural is applied to what exceeds one.

In the verse, on all the opinions, there is taghlib (the predominance of one gender term over the other), meaning: those are exalted above what the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk) say about them of baseless lies.

The subject of the mentioned attributes was made to be women and men, as you have heard, related by al-Tabarani from Ibn 'Abbas within a lengthy report, and the Imamiyyah (Imami Shi'a) related it from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with them both. Abu Muslim, al-Jubba'i, and a group chose it, and it is the more apparent view in my opinion. A different report from Ibn 'Abbas, which al-Tabarani also transmitted, as did Ibn Mardawayh and others, states that ( the wicked and the good ) are attributes of the words (al-kalim), and ( the wicked men and the good men ) are attributes of the two wicked groups among the people. This was also related from al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. According to this, ( the wicked men ) includes men and women by way of taghlib, and likewise ( the good men ). ﴿Those﴾ refers to the good ones, and the pronoun in ﴿they say﴾ refers to the two wicked groups. It was also said that it refers to the slanderers (al-afikin), meaning: the wicked words are for the wicked men and women, that is, specific to them and attached to them, and they should not be said about anyone else. Likewise, the wicked of both groups deserve to have wicked words said about them, and the good words are specific to and truly belong to the good of both groups, and they deserve to have good words said about them. ﴿Those, the good ones, are cleared of being characterized by what the wicked say﴾. It was also said that the slanderers say it about them, and so its outcome is the exoneration of the Truthful One, may God be pleased with her, as well.

It was also said: the meaning is that the wicked words are specific to the wicked of the two groups of men and women, and do not proceed from anyone else. The wicked of both groups are specific to the wicked words and exposed to them. The good words are for the good of both groups, that is, specific to them, and do not proceed from anyone else. The good of both groups are specific to the good words, and nothing else proceeds from them. ﴿Those, the good ones, are cleared of what the wicked say﴾, meaning: something like that does not proceed from them. This was related from Mujahid. The expression on this view involves the omission of a genitive attached to "ma" (what), and its outcome is the disparagement of the slanderers and the exoneration of those who said, ﴿Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, great forgiveness, for what humans cannot avoid of sin, and the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of the near ones (muqarrabun). ﴿And a noble provision﴾, which is Paradise, as most of the commentators said.

[Page 132]

This is supported by His words in Surat al-Ahzab concerning the Mothers of the Believers: ﴿And We have prepared for her a noble provision﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31]. For the meaning there is Paradise, by the context of "We have prepared", and the Qur'an explains part of itself by part. In these verses there is what there is of indication of the virtue of the Truthful One. And if you were to turn over the entire Qur'an and search for what the disobedient are threatened with, you would not find that God, mighty and majestic is He, has been severe in anything as severe as in the slander, and this also indicates her virtue. She, may God be pleased with her, used to speak of God's blessing upon her by the revelation of that concerning her.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from her that she said: "There are qualities in me that were not in anyone among the people except what God gave Mary, daughter of 'Imran. By God, I do not say this boastfully over my co-wives." It was said: "And what are they?" She said: "The angel came down with my image, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married me when I was seven years old, I was brought to him when I was nine, I was married to him as a virgin, and no one among the people shared me with him. Revelation came to him while I was with him under one blanket, I was among the most beloved people to him, and verses of the Qur'an were revealed concerning me that nearly destroyed the community because of them. I saw Gabriel, peace be upon him, and no one of his wives saw him except me, and he died in my house, and no one attended him except the angel and I."

Ibn Mardawayh related from her that she said: "My exoneration came down from heaven, and I was created good, in the presence of one good, and I was promised forgiveness and a great reward." In His, glorified is He, words: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a noble provision﴾, on the basis that it includes 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, it refutes the Rafidah (the rejectors) who say that she disbelieved and died upon that, and God forbid, because of the incident of the Battle of the Camel, along with other things they fabricated and attributed to her. Among what also refutes that claim is the statement of 'Ammar ibn Yasir in his sermon when the Commander (the Amir), may God honor his face, sent him together with al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, to summon the people of Medina and Kufa to mobilize: "Indeed I know that she is the wife of your Prophet, peace be upon him, in this world and the Hereafter, but God has tested you to know whether you obey Him or obey her."

Among the things that are a source of wonder is what I saw in some books of the Shi'a, that she was removed from the Mothers of the Believers after that battle, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Commander, may God honor his face: "I have permitted you, after my death, to divorce from the marriage whomever of my wives you wish." So the Commander, may God honor his face, removed her from that because of what had proceeded from her with him, what proceeded. By my life, this is something that almost makes the bereaved laugh. And the Commander's good treatment of her, may God be pleased with her, after his taking control of the army that accompanied her, which is well-established with both parties, refutes that. We do not doubt her virtue, may God be pleased with her, because of these verses and because of what has come in praise of her from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And had there been nothing of that except what

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah related from Anas, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The virtue of 'A'ishah over the women is like the virtue of tharid over food.'"

Yet, despite this, I do not say that she is more excellent than his noble daughter (ﷺ), Fatimah al-Zahra', may God be pleased with her, and the point is not hidden. On this matter there are discussions that should be sought in their proper place. Then, what I see is that the sending down of these verses concerning her was for greater attention to the status of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and to comfort the heart of his companion, the Truthful One, may God be pleased with him, and likewise the heart of his wife Umm Ruman, for that slander had afflicted both of them with what God alone knows. And also for the greater attachment of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, to Him, mighty and majestic is He, along with her virtue and purity in herself.

It has come in a strange report that Ibn al-Najjar mentioned in Tarikh Baghdad with its chain of narration from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was sitting with the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, to gladden her eye with the declaration of her innocence, and she was weeping. She said: 'The near and the far have abandoned me, until even the cat has abandoned me, and no food or drink was offered to me, so I would sleep while hungry and thirsty. Then I saw in my dream a youth who said to me: "What is the matter with you?" I said: "I am grieved by what the people have mentioned." He said: "Call upon these supplications, and God will relieve you of it." I said: "And what are they?" He said: "Say: O Bestower of blessings, O Repeller of calamities, O Reliever of distresses, O Dispeller of darkness, O Most Just of those who judge, O Sufficient against the wrongdoer, O Protector of the wronged, O First without a beginning, O Last without an end, O One who has a name without a kunya. O God, make for me a relief and a way out from my affair."' She said: 'I awoke, and I was sated and refreshed, and God had sent down my relief.'" This supplication is called the supplication of relief (du'a' al-faraj), so let it be memorized and put into practice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 1 of 2):

Then, after He (Mighty and Majestic) had detailed the deterrents against fornication and against accusing chaste women of it, He began to detail the deterrents against what might lead to one of those two, namely the mixing of men with women, and men entering upon them during times of seclusion, and the teaching of beautiful manners and pleasing conduct that brings about happiness in both abodes. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾, etc. The occasion of revelation, according to what al-Firyabi and others narrated through the chain of 'Udayy ibn Thabit, from a man of the Ansar: "A woman said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither a child nor a parent. Then someone comes and enters upon me. So how should I act?' Then there was revealed ﴿O you who have believed﴾, etc."

The attribution of "houses" to the pronoun of the addressees is a lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas, the lam indicating exclusive association). Some say that what is meant is the specification of ownership (al-ikhtisas al-malaki), and describing the houses as "other than your houses" in this sense is a departure from the customary situation, in which each person dwells in what he owns. Otherwise, the hirer and the lender are also prohibited from entering without permission.

Some of them said: What is meant is the specification of dwelling, i.e., "other than your houses in which you dwell." Because the hirer and the lender being prohibited, like others, from entering without permission is evidence that the specification of ownership is not intended. So that is to be understood as the aforementioned specification, and there is no need to say that this is a departure from custom.

It was read ﴿houses other than your houses﴾ with a kasra on the ba' (bayt, "houses" as "buyut") for the sake of the following ya' (i.e., "bi-yuti" rather than "buyuti" in that reading). ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾, i.e., you seek permission from whoever holds the authority to grant permission from their owners. This interpretation was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It contradicts what al-Hakim narrated and declared authentic, as did al-Diya in al-Mukhtara, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and other people, from him: that he said regarding ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾: "The scribe erred, and it is only ﴿until you seek permission﴾ (hatta tasta'dhinu)." But Abu Hayyan said: Whoever narrates from Ibn 'Abbas that he said this is one who discredits Islam and is a heretic in the religion, and Ibn 'Abbas is innocent of that statement. End of quote.

You know that al-Hakim's declaration of authenticity is not relied upon by the imams of hadith. However, this report has many chains, and the book al-Ahadith al-Mukhtara of al-Diya is a reliable book. Al-Sakhawi said in Fath al-Mughith, in classifying the people of the musnad collections: "Among them are those who limit themselves to what is fit for proof, like al-Diya in his al-Mukhtara." And al-Suyuti, after enumerating in the preface to Jam' al-Jawami' the five books: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sahih Ibn Hibban, al-Mustadrak, and al-Mukhtara of al-Diya, said: "All that is in these five books is authentic."

The hafiz Ibn Rajab narrated in Tabaqat al-Hanabila from some of the imams that he said: "The book al-Mukhtara is better than the Sahih of al-Hakim." So the presence of this report there, along with its multiple chains as mentioned, makes what Abu Hayyan said unlikely. Ibn al-Anbari answered this report and similar discrediting reports, on the apparent level, by the (mutawatir) transmission of the Qur'an narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). And some of them will come later in the tafsir of this surah, God willing, with the answer that the narrations are weak and are contradicted by other narrations from Ibn 'Abbas as well as from others, and this is apart from Abu Hayyan's criticism. Ibn Ashtah answered all of that by saying that what is meant is an error in choice, and leaving what is preferable according to his opinion (may Allah be pleased with him), in order to gather the people upon it from among the seven ahruf (modes of recitation), and not that the one who wrote the error was outside the Qur'an.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti chose this answer and said: "It is more preferable and more firmly grounded than the answer of Ibn al-Anbari." It is not hidden from you that interpreting Ibn 'Abbas's words in this way is not free from remoteness, because what was mentioned is contrary to the apparent meaning of his words. Also, Ibn 'Abbas supposed the preferability of what all the companions (may Allah be pleased with them) agreed upon in contrast to it, from what he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the final recitation (al-'ardah al-akhirah), by his own judgment. It seems they regarded adhering to that as easier than denying the report's transmission from Ibn 'Abbas despite its multiple chains and al-Diya's inclusion of it in his al-Mukhtara. What encourages this denial is the belief in the greatness of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), and the established consensus on the mutawatir transmission contrary to what the apparent meaning of his words requires. So reflect.

The use of "isti'nas" (seeking familiarity) in the sense of "isti'dhan" (seeking permission) is based on the view that it is an form of "istif'al" from "anasa al-shay'" with the long vowel, meaning he knew it or saw it; and seeing it is a path to knowledge. So "isti'nas" is seeking to know, and the one who seeks permission is one who seeks knowledge of the situation, seeking to uncover whether his entry is desired or not.

It was also said that "isti'nas" is the opposite of "isti'hash" (feeling estrangement), so it derives from "uns" (intimacy) with a damma, the opposite of wahshah (loneliness). What is meant by it is being given permission. So it is as if it were said: "until permission is granted to you," for whoever knocks on the house of another does not know whether he will be permitted or not. So he is like one who feels estranged because the situation is hidden from him, and when he is given permission he feels at ease. In this he is using a kinayah or majaz. It was also said: "isti'nas" derives from "insi" (people, humankind) with a kasra, meaning "the people," i.e., "until you seek knowledge of who is in the houses of the people." This was judged weak, because it involves deriving a verb from a non-derivative noun, as in al-musrij (the one who lights a lamp), which is said to be derived from al-siraj (the lamp); and because knowing who is in the house is not sufficient without permission, so it gives the false impression that entry without permission is allowed. Some people preferred it for its suitability to His saying: ﴿But if you do not find anyone in them﴾. But this weakness is not countered by what you have heard.

Al-Tabari held that the meaning is: "until you make the people of the house feel at ease about you, by seeking permission and the like, and make yourselves feel at ease by knowing that they have become aware of you." And what is in this is not hidden. It was also said: the meaning is "until you seek knowledge of the people of the house," and what is meant is: "until you teach them in the most complete manner." What guides to this is what was narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: "We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is isti'nas?' He said: 'A man speaks with tasbih, takbir and tahmid, clears his throat, and the people of the house are notified.'"

And what Ibn al-Mundhir and a group narrated from Mujahid, that he said: "tasta'nisu" means "they clear their throats and cough."

It was also said that what is meant is "until you make the people of the house feel at ease by informing them with tasbih or the like." The two reports mentioned do not reject this, and both opinions, as you see, [are weak]. Regarding the implication of what was mentioned of the interpretation of isti'nas in the report, according to what was previously said, there is a discussion which we will point to, God willing. ﴿And greet its people﴾, i.e., those who dwell in them. The apparent meaning of the verse is that seeking permission comes before greeting, and some have said so.

Al-Nawawi said: The correct and preferred view is to give precedence to the greeting over seeking permission. For al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The greeting before speech.'" And Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad narrated from Abu Hurayrah regarding one who seeks permission before greeting: "He is not granted permission until he greets." Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Wahb in Kitab al-Majalis narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "My father sent me to Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), so I came to him and said: 'Shall I come in?' He said: 'Enter.' When I entered he said: 'Welcome, nephew. Do not say "Shall I come in?" but say "Peace be upon you." If it is said "And upon you," then say "Shall I enter?" If they say "Enter," then enter.'"

Qasim ibn Asbagh and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) sought permission to enter upon the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon you. May 'Umar enter?'" Al-Mawardi chose a distinction, which is that if the eye of the one seeking permission falls upon the people in the house before he enters, he gives precedence to the greeting; otherwise he gives precedence to seeking permission. The apparent meaning is that seeking permission is by what clearly indicates a request for permission, and the well-known established wording in this is "May I enter?" as you have heard. It is also permissible that it be by what is understood from it generally, and they counted tasbih, takbir and the like among it, by which the people of the house are notified of the one who has come, for their notification indicates that they have granted what he requested. They applied to this the aforementioned hadith of Abu Ayyub and the statement of Mujahid. According to what is narrated from 'Ata', it is obligatory upon every adult male, and one time suffices for it, as the apparent meaning of the verse requires.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It used to be said: seeking permission is three times. Whoever is not granted permission in these three should return. The first time, the household hears. The second time, they prepare their caution. The third time, if they wish they grant permission and if they wish they refuse." Regarding the command to return after three, there is a raised hadith narrated by Malik, al-Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that one should not exceed three unless one is certain that those in the house did not hear. The apparent meaning of the verse is the legislation of seeking permission when one wishes to enter upon mahram relatives. Malik narrated in al-Muwatta' from 'Ata' ibn Yasar that "a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Should I seek permission to enter upon my mother?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'She has no servant other than me; should I seek permission to enter upon her every time I go in?' He said: 'Would you like to see her naked?' The man said: 'No.' He said: 'Then seek permission to enter upon her.'"

Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "It is obligatory upon you to seek permission to enter upon your mothers and your sisters." This also, according to what some reports indicate, is legislated for women when they wish to enter houses other than their own. For Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umm Iyas, who said: "I was with four women seeking permission to enter upon 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her). I said: 'Shall we enter?' She said: 'No.' One of them said: 'Peace be upon you. Shall we enter?' She said: 'Enter.' Then she said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾, etc." If this is authentic, then there is a kind of generalization (taghlib) in the verse. The reason for the legislation of seeking permission for them is similar to the reason for its legislation for men, for the people of the house may be in a state they do not like women to see, just as they do not like men to see it.

It is authentically established from a hadith narrated by the two Shaykhs and others: "Seeking permission was only instituted because of looking." For this reason, one should not look into the interior of the house before seeking permission. Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever believes that I am the Messenger of Allah, let him not enter upon the household until he seeks permission and greets. If he looks into the interior of the house, then he has entered."

And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as Abu Dawud and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr, when he came to the door of a people, did not stand directly facing the door, but from its right or left side, and he would say: "Peace be upon you." That is because the houses at that time had no curtains, so facing the door might lead to looking. The apparent meaning of the verse also indicates the legislation of seeking permission for the blind man, for he is included in the generality of the relative pronoun, and its wisdom is disliking that he become aware, through hearing, of what the people of the house do not want him to know, such as speech, for example.

In al-Kashshaf: "Seeking permission was legislated so that one does not come to know the states which people ordinarily conceal from others and guard against anyone knowing of. It was not legislated so that the blind man would not see someone's nakedness, nor so that his eye would not fall upon what is not lawful to look at, only." This is a fine reason, except that holding this view requires saying that the statement of the Prophet ﷺ, "Seeking permission was only instituted because of looking," is an example of the general case (kharaja makhraj al-ghalib, stated in the manner of the usual case).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 2 of 2):

It is introduced with innama (إنّما) for the sake of greater emphasis (li-mazid al-i'tina'), not for restriction (li-l-hasr). The scholars have indeed stated that innama comes for this purpose, so do not overlook this. Then know that istidhan (seeking permission) and taslim (greeting with peace) are distinct, but the apparent meaning of some reports suggests that istidhan is included within taslim, just as others suggest that it is distinct from it and not included in it. The reason for counting it as part of taslim is that without it, it is as if it did not exist, since the sunnah regarding it is that it be coupled with taslim.

Moreover, in the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i): "until you greet its people and seek permission" (حَتّى تُسَلِّمُوا عَلى أهْلِها وتَسْتَأْذِنُوا). ﴿That﴾ (ذَلِكُمْ) is a reference, according to what has been said, to entering by means of istidhan and taslim, which is understood from the speech. It has also been said that it refers to what is mentioned implicitly within the two verbs to which the limit is set, namely istidhan and taslim. ﴿is better for you﴾ (خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ) than entering suddenly and entering upon the greeting of the Jahiliyyah.
