For a man among them, when he wished to enter a house other than his own, would say: "Hayyitum sabahan, hayyitum masa'an (may you be greeted with good morning, may you be greeted with good evening)," and then enter, and perhaps he would find the man with his wife under a blanket. The superiority (khayriyyah) of the preferred over the other is said to be, according to their assumption, because of the humiliation in waiting, and because of the absence of the Jahiliyyah greeting, which is good, as is the custom of people today in their saying: "Sabah al-khayr, masa' al-khayr." But perhaps the better view is to say that this is of the kind of "the vinegar that is sweeter than honey" (al-khall ahla min al-'asal).

He also permitted that ﴿khayr﴾ (خَيْرٌ) be an adjective, in which case there is no need for an estimated element (taqdir). The saying of the Exalted, ﴿so that you may remember﴾ (لَعَلَّكم تَذَكَّرُونَ), is a causal clause (ta'lil) according to what a group has chosen, with an omitted element, meaning: "You were guided to that," or "It was said to you: this, so that you may remember, take heed, and act in accordance with its requirement."

﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَجِدُوا فِيها أحَدًا﴾ by which is meant that the houses are empty of their people, ﴿فَلا تَدْخُلُوها﴾ and wait, ﴿حَتّى يُؤْذَنَ لَكُمْ﴾ by permission from the one who has the authority to grant permission, when you find him. The reason for this is that entering empty houses without permission invites gossip and talk, and involves disposing of another's property without his consent, which resembles wrongful seizure. This verse explains the ruling concerning houses empty of their occupants, just as the first verse explains the ruling concerning houses in which their occupants are present.

It is also permitted that this be a confirmation of the command to seek permission (isti'nas), and that it is obligatory and that the matter depends upon it. The meaning would then be: "If you do not find in them anyone from among those who grant permission, that is, one who has the authority to grant it, then do not enter them," and so on. This implies the prohibition of entering a place containing someone who does not have the authority to grant permission, such as a slave or a child, without the permission of the one who has that authority. Whoever chose the first interpretation said: the prohibition of what was mentioned is established by the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass, implicit meaning of the text), so consider this carefully. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَجِدُوا﴾ up to its end, rather than "If there is no one in them," because what is taken into account is finding that they are empty of their people entirely, or empty of anyone who has that authority, whether or not anyone was actually in them. So it has been said. Accordingly, the meaning of their statement in explaining this, "that they are empty," is that they are empty according to belief, and the same applies to its counterpart, so do not be heedless. Furthermore, the ruling derived from the two verses has been specified by the Sharia, which permitted entering to remove a wrong that can only be removed by entering without the permission of the people of the house, and entering an empty house to extinguish a fire in it, or the like.

The jurists have mentioned the cases in which one enters without permission from the one who has the authority to grant it, so refer to them. It has also been said that what is meant by "permission" in His, glorified is He, saying ﴿حَتّى يُؤْذَنَ لَكُمْ﴾ is that which encompasses permission given explicitly (dalalatan) and permission given by the Sharia (shar'an), and for this reason it occurred in the passive form. In that case there is no need to resort to the view of specification, though this is obscure. ﴿وإنْ قِيلَ لَكُمُ ارْجِعُوا فارْجِعُوا﴾ that is, if you are told by the people of the house to return, whether the one who tells you has the authority to grant permission or not, then return and do not insist. ﴿هُوَ﴾ that is, returning, ﴿أزْكى لَكُمْ﴾ that is, purer for you than what is not free from obstinacy, contentiousness, and standing at the doors after the aforementioned statement, which is the filth of baseness and meanness; or more beneficial for your religion and your worldly life. Here ﴿أزْكى﴾ is from purification (zakah) in the sense of growth.

It is evident that the form af'al in both senses is for intensification. We have restricted standing at the doors to what you have heard, because in that case there is no baseness at all. It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he used to go to the houses of the Ansar to seek hadith; he would sit at the door and not ask permission until they came out to him. When they came out and saw him, they would say: "O cousin of the Messenger of Allah, if only you had informed me of your whereabouts!" He would reply: "Thus we have been commanded to seek knowledge." It seems that he, may Allah be pleased with him, regarded this as humility, and it is among the strongest causes of success for the seeker of knowledge. Allah, mighty and majestic, has given me a full share of it, so I was the most humble of the students and the most devoted in service to the teachers, and praise be to Allah, Exalted is He, for that. ﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ عَلِيمٌ﴾ So He knows what you do and what you leave undone of that which He has obligated you to, and He will recompense you for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 29:

﴿There is no blame upon you for entering﴾ — that is, without seeking permission — ﴿houses not inhabited﴾, that is, houses set up not for the habitation of a specific group only, but for anyone who needs to make use of them, whoever he may be, without taking them as a dwelling, such as caravanserais (ribat), inns (khanat), shops (hawanit), bathhouses (hammamat) and others, for they are prepared for the benefit of people in general, as indicated by His saying, ﴿wherein is provision for you﴾. This phrase is either a descriptive clause for "houses," or a resumptive clause functioning as a justification for the negation of blame. The meaning is: in them there is a right of enjoyment for you, such as sheltering from heat and cold, storing goods and belongings, buying and selling, bathing, and other uses that befit the nature of houses and their interiors. Therefore there is no harm in entering them without permission from those within them beforehand, nor from the one who manages their affairs and oversees their administration.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, on the authority of Muqatil, that when the words of the Most High, ﴿O you who believe, do not enter﴾, etc. were revealed, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about the merchants of Quraysh who travel between Makkah, Madinah, Syria and Bayt al-Maqdis, and who have known houses along the road? How are they to ask permission and greet, when there are no inhabitants in them?" So He, glory be to Him, granted a concession in that, and revealed His saying, ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ etc.

By "the known houses" Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) meant the inns along the roads, but the verse is more general than that, and the specific occasion of revelation carries no restrictive weight. What was related from Ibn Jubayr, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Dahhak and others, interpreting it as referring to these, is by way of example (tamthil). Likewise what a group related from Ata', Abd ibn Humayd and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, that they are the ruined houses entered for relieving oneself. As for what was related from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah as well, that they are the houses of Makkah, this too is by way of example; but the soundness of that depends on the view that the houses of Makkah are not owned and that people share them, and you know the disagreement on this question.

Abu Dawud related in al-Nasikh, and Ibn Jarir from Ibn Abbas, that the words of the Most High, ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾, were abrogated (nusikha) by His saying, ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, etc., and that He excepted from it the houses that are not inhabited. The hadith of the exception was also related from Ikrimah and al-Hasan, and it is what the apparent sense of Muqatil's report requires. Al-Zamakhshari adopted this view, and Abu Hayyan criticised him, saying that this does not make it clear that the first verse concerns owned and inhabited houses, while this verse concerns permitted houses which no one person has exclusive right to. What the sound reasoning requires is that the houses mentioned earlier are more general than these houses, so that what is mentioned here is a specification of that, and it is what is meant by the exception. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

﴿And Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾: a warning to whoever enters any of these places for corruption or for spying upon private matters.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 30:**

﴿Say to the believing men﴾ This begins the statement of general rulings that apply to all believers. The ruling concerning those who seek permission when entering houses falls under them as a first-level inclusion. The address is turned away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the commands and prohibitions within this section are delegated to him, peace and blessings be upon him. It has been said that this is because these are obligations concerning many particular matters that occur frequently, so the one who issues them and manages them is a guardian and overseer over them. It has also been said that this is because some of the believers came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as one who requests that he tell them what is in the sphere of speech.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "A man passed by in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on one of the roads of Madinah, and he looked at a woman, and she looked at him. Satan whispered to them both that neither had looked at the other except out of admiration for him. While the man was walking alongside a wall, looking at her, the wall met him and split his nose. He said, 'By Allah, I will not wash off the blood until I come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and inform him of my affair.' So he came to him and related his story. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'This is the punishment for your sin.' Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾."

The object of "say" (qul) is implied. The word "yaghuddu" (they should lower) is a response to the imperative "qul" (say), because it includes the meaning of the conditional particle. It is as if it were said: "If you tell them, 'Lower,' they will lower." This indicates that, owing to their great readiness to obey, their action is never separated from his command, peace and blessings be upon him, and that his command is like the cause that necessitates it. This is the well-known view.

It has also been permitted that "yaghuddu" be a response to the implied imperative that is the object of the verb "say." It has been objected that a response must differ from the thing being responded to, either in the verb and the subject, as in "come to me and I will honour you," or in the verb alone, as in "submit and you will enter Paradise," or in the subject alone, as in "stand, and I will stand." It is not permitted for the two to agree in the subject. Furthermore, the imperative is addressed directly, whereas "yaghuddu" is in the third person, and this is not permitted. It has been replied to this: why would it not be permitted that it be of the type of "whoever's migration was..." in the hadith? And it is not granted that an imperative cannot be answered with a verb in the third person when it is reported by speech, since shifting between persons is permitted in that case. There is a discussion here. Whoever is fair does not regard this view as sound, and it is, despite its flaws, very contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Tabarsi and others permitted that "yaghuddu" be in the jussive mood, governed by an implied imperative lam (lam al-amr, the particle of command), because "qul" (say) indicates it. That is: "Say to them, 'Let them lower.'" In this case the clause is in the accusative position as the object of "say." The meaning of "ghadd al-basar" (lowering the gaze) is closing the eyelid over the eyelid.

As for "min" (from) in "min absarihim" (from their gazes), it has been said to be an extra particle (silah). Sibawayh rejects this in such a context, and permitting it is the view of al-Akhfash. Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is valid for min to be for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), and it is valid for it to be for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah)." Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) criticised this: "No ambiguous term precedes it, so that min could be for specifying the kind. Moreover, the correct view is that it is not among the functions of min to specify the kind." The majority view is that here it is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the intended meaning is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and limiting it to what is permitted. Making lowering the gaze from some of what is seen into lowering part of the gaze is, as in al-Kashf (al-Kashshaf), a fine metonymy (kinayah). Lowering the gaze from what makes looking at it forbidden is obligatory, while a sudden glance in which one does not intend to look is excused.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours.'"

Allah the Glorified began with guidance to lowering the gaze because in that is closing the door to evil, for looking is a gateway to many evils, and it is the messenger of adultery and beyond it immorality. Some of them said:

Every calamity begins from a glance,
and most of the fire comes from a spark that was thought small.
So long as a man has an eye that turns it about,
he is exposed to danger among the eyes of others.
How many a glance has done to the heart of its doer
what arrows do, without a bow or a string.
It pleases its looker, but harms his thought;
no welcome to a pleasure that returns with harm.

It is apparent that the guidance is for each one of the believers, and the plural form does not preclude this. It is also apparent that "the believers" is more general than the servants and others. Some claimed that it is permissible for the intended meaning to be the servants, and the believers who are sincere, so that the meaning would be: "Say to the perfect believers that they should lower their gazes, ﴿and guard their private parts﴾," that is, from what is not lawful to them, such as adultery and sodomy. The particle "min" (partitive) is not used here as it was used earlier, because there is no fine metonymy in it, as is the case there. In al-Kashshaf: "Min entered with lowering the gaze but not with guarding the private parts, to indicate that the matter of looking is broader. Do you not see that there is no harm in looking at the hair, breasts, bosoms, upper arms, shins and feet of mahram women? Likewise, slave girls displayed for sale, and a non-mahram woman's face, palms and feet may be looked at according to one of the two narrations. As for the matter of the private parts, it is restricted. Sufficient to show the difference is that looking is permitted except for what is excluded from it, while intercourse is forbidden except for what is excluded from it." End of quotation.

The author of al-Fara'id said: "It may be said that the intended meaning is lowering the gaze from non-mahram women, and some parts of non-mahram women may lawfully be looked at, but as for the private parts, there is no way at all to make them lawful with respect to non-mahram women. So there is no reason for min to enter there." There is room for reflection on this.

It has been said: min was not used here because the intended meaning of guarding the private parts is concealing them.

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah that he said: "Every verse in which guarding the private parts is mentioned means from adultery, except this verse in Surah al-Nur, ﴿and they guard their private parts﴾ and ﴿and they guard their private parts﴾ [for women], which means that no one should see them." A similar report was narrated from Abu Zayd. Covering is commanded absolutely.

It has been objected to this that uncovering is permitted in certain places, so if min had been used, it would have indicated that. And explaining the guarding of the private parts here specifically as covering them has been said not to be free from remoteness, because it contradicts what occurs in the Noble Qur'an, as the one who explained it in the way mentioned has acknowledged.

Some scrupulous scholars chose that the intended meaning of that is guarding the private parts from leading to what is not lawful, and guarding them from exposure, because guarding, since its complement is not mentioned, includes both types. He mentioned that guarding from exposure entails the other in two ways: that exposure is ordinarily not free of uncovering, and that guarding from exposure, or rather the command to conceal entirely, is for guarding from leading to what is unlawful. From here you will know that the weakness of what was narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd lies in the fact that the verse does not address guarding the private parts from adultery, and so they did not hit the mark.

﴿That﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of lowering the gaze and guarding, ﴿is purer for them﴾, that is, more cleansed from the filth of doubt, or more beneficial in terms of religion and worldly life, for looking is a messenger of adultery, and in it are religious or worldly harms that are not hidden. The form "afʿal" (purer) here is for intensification (mubalaghah), not for comparison (tafdil).

It has been permitted that it be for comparison, in the sense of "purer than everything beneficial or distancing from doubt." It has also been said, in the sense that it is more beneficial than adultery and forbidden looking, since they imagine the pleasure of that to be a benefit. ﴿Indeed Allah is Aware of what they do﴾, nothing is hidden from Him of what proceeds from them of deeds, among which is roaming the gaze, using all the senses, moving the limbs, and what they intend by that. So let them be wary of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in everything they do and everything they leave undone.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze﴾, so that they do not look at what it is not lawful for them to look at, such as the awrah (intimate parts) of men and women, which is the area between the navel and the knee. In al-Zawajir of Ibn Hajar al-Makki it is stated: Just as a man's looking at a woman is forbidden, her looking at him is forbidden too, even without desire and even without fear of temptation. Yes, if there is a mahram relationship between them by lineage, fosterage or marriage, each may look at everything other than the area between the navel and knee of the other. What is mentioned in some books of the companions (the Hanafi jurists) is that if her looking at other than the navel and knee is with desire, it is forbidden, but without desire it is not forbidden. Yes, lowering her gaze from strangers altogether is more fitting and better for her.

For Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, and al-Nasa'i, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, related from Umm Salamah that she was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Maymunah. She said: "While we were with him, Ibn Umm Maktum came and entered upon him, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Veil yourselves from him.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he is blind and cannot see.' He said: 'Are you two blind? Do you not see him?'"

Those who hold that it is forbidden for a woman to look at any part of a non-mahram man in absolute terms use this as evidence. It is not far-fetched to say that it is forbidden for a woman to look at another woman at other than the area between the navel and knee if it is with desire, and it is not unlikely that this occurs, for many women who practise sihaq (lesbianism) do so, and we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted.

﴿And guard their private parts﴾, i.e., from what is not lawful for them, such as fornication and sihaq, or from exposure, or from what encompasses all of that. "Exposure" (al-ibda') ﴿and not display their adornment﴾, i.e., what they adorn themselves with, such as jewellery and the like, ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, i.e., except what custom and natural disposition have made it usual for to appear, and the basic principle concerning it is that it is visible, such as a ring, a plain ring (al-fatkha), kohl and henna. There is no blame for displaying these to strangers. The blame lies only in displaying the adornment that is hidden, such as the bracelet, anklet, armlet, necklace, crown, sash, and earring.

Mentioning the adornment rather than its locations serves to emphasise the command to cover up, because these adornments are placed on parts of the body which it is not lawful to look at except for those excepted later in the verse, namely the forearm, shin, upper arm, neck, head, chest and ear. He forbade displaying the adornments themselves so that it would be known that looking at them is not lawful when they are attached to those locations. The evidence is that looking at the adornment itself, which is not attached to those locations, such as looking at a woman's bracelet being sold in the market, is not disputed as permissible. If looking at the locations themselves is firmly established as dangerous and fixed in prohibition, this shows that women have a duty to be very careful in covering them and to fear Allah the Exalted in uncovering them. So says al-Kashshaf.

Al-Tibi said that this indicates that what is mentioned is by way of metonymy, like the saying: "So-and-so is clean of collar and clean of hem."

The author of al-Fara'id said: This is from the figure of speech in which the name of what resides is applied to the place, so the meaning of "adornment" is its locations, and the prohibition of looking at the locations is established by the explicit wording through its indication, which is stronger. There is discussion in this.

It has been said: the speech is on the assumption of an omitted noun, i.e., "do not display the locations of their adornment." Ibn al-Munir said: the adornment is in its literal sense, and what comes later, if Allah wills, in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and let them not stamp their feet﴾, the verse, confirms that displaying the adornment is what is intended by the prohibition. Also, if the meaning of "adornment" were its locations, it would follow that it is lawful for strangers to look at the visible locations of the visible adornments, and this is false, because the whole body of a free woman is awrah, and it is not lawful for anyone other than a husband or mahram to look at any part of it except out of necessity, such as treatment or bearing witness. You know that Ibn al-Munir was a Maliki and what he said is based on his school, while what al-Zamakhshari said is based on the well-known position of Imam Abu Hanifah, that the visible locations of adornment, namely the face, the two palms and the two feet, are not awrah at all, and so looking at them is not forbidden.

Page 141

Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that "Asma' bint Abi Bakr entered upon the Prophet ﷺ wearing thin clothes, and he turned away from her and said: 'O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not appropriate for anything of her to be seen except this,' and he pointed to his face and his palm, ﷺ."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾: the surface of the face and the inside of the palm.

Both of them related from Ibn Umar that he said: the face and the two palms. Perhaps the two feet, in their view, are like the two palms, except that they did not mention them, being content with knowledge by analogy, since the hardship in covering them is greater than the hardship in covering the palms, especially for most poor Arab women who walk in the streets to attend to their affairs. The school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, as in al-Zawajir, is that the face and the two palms, both their backs and their fronts up to the two wrists, are awrah in a woman's looking, even her mother's, according to the more correct view, although they are not awrah for a free woman in prayer. In al-Minhaj and its commentary by Ibn Hajar, in the chapter on conditions of prayer: the awrah of a female slave, even partly owned, a mukatabah or umm walad, is like the awrah of a man, the area between navel and knee, according to the more correct view. The awrah of a free woman, even one who is not yet discerning, and of a free hermaphrodite, is everything other than the face and the two palms. Looking at them is forbidden as with what exceeds the awrah of a female slave, because that is a likely cause of temptation. In seclusion it is obligatory to cover the private part of a female slave as with a man, and the area between navel and knee of a free woman only, except for a minor need such as cooling off or fear of dust on a garment one has adorned, end of quote.

Al-Zawajir mentions the prohibition of looking at any part that has separated from a woman, because seeing a part may lead to seeing the whole, so it is fitting that looking at it is also forbidden. Indeed it says: Our imams forbade looking at the paring of a woman's fingernail that has separated, even from her own hand. Some Shafi'i scholars held that looking at the face and palm is permissible if there is no fear of temptation, but this is not relied upon among them. Some of their eminent scholars, after citing the verse as evidence that the awrah of a free woman is what is other than these two, explained what appears as the face and two palms, and gave as the reason for forbidding looking at them the likelihood of temptation. This shows that not everything whose looking is forbidden is awrah. You know that permitting the display of the face and two palms, as the verse implies according to them, together with the view that looking at them is forbidden in absolute terms, is very far-fetched, so reflect. Know that if the intended meaning is the prohibition of displaying the locations of adornment, and it is said that the general sense includes the face and the two palms, and one maintains that they are awrah and that displaying them to anyone other than those excepted later is forbidden, then the exception in the words of the Exalted ﴿except what appears thereof﴾ may be a ruling established by indication, namely blame in the abode of recompense. The meaning would be that what appears from them without display, as if the wind had uncovered it, for example, is something for which they are not held accountable in the abode of recompense. In the same ruling is what it is necessary to expose for something like bearing witness or a physician's treatment. Al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group of others related from Ibn Mas'ud that what appears is the garments and the outer cloak (al-jilbab). In another narration it is restricted to the garments, and Imam Ahmad also restricted it to them. The term "adornment" has been applied to them in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], according to al-Bahr. Some narrations from Ibn Abbas state that what appears is the kohl, the ring, the earring and the necklace.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ikrimah that it is the palm and the hollow of the throat, and from al-Hasan that it is the ring and the bracelet. Other things have also been related. It is not hidden that some reports clearly carry the word "adornment" in its ordinary sense, and some clearly carry it to mean its locations. Ibn Bahr said: "adornment" applies both to the beauty of creation which Allah the Exalted has made, and to what one adorns oneself with of fine clothing. The intended meaning in the verse is the prohibition of displaying these to those who are not forbidden, and it excepts what cannot be concealed at some times, such as the face and the extremities. Some denied that "adornment" applies to natural form. In al-Bahr it is said: "The closer view is that it is included in adornment, and what adornment is finer than a well-proportioned natural form?"

﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests (juyub)﴾: this is guidance on how to conceal some locations of adornment after the prohibition on displaying them. Khumur is the plural of khimar, and its plural for few is akhmirah; both plurals are regular. It is the head-covering which a woman throws over her head, from the root khamr meaning cover. Juyub is the plural of jayb, which is an opening at the top of a shirt through which part of the body appears. Its root is said to be from al-jayb meaning cutting. In al-Sihah it is said: "I cut the shirt, I cut it and I cut it, when you widen its neck opening." The rajaz poet said:

"She began to cut the dark night's collar, the collar of the warrior's armour..."

This application to the neck opening is the well-known usage in the language. As for applying it to the side pocket used for placing dirhams and the like, as is common among us today, this is not from the speech of the Arabs, as Ibn Taymiyyah stated, but it is not an error in terms of meaning. The intended meaning of the verse, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr, is that He commanded them to cover their necks and chests with their head-coverings so that nothing of them would be seen. The women used to cover their heads with the khimar and let it hang down behind the back, as was the pre-Islamic custom, so their necks and some of their chests would show. It is authentically related that when this verse was revealed, the women of the Muhajirun hastened to comply with what it contains, so they tore their izars and covered themselves with them, affirming and believing in what Allah the Exalted sent down in His Book.

"Yadrib" is used with "ala" according to Abu Hayyan because it is implicitly given the meaning of placing and casting. It has been said it means tightening. The apparent sense of al-Raghib's words is that it takes "ala" without implicit meaning. Abbas related from Abu Amr the reading "wa-liyadribna" with a kasra on the lam. Several of the seven readers read "juyubihinna" with a kasra on the jim, while the damma is the original form, since the pattern fi'l, in its plural, takes the form fu'ul in both sound and weak roots, like fulus and buyut, and the kasra is for harmony with the ya'. Al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a poor dialect.

﴿And not display their adornment﴾: the prohibition is repeated in order to make an exception from it of some materials of permission with regard to the viewer, after an exception from it of some materials of necessity with regard to what is viewed, ﴿except to their husbands (bu'ulatihinna)﴾, i.e., their husbands, for they are the ones primarily intended by the adornment, and the women are commanded to adorn themselves for them. Indeed, they have the right to beat them for abandoning it, and they have the right to look at the whole of their bodies, even the customary place, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim.

Most Shafi'is disliked looking at that, and some prohibited it. It has been said that it is contrary to what is preferable, and this, as al-Khafaji said, is the position of the Hanafis, and its details are in al-Hidayah. In what we have mentioned there is an indication of the reason for giving precedence to "their husbands."

[Page 143]

﴿or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters﴾. This is because of the necessary, constant mixing between them and these men, and because the risk of temptation from them is unlikely. They may look at what is normally visible of the women during service and work in the household. This ruling does not apply only to the nearest fathers, but to the fathers of fathers, however far back they go. Likewise, the fathers of mothers are in the same position. Similarly, it does not apply only to sons and the biological children, but includes the sons of sons and the sons of sons' sons, however far down they go. By "brothers" is meant what includes both full brothers, who share the same father and mother, and half-brothers through the father (banu al-'illat), who are the sons of a man by different wives, and half-brothers through the mother (al-akhyaf), who are the sons of a woman by different fathers. The same is said about sisters. He used "banu" (sons of) with them instead of "abna'" (sons) because it better suits the general sense, and it is more commonly used for a group that traces back to one person even when the kinds of kinship among them differ. Do you not see that you often hear "banu Adam" and "banu Tamim," and rarely hear "abna' Adam" and "abna' Tamim"? In the case under discussion, a woman may have a full nephew through a brother, a nephew through a half-brother through the father, and a nephew through a half-brother through the mother all at once. Indeed, she may have several nephews through a full brother, or full brothers, or half-brothers through the father, or nephews through a half-brother through the father, or brothers through the mother, in the same way. Something similar can happen with the son of a sister, but the half-brothers through the father (banu al-'illat) cannot be imagined here, just as the half-brothers through the mother (al-akhyaf) cannot be imagined in the case of the sons of a brother. The gathering of these relations in the sons of the women and the sons of their husbands is possible, though it is not of the same standing.

It has been said that "banu" was chosen in the last two cases because if "abna'" had been used, two hamzas would have come together: one the hamza of "abna'" and the second the hamza of "ikhwan" or "akhawat." Yet, even with this, the question is not fully settled, since the questioner may then ask: "Why was 'abna'' chosen in the first two cases instead of 'banu'?" This requires an answer such as: it was chosen because it suits "aba'" (fathers) better. It has also been said that "abna'" was chosen in the first two for this reason, and "banu" was chosen in ﴿the sons of their sisters﴾ so that the genitive and the possessor would be of one kind. In "banu akhwanihinna" it was chosen for harmony of sound (al-musha-kalah). There is much to say about this. God did not mention the paternal and maternal uncles, although, as al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said, they are like the other close kin (mahram, those one may not marry) in permitting the display of adornment to them. It has been said that this is because they are in the position of brothers, since the grandfather, whether the father's father or the mother's father, is in the position of a father, so his son is in the position of a brother. It has also been said that God did not mention them because it is more cautious for the women to cover themselves before them, out of fear that they might describe the women to their sons, which would lead to the sons looking at them. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Shaybah related this from al-Sha'bi. There is in this a clear indication of the obligation to cover oneself from non-mahram men.

It has been objected that this reasoning applies to the fathers of the husbands as well, since if they saw the women's adornment they might describe them to their sons, who are not mahram, and this would lead to those sons looking at them, especially if the women were unveiled. It has also been said that they were not mentioned because the fathers are sufficient to mention, since they stand in the same position as the uncles, especially, and the word "father" is often applied to the paternal uncle. From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am 6:74], although Azar was his uncle. Further, the mahram relationship that permits display may arise through nursing as well as through blood. So it is permitted for them to display ﴿their adornment﴾ to their fathers and sons, for example through nursing, ﴿or their women﴾, meaning the women who are specifically close to them through companionship and service, from among the free believing women. For unbelieving women do not scruple to describe them to men, so in displaying adornment to them they are like non-mahram men. There is no difference in this between a doll and other things. Most of the early scholars (al-salaf) held this view.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah, may God be pleased with him: "To proceed: it has reached me that some women among the Muslim women enter the bathhouses with the women of the polytheists. Put a stop to this. It is not lawful for a woman who believes in God and the Last Day to see the nakedness of another woman except one who is of her own religious community." In the Rawdah of al-Nawawi, regarding a dhimmi woman looking at a Muslim woman, there are two opinions. The more sound of them according to al-Ghazali is that she is like a Muslim woman. The more sound according to al-Baghawi is prohibition. In the Minhaj of al-Nawawi, the more sound opinion is the prohibition of a dhimmi woman looking at a Muslim woman, and its implication is that she is with her like a non-mahram man. A group of Shafi'is relied on this. Ibn Hajar said: the more sound opinion is the prohibition of her looking at what is not normally visible during service, from a Muslim woman who is not her mistress or mahram. The entry of the dhimmi women upon the Mothers of the Believers, mentioned in the sound hadiths, is evidence for the permissibility of her looking at what is normally visible during service. Imam al-Razi said: the position is that she is like a Muslim woman, and "their women" means all women. The statement of the early scholars is taken to mean recommendation, and this view is more lenient for people today, since it is nearly impossible for Muslim women to veil themselves from non-Muslim women.

﴿or those their right hands possess﴾, that is, of the female slaves, even if they are unbelievers. As for male slaves, they are like non-mahram men. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, and one of two opinions in the school of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and many Shafi'is have deemed it sound. The other opinion is that they are like mahram. Al-Minhaj and its commentary by Ibn Hajar also state that the more sound opinion is that the just male slave may look, but mere chastity against fornication is not enough, and this excludes a slave owned jointly, a partly freed slave, and a mukatab (a slave contracted to buy his freedom), as stated in al-Rawdah from al-Qadi, who approved it, although they went to great lengths to refute it. He is returned to his mistress, who must be just, like the looking of a mahram. So he may look at what lies outside the area between the navel and the knee, and she may look at him in the same way. He is also treated like a mahram regarding seclusion and travel. End of the summary. Ibn al-Musayyib held that the slave is like the female slave, but then he retracted and said: "Let not the verse of al-Nur deceive you, for it concerns females and not males," and he gave the reason that they are males who are neither husbands nor mahram, and desire is present in them, since marriage is permitted for them in general, as stated in al-Hidayah.

It was related from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin that they said: the slave may not look at the hair of his mistress. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Tawus that he was asked: "Does a boy see a woman's head and feet?" He said: "I do not like it, except for a boy who is still young. As for a man with a beard, no." This is the view of 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah, may God be pleased with them. It was also related from some of the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may God be pleased with them, that it is permissible for the male slave to look at what those excepted above (the mahram) may look at from his mistress. It was related from 'A'ishah that she used to comb her hair while her slave watched her, and that she said to Dhakwan: "When you place me in the grave and leave, you are free." It was related from Mujahid that the Mothers of the Believers did not veil themselves from their mukatab slaves so long as he still owed them a single dirham.

Ahmad in his Musnad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, may God be pleased with him, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, with a slave whom he had given her. Fatimah had a garment which, when she covered her head with it, did not reach her feet, and when she covered her feet with it, did not reach her head. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw what she was suffering, he said: 'There is no harm for you. He is only your father and your slave.'"

What the apparent meaning of the verse requires is that there is no distinction between male and female, because of the generality of "ma" (what). Also, if only females had been meant, it would have said ﴿or their female slaves﴾, which is more concise and is explicit about the intended meaning. When the above report is added to this, the view that there is no distinction becomes stronger, and escaping it is difficult. The best answer that has been given concerning the report is that the boy in it was a child, since "ghulam" (boy) is literally applied to such a child. Consider this. By attributing the possession to them, the husband's slave is excluded. He and the non-mahram man are equal. It has been said that some scholars treated him as a mahram, on the basis of the reading ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾.

﴿or male attendants who have no physical need [of women]﴾, meaning those who follow in order to obtain some of the leftover food, not those who have need of women. These are the old men advanced in years whose desires have faded, and the eunuchs (mamsuhun) whose male organs have been cut off, and castrated men. Regarding the impotent man (al-majbub), who has had his penis cut off, and the castrated man (al-khasi), who has had his testicles removed, there is disagreement. It is preferred that both are subject to the prohibition of looking, like other non-mahram men. Mu'awiyah held that it was permissible to look at a castrated man, but his opinion is not relied upon. It is said that he was the first to take eunuchs into service. It is related from Maysun al-Kalbiyyah that Mu'awiyah entered upon her with a eunuch, and she covered herself from him. He said: "He is a eunuch." She said: "O Mu'awiyah, do you think that mutilating him makes lawful what God has forbidden?" One may not use as evidence the report that "al-Muqawqis gave the Prophet (ﷺ) a eunuch, and he accepted him," since there is no indication in it that it was permissible to bring him in to women.

Ibn Jarir and a group related from Mujahid that "those who have no physical need" means the simpleton who does not understand matters concerning women. This is also related from Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with him. Ibn Jubayr said that it means the one afflicted with mental weakness, and similar to him is the madman, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it means the mukhannath (effeminate man) whose penis does not become erect. But Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others related from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "A man who was a mukhannath used to enter upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they counted him among those who had no physical need. One day the Prophet (ﷺ) entered while he was with one of his wives, and he was describing a woman, saying: 'When she comes forward, she comes with four [folds], and when she turns back, she turns with eight.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do you not see that this one knows what is here? He must not enter upon you.' So they veiled him from them." It has also been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) expelled him, and he used to frequent al-Bayda' every Friday, begging for food.

Perhaps the better course is to understand "those who have no physical need" as those who have no need of women and know nothing of their affairs, such that their souls do not incite them to immorality and they do not describe the women to non-mahram men. I do not see that merely lacking need of women is sufficient for those with physical need, since by it the harm of display is not completely removed, as is not hidden. It seems the report contains a kind of allusion to this. The Minhaj and its commentary by Ibn Hajar, may God have mercy on him, state: the more sound opinion is that the looking of the castrated man (al-mamsuh), whose penis and both testicles are removed, is permitted, on condition that no desire for women remains in him at all, and that he is Muslim when the woman is Muslim. Even if he is a non-mahram man, it is like the looking of a mahram towards a just non-mahram woman. He may look at what lies outside the area between the navel and the knee, and she may look at him in the same way. He is also treated like a mahram regarding seclusion and travel. From this it is known that the example of the castrated man given earlier is not absolute. As for the old man who is decrepit and the mukhannath, according to the Shafi'is they are not like the castrated man in regard to looking at non-mahram women. They also agreed that the madman must be veiled from, so take note.

The word "ghayr" (other than) in the genitive is said to be in apposition, not as an adjective, because an adjective would require an unnatural explanation. Some scholars treated "al-tabi'in" (those who follow) as indefinite because they are not specified, as al-Zajjaj said. Or "ghayr" is made definite by its genitive here, as in al-Fatihah, though this is open to question. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "ghayr" in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal) and as an exception (istithna').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 3 of 3):

﴿or the children who have not yet attained awareness of women's private parts﴾ That is, the children who do not know what 'awrah (private parts) is and cannot distinguish between it and other things. [Here] ﴿have not yet attained awareness﴾ and so on is taken from the expression "zahara 'ala al-shay'" (he came upon the thing) when he became aware of it, so it is used as a metaphor for that. Or [it means] those who have not reached the limit of desire and the capacity for intercourse, [here] taking "zahara 'ala fulan" to mean he overpowered him when he became stronger than him, and from it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿so they became victorious﴾ [al-Saff: 14]. This includes the child described by the mentioned attribute in this sense, and also the adolescent in whom no yearning for women has become apparent. Some of the imams of the Shafi'i school have stated that he is like the adult, so it is obligatory to veil from him according to the more correct view, like the adolescent in whom that has become apparent. It also includes those younger than the adolescent, but only those who describe what they see as it is. They have stated concerning one younger than the adolescent that if he has this quality, he is like a mahram, and otherwise he is like one who does not exist, so it is permissible in his presence to do what is permissible in seclusion. So do not be negligent.

It is apparent that "al-tifl" (the child) is conjoined to the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿to their husbands﴾, or to what follows it of its counterparts, not to "al-rijal" (the men). The words of Abu Hayyan are apparent in saying that it is conjoined to it, and this is nothing [of substance]. Then, it is a singular noun preceded by the definite article of the genus, so it is general, and for this reason, as he said in al-Bahr: it is a descriptor of the plural, so it is as if it were said: "or the children," as is narrated from the codex of Hafsa. Similar to this is their saying: "The yellow dinar ruined the people, and the white dirham." It was also said that it is a singular placed in the position of the plural, and similar to it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then He brings you out as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67].

It was objected that placing the singular in the position of the plural is not analogical according to Sibawayh, and what is here, according to him, is from the category of the singular defined by the definite article of the genus, and it is general, as evidenced by the validity of exception from it. The mentioned verse may be, in his view, in the sense of "then each one of you comes out as a child," as was said concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31], that it is in the sense of "she prepared for each one of them a couch," so it is not necessary that "tifl" there be of what is not analogical in his view. Al-Raghib said: "tifl" is used for the plural as it is used for the singular, and al-Jawhari stated this explicitly. Likewise some grammarians said: it is originally a verbal noun, so it applies to the few and the many, and the matter according to this is very apparent. "Al-'awrat" is the plural of 'awrah, which originally refers to that which one guards against being seen, and it became predominantly used for the private parts of the man and the woman. The dialect of most of the Arabs is to pronounce the waw in the plural with a sukun, and this is the reading of the majority.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "'awarat" with a fatha on the waw. The well-known view is that vocalizing the waw, and likewise the ya', in this kind of plural is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah. Ibn Khalawayh reported in his book Shawadhdh al-Qira'at that Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read "'awarat" with a fatha, then said:

"We heard Ibn Mujahid say: it is a lahn (linguistic error). He only called it a lahn and an error due to the transmission; otherwise it has a standing in Arabic, for the Banu Tamim say: rawdat, jawazat, and 'awarat with a fatha in them, while the rest of the Arabs use the sukun." Al-Farra' said: the Arabs lighten this, except Hudhayl, who make heavy what is of this type of the ya' and waw roots. One of them recited to me:

"Abu bayda't ra'ih mu'addab
raqiq bi-masḥ al-mankabayn sabuh"

﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾, that is, what they hide from sight. ﴿of their adornment﴾: that is, let them not strike the ground with their feet so that their anklets jingle and it becomes known that they wear anklets, for that stirs men's inclination towards them and gives the impression that they have an inclination towards men. Ibn Jarir narrated from Hadrami that a woman made an anklet of silver and made one of jizi' (a kind of stone/bead), then she passed by a group of people and struck with her foot, so the anklet fell upon the jizi' and it made a sound, and Allah the Exalted sent down: ﴿and let them not stamp﴾, and so on. Women today put beads and the like inside the anklet, so when they walk with it, even if they walk gently, it makes a sound. They also have types of ornaments other than the anklet that make a sound when walking, especially when accompanied by the striking of the foot and heavy treading. Some people are stirred in their desire by the jingling of ornaments more than by seeing them. In the prohibition of displaying the sound of ornaments after the prohibition of displaying their adornment, there is what is not hidden of the prohibition of displaying their places. It may be inferred from this prohibition the prohibition of listening to their voices.

What is mentioned in the authoritative books of the Shafi'i school, and to which I incline, is that the voice of women is not 'awrah, so listening to it is not forbidden unless one fears temptation from it; and likewise if one finds pleasure in it, as al-Zarkashi investigated. As for the Hanafis, the Imam Ibn al-Humam said: "It is stated in al-Nawazil that the tone (naghmah) of a woman is 'awrah, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Glorification (tasbih) is for men, and clapping is for women.' So it is not proper for a man to hear her," end of quote.

Then know that among what is included in the adornment whose display is forbidden, in my view, is what most affluent women in our time wear over their garments and cover themselves with when they go out of their houses: a cloth woven of silk of many colors, with golden or silver embroidery that dazzles the eyes. I consider that allowing their husbands and the like to permit them to go out in it and walk with it among non-mahram men is a sign of little jealousy, and this affliction has become widespread. Similar to it is what has also become widespread: the lack of veiling by most women from their husbands' brothers, and the husbands' indifference to this, and they often order them to do it. Sometimes a woman veils from them for days after the marriage until they give her some ornament or the like, and then she shows herself to them and no longer veils from them. All of that is what Allah the Exalted and His Messenger ﷺ have not permitted. Such examples are many. There is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you﴾: a shift of address, turning it away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to all, by way of predominance (taghlib), to show the complete concern with what is within its scope, namely the matter of repentance, and that it is among the greatest of true matters, in that the Exalted and Glorified One is the one who commands it, since hardly anyone among the responsible persons is free from some kind of neglect in fulfilling the duties of obligations as they should be, especially in refraining from desires.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Muslim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have narrated from al-Agharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'O people, repent to Allah, for I repent to Him a hundred times every day.'"

The meaning of repentance according to this is repentance from what is present in the state [one is in]. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning is repentance from what they used to do before, such as casting glances and other things. Although this is erased by Islam, it still requires remorse for it and the resolve to refrain from it whenever one remembers it. They have said: this is required of every penitent for a sin whenever he remembers it. From this it is known that what many do of those who claim repentance, by relating their sins with boastfulness and relish, is evidence of the lack of sincerity of their repentance.

In repeating the address with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O believers﴾ there is an emphasis on the obligation, and a notice that the attribute of faith necessitates compliance absolutely, and it is evidence that sins do not take one out of faith. Ibn 'Amir read "ayyuhu al-mu'minun" with a dammah on the ha'. Its basis is that it was fatha because it came before the alif, and when the alif fell due to the meeting of two sukun, it made its vowel follow the vowel of what preceded it. The dammah of the ha' that is for alerting after ayyu is a dialect of the Banu Malik, a group whose representative is Shaqiq ibn Maslamah. Some stopped with a sukun on the ha' because it was written in the codex without an alif after it.

Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub stopped with an alif, contrary to the orthography, as in al-Nashr. ﴿so that you may prosper﴾: that is, so that you may succeed thereby in the happiness of both abodes; or it is hoped for, so there is no ruling.

﴿And marry off the unmarried (al-ayama) among you﴾. After He (glorified be He) had forbidden fornication and its near and remote precursors, He commanded marriage. Although marriage is intended in itself, as the means by which the species endures in a manner free from the confusion of lineages, it is also a deterrent from that (fornication).

(Al-ayama): as transmitted in al-Tahrir from Abu 'Amr, and as al-Zamakhshari adopted, it is a metathesized (maqlub) form of ayaim, the plural of ayyim, because the pattern fay'al is not pluralized as fa'alى. That is, its original form was that, then the mim was moved forward and given a fatha for lightness, and the ya' was changed to an alif because it was vocalized and preceded by an open vowel. Ibn Malik and those who followed him held that it is an irregular plural with no metathesis, its pattern being fa'ala, and this is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's statement.

(Al-ayyim): al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: every male without a female with him, and every female without a male with her, whether virgin or previously married. It is also said: "amm" and "amit," when they have not married, whether both were virgins or both had been married. And a poet said:

"If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried, I too will remain unmarried, even though I am more inclined to remain so than you are."

Al-Tabrizi said in his commentary on the Diwan of Abu Tammam: this word is frequently used of a man whose wife has died and of a woman whose husband has died. In older poetry there is evidence that it applies both through death and through a husband's leaving without death. Al-Shammakh said:

"It pleases my eye that I hear that she (the woman) is ... and though I do not attain her, she is an unmarried woman who has not been wed."

End of quotation. In the commentary on Sibawayh's Book by Abu Bakr al-Khaffaf: the ayyim is the one who has no husband, and originally it is one who had been married but lost her husband through a calamity that befell her. Then it was said of a virgin figuratively, because she has no husband. From Muhammad (it is reported) that it means a previously married woman, and he argued for this from what was reported: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The ayyim has more right over herself than her guardian, and the virgin is consulted about herself, and her permission is her silence."

Here he contrasted the ayyim with the virgin. It is possible that the word is shared (between both meanings), but it is intended here in the former sense because of the contrast. Most scholars, however, follow what al-Nadr said.

[Page 148]

That is: marry off those who have no spouse among free men and free women. ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾. The address is to guardians and masters. The meaning of "righteous" (al-salah) is its legal (shar'i) meaning, and it is taken into account concerning slaves, because one among them who lacks righteousness is not fit for his master to care for his affairs, to be solicitous of him, or to exert himself in arranging what is necessary for his welfare, legally and customarily, by spending wealth and resources. Indeed, his marriage might even cause harm to the master, so it is his duty to keep him with him. Since those among free men and free women who lack righteousness are not in this position, their righteousness was not taken into account. It has also been said that "righteous" means its linguistic meaning, that is, those fit for marriage and capable of fulfilling its rights. The command here has been said to be obligatory, and the people of the literal (Zahiri) school held this. It has been said to be recommended (nadb), and the majority held this.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Razi that although the verse implies obligation, the salaf unanimously agreed that obligation was not intended. Several things indicate this. First, if marrying off were obligatory, its transmission through the practice of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the salaf would have been widespread and well known, because the need is general. Since we find that in his time, peace be upon him, and in all subsequent eras, there were unmarried men and women and no one objected, it is established that the command did not intend obligation. Second, we agree that if a previously married woman refuses to marry, the guardian cannot compel her. Third, all agree that a master is not obligated to marry off his female slave or male slave, and by the conjunction (in the verse), the non-obligation applies to all. Fourth, the term "unmarried" (al-ayama) includes men and women, so if it is obligatory for guardians to marry off men with their consent, it is obligatory for women too. End of quotation.

Al-Imam himself said: the apparent meaning of the command is obligation, so it indicates that a guardian is obligated to marry off those under his guardianship. Once this is established, it follows that marriage is not permitted except through a guardian, since otherwise the one under guardianship would deprive the guardian of the ability to fulfill this obligation, and that is impermissible.

The reply to what was transmitted from Abu Bakr is that all he mentioned are specifications that have entered the verse, and a general term remains authoritative after specification. Therefore, when a woman asks her guardian to marry her to an unmarried man, it becomes obligatory. End of quotation. In al-Iklil it is said that whoever permits marrying slave women without condition, and a slave marrying a free woman, has used the general wording of the verse as evidence.

You know that it has not remained general. What I incline to is that the command expresses bare request, that the meaning of marrying off is assistance, mediation in the marriage, or enabling it, and that the validity of marriage in some cases depends on a guardian, which is known from another evidence.

Using this verse as evidence for requiring a guardian, and for his right of compulsion in some cases, is not free from debate, and to complete it is like pulling out thorns (kharṭ al-qatād; i.e., an impossible task). So reflect.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid read ﴿min 'ubaydikum﴾ with a ya' in place of the alif and with a fatha on the 'ayn. It is like 'ibad, the plural of 'abd, except that its use for slaves is more common than the use of 'ibad for them.

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾. The apparent meaning is a promise from Allah, mighty and majestic, of enrichment. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It is not unlikely that this is a way of closing the door to using poverty as an excuse and considering it a barrier to marriage.

There is an implied condition in the verse, namely the will (of Allah). So it is not objected that many poor people married and did not attain wealth. The evidence for this implied condition is His saying: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. That this verse was revealed concerning preventing the disbelievers from the Sacred Mosque does not negate its being evidence, as some imagined. Or (the evidence is) His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, i.e., rich, possessing abundance, whom the enriching of creatures does not diminish, since His favor has no end and His power has no limit; ﴿All-Knowing﴾, who extends provision to whom He wills and measures it as wisdom and benefit require. The matter of this ultimately returns to the will, and this is the secret in choosing "All-Knowing" rather than "Generous," even though "Generous" would fit "All-Encompassing" better when considered superficially.

In al-Intisaf: if it is said that the Arabs are like that, since their wealth is also contingent on the will, there is no point in the specification. The answer is that it has become established in the natures inclined to means that dependents are a cause of poverty and their absence is a cause of abundance of wealth. So this deeply rooted misconception is intended to be cut off, by showing that Allah may increase wealth despite many dependents, which in imagination is a cause of scarcity of wealth, and poverty may occur in celibacy, as reality attests. This shows that the imagined connection is false, and that wealth and poverty are by the act of Allah, the Causer of causes, and depend only on the will. So when the one marrying knows that marriage does not cause hardship, he will not be prevented from beginning it. The meaning of the verse then is that marriage does not prevent them from the wealth of Allah's bounty. He expressed the negation of marriage being a barrier to wealth by its existence together with wealth. Similar is His saying: ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], for its apparent meaning is a command to disperse upon the conclusion of prayer, and the intention is to establish the removal of the barrier, namely that once prayer is concluded there is no barrier to dispersing. He expressed the negation of the barrier to dispersal by something that requires dispersal, for emphasis. End of quotation.

Some said, distinguishing the married from the single: enrichment is closer for the married, and the connection of the will to him is more hopeful, because the text explicitly mentions his promise, unlike the single person. This is also found to be the case when inquired into.

It was objected that this overlooks His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 130], and similarly His saying (glorified be He): ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep chaste﴾ etc. The author of al-Kashshaf pointed out that in this verse and the one following it there is a promise of enrichment for both the married and the single together, so there is no objection to the question. He said: He (exalted) commanded guardians not to mind the poverty of a suitor once righteousness exists, trusting in Allah's kindness in enrichment. Then He commanded the poor to be chaste until they find wealth, as encouragement for them, and He incidentally included that the basis of the matter is chastity and righteousness under both circumstances, and this is the answer to the objector's question. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from you that the reports indicating the promise of enrichment for the one who marries are numerous, but we have not found any report concerning a promise to the single person who is not in the state of marriage as such.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three are a right upon Allah, that He help them: the one who marries seeking chastity, the mukatab (slave seeking to buy freedom) who seeks to pay, and the one who fights in the way of Allah."

Al-Khatib in his History transmitted from Jabir who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) complaining to him of poverty, so he commanded him to marry."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Obey Allah in what He has commanded you concerning marriage; He will fulfill for you what He promised of wealth. He (exalted) said: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: Seek wealth through marriage (al-ba'ah). In another wording: Seek wealth through marriage. Allah (exalted) says: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

Al-Tha'labi and al-Daylami transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Seek provision through marriage."

Along with other reports. For the enrichment of a poor man who marries there is a customary cause: his increased concern in earning and his complete striving in pursuit, since he has been tested with one whose maintenance is legally and customarily binding on him. To this is added the woman's assistance to him and her help to him in the affairs of his livelihood. This is common among the Arabs and the people of villages; we have found among them one whose wife suffices him for the matter of his livelihood and hers, through her occupation. Often, children are added to this, so the matter of mutual support and cooperation grows stronger. Sometimes the woman has relatives from whom he receives help according to his in-law relation with them, which is not found for the single man. This poor man who is marrying shares with the poor man who is about to marry the greater concern for earning, but this concern is for obtaining what he will marry with, and perhaps also for obtaining what improves his condition after marriage. It is not hidden that the condition of a married woman and that of a woman about to marry is similar to the condition of a man, and the difference is slight.

This said, the apparent meaning of some scholars' statements is that what was mentioned concerning the unmarried and the righteous is general, and the reference of the pronoun in the masculine is clear. It has been said that it is specific to free men and free women, and al-Tabarsi explicitly stated this, because slaves do not own property; even if they own, they do not inherit or bequeath. The one that is understood from enrichment by bounty is that they own that by which wealth is attained and need is removed, and this is not realized while slavery continues. Yes, if by enrichment is meant expansion and removal of need, whether through what one owns or not, then there is no harm in the generality. So reflect.

It was also permitted that the verse concerns free persons only, the meaning being a prohibition to guardians from using their poverty as an excuse when they are asked for marriage. And that it concerns men seeking marriage in general, with the meaning again being a prohibition to guardians from this as well. So reflect on all of this.

Some scholars argued, as Ibn al-Furs said, from the verse that marriage is not annulled by inability to provide maintenance, because He (glorified be He) promised enrichment in it. There is an objection to this that is not hidden.

[Page 150]

﴿And let those who cannot find a means of marriage keep themselves chaste, until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾: this is guidance for those who have desire but are unable to meet the preliminaries and means of marriage, directing them to what is better and more fitting for them. That is, let him strive for chastity (*'iffah*) and the preservation of the self. ﴿Those who cannot find a means of marriage﴾: that is, the means of marriage, or they are not able to afford what one marries with, namely wealth. (Here *fa''al* is taken to be an instrument noun, like *rukkab*, meaning what is ridden.) ﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾: a generous promise of favour to them with wealth, and of kindness towards them in their striving for chastity, and of strengthening their hearts. It is also an announcement that the bounty of the Exalted is more worthy of making one chaste and closer than the righteous.

Some of the Shafi'is have used this verse as evidence for the recommendation (*nadb*) of abstaining from marriage for one who does not possess its prerequisites while feeling intense desire (*tawaqan*). Many people, however, held that marriage is recommended for him, based on the verse ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾. They interpreted the command to chastity in this verse as applying to one who has not found a wife, by taking *fa''al* as an adjective in the sense of a passive participle, like *kitab* in the sense of *maktub*. But it is not hidden that the stated goal (enrichment) makes this interpretation remote. Poverty does not necessarily imply lacking the prerequisites (*uhbah*), which they explain as the dower (*mahr*), the clothing for the period of consummation, and the maintenance of its day.

What is mentioned in the authoritative works of our (Hanafi) school is that marriage becomes obligatory (*wajib*) at intense desire, that is, strong longing, such that one fears falling into fornication (*zina*) if he does not marry. Likewise, it seems, if he cannot restrain himself from forbidden looking or from masturbation by hand. It becomes an obligation (*fard*) if he cannot avoid fornication except by it, that is, if he is unable to resort to a concubine (*tasarri*) or to fasting, which breaks desire, as indicated by the hadith: "Whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield (*wija'*) for him." So if he is able to do any of these things, marriage no longer remains an obligation of individual duty (*fard 'ayn*) or a necessary obligation, but becomes, or something else, whatever prevents him from falling into what is forbidden. Both of these divisions are conditional on possessing the dower and the maintenance. Al-Bahr added another condition to both, namely the absence of fear of injustice. Then he said: If the fear of falling into fornication if he does not marry conflicts with the fear of injustice if he marries, the second is given precedence, and marriage is then disliked (*makruh*), as Kamal (Ibn al-Humam) stated in al-Fath. Perhaps this is because injustice is a sin connected with the servants (of Allah), unlike preventing oneself from fornication, and the right of the servant takes precedence in a conflict, since he needs it, while the Master, the Mighty and Majestic, is self-sufficient. End of quote. The implication of this is that it is also disliked when one does not possess the dower and maintenance, since these too are a right of the servant, even if he fears fornication. However, they mentioned that borrowing for the dower is recommended. The implication of this is that it is obligatory if he fears fornication even if he does not possess the dower, provided he is able to borrow it. This conflicts with the earlier condition, unless it is said:

[Page 151]

The condition is possession of maintenance and the dower, even by borrowing. Or it may be said: this applies to one who is unable to earn and has no means of repayment.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that what they stated about the recommendation of borrowing should be understood as recommended when one believes he will be able to repay. In that case, if it is recommended with this belief, provided he is safe from falling into fornication, it should be obligatory when fornication is certain. Indeed, it should be obligatory then even if he does not strongly believe he will be able to repay. In my view he is excused before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if he marries and dies without leaving repayment. So reflect. It is disliked when there is fear of injustice, as you have heard, and forbidden when injustice is certain, because marriage was legislated for the benefit of protecting the self and attaining reward, whereas through injustice one commits sin and perpetrates prohibited acts, so the benefits vanish because these harms outweigh them. It is a strongly emphasized sunnah (*sunnah mu'akkadah*), according to the more correct view, when one has the capacity for intercourse, the dower and the maintenance, with no fear of fornication or injustice, and no neglect of obligations and sunnas. If he lacks any of the first three, or fears any of the last three, marriage is not a sunnah for him, as al-Kasani stated in Bada'i'. It is understood from al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir by Ibn Nujaym that its being a sunnah depends on intention. Al-Fath mentioned that if it is not accompanied by intention, it is permissible (*mubah*), because its purpose then is merely the satisfaction of desire, whereas worship is based on the opposite, so one is not rewarded for it. The intention by which one is rewarded is to guard himself and his wife from what is forbidden, and likewise the intention to beget children through whom Muslims increase, and likewise the intention of following the Prophet (ﷺ) and complying with the command. In our (Hanafi) school this is better than occupying oneself with learning and teaching, as in Durar al-Bihar, and better than devoting oneself to voluntary worship, as several scholars have explicitly stated. In some authoritative works of the Shafi'i books it is stated that marriage is recommended for one who needs it and has the capacity of the dower, clothing for the period of consummation, and maintenance for its day. It is not recommended for one who is in the land of war (*dar al-harb*) to marry at all, out of fear that his child will be raised in their religion and enslaved. It must be understood as applying to one who does not strongly believe he will commit fornication if he does not marry, since a certain, immediate benefit takes precedence over a future, imagined benefit. If he lacks the capacity, it is recommended to abstain, according to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And let them keep themselves chaste﴾ (the verse), and to break his desire by fasting, according to the hadith. That heat and desire are aroused is only at the beginning of it, so if desire is not broken by it, he may marry. He should not break it with something like camphor, for that is disliked, indeed forbidden for both man and woman if it leads to despair of offspring. The statement of a group that the hadith indicates the permissibility of cutting off the capacity for intercourse by means of medicines is rejected, since medicines are dangerous, and some people used camphor and it produced lasting illnesses in them; then they tried to contrive to restore their capacity with costly medicines, but these did not benefit them. If he does not need marriage, it is disliked for him if he lacks the capacity. If he has the capacity but does not need it, then it is not disliked for him, since he is able to marry, and his purposes are not confined to intercourse. Devoting oneself to worship is better than it. If he does not devote himself to worship, then marriage is better according to the more correct view, as al-Nawawi said, because idleness leads to immoral acts. If he has the capacity but has a defect, such as old age, a chronic illness, or impotence of the same kind, it is disliked for him, since he has no need of it, and the woman is not protected, which generally leads to her corruption. With this, the statement of al-Ihya' is refuted, which says that it is a sunnah for one such as a eunuch to marry, in imitation of the righteous, just as it is a sunnah to pass a razor over the head of one who is bald. The statement of al-Fazari, that is, he forbade and rejected it for one such as a castrated man, and that need is not confined to intercourse. If these circumstances arise after the contract, does the ruling for beginning apply to them? Al-Zarkashi hesitated about this, and the second is the correct view, as is evident. End of quote.
