In this there is something not addressed in the books of our (Hanafi) companions as far as I know, but our principles do not reject it.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning is that the verse is specifically addressed to men, for they are the ones commanded to chastity when unable to meet the preliminaries and means of marriage. Yes, it is possible to say that it is general, with the consideration of predominance (*taghlib*), if by marriage is meant what one marries. But you know what is involved in this. And do not imagine from this that it does not recommend chastity for women at all, for it is evident that it may be recommended in some cases. Indeed, whoever reflects even slightly sees that the rulings apply to their marriage. But I have not seen anyone among our companions explicitly state this. Yes, some Shafi'is transmitted from al-Umm the recommendation of marriage for a woman with intense desire, and added to her one who needs maintenance and fears being molested by wicked men.

[Page 152]

In al-Tanbih: a woman for whom marriage is permissible, if she needs it, it is recommended for her. Al-Adhra'i transmitted it from the companions of al-Shafi'i, then examined whether it is obligatory for her if the wicked cannot be warded off from her except by it. Fasting has no place in this. From what has been mentioned, the weakness of al-Zinjani's statement becomes known: it is recommended for her unconditionally, since there is nothing upon her, together with what it involves of caring for her affairs and protecting her. Also weak is the statement of another: it is not recommended for her unconditionally, because she has grave rights toward her husband which she cannot easily fulfil. Indeed, if she knows about herself that she will not fulfil them and has no need of it, it is forbidden for her. End of quote. It is not hidden that what he mentioned afterwards is even more appropriate.

Some have used the verse as evidence for the invalidity of temporary marriage (*nikah al-mut'ah*), because if it were valid, chastity would not be specifically required of one who lacks the dower; and the apparent meaning of the verse requires it. This does not imply the prohibition of ownership by right hand (*milk al-yamin*), because one who cannot marry for lack of dower generally cannot buy a slave-girl either. This was mentioned by al-Kiya, and it is as you see.

﴿And those who seek the writing﴾: after commanding Allah, glorified is He, to marry off the righteous among the slaves who deserve to be married, He commanded, Mighty and Exalted is He, that those among them who are entitled to it be given a contract of manumission, so that he becomes free and disposes of himself. Ibn al-Sakan, in *Ma'rifat al-Sahabah*, transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Subayh who said: I was a slave of Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, so I asked him for the contract of manumission, but he refused, so the verse ﴿And those who seek﴾ and so on was revealed. From this it is hinted that the aforementioned 'Abd Allah was the first to be given a contract of manumission. Perhaps it is imagined from this that the contract of manumission was known before. But al-Khafaji transmitted from al-Damiri that he said: *al-kitabah* is an Islamic term, and the first to be given a contract of manumission by the Muslims was a slave of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, called Abu Umayyah. Ibn Hajar also explicitly stated that it is an Islamic term unknown to the pre-Islamic period. And Allah knows best.

*Al-kitab* is the verbal noun of *kataba*, like *al-mukatabah*, and its counterpart is *al-'itab* and *al-mu'atabah*, meaning: those among you who ask for the contract of manumission. ﴿From what your right hands possess﴾: whether male or female. In our (Hanafi) school, legally it is the freeing of the slave in the hand immediately and in the neck eventually. Its pillar is an offer with the word *kitabah* or what conveys its meaning, and the acceptance, such as the master saying: "I have made a contract of manumission with you for such and such a dirham, which you will pay to me, and you will be freed," and the slave says: "I accept." By this he leaves the master's hand but not his ownership. When he pays the entire price, he is freed and leaves his ownership. Its literal meaning is the writing of letters, that is, their gathering, and it is applied to what has been mentioned because it combines the freedom of the hand with the freedom of the neck. Or because the price is usually paid in instalments, some of which are added to others. Or because the slave writes down on himself for his master his price, and the master writes down for him the freedom. This is more suitable to the form of the verbal noun *mufa'alah*, meaning *mukatabah*.

In *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*: They said: its meaning is: "I have written for you upon myself that you be freed by me when you fulfil the wealth, and you have written for me upon yourself that you fulfil that," or "I have written upon you the fulfilment of the wealth, and I have written for the freedom with him." Then he said: The truth is that *mukatabah* is the name of the contract resulting from the combined statements of the owner and the slave, like the other legal contracts concluded by offer and acceptance. There is no doubt that this does not truly proceed except from the two contracting parties, and the function of each of them in reality is only to bring one of its two halves, expressing what is completed from his side and proceeds from him of his own action, without addressing what is completed from the other party's side and proceeds from his own action. However, since each of these two actions cannot be realized in itself except as dependent on the realization of the other, because the obligation of freedom in exchange for the price on the part of the master cannot be conceived of or realized except by the obligation of the price on the part of the slave, just as the contract of sale, which is the transfer of ownership of the sold item for the price from the seller, cannot be realized except by his acquiring it from the buyer, there is no alternative but to make each of them responsible for the other at the time of the formation. Just as the seller's saying "I have sold" is a formation of the contract of sale, in the sense that it is an effecting of what is completed from him primarily, and of what is completed from the buyer's side secondarily, as an effecting that depends on his opinion, with a dependence resembling the dependence of an unauthorized contract (*'aqd al-fudul*), so likewise the master's saying "I have made a contract of manumission with you for such and such" is a formation of the contract of *kitabah*, that is, an effecting of what is completed from its side, namely the obligation of freedom.

[Page 153]

By way of the counterpart of the exchange (al-badal) it is primarily an offer (ijab), and what is completed on the part of the slave is the undertaking of the exchange implicitly, as a unilateral declaration (iqa') dependent upon its acceptance; so when he accepts, the contract (al-'aqd) is complete. End quote. By this, a difficult problem that arises concerning the attribution of contract verbs is resolved. The problem is that if the pillar (rukn) of each of them is the offer (ijab) and the acceptance (qabul), it follows that a statement such as "I sold this for that" (bi'tu kadha bi-kadha), for example, would not be valid, because the speaker has only effected what is completed on his own side, and that is not a legal sale (bay' shar'i), since a legal sale requires another act, namely the acceptance of the buyer, which the speaker in question did not effect.

The summary: attributing the verb "sold" (ba'a) to the first-person speaker entails that he effected the sale, although he effected only one of its two pillars, so how can the attribution be valid? The way this problem is resolved by what has been mentioned is evident. However, it has been objected to this that it contains a claim which the intuition of every rational contracting party refutes. Do you not see that when you say "I sold," for example, there does not occur to your mind any implicit effecting by you of the purchase by another, a unilateral declaration dependent on his opinion at all; rather, the most that comes to mind is that he effects the purchase, not your effecting of his purchase in the manner of an unauthorized agent (fudhuli). Whoever claims that has contradicted his own intuition.

It is answered that implicit matters are sometimes taken into account legally even if they are not intended, as is indicated by the fact that in the statement of one who says to another, "Free your slave on my behalf for such-and-such," and he frees him, they took into account an implicit sale with its two pillars, even though the speaker did not have that in mind or intend it.

It has been examined in this regard that they took into account first the manumission (itq), which is the signified meaning of the utterance and what is intended by it, giving preference to the side of freedom. Then, when they saw that this depends on ownership (al-milk), which depends on sale according to the prevailing custom, they took into account the sale in order to complete for them the first consideration. They did not regard it as a signified meaning of the word "manumission" at all, such that intention would be a condition, even though their calling it an implicit sale might give that impression. This differs from what we are discussing, as you have heard, since the effecting of acceptance is a precondition for the very quiddity of the legal sale, and it is regarded as an implicit signified meaning of it, to the extent that it becomes in their understanding, as the apparent sense of the words of al-Irshad suggests, something like "I sold" meaning "I effected an offer from me primarily and an acceptance from you by delegation." And in such a case the existence of intention is evident. Since intuition negates the intention to effect acceptance by delegation, it is known that it is not an implicit signified meaning.

Some people have escaped the problem by holding that the sale is the offer, and that acceptance is a condition of its validity; so the statement of the speaker "I sell" is a creation of a sale that may or may not be valid, and when the other says "I buy," validity becomes determined. They also hold that the statement that the pillar of sale is offer and acceptance is one of the common loose usages. Or they hold that "sale" and similar terms have two usages: one, the contract resulting from the combination of offer and acceptance, as in your saying, "The sale took place between Zayd and 'Amr"; and the second, the offer alone, as in your saying, "I sold him such-and-such, but he did not buy." The sale signified by the performative "I sell" belongs to this category, so there is no problem in attributing it to the speaker. Reflect and ponder.

On this subject there are discussions which we have left out, fearing excessive digression from what we are concerned with. And God is the one who grants success.

(And) "those who" (alladhina) may be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so write (contract) with them﴾. This is with the supposition of a verb of saying, according to the well-known view that a performative sentence cannot be a predicate of the subject except in that way. Some verifiers said: there is no need for such an interpretation in a case like this, because it has the sense of a conditional and its consequent, and for this reason the predicate is introduced with the particle fa'.

It may also be in the accusative position, as the object of an omitted verb that the mentioned verb explains, and the particle fa' in it implies the conditional as well. In al-Bahr: it is permissible to say, "Zayd, so strike him," and "Zayd, strike him." When the particle fa' enters, the sense is "Be alert, so strike." Thus the fa' is in response to an omitted imperative. End quote. You know that this is not needed in the verse. Some eminent scholars mentioned that the fa' in it on the second possibility is because the explanation should follow what is explained, and what is meant is a writing after a writing, since there are many masters, and so there is not a command to the master with respect to a single contract-writer. End quote. This resembles speaking in a foreign tongue.

The command is for recommendation (nadb) according to the correct view. It has been said that it is for obligation (wujub), and this is the position of 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, Ibn Sirin and Dawud. And what 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas ibn Malik, who said: Sirin asked me for a contract of manumission (mukatabah), and I refused him. So he went to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and he came to me with the whip and recited His statement, exalted is He: ﴿so write (contract) with them﴾ etc. In another narration: "Write a contract with him, or I will strike you with the whip." This is clearly in favor of the view of obligation.

The majority of the imams, such as Malik, al-Shafi'i and others, hold that the contract of manumission after the request and the fulfillment of the condition to come, God willing, is recommended. Nevertheless, those among them who said that the apparent sense of the command is obligation, like al-Shafi'i, did not hold to its apparent sense here, because it comes after a prohibition, namely the sale of his property for his property, which is a permission; and he claimed that its recommendation is from another proof. The apparent sense of the verse is the permissibility of the contract whether the price is immediate, deferred, paid in installments, or not in installments, because of the absoluteness of the expression. To this the Hanafis went.

The majority of the Shafi'is held that it is a condition that it be paid in at least two installments, so it is not permitted without a term and installments in any form. It was said that if the master's ownership is of part of the slave and the rest is free, a term and installments are not required; their verifiers rejected this, and they answered the claim of the verse's absoluteness by saying that the contract of manumission implies installments, so it dispenses with the restriction, because he writes that he will be freed when he pays what is due upon him, and such a thing cannot be immediate.

They also objected to the view that an immediate contract is valid, saying that if the contract were made immediate, the demand would be directed at him immediately, and he would have no property with which to pay, so he would fail to pay and be returned to bondage, and the purpose of the contract would not be achieved. This is like a salam contract for something not available at the time the term falls due, which is not permitted. You know what is in the claim that the contract implies installments, and that it harms the Shafi'is, because the installment which the contract implies by their own claim is realized with one installment, so it should be permitted with one installment, as the majority of scholars held, whereas they do not permit that and require two or more. What they mentioned in the objection is nothing, for there is no inability when the Muslims are commanded to help him with charity, gift and loan. Analogy with salam does not hold, because the difference is clear. Perhaps what was mentioned is like a sale to one who does not own the price, and there is no doubt about its validity; so it was said, but there is room for discussion in this.

Ibn Khuwayzmandad said: if the contract is for immediate property, it is a manumission for property and not a contract of manumission. The difference between manumission for property and mukatabah is mentioned in its proper place. ﴿If you know good in them﴾, that is, trustworthiness and capacity for earning, and by these two al-Shafi'i interpreted "good." Al-Baydawi mentioned that this interpretation was narrated as a marfu' report, and something similar came in some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas. Others interpreted trustworthiness as not squandering property. It was said that the meaning may be uprightness (adalah), but on this interpretation the recommendation of the contract requires that the slave not be known for spending what is in his hand on disobedience, since such a person is not hoped to be freed by mukatabah.

Abu Dawud in al-Marasil and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning His statement, exalted is He, ﴿so write (contract) with them if you know good in them﴾: 'if you know in them a craft.'" Its apparent sense is sufficiency with capacity for earning and not requiring trustworthiness. This is a view Ibn Hajar reported from some of them, and he criticized it by saying that if the mukatib is not trustworthy, he will squander what he earns, so the purpose is not achieved.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, Qatadah, Ibrahim and Abu Salih that they interpreted "good" as trustworthiness. The apparent sense of their words is sufficiency with it and not requiring capacity for earning. Ibn Hajar also reported this from some of them and criticized it by saying that if the mukatib is not capable of earning, there is harm to the master in his mukatabah, and there is no assurance of his support by such things as charity and zakat.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he interpreted "good" as property. A group transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Ibn Jurayj, and it was reported from Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak. It was criticized as weak both in wording and meaning. As to wording, because one does not say "mal" (property) in this regard but rather "'indahu" or "lahu mal" (he has property). As to meaning, because the slave has no property, and because the understood sense of "good" is other than that, although "good" is applied to property in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves good, that he make bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. It was answered that for these eminent scholars "good" may mean the capacity to earn property, but they mentioned what is the primary purpose of it, out of laxity in expression, and there are many similar cases.

Abu Hayyan said: what appears from usage is that it is religion; one says, "So-and-so has good in him," and nothing comes to mind except righteousness. It was criticized: this does not fit the context and would imply that one should not write a contract with a non-Muslim. Many of our companions interpreted it as: that they not harm the Muslims after manumission, and they said: if there is strong suspicion of harm to them after manumission, then the better course is to refrain from writing a contract with them. The apparent sense of the conditional clause is that if they do not know good in them, it is not recommended for them to write a contract with them, or it is not obligatory upon them. This is due to the disagreement over whether the command is for recommendation or obligation, so the verse does not indicate impermissibility when the condition is absent; for what is required by the absence of the condition is only the absence of the conditioned matter, and in the verse there is only the command, which indicates either obligation or recommendation. Whoever said it is for permissibility held that the condition here has no implication, since it follows the customary practice regarding a contract with one whose goodness is known, so it was said. What I hold is that the contract is forbidden when the master knows that the mukatib, if freed, would harm the Muslims.

In the Tuhfah of Ibn Hajar, in the chapter on mukatabah, under al-Nawawi's words, "it is recommended if a trustworthy, strong slave who is capable of earning requests it, and it is never disliked in any case," the text is: "But al-Bulqini's inquiry is that it is disliked for a wicked person who would waste his earnings in sin; and if the master took control of him he would be prevented from that. He and others said: rather, the matter reaches prohibition," that is, the analogy of the prohibition of charity and loan when one knows that the recipient will spend them on something forbidden. Then I saw al-Adhra'i investigate it regarding one who is known to earn by way of sin, and it is explicit in what I mentioned, since the basis is enabling him through it to do what is forbidden. End quote. What he mentioned as the basis exists in this case, as we have said. Then, by knowledge is meant strong assumption, which is the basis of most legal rulings.

﴿And give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾. The apparent sense is a command to masters to give the mukatabin some of their property as assistance to them, and in its ruling is the remission of some of the mukatabah money. What suffices in this is the least that counts as property.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bayhaqi and others transmitted through 'Abd Allah ibn Habib from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A quarter is to be remitted for the mukatab." This also came in some narrations as a mawquf report from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said: it is the more correct view, and perhaps that is his own ijtihad, may Allah be pleased with him. The claim that this is not said on the basis of opinion and therefore has the status of a marfu' report is not accepted. On account of this report, and the statement of Ibn Rahawayh: the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) agreed that the quarter is what is meant by the verse. They said: the better course is to give a quarter. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan approved

The Shafi'is, however, say it is obligatory, since nothing diverts the command from obligation. They state that it binds the master (sayyid) or his heir, to be paid before the expenses of burial (ta'hiz).

As for remitting part of the debt owed by a mukatab (a slave who has contracted with his master to buy his freedom in installments), where the contract (kitabah) is valid, or paying back part of what was contracted for after it has been received, or paying it in kind: remission is preferable to payment, because it is what was transmitted from the Companions, and because the aid it gives is certain, whereas what is paid may be spent on something else. It is best in the final installment. The more correct view is that the time of obligation is before manumission, and it becomes urgent once only enough of the installment remains to cover what is due under the contract. It has spread that people say remission is obligatory. This is refuted by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The mukatab is a slave as long as a single dirham remains owed to him." For if remission were obligatory, the remainder would necessarily fall away. Also, if remission were obligatory, its obligation would depend on the contract, so the contract would be both the cause of an obligation and the cause of its cancellation at once. Furthermore, it is a contract of exchange (mu'awadhah), and so one cannot be compelled to grant remission, as in sale.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿آتُوهُم﴾ ("give them") is "lend to them." It has also been said that it is a command to them to spend on them after they have paid off and been freed. The attribution of the wealth to Him and the description of it as His giving to them (ـ"that Allah has given you") serves to urge compliance with the command by making the commanded act certain. For keeping in mind that the wealth reaches them from Him, glorified is He, while He, mighty and majestic, is the true owner of it, is among the strongest motives for spending it in the way commanded. It has also been said that it is a command of recommendation (nadb) addressed to all Muslims to help the mukatabun by giving them charity.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that he commanded the rulers to give them from the zakat. This is similar to what al-Zamakhshari mentions in the Kashshaf: that he commanded the Muslims, as an obligation, to aid the mukatabun and to give them their share which Allah has appointed for them in the public treasury (bayt al-mal), like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وَفِي الرِّقَابِ﴾ ("and for freeing slaves"). This is according to Abu Hanifa and his companions. It is lawful for the master, if he is wealthy, to take back what was given in charity to the mukatab, because of the change of ownership (tabaddul al-milk), as in the case where he buys charity from a poor man or the poor man gives it to him as a gift. For the mukatab then owns it as charity, and the master owns it as a return for the freedom. The same ruling applies if the mukatab becomes unable to pay the rest after paying part of it, and is returned to slavery, or is freed by some means other than the contract. The reason of change of ownership also applies according to Muhammad (al-Shaybani), though there is some obscurity in this, because what was taken was not given as a return for freedom. As for the case of return to slavery, it is clear; and as for the case of freeing by means other than the contract, it is because freedom was not conditioned on paying that. Consider this carefully.

Abu Yusuf explained the matter by saying that there is no impurity (khubth) in charity itself; the impurity lies in the act of the one who takes it, since it is a humiliation of the recipient, and that is not permitted without need. And taking it has not been done by the master. It was objected to him that this contradicts the description of charity as "the filth of people" in the hadith.

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that if the mukatab is returned to slavery or freed by means other than the contract, the master must return what he took, unless it has been destroyed before that, because what was given to the mukatab did not reach its proper place and the intended purpose was not achieved by it.

Al-Tibi said: From this it becomes clear that analogizing this to the charity that was bought from the poor man is not valid. In my view the criterion is the difference of the two aspects of ownership. Whenever that difference is established, no doubt remains regarding its lawfulness.

It is authentically reported that "Barirah, the freed-woman (mawlah) of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, came after her manumission with beef, and 'A'ishah said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'This is what was given in charity to Barirah.' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It is charity for her, and a gift for us.'" So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, pointed to its lawfulness for the Family of the House (Ahl al-Bayt), for whom charity is not lawful, because of the difference of the two aspects of ownership. Reflect on this. The mukatabah has many rulings, which are to be sought in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿وَلَا تُكْرِهُوا فَتَيَاتِكُمْ عَلَى الْبِغَاءِ﴾ ("And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution")

Muslim and Abu Dawud transmitted from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a slave-girl belonging to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, called Masikah, and another called Umaymah, he used to compel them to fornication. They complained of that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy had a slave-girl called Mu'adhah. Whenever a guest arrived, he would send her to him to have intercourse with him, seeking reward from him and honor for himself. The slave-girl came to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and complained of that to him. Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, who ordered that she be taken from him. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy shouted: 'Who will excuse us from Muhammad ﷺ, who overpowers us regarding our slaves?' Then the verse was revealed."

It has also been said: "This accursed man had six slave-girls: Mu'adhah, Masikah, Umaymah, 'Umrah, Arwa and Qutaylah, whom he compelled to prostitution and to whom he imposed taxes. Two of them complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed."

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning two men who used to compel two of their slave-women to fornication, one of them being Ibn Ubayy.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that they used to compel their slave-women to fornication in the Jahiliyyah, taking their wages, and they were forbidden from this in Islam, and the verse was revealed. A similar report is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. According to all the reports, the address is not restricted to the people concerning whom the verse was revealed, but is general to all who are responsible (mukallafun).

The word fatayat is the plural of fatat. Each of fata and fatat is a well-known metaphor for the male slave and the female slave in general. The Lawgiver ﷺ commanded that they be expressed with the possessive pronoun of the first person (my) attached, rather than as "slave" and "slave-girl" with the pronoun attached to them. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my slave-girl,' but say 'my young man' (fata-ya) and 'my young woman' (fatati)." It seems that he ﷺ disliked servitude to anyone other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and there is no restriction on Him, glorified is He, in attributing the latter two to other than Him, exalted is His majesty. And the expression mentioned in this discussion, considered in its original meaning, has a fine placement and added appropriateness to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿عَلَى الْبِغَاءِ﴾ ("to prostitution"). Al-Bahr says that prostitution is the fornication of women, in that it proceeds from their youthful ones, because they are the ones from whom it is generally expected, rather than the aged and the young girls.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿إِنْ أَرَدْنَ تَحَصُّنًا﴾ ("if they desire chastity") is not meant to restrict the prohibition to the case where they desire to abstain from fornication, excluding other cases from its ruling, as when compulsion occurs because of their dislike of fornication with a particular man, or at a particular time, or in a particular place, or for other such reasons that in general justify the compulsion. Rather, it serves to preserve the custom of those concerning whom the verse was revealed, for they used to compel them to prostitution while they wished to keep chaste, together with the strength of their desire that commands immorality and their deficiency in knowing the matters that call to good and restrain from ugly deeds. In this there is an addition for disparaging their condition and condemning the ugly deeds they committed, which is not hidden. For whoever has even a little manliness hardly accepts the immorality of those in his house from among his slave-women, let alone commanding them to it or compelling them to it, especially when they desire chastity. And it intensifies the reprehensibility, as the expression "they desire" in the past tense indicates. The use of the word "if" (in) rather than "when" (idha) is because the desire for chastity among slave-women is like a rare exception; or it serves to announce the obligation to desist from compulsion when the desire for chastity is in the realm of doubt and uncertainty, so how much more so when it is certain to occur, as is the actual case. From the justification of this condition, together with what we have indicated of fine explanation, it is understood that the placement of "fatayat" here, considered in its original meaning, is that it has no implied restriction (mafhum) even if it is taken as a qualifier. For the condition for recognizing an implied restriction, according to those who hold it, is that the mentioned item must not have come out in the usual manner. Some have used the verse to refute the view that implied restriction is valid, saying: "If it were recognized, it would entail permissibility of compulsion when there is no desire for chastity, whereas compelling to fornication is impermissible in any circumstance by consensus (ijma')." What we have mentioned makes clear the answer to this.

In the commentary of al-Adud on the Mukhtasar of Ibn al-Hajib, the answer to this is given: first, that it is among what came out in the usual manner, since what usually happens is that compulsion occurs when there is a desire for chastity, and there is no implied restriction in such a case. Second, that the implied restriction did indicate that, but it has been negated by a stronger contrary evidence, namely consensus. This may be answered by saying that it indicates the absence of prohibition when there is no desire, and that this is established, since compulsion is not possible at that time: for when they do not desire chastity, they are not compelled to prostitution, and compulsion is merely the imposition of a disliked act; and when there is no compulsion, the prohibition does not attach to it, because the condition of responsibility is possibility. And the absence of prohibition does not entail permissibility. End of quotation. Perhaps what we have mentioned first is the better. Many have made the addition of disparagement and condemnation a separate answer with a slight change, and there is no harm in that.

Some have claimed that ﴿إِنْ أَرَدْنَ﴾ refers back to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَأَنْكِحُوا الْأَيَامَى مِنْكُمْ﴾ ("And marry the single among you"). This is something from which wonder arises. In sum, there is no proof in this for those who refute the view of implied restriction. Likewise, they have no proof in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لِتَبْتَغُوا عَرَضَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا﴾ ("seeking the goods of this worldly life"). For it, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, is a qualifier of the compulsion, not because it is the basis for the prohibition of it, but because it is what is customary among them as well. It is mentioned to condemn them for what they do, since they risk a great burden for the sake of a paltry gain. That is: do not do what you are doing, compelling them to prostitution, in pursuit of a fleeting enjoyment that is about to vanish. So "seeking" here means the seeking that is accompanied by attaining the sought thing and actually enjoying it, since that is the proper meaning for it to be the aim of the compulsion and to be consequent upon it, not the bare seeking which precedes and motivates it. And the "goods of the worldly life" are not restricted to their earnings, namely the wages they take for fornication, although many reports apparently suggest this. Rather, they include also the children born of fornication. This was the explanation given by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as transmitted from him by Ibn Abi Hatim. Some reports suggest that they used to compel them to fornication for the sake of the children.

Al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted with an authentic chain from Ibn 'Abbas that a slave-girl of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy used to commit fornication in the Jahiliyyah, and bore him children from fornication. When Allah, exalted is He, forbade fornication, he said to her: "What is the matter with you that you do not commit fornication?" She said: "By Allah, I will never commit fornication again." He beat her, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿وَلَا تُكْرِهُوا﴾ ("And do not compel") the verse. This and similar reports do not necessitate restricting the "goods" to the children, as is not hidden.

I have heard that some tribes of the Bedouins of Iraq, such as the family of 'Izzah, command their slave-girls to commit fornication for the sake of the children, like the practice of the Jahiliyyah. This is not surprising from the Bedouins, especially in such eras in which many of the gardens of the legal rulings (riyad al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah) have been obliterated in many places by a storm (i'sar). For they are the most deserving of not knowing the limits of what Allah has revealed. There is no power and no strength except with Allah.

**Part 4 of 4**

His words, "And whoever compels them" to its end, form a resumptive sentence (*jumla musta'nifa*), brought in to confirm the prohibition and to stress the obligation to act, by explaining that the compelled women are freed from the punishment of the one who compels them. The expression is a metaphor, and the harm of compulsion returns to the compellers, which is an allusion. That is, "And whoever compels them to what has been mentioned, namely prostitution, **[then indeed Allah, after their being compelled, is Forgiving, Merciful]** to them." This is as in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, which Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him, but with "lahunna" placed before "ghafurun rahim." It is also narrated in the same way from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. According to what has been said, the words "after their compulsion" point to this, meaning "after their being compelled." Here the compulsion is a verbal noun of the passive form, and placing it between the particle *inna* and its predicate signals that this is the cause of forgiveness and mercy.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "Ghafurun rahim" is for them (the women) and not for them (the men). Al-Hasan, whenever he recited the verse, would say: "Lahunna, by Allah, lahunna."

The specification of this for the women, and the restriction of its basis to what you have heard, along with the earlier mention of the compellers, also indicates in the conditional clause that the compellers are entirely deprived of forgiveness and mercy. It is as if it were said: "No, for them" or "No, for him." Because this supposition is evident, the conditional noun (*ism al-shart*) is treated as not needing a returning pronoun (*'a'id*) in the conditional sentence, according to the more correct view, as in *al-Mughni*. It has also been said, regarding the question of the returning pronoun, that "their compulsion" is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the genitive construction, with the object as its genitive complement, and the subject of the verbal noun is an omitted pronoun returning to the conditional noun. The omitted element is like the stated one, and the sense is "after their compulsion of them." Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that they do not count the omitted subject of a verbal noun among the linking elements (*rawabit*) in constructions like "Hind was amazed at the striking of Zayd" (where the sense is "at her striking of Zayd"). They did not permit this structure, and there is no difference between that and what we are discussing. It has also been said that the answer to the condition is omitted, and what is stated is a reason for what is understood from that omitted answer. The sense is: "And whoever compels them, then upon him is the burden of their compulsion, which does not extend to them. Then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving, Merciful to them." But this involves deviating from the apparent meaning and adding an excessive ellipsis without necessity, and the claim that this is for the causal link of the answer to the condition is of no value.

Al-Bahr (*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan) says: "The correct view is that the supplied words are 'Forgiving, Merciful to them,' so that the answer to the condition contains a pronoun returning to the conditional noun, which is the subject of the answer clause, and this is conditional upon repentance." But this undermines the eloquence of the sublime composition and diminishes the matter of the prohibition in a context of severe warning, and the linking does not depend on this. Similar to it is what has been said: that the supplied words are "for both of them." The preferred view is what has preceded. As for the prepositional phrase in the reading of the one I heard about, Ibn Jinni said: it is connected to "ghafur," because it is closer to it, and because *fa'ul* is more firmly transitive than *fa'il*. It may also be connected to "rahim," because of the preposition, if it is considered a predicate following a predicate. It is not taken as a qualifier of "ghafur," because a qualifier cannot precede what it qualifies, and a complement can only occur where its governing element occurs, which is not the case with the predicate. Also, it is better in the predicate, because the rank of mercy is higher than the rank of forgiveness, since forgiveness is caused by it. Thus it is as if it precedes in meaning, even if it follows in wording. The sense, with its connection to both, is clear.

Making forgiveness for them conditional on their being compelled, though they bear no sin, is based on the principle that the compelled person is not legally responsible, and there is no sin without responsibility. The detailed treatment of this issue belongs to the books of legal theory (*usul*). It has been said that this is because of the severity of punishment for the compelled person: since the compelled woman, despite the existence of an excuse, is nearly subject to punishment and in need of forgiveness, what then of the compelled man? It is also to indicate that the legal limit of compulsion, and the endurance one must maintain until one reaches it, is narrow, so that a person commits the act, and Allah, by His kindness, forgives that. It has also been said that this is to emphasize the gravity of fornication, and to urge the compelled women to strive to stay away from it. Or it is because of the consideration that these women, even though they are compelled, cannot be entirely free, in the midst of fornication, from some trace of willing submission, by the innate human disposition.

[p. 159]

[p. 160]

**﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that make things clear﴾** [34. 40]. This is a new statement, introduced among the preceding and following verses to show the greatness of their matters, which call for wholehearted commitment to acting upon their content. It opens with an oath, expressed by the *lam* of emphasis, to highlight the full care given to this matter. The meaning is: "By Allah, We have certainly sent down to you, in this noble surah, verses that make clear everything you need clarified, such as the *hudud* (the prescribed penalties), the other rulings, the etiquettes, and other matters that are among the foundations of such clarification."

Regarding **«مُبَيِّنَاتٍ»** (*mubayyināt*, "making clear"): the word may be transitive with its object omitted, and the attribution of the clarifying to the verses is then metaphorical (*majāzī*). Or the meaning may be "verses that are evident, which the earlier scriptures and sound minds have confirmed." Or **«مِن بَيْنَ»** (*bayyana*) may be intransitive in the sense of *tabayyana* ("to become clear"), meaning verses whose being verses from Allah the Exalted has become clear. From this comes the proverb: "The morning has made itself clear to the one with two eyes."

The two Harams (the scholars of Makkah and Madinah, *al-Ḥaramayn*), Abu ʿAmr, and Abu Bakr read **«مُبَيَّنَاتٌ»** (*mubayyanāt*) in the passive form, meaning verses that Allah the Exalted has made clear, rendering their indication of the rulings, the *hudud*, and other matters evident. It is also permitted that the original sense is "verses in which the rulings are made clear," so the adverbial expression was extended by treating it as an object.

Page 160

**﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾**: this is coordinated with **﴿āyāt﴾** ("verses"). The meaning is: "And We have sent down an *mathal* (example, parable) of the kind of the examples of those who passed away before you, from the wondrous narratives and the parables struck for them in the earlier scriptures and in the sayings transmitted through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them." Thus it includes, in a preliminary way, the story of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, which parallels the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the story of Maryam, may Allah be pleased with her, in that what was attributed to ʿĀʾishah of the slander was similarly attributed to them, and Allah cleared them both of it. It also includes the other examples mentioned in this noble surah. This is more suitable to the statement's following with what will come, if Allah wills, of illustrations, by restricting the verses to the preceding matters and confining the *mathal* to the wondrous narrative alone.

**﴿and an admonition﴾** by which you are admonished and restrained from what is unbefitting, such as the forbidden and disliked acts and everything else that harms the good of manners. It refers to what preceded of verses and examples, since it is evident that they are admonitions in the sense mentioned. The mere difference in designation, treated as if it were a difference in essence, is sufficient for coordination. The verses have been specified as those that clarify the *hudud* and rulings, and the admonition as that by which one is admonished, such as His saying: **﴿And let not compassion for them seize you in the religion of Allah﴾** [al-Nur: 2], and His saying: **﴿Why, when you heard it﴾** [al-Nur: 12], and other verses that concern etiquettes. The admonition is qualified by His saying:

**﴿for those who are mindful of Allah﴾**, although it encompasses all people according to the scope of the sending down, in order to urge the addressees to seize the opportunity of being counted among the God-fearing, by indicating that they alone are the ones who benefit from its effects and draw from its lights. It has been said: the intended meaning of the "clarifying verses," the "examples," and the "admonition" is all that is in the glorious Qur'an of verses, examples, and admonitions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 1 of 6):

﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.﴾ Al-nur (light) in the language, as Ibn al-Sikkit said, is al-diya' (radiance). This is evident in that there is no difference between al-nur and al-diya'. Yet a group has distinguished between them, although the application of each to the other is common. Al-Imam al-Suhayli, in al-Rawd, said regarding the verse of Waraqa:

"And radiance appears in the lands, a light by which the creation is set to stir."

He clarifies that al-nur and al-diya' differ: al-diya' is what spreads out from al-nur, and al-nur is the origin. In the Revelation: ﴿So when it lit up what was around it, Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance (diya') and the moon a light (nur)﴾ [Yunus: 5], because the light of the moon does not spread from it what spreads from the sun, especially at the two ends of the month. The philosophers said: diya' is what belongs to a thing from its own essence, and nur is what is poured onto it from facing a luminous body. On this basis, it is claimed by their Islamic followers, came the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾. The variation of the moon's phases by its nearness to and distance from the sun, together with its eclipse at the time the earth comes between it and the sun, is evidence that its light is poured onto it from facing the sun. You know that in this there is a debate among the scholars of Islam, and we have already presented what is in it in another place. Perhaps the most appropriate basis for the distinction is what preceded just now in al-Suhayli's words.

Some verifiers have mentioned that it is known from their words that each of al-nur and al-diya' has a rhetorical aspect: the rhetorical aspect of al-nur is that it is the origin and source of al-diya', and the rhetorical aspect of al-diya' is that seeing in actuality occurs through its intervention. Some claimed that al-nur in absolute terms is more eloquent than al-diya', because of the verse we are concerned with. There is a discussion of this which, God willing, will be known during its interpretation. Know that the philosophers differed about the reality of light. Some of them claimed that it is small bodies that separate from the luminous object and connect to the illuminated object. This was refuted in several ways. The first: if it were a moving body, its motion would be natural, and natural motion is toward one direction only, not all directions; yet light falls on a body in every direction it has. The second: if it enters through a niche and then we seal it at once, those luminous parts either remain in the house, and then the house must be lit as it was before sealing, which is not the case; or they exit through the niche before it is sealed, which is impossible, because the sealing was the cause of their cessation, so it must have been prior to it either in essence or in time; or they are not remaining at all, which means a body has come between two bodies causing the annihilation of one of them, and this is known to be false. The third: that those small bodies are lights either is identical with their being bodies, which is false, since the concept of luminosity differs from the concept of corporeality; or it is different from it, in that those bodies carry that quality separated from the luminous object and connected to the illuminated object. If those bodies are not perceptible, this is plainly false, since then how could they be an intermediary for the perception of others? And if they were perceptible, they would be veils over what is behind them, and it would necessarily follow that the more they gather, the more they veil; but the matter is the reverse, for light, the more its power increases, the more it manifests. The fourth: when the sun rises above the horizon, the whole face of the earth is lit at once, and it is far-fetched that those parts should move from the fourth sphere to the face of the earth in that subtle instant; and its state is not hidden according to the view that the spheres cannot be pierced. The fifth: the separation of parts from the stellar bodies entails wasting and diminution, and the emptying of their places of the full measure of their magnitude or the measure of their parts, or their being constantly dissolving while replacement is supplied for what dissolves from their mass; thus their bodies would be nourishing bodies that are transmuted, generated and corrupted, and that is impossible for celestial things.

Some of their later scholars criticized these arguments as extremely weak. As for the first, that light is a body does not necessitate that it is moving, nor that its origination is by motion; rather it is something that exists all at once without motion. As for the second, one may say: the subsistence of what is made without matter occurs only through the agent that makes it, with the condition that the obstacle preventing the outpouring is absent; so when an obstacle arises, the outpouring does not occur, and what was poured out ceases without matter remaining from it, because its existence did not come about through the sharing of matter, so its non-existence is likewise. Thus, at the closing of the door that prevents the outpouring, the ray ceases from the house all at once. There is no difference in this between it being an accident or a substance, and the secret in both is that light in general does not come about through the affectation of matter or the sharing of hyle, as with the other substances and accidents that are subject to affection; therefore none of them ceases all at once even if a barrier were supposed between them and the active principle, except after a time and a transformation. As for what was mentioned third, its answer is that difference in concept does not contradict unity and identity in existence; so what was stated is a sophism arising from confusion between the concept of a thing and its reality. As for what was mentioned fourth and fifth, their basis is separation and cutting of distance, not mere substantiality and corporeality.

That said, some held that it is an accident of the perceptible qualities, and they said: it is independent of definition like all perceptible things. Its definition as "the first perfection of the transparent insofar as it is transparent," or as "a quality whose seeing does not depend on seeing something else," is a definition by what is more obscure; and it seems the intent of this is to alert to some of its properties. Among these are those who said: it is the very appearance of color, and among them are those who held that they are different and argued with several arguments. The first: the appearance of color indicates the renewal of a matter, so it is either the color itself, or a relational attribute, or a non-relational one. The first is false, because light is either made to be an expression for the renewal of color or for the renewed color; the first requires that it not be illuminated except at the instant of its renewal, and the second makes light itself the color, so the saying "light is the appearance of color" no longer has meaning. If they make light a real quality additional to the essence of the color and name it "appearance," then that is a verbal dispute. If they claim that this appearance renewed as a relational state, then that is false, because light is a non-relational matter; otherwise it would be a mental thing falling under the category of the relative and not perceptible at all. Yet the visual sense is affected by it, and is harmed by the intense of it until it is nullified. Mental things do not produce this kind of effect; so if it is not possible for a relational matter, it cannot be explained as a relational state. The second: whiteness may be luminous and shining, and so may blackness; so if the light of each were the very essence of each, some light would be the opposite of some other light, which is impossible, since the opposite of light is darkness. The third: color exists without light, as in a colored body in darkness; and likewise light exists without color, as in crystal when light falls on it; so they are different, since each exists without the other. The fourth: a red body, for example, when luminous, is reflected toward an opposite object; sometimes the light is reflected from it to another body, and sometimes both color and light are reflected from it when they are close, so that the reflected object becomes red. If light were merely the appearance of color, it would be impossible for it to give another a simple luster. One cannot say: this glare is an expression of the manifestation of the color in that receptive thing; for it is said: then why, when the color of the reflecting body intensifies, does its light obscure the light of what is reflected toward it, nullify it, and give it its own color?

Some later scholars said: it has been settled that sensible light, insofar as it is sensible, is an expression for the mode of existence of the seeing substance present to the soul in another world; as for what is outside corresponding to it, its existence does not exceed the existence of color. The arguments mentioned for their difference are flawed. As for the first argument, it is flawed in that the appearance of color is an expression for its existence, and it is a real attribute which by nature can be attributed and related to the perceiving power, and in this respect renewal occurs to it. As for their saying that this requires light to be the very color, we say: yes, but they are different in conception, just as existence and quiddity in everything are identical in essence yet differ in conception. Light and luminosity, in meaning, return to a specific existence accidental to some bodies; darkness is an expression for the total absence of that specific existence; shadow is an expression for its absence in part; and color is an expression for a mixture occurring between the bearer of this luminous existence and the bearer of its absence, in various modes. So the colors are nothing but degrees of compositions of lights. The proofs brought to refute this are weak. Thus the saying "light is the appearance of color" is sound, and the saying of one who says it is other than color is also sound, because light as light does not vary, since no mixture or admixture with absence or darkness is considered in it, whereas colors vary. As for the second argument, it too is dismissed by what has been laid down, and because although color is none other than light, the degrees of lights differ in intensity and weakness; and along with this difference they may differ in other respects according to many compositions and mixtures that occur between numbers of light and its possibility, actuality, root and branch, and numbers of darkness, meaning the absence of that light, its possibility, actuality, root and branch. For these colors are material matters for the most part, or connected to matter, and matter is a stronghold against division and composition between existences and non-existences and possibilities. So it is no wonder that from the various combinations of light with darkness these colors we see arise; those divisions occur in their substrates in the stated manner, and then another light falls upon them by facing the luminous source.

Whoever says that light is the very color does not say that every light is the very essence of every color, just as whoever says that existence is the very quiddity does not say that every existence is the very essence of every quiddity, lest it follow that no existence is not shared by another existence, nor is any existence opposed to another existence. Colors therefore differ in their rulings, and some of them are opposites, but insofar as they are colors, not insofar as they are lights, just as existents differ in their rulings and some

Page 163

...things that are opposites, but not as quiddities (māhiyyāt) in their own right, rather as existents (mawjūdāt), even though existence and quiddity are one. As for the third aspect, its refutation is easy, as is clear from what precedes. Likewise the fourth aspect is dispelled with the slightest reflection. The non-appearance of a colour may be due to the weakness of the light falling on an object, and it may be due to the intensity of the light. So what falls on the opposite surface, from the reflection of a coloured luminous body, may be only its light, and that happens when the light and the colour are both deficient, or when the receptivity of the opposite receiving body is deficient. And it may be both together, because of their strength and the strength of the receptivity of the body to which the reflection is directed. However, the discussion of reflections is lengthy. As for the reflection from a luminous body onto another body, where its light but not its colour is transmitted, this may be because of its polish, for a polished thing may have a colour and a light. But what is reflected from it onto its opposite is nothing but what arises from another luminary through its mediation, according to a specific positional relation between them and it, not the colour and light that inhere in it. So what is reflected onto that opposite is nothing but the light alone from that luminary, not from what is reflected from it, unless the body onto which it is reflected is also a polished body, in which case there is imprinted in it a representation of both, that is, of the light and the colour, or of one of them.

This is the furthest that they have said concerning the sensible light by which bodies appear to the eyes. They have another usage of light, which is that which is manifest in itself and makes other things manifest. They said: in this sense it is equivalent to existence, or even identical with it, so it is a simple reality like existence, divided as existence is divided. Among it is a light that is necessary in itself, dominant over all else; and among it are intellectual, soul-related and corporeal lights. The Necessary Being, exalted is He, is the Light of lights, of unlimited intensity, and all else besides Him, glorified is He, are lights of limited intensity, in the sense that above them there is what is more intense than them, although some of them, such as the intellectual lights, have effects that do not stop at any limit. All of them are flashes of His light, mighty and majestic is He, even the dense bodies, for they too, in terms of existence, are not free of light, but it is mixed with the darknesses of non-existence and contingent possibilities. Now that you know this, know that applying the term light to God, exalted is He, in the linguistic and the judgmental sense mentioned above, is not correct, because He is utterly exempt from corporeality, quality and their necessary attributes. However, applying it to Him, glorified is He, in the sense mentioned, namely that which is manifest in itself and makes others manifest, has been permitted by a group, among them the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali, for after mentioning in his treatise Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche of Lights), along with the meaning of light and its degrees, he said, may his secret be sanctified: "When you know that light returns to manifestation and making manifest, know that there is no darkness more intense than the concealment of non-existence, for the dark is called dark because it is not apparent to sight, although it exists in itself. So that which is not existent at all, how could it not deserve to be the ultimate in darkness?"

And in opposition to it is existence, which is light, for a thing does not appear to others unless it appears in its own essence. Existence is divided into that which belongs to a thing from its own self and that which belongs to it from another. What has existence from another, its existence is borrowed, for its own self, and indeed, if its essence is considered in terms of its essence, it is pure non-existence; it is only existent in terms of its relation to another, and that is not real existence. So the real existence is God, exalted is He, just as the real light is God, mighty and majestic is He. He had said before this: I say, and I do not mind, that applying the name light to other than the First Light is purely metaphorical, for everything other than Him, glorified is He, if its essence is considered in terms of its essence, then in itself, in terms of its essence, it has no light; rather its luminosity is borrowed from another, and its borrowed luminosity has no subsistence in itself but in another, and attributing the borrowed to the borrower is purely metaphorical. He interpreted the light in this verse, that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ in this sense. Then he pointed to the aspect of the annexation to ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾ by his saying: It should not be hidden from you, after you have known that He, exalted is He, is the Light and there is no light other than Him, and that He is all the lights and the universal light, for light is an expression for that by which things are disclosed, and higher than it is that by which it is disclosed, and that to which it belongs and from which it comes, and there is nothing above it
[page 164]
of light from which it derives its borrowed light and its support; rather that belongs to it in its own essence, by its essence, not from another. Then you have known that this is not characterised except by the First Light. Then you have known that the heavens and the earth are filled with light of two strata: light in the sense attributed to sight, and light attributed to insight, that is, to beauty and intellect, like the light of the stars, the substances of the angels, and the visible lights that spread over everything on the earth, and the lights of prophethood and the Qur'an, and so on.

This is a Sufi approach, and the Sufis do not shrink from saying that He, glorified is He, exalted above what the wrongdoers say to a great height, is All, indeed He is He, and there is no quiddity-ness (huwiyya) for anything else except metaphorically. They say: "There is no god but Allah" is the monotheism of the common people, while "There is no god but He" is the monotheism of the elect, because it is more complete, more specific, more comprehensive, more truthful, more subtle and more inclusive, bringing its adherent into pure singularity and sheer unity. Al-Ghazali also said this in the aforementioned treatise. You know that this is something not reached by the light of inferential reasoning; rather it is a stage beyond the stage of the intellect, and it is not reached except by the light of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) permitted that the meaning of light in the verse is the Originator, as if it were said: Allah is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. The basis of this is that it is a metonymy (majāz mursal) by consideration of a necessary meaning of light, namely manifestation in itself and making others manifest. It was also said: it is a metaphor (isti'āra), the borrowed-from being light in the sense of that which is manifest by itself and makes other things manifest, and the borrowed-to being the Necessary Existent who brings into existence what is other than Him. And it was said that its meaning is the Bestower of perception and its giver, as a metonymy or a metaphor, and the speech is by elision of a modifier, i.e. the light of the people of the heavens and the earth. This is close to what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth": the Guide of the people of the heavens and the earth. This is a good interpretation. In another narration, transmitted by Ibn Jarir from him, may Allah be pleased with him, he interpreted light as the Governor, saying: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth, He governs the affair in them." This was also related from Mujahid. Some made this a eloquent simile (tashbih baligh).

The point of resemblance is that each of governance and light is a cause of being guided to benefits. It was also permitted that there is here a declarative metaphor (isti'āra taṣrīḥiyya).

It was objected that mentioning both sides of the simile, namely Allah, exalted is He, and the light, contradicts that. It is answered that their mention contradicts it only if it is in a manner that indicates a simile, and each of the likened and the likened-to is mentioned exactly; but here Allah, glorified is He, did not liken Himself to light; rather He likened the Governor to it. And a particular that the likened applies to, or a universal that includes it, does not contradict that, as al-Zamakhshari indicated in several places in his work, and the masters of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) stated it. It was also said: the meaning is the one free from every defect, and from this is their saying: a woman nuwār, meaning one innocent of suspicion and of immorality; and this too is from the domain of metaphor. It was also said: the speech is by elision of a modifier, as in "Zayd is generous" meaning "possessor of generosity," i.e. "possessor of light." It is supported, as was said, by His saying after ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ and ﴿Allah guides to His light﴾.

It was also said: nūr in the sense of munawwar (illuminated/illuminating). This was related from al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak, and a group of exegetes adopted it. It is supported by the reading of some who read munawwir (the illuminator), and likewise the reading of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Abu Ja'far, 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Makki, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Thabit ibn Abi Hafsa, al-Qawrasi, Muslima ibn 'Abd al-Malik, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas ibn Abi Rabi'a: "nawwara" as a past-tense verb, and "al-ard" in the accusative. His illumination, glorified is He, of the heavens and the earth, was said to be by the sun, the moon and the rest of the stars, and it is attributed to al-Hasan and those with him. It was also said: the illumination of the heavens is by the angels, peace be upon them, and the illumination of the earth by the prophets, peace be upon them, and the scholars; and it is attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The illumination on the first view is sensible, and on the second it is intellectual. It was also said, and this is what he chose: His illumination of them, glorified is He, by what is in them of the signs of creation and of revelation,
[page 165]
which indicate His existence, His oneness and all His attributes, mighty and majestic is He, and which guide to the welfare of life and the hereafter. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf musawwiq), either to establish that His clarification, indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you manifest verses﴾ and so on, is not restricted to what came in this noble surah; or to affirm the clarity contained in the glorious Qur'an. Something like this may be applied on some of the earlier views concerning the meaning of light, and it is a strong aspect of the connection of the verse with what precedes it, and something like it can hardly appear in respect of some other views. Al-'Allama al-Tibi, in explaining the connection, stated words containing both the worthless and the valuable; if you wish to see them, return to him.

The specifying of the heavens and the earth in mention is because they are the well-known abode of the responsible beings, who need what guides them and directs them, as has preceded.

Al-'Allama al-Baydawi, after mentioning several possibilities regarding the meaning of light, said: the annexing of it to them serves to indicate the breadth of its radiance, or because they include the sensible and intellectual lights, and the limitation of human perceptions regarding them, and regarding what is connected to them and what is indicated by them. It was also said: the intended meaning of them is the whole world, like the use of "the Emigrants and the Helpers" for all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

This was objected to: this is the use of the name of a part for the whole, metaphorically, and al-Taftazani's Talwih stipulated that the whole be compounded in a real composition, and it is not established in the language that "earth" is used for the totality of earth and heaven, or "human" for the son of Adam and the beast. It is answered: it is not necessarily a metaphor, since it may be a metonymy (kinaya). Even if it be granted, what is in the Talwih is not agreed upon, or it is a majority usage. Al-Zamakhshari, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nothing on the earth or in the heaven is hidden from Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 5], mentioned that He expressed the whole world by the heaven and the earth. Al-'Allama, in his commentary on it, said: it is the use of the part for the whole; the meaning then is: Allah is the Light of the whole world. ﴿The likeness of His light﴾, that is, His rational and revealed proofs in the heavens and the earth, by which He guides whom He wills to what is good for him. This was related from Abu Muslim, and the Qur'an fits this in a primary way. And from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam, the meaning of light here is the Qur'an, as what precedes indicates, when it described His verses as sent down and clarifying. He also explicitly called it light in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174]. It was also said the meaning is the Truth, for light has been used as a metaphor for it, just as darkness is used as a metaphor for falsehood, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqara: 257], that is, from kinds of falsehood to truth; and the basis of the resemblance is manifestness. And among their proverbs: "The truth is clear." This suffices for the permissibility of the metaphor, and it does not depend on the realisation in the truth of what is in light of the meaning of making manifest. Yes, if that too is realised, it is light upon light. But he preferred the weakness of interpreting it by what was mentioned rather than the Qur'an, because it is incompatible with the context of explaining the status of the verses and describing them with the clarification mentioned, together with the absence of any prior mention of the Truth.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 3 of 6):

In al-Kashf: "The intended meaning of 'the truth' by which light is explained is that which is the opposite of falsehood (batil), and it encompasses monotheism (tawhid), the sacred laws (shara'i), and what is indicated by the evidence of revelation (sam') and reason ('aql). The intended meaning is not that the heavens and the earth are two proofs of the existence of their Originator (fatir); rather, that too falls within the general scope of the wording." End of quotation. It is weak as to this, and the weakness of this is evident. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the guidance (huda) indicated by the clear verses. It has also been said: guidance in general. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The likeness of His light is the likeness of His guidance in the heart of the believer." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Anas that he said: "Indeed my God says: My light is My guidance." Some have mentioned that explaining it as guidance is the preference of most scholars, and that explaining it as truth in the general sense agrees with it. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the knowledge and sciences which He, glorified and exalted, poured into the heart of the believer, and the attribution of this to Him, glorified is because He is its bestower, exalted is He. It is also reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Dahhak that its explanation is faith (iman) which He, glorified is He, gave the believer and granted him success in.

Page 166

In some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that it is explained as the acts of obedience with which He, great is His majesty, adorned the heart of the believer, so it includes faith and all other praiseworthy inner actions of the heart. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "His light" is His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), and the application of the term "light" to him, upon him be prayers and peace, has come in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15], according to one opinion. It has been said other than this, which you will know, God willing, exalted is He. The pronoun, according to all these opinions, refers to Him, exalted is He, as is the apparent meaning.

He permitted the pronoun to refer to the believer, and this is narrated from 'Ikrimah and is one of the narrations; al-Hakim authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It is also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Indeed, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif transmitted from al-Sha'bi that he said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "the likeness of the light of the believer." Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abu al-'Aliyah that Ubayy recited "the likeness of the light of whoever believed in Him," or he said: "the likeness of whoever believed in Him."

In al-Bahr it is narrated from Ubayy that he recited "the likeness of the light of the believers." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), and a group narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas from Ka'b al-Ahbar, and Abu Hayyan related it from Ibn Jubayr as well. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an, and it has been said to refer to faith. There is no concealing that referring a pronoun to something not mentioned in the speech, when the speech contains nothing that indicates it, or when it does contain something but its indication of it is hidden and highly contrary to the apparent meaning, is especially so when the intended purpose of the speech is lost under that reading. The intended meaning of "mathal" here is the amazing description, i.e., the description of His light, glorified is He, which is of marvelous import. ﴿Like a niche﴾, i.e., like its description in illumination and enlightening. Abu Hayyan said: i.e., like the light of a niche (mishkah), which is a non-piercing recess (kuwwah), as Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, Ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn 'Iyad and the majority said. Abu Musa said:

It is the small iron or lead piece in which the wick sits within the glass vessel. From Mujahid: it is the iron on which the lamp is hung, and this, as you see, is not right; the reliance is on the opinion of the majority. From Ibn 'Atiyyah: it is the most correct of the opinions. In all of them it is a loanword from Abyssinian (Habashi), arabized, as Ibn Qutaybah and al-Kalbi and others said. It has been said that it is Roman (Rumi) and arabized. Al-Zajjaj said, as in Majma' al-Bayan: it is possible that it is Arabic, in which case it is of the form mif'alah, and the original is mashkuwah; the waw became alif because it is vowelled and the preceding letter is open. Ibn Jinni went to the view that the origin of its alif is waw, and he argued for this by the fact that the Arabs have inclined it toward the inclination of the waw, as they did with al-salat.

Al-Kisa'i, by the transmission of al-Duri, read with imalah (inclination) ﴿in it is a lamp﴾: a large, piercing lamp. It has been said that the wick is kindled. ﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾: in a lamp of pure, bright glass. The vowelling of the zay (in zujajah) with damma is the dialect of the Hijaz, and with kasra and fatha is the dialect of Qays. With fatha, Abu Raja' and Nasr ibn 'Asim read, in the transmission of Ibn Mujahid.

Some also read with kasra, and likewise it is read with both in His saying: ﴿The glass is as if it were a star, brilliant (durri)﴾: shining, sparkling, like a flower in its clarity and its brightness. It is attributed to durr (pearl), so its measure is fi'li. He permitted that its origin be dara'a with a hamzah at its end, as Hamzah and Abu Bakr read, so it became ya' and was assimilated into the ya', so its measure is fa'il, and it is from al-dar' meaning repelling, for it repels darkness by its light, or it repels some of its light by some of its shine. He permitted that it be from al-dar' meaning running, but it is not so; and like it is what is said, that it is from daraa when it rises and surprises. It is not concealed from the one who investigates that fa'il is rare in their speech. In al-Lubab: fa'il is strange, with no parallel except murig (for dyed-yellow stuff), or what grew fat of horses, and 'aliyyah, sirriyyah and dhurriyyah, as Abu 'Ali said. In al-Bahr: mirrikh, which is in the inside of the dry horn, was also heard, and it has two dialects, with damma and kasra on the mim. Al-Farra' said: only murig was heard, and it is non-Arabic (a'jami). Sibawayh counted that among the patterns of the Arabs, and some did not establish this measure at all.

Page 167

Abu 'Ubayd said: the origin of "dara'a" is duru'un like sabuh, so the damma was made into kasra for heaviness, and the waw into ya' because of the breaking of the letter before it, as they said in 'utuw: 'atiy. So its measure is fu'ul, and likewise it has been said of sirriyyah and dhurriyyah. Some made sirriyyah from sirr, which is marriage or concealment, and the damma is one of the changes of the nisbah, so its measure is fi'liyyah, as in the Sihah.
