Al-Akhfash holds that it is from surur (joy), and the last ra' was changed into ya', which is familiar in the verb, for they said: tusurrirat jariyah and tusurriyat, as they said: tazannanat and tazanniyat. So its measure on this view, as al-Khafaji said, is fa'ilah. Some made dhurriyyah a nisbah to dharr, against analogy, because of their being brought out like the dharr from the back of Adam, peace be upon him.

Qatadah, Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Dahhak read "duriyya" with fatha on the dal; this is narrated from Nasr ibn 'Asim, Abu Raja', and Ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Zuhri read "duriyya" with kasra on the ra'. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "duri'a" with kasra and a hamzah at its end, and this is a common pattern in nouns, like sikkin, and in adjectives, like sikkir. Qatadah also, and Aban ibn 'Uthman, Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Raja', 'Amr ibn Qa'id, al-A'mash and Nasr ibn 'Asim read "duri'a" with hamzah and fatha on the dal. Ibn Jinni said: this is rare; there is nothing preserved of it except sikkinah with fatha on the sin and shadda on the kaf, in a dialect transmitted by Abu Zayd. It was read "da'riyy" with the hamzah placed before the ra' as a sakin, and this is among the rare anomalous readings. In the repetition of "the lamp" and "the glass" as definite, after their previous mention as indefinite, and the report about them with what follows, with the speech being coherent, if it were said: like a niche in which is a lamp, in a glass, as if it were a star brilliant, there is in this the magnifying of their matter, the raising of their station, by explanation after ambiguity and detail after generality, and by affirming what follows them for them by way of report, which indicates the primary intent, rather than the descriptive form which indicates mere affirmation in general, which is not hidden. The first clause is in the place of raising, as an attribute of "lamp," and the second clause is in the place of lowering, as an attribute of "glass," and the relative particle is dispensing with the connecting pronoun, as in Majma' al-Bayan and Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim. It is as if it were said: in it is a lamp which is in a glass which is as if it were a brilliant star. ﴿It is lit from a tree﴾: i.e., the kindling of the lamp begins from a tree ﴿blessed﴾: i.e., abundant in benefits, by its wick being fed with its oil. It has been said that it was described as blessed only because it grows in the land which God, exalted is He, blessed for the worlds. It has been said that seventy prophets, among them Abraham, peace be upon him, prayed for blessing in it. ﴿Olive﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tree﴾. Abu 'Ali said: it is an explanatory apposition to it. It has been said that seventy prophets, among them Abraham, peace be upon him, prayed for blessing in it. ﴿Olive﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tree﴾, and Abu 'Ali said: it is an explanatory apposition to it. This is based on the view of the Kufans, who permit explanatory apposition in indefinites; as for the Basrans, they permit it only in definites.

In the indefiniteness of the tree and its description with blessing, then the substitution for it or its explanation, there is magnification of its status.

Indeed, in a hadith the praise of olive oil has come, because it is from it. 'Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad, and al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah transmitted from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Eat with olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."

Al-Bayhaqi transmitted from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that olive oil was mentioned in her presence, and she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to order that it be eaten, used as an ointment, and applied as nasal drops, and he would say: 'It is from a blessed tree.'"

It is praiseworthy in itself. In the hadith it is a cure for hemorrhoids (basur). The physicians have mentioned for it many benefits. "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to eat bread with it," and "the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, ate tongue (lisan) cooked with barley, in which there was olive oil and spices." So let this be noted.

Al-Akhawan, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatadah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, 'Isa and al-A'mash read "tuqadu" with the ta' of two dots from the form of the present tense of aw qada, in the passive voice, so that the pronoun standing in place of the subject refers to the glass; and the attribution of the verb to it is said to be by way of hyperbole. It has been said that it is with an implied noun, i.e., "its lamp." Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Qatadah also, Ibn Muhaysin, Salam, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "tuqadu" with the upper ta' as well, the present of tawaqqud, and its original is natawaqqadu with two ta's, so it was lightened by dropping one of them. Al-Khafaji mentioned that this is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir, and the attribution in it is to the glass, as has passed. Qatadah, Salam and al-Sulami also read "yuqadu" with the ya' from below, as the present of tawaqqada too, and it came thus from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, and its original is yatawaqqadu, i.e., the lamp, so the ta' was dropped. This is not known with the ya'; what is known is the dropping upon the meeting of two identical ta's.

The explanation of this, according to Ibn Jinni, is that a letter of the present-tense prefix was assimilated to another letter of the present-tense prefix, meaning the ya' to the ta', so it was treated as its treatment, just as the ta' and nun in ta'addan and na'uddu were likened to the ya' of yu'eddu, so the waw was dropped with them, as it was dropped in it, because it occurred between a ya' and a kasra.

And it was read "tuqadu" with the ta' from above, in the form of the past tense of tafa''ul, and the pronoun refers to the lamp, meaning: beginning, the lamp is kindled from a tree.

[p. 169]

"Neither eastern nor western": that is, it receives the sun all the time. No mountain or tree shades it, and nothing blocks the sun from it from its rising until its setting. This is best for its oil. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Kalbi, and it is an explanation by a necessary implication of the meaning, namely that it is situated between east and west. It is also narrated from Ibn Zayd that it means it is neither from the trees of the east nor from the trees of the west. This is because what belongs to only one of the two directions yields less oil and gives weaker light. Rather, it is from the trees of al-Sham (Syria), which lies between the east and the west, and its olives are of the finest quality. Abu Hayyan said in his Tadhkirah: The meaning is that it is never in a place of sunshine, that is, a place no shade reaches, and never in a place of shade, that is, a place the sun does not reach. The summary is that the olive tree is not reached by the sun exclusively, nor by shade exclusively, but at one time this reaches it and at another time that. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is not eastern only, nor western only, but it is both eastern and western, that is, the sun reaches it at its rising and at its setting. You know that a qualifier must be supplied after each of "eastern" and "western", as you have heard, so that the negation applies to it. Then the construction conveys the combination of both matters. Otherwise the apparent meaning is the negation of both. It is also said from al-Matla' that this is like the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"In the hands of men who have not sheathed their swords,
and the slain have not been many by them when they were drawn."

Its meaning is that they have not sheathed their swords and have made many slain by them. Al-Kashf (Zamakhshari's commentary) objected to this, saying there is no proof from the verse for this, since it may mean that they have not sheathed them, being those who did not make the slain many, as a circumstantial clause (hal). In that case the meaning mentioned is clearly conveyed.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is in a tree surrounded by other trees, so it is not exposed either from the east or from the west. This was objected to, on the grounds that this cannot be authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, because if it had this attribute its fruit would be blocked.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that this is a parable, and that it is not from the trees of this world, since if it were in this world it would be either eastern or western. It is narrated from Ikrimah that it is from the tree of Paradise. Perhaps he asserted this because of what al-Hasan said, but its problems are not hidden.

al-Dahhak read "lā sharqiyyatin wa lā gharbiyyatin" with nominative (raf') endings, meaning: it is neither eastern nor western.

Abu Hayyan said: That is, it is neither eastern nor western. Perhaps what we have mentioned is better. The clause is in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for "olive tree" (zaytūnah).

﴿Its oil would almost give light, even if no fire touched it﴾. That is, it is in such purity and brightness that it would almost shine by itself, without fire touching it at all. The word "law" (even if) in such contexts is not intended to show that one thing is absent because another is absent in past time. Therefore no answer (jawab) is noted for it, as an answer deleted with confidence in what precedes it indicating it, unless the aim is to show grammatical analysis according to the technical rules of the grammarians. Rather, it serves to affirm the truth of what the preceding statement conveys, whether affirmative or negative, in every state of affairs assumed to accompany it in general, by placing it upon the most remote of them. The "wa" (and) attached to it is for conjoining the mentioned clause to a deleted clause opposite to it, according to al-Jazuli and those who agree with him. The two clauses together occupy the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the affirmative or negative verb. The estimate of the noble verse is: "Its oil would almost give light if fire touched it, and even if fire did not touch it," that is, it shines in every state, whether the condition of illumination is present or absent. The first clause is deleted, as is common in this construction, with confidence in the clear indication of the second clause.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The "wa" is for the circumstantial clause, and its implication is that "law" together with what follows is a circumstantial clause. So the estimate is "while it is the case that, whether something is or is not so," that is, supposed to be established or not established. But al-Zamakhshari, and al-Marzuqi with him, estimate: "even if the circumstance were so." This was objected to on the grounds that conditional particles are not fit for the circumstantial sense, because they imply non-realization while the circumstance implies the opposite. For this reason he held that the conditional sense has been stripped from it, and that it is interpreted as a circumstance, just as a circumstance can carry the meaning of a condition, as in "I will do it, whatever happens," meaning "if this or something else happens." For this reason it does not need an answer at all. It is said that he estimated the circumstance after "law" to show that he intended to make the clause a circumstance before the conditional sense entered, which contradicts it, and then "law" was introduced to indicate that it is a circumstance not realized. Al-Radi objected to the claim that it is a conjunctive particle, on the grounds that if it were so, the conjoined element would have been stated in usage, and it is not so. He held that it is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah).

Parenthesis is permitted at the end of a statement, and its purpose is emphasis. His objection was answered on the grounds that the clear following of the answer from the conjoined element made mention of it unnecessary, so that mentioning it would be repetition. It is also answered with the clause after which the majority conjoin and approve, namely that it is conjunctive, and that the two clauses together occupy the position of a circumstance as stated, which removes the supposed conflict between the conjunctive reading and the conditional sense here, so reflect.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan read "yamassuhu" with the yā' (third person masculine), and the separation (fasl) and the fact that the subject is not a feminine of real gender made it acceptable.

﴿Light upon light﴾. That is, it is a great light, situated upon light. This is on the basis that "nūr" is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the prepositional phrase is connected to a deleted verb in the position of a qualifier to it, emphasizing the grandeur indicated by the indefiniteness. The clause is a summary (fadhlakah) of the parable, a statement of what resulted from it, and a preparation for what follows. So the pronoun refers to the light whose great attribute has been likened by what you have heard, not to the light that is the thing compared. Taking it to refer to the latter, as some have said, is not fitting for the glorious revelation. The meaning of its being light upon light is not that it is one specific light, or an unspecified light, upon another light like it, nor that it is merely a combination of two lights, but that it is a light that has multiplied without limit, since its multiplication is not bounded by a specific measure. This is with the determination of the degrees of multiplication of what has been likened, namely the light of the niche (mishkat), by what has been mentioned, since this is the furthest degree of multiplication usually. For a lamp in a confined place, like a niche, is brighter for it and gathers its light more completely, because of the joining of the reflected ray to the original ray. This is unlike a wide place, where the light spreads and disperses. The lamp (qindil) is the most helpful thing for increasing illumination, and so is the oil and its purity. Beyond these degrees there is nothing that increases its light in brilliance and extends it with the illumination of another degree usually.

It seems to me that the comparison contained in the noble verse is the comparison of an intelligible thing, namely His light, may He be exalted, with the meaning of His proofs, may He be glorified. But inasmuch as they are proofs, or the Qur'an, or the monotheism and laws, and what they indicate by the evidence of revelation and reason, or the guidance, or the like, they are likened to the sensible thing, which is the light of the niche, described in an exaggerated way. The thing compared has no parts from which the resemblance is abstracted in order to build upon it that it is compound or separate. He mentioned that if the intent is to compare light in the sense of guidance, which the clear verses indicate, then it is compound intellectual similitude (tashbih), in which the abstracted configuration is compared with another configuration. For light, although its wording is singular, indicates a plurality. Likewise, if the intent is to compare what the light of God, may He be exalted, has placed in the heart of the believer of knowledge and insight, with the light of the niche radiating from its lamp.

In al-Hawashi al-Tayyibah al-Tayyibiyyah, after choosing that the intended "light" is guidance by a revelation He sends down and a messenger He raises, there is what is clear that the comparison is a divided similitude. Indeed, he explicitly stated this at the end, and he argued for it by saying that the repetition in the verse requires it. He spoke at length on this point. Among its contents is that the things compared in this sense are: the breast of the Messenger (ﷺ), his noble heart, the divine subtle faculty within it, and the Qur'an, and what the heart is affected by when it draws upon it. The detail is that he likened his breast, upon him be prayers and peace, to the niche, because it is like an opening with two faces. From one face it draws light from the illuminated heart, and from the other that drawn light overflows upon creation. This is due to his readiness, through the expansion of his breast twice: once in his childhood, and once at his Night Journey. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So is one whose breast God has opened to Islam, and who is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. This is a sound comparison, which has become famous from a group of the exegetes. Muhyi al-Sunnah narrated from Ka'b: "This is the likeness God struck for His Prophet (ﷺ): the niche is his breast, the glass is his heart, the lamp in it is prophethood, and the blessed tree is the tree of prophethood." The Imam narrated from some of them that the niche is the breast of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, the glass is his heart, and the lamp is the religion that is in his heart. In the Haqa'iq of al-Sulami, from Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz: the niche is the chest of Muhammad (ﷺ), the glass is his noble heart, and the lamp is the light that is in it.

He likened the heart of the one upon whom be God's blessings and peace to the glass described as a shining star, because of its clarity, its brightness, and its purity from the turbidity of desire and the stain of the commanding self, and from the reflection of the light of the subtle faculty upon it. The holy subtle faculty blazing in the heart is likened to the piercing lamp.

Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Hearts are of four kinds: a heart that is most pure, in which there is like a lamp that shines...' — and in it — 'As for the purest heart, it is the heart of the believer; its lamp is in it, its light is in it.'" The hadith is [given] in full.

He likened the Qur'an itself to the blessed tree, because its root is firm, its branches spread, and it yields fruits without end. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿A good word is like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branch is in heaven. It gives its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 24-25], the verse. Muhyi al-Sunnah narrated from al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd that the blessed tree is the tree of revelation, "its oil would almost give light": the proof of the Qur'an would almost become clear even if it were not recited.

He likened what the noble heart of the one upon whom be God's blessings and peace draws from the Qur'an, and the beginning of its strengthening from it, to pure oil. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Just as He, glory be to Him, made the Qur'an the cause of its kindling from Him, in His saying: ﴿kindled from a blessed tree﴾, so He made its light derived from the reflection of the light of the subtle faculty upon it, in His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿even if no fire touched it﴾.

According to what has been mentioned, the meaning, in the sense of the pupil of the eye, is: the secret of the Qur'an almost appears to creation before the call of the Prophet (ﷺ). There is in this a touch of the meaning of the poet's words:

"The glass has become thin, and the wine has become thin,
so they resemble one another, and the matter has become uniform.
It is as if it were wine and there were no cup,
and as if it were a cup and there were no wine."

From this the tree is described as neither eastern nor western. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) is likened to the shining star, and that the blessed tree is Ibrahim, upon him be peace. The meaning of "neither eastern nor western" is that he was not a Christian who prays toward the east, nor a Jew who prays toward the west. The pure oil is the religion of Ibrahim, upon him be peace. It may be said, on the division of the comparison, but...

[p. 171]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 5 of 6):

according to another lawgiver, who likened the Qur'an to the lamp, as has preceded, and likened his own pure and purified self (ﷺ) to the tree, because it is planted in the soil of religion, its branches spreading up to the sky of faith, its fruits hanging down toward the expanse of sincerity and excellence. This is due to its uprightness in accordance with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], not leaning toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. This is the meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾. And there is resemblance between what is extracted from those fruits, after complete purification for readiness and for accepting impressions, and the pure oil, due to the abundance of the strength of its preparedness for being illuminated, being oily and capable of catching fire. For this reason the olive tree was singled out, because the core of its fruit is the oil with which lamps are kindled. This oil was singled out for its greater brightness together with little smoke. The oil of his preparedness, God's blessings and peace be upon him, nearly gives light, by its purity and purity of nature, even if the light of the Qur'an did not touch it. Al-Baghawi related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: "The virtues of Muhammad (ﷺ) almost became apparent to people before he was revealed to." Ibn Rawaha said:

Had there been in him no clear signs,
his very presence would have informed you of his news.

In Haqa'iq al-Sulami, the likeness of His light in His servant who is sincere: the niche is the heart, the lamp is the light cast into it, and the knowledge which illuminates in the heart of the knower by the light of success, kindled from a blessed tree, illuminates a blessed person; inner lights become evident through outward manners, and the goodness of his dealings is an olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, a pure jewel that has no share in this world or in the Hereafter, because of its being specially connected to the Mighty, the Forgiving, and its being singled out for the Single, the Overpowering, and so on.

Some have made the likeness a composite imagined likeness, on the basis that what is meant by the light being likened is guidance, insofar as it is surrounded by the darkness of people's imaginings and fancies.

On this view it would be apparent that the particle "ka" (like) should enter upon the lamp rather than the niche which contains it. Hence it has been said that there is an inversion (qalb) in the verse. Some have justified its entry upon the niche by saying that the container is mentioned before the contained in the eye's perception, so the word order placed it first and the particle "ka" entered upon it in keeping with this. It has also been said that on this view too the likeness is a divided likeness, since it likened guidance to the lamp and the ignorances to the darkness they entail. But this, as you see, is weak.

Some people have made the likeness divided, but built their discourse on what the philosophers established, so they took the light being likened to be what God, exalted is He, has bestowed upon His servants of the five perceptive faculties arranged in order, upon which livelihood depends. These are: the sensitive faculty, meaning the common sense which perceives sensible things through the spies of the five outward senses; the imaginative faculty which preserves the forms of those sensible things so that they may be presented to the rational faculty whenever it wishes; the rational faculty which perceives universal realities; the cogitative faculty which takes rational knowledge and composes it in a way by which knowledge of unknown things is attained; and the holy faculty which is peculiar to the prophets and saints, in which the flashes of the unseen and the secrets of the kingdom become manifest. They took what lies within the scope of the particle "ka" to be an expression of matters, each of which is likened to one of these five. He said: I likened the sensitive faculty to the niche, insofar as its seat is a hollow in the front of the brain, like a window in which the outward senses place what they sense, and by it there is illumination. He likened the imaginative faculty to the glass, insofar as it receives the perceived forms from all sides, just as the glass receives sensible lights from all sides, and insofar as it holds and preserves the rational lights as glass preserves sensible lights, and insofar as it is illuminated by what the intelligibles contain. The rational faculty was likened to the lamp, for its illumination by perceptions and knowledge. The cogitative faculty was likened to the blessed tree, insofar as it yields many results which are like the fruits of the tree. It was regarded as an olive tree because it has a virtue over the other trees, insofar as the core of its fruit is
page 172
the oil which has many benefits, among which is that it is the material of lamps and of sensible lights, and which alone among all oils has the special quality of greater brightness and little smoke. Taking the description "neither of the east nor of the west" as applying to the likened item is due either to the cogitative faculty being abstracted from corporeal attachments, or to the fact that its benefit is not restricted to the side of forms nor to the side of meanings. The holy faculty was likened to the oil which nearly gives light without fire touching it, insofar as, because of its perfect purity and intense readiness, it needs no teaching or reflection. An objection was raised that the proper arrangement of the noble composition on this view would be: "His light is like a niche, and a glass, and a lamp, and a blessed tree, an olive, and oil which nearly gives light, even if no fire touched it," so as to indicate the likening of each one to each one. It is answered that since each of these faculties takes what it perceives from what precedes it, just as the contained takes from its container, God, glorified is He, indicated this by the particle of containment, showing the wondrous craft of His, glorified is He, and His wisdom, exalted is His majesty.

It is also permitted that what is meant is the likening of the light, by which is meant the rational faculty of the soul, with its levels, to that. Its levels are four. The first: that the soul is empty of all necessary and acquired knowledge, yet prepared for it, as at the beginning of childhood; the rational faculty at this level is called the material intellect (al-'aql al-haylani), because it is like matter in that in itself it is empty of all forms and receptive of them. The second: that it employs its instruments, that is the senses, in general, so that primary knowledge is acquired for it, and it becomes prepared to acquire theoretical knowledge; the faculty at this level is called the intellect in habit (al-'aql bil-malaka), because the faculty of moving to theoretical matters is attained through those primary matters. The third: that theoretical matters become stored with it and it attains the habit of recalling them whenever it wishes, without fresh acquisition; the faculty at this level is called the intellect in actuality (al-'aql bil-fi'l), because those sciences are attained by it with a potentiality close to actuality. The fourth: that the primary sciences are arranged and it perceives the theoretical sciences, witnessing them actually; the faculty at this level is called the acquired intellect (al-'aql al-mustafad), because it benefits from the active intellect (al-'aql al-fa''al). So the faculty of the first level is likened to the niche, empty at the outset of the lights of sense, prepared to be illuminated by them; to the second level, the glass, shining in itself, receptive to the lights poured upon it from an external source; to the third level, the lamp whose wick is kindled, saturated with oil; and to the fourth level, the multiplied light referred to by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿light upon light﴾. Shaykh Ibn Sina, after explaining the levels, applied the words of the revelation to them. In al-Muhakamat he verified the order of arrangement therein, since he made the glass in the niche and the lamp in the glass: there is pure readiness, as in the first level; readiness for acquisition, as in the second level; and readiness for recall, as in the third level. There is no doubt that readiness for acquisition is according to pure readiness, and readiness for recall is according to readiness for acquisition. Thus the glass, which is the intellect in habit, is as if it were in the niche, which is the material intellect, and the lamp, which is the intellect in actuality, is in the glass, which is the intellect in habit, since it arises only through the attainment of the intellect first. And since the intellect in habit passes from potentiality to actuality only through reasoning, or through intuition, or through the holy faculty, he referred to reasoning by the olive tree, to intuition by the oil, and to the holy faculty by "its oil nearly gives light." He also answered what might appear as a mismatch between this and the noble composition, since it described the tree with the attributes you have heard. These are distinct matters, and it is not permissible to describe one of them by the other; the olive tree is one thing, and when it advances through its stages there results oil; when that oil advances in quality it nearly gives light. Likewise, acquisition is a soul-faculty which is reasoning, and when it advances it becomes intuition; then there is the holy faculty. Though these are distinct, they return to one thing, like the tree.
page 173

He also mentioned that His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾ indicates that it is not of the world of sense, which never lacks one of two conditions. It is not hidden from you that this, despite its strain and its being built on what the philosophers established, who are in blindness regarding the light of the Shari'ah, and God, exalted is He, has a fine verse about them:

Brotherhood was severed from a group
in whom there is a sickness from the Book of al-Shifa'.
They died upon the religion of Aristotle,
and we lived upon the Sunnah of the Chosen One.

It does not suit the context, nor do its parts harmonize with it; and in it there is what implies that His saying: ﴿light upon light﴾ falls within the likeness, and there is disagreement on this. Then know that with the help of what we have mentioned, one can know the state of the likeness according to the other opinions regarding the meaning of the light; and perhaps what we have mentioned is more complete in light and more evident in clarity. God, exalted is He, knows best the realities of matters. ﴿And whoever God does not grant light, for him there is no light﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. ﴿God guides to His light﴾ [al-Nur: 35], that is, He, glorified is He, guides with a special guidance that certainly conveys to the sought goal, to that mighty light of great rank. The expression of it in the place of the pronoun is to increase its establishment and to affirm its intrinsic grandeur by its relational grandeur, arising from its being attributed to His pronoun, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Whom He wills﴾: His guidance of His servants, by His, glorified is He, granting them success to understand the aspects of the indication of the rational and transmitted proofs by which He illuminated the heavens and the earth, in a manner by which they benefit; or by His granting them success to understand what is in the Qur'an of indications of its truth and that it is from Him, mighty and majestic is He, such as its inimitability, its reports of the unseen, and other things that necessitate belief. There are other possibilities according to the opinions regarding the light. In any case, it contains an announcement that the basis and foundation of this guidance is nothing but His, exalted is He, will, and that displaying the causes without it is far from leading to the goals:

When success is not an aid to the seeker,
the path of guidance is hard for him to attain.

﴿And God strikes parables for people﴾ within the folds of guidance according to what their state requires, for striking a parable has a great role in the matter of direction, since it is the presentation of the intelligible in the form of the sensible and the depiction of abstruse meanings in the image of the familiar. For this reason, He, exalted is His majesty, likened His light, meaning by it what includes the Qur'an or the clear Qur'an alone, to the light of the niche. The expression of the sublime Name in the place of the pronoun, according to what is in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, is to announce a difference between what is attributed to Him, exalted is He, of the special guidance and the striking of parables, which belongs to the category of general guidance, as its linking of the first to "whom He wills" and the second to "people" in general makes clear.

"And Allah is Knowing of all things," whether intelligible or perceptible, apparent or hidden. Among the requirements of this knowledge is that His will, exalted is He, be related to guiding those among people who are fit for it and deserve it, to the exclusion of others, because of the contravention of wisdom, which is the basis of creation (takwin) and legislation (tashri'). It also requires that His general guidance, glorified is He, take various forms and diverse methods, according to what their circumstances require, and by which the proof is established against them for Him, exalted is He. The sentence is an i'tiraḍ (parenthetical clause) of a concluding (tadhyil) type, confirming what precedes it. It was said that it was brought as a promise of reflection upon the parables and a warning to whoever paid them no heed. It was said that it explains that the benefit of striking parables, which serve for clarification, is only for people, and that this is not the case. The mention of the glorious Name is to emphasize the independence of the sentence and to indicate the cause of the judgment, and of what was mentioned just before, namely the difference in the state of the object of the judgment, both in its essence and in its relation.

**[Page 174]**

*"In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned. He is glorified therein morning and evening by men"* (24:36). The phrase **"men"** (*rijal*) begins a new, resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that explains the condition of those who were granted guidance to that light. It also mentions some of their inward and outward acts. The prepositional phrase, namely the phrase *"in houses"* (*fi buyut*) that is the complement of **"He is glorified"** (*yusabbihu*), is repeated with *"therein"* (*fiha*). This repetition was used for emphasis (*tawkid*) and to remind the reader of what came earlier in the sentence. It also signals that the fronting of the phrase is for emphasis, not for exclusivity. Similar examples of this repetition for emphasis include Allah's words: *"So in the mercy of Allah they abide therein forever"* (3:107), and your saying: "I passed by Zayd, by him." Some grammarians parsed such constructions as *badal* (substitution/apposition), as in the commentary on *Sharh al-Tashil*. In *al-Mughni*, it is said that it is an emphasis of the particle by repeating what it governs in pronominal form. The prepositional phrase is not an emphasis of the prepositional phrase, because the apparent (noun) is stronger and is not emphasized by a pronoun. Nor is the genitive noun a substitution by repeating the preposition, because a pronoun is not substituted by an apparent noun. Some grammarians permitted it only by analogy. You should know that what has been mentioned is not valid, because the whole is either a substitution or an emphasis. The apparent noun was used to avoid repetition. **"Men"** (*rijal*) is the subject (*fa'il*) of **"He is glorified"** (*yusabbihu*). It is placed after the adverbial phrases because its description has some length, and placing it first would disrupt the good arrangement of the sentence.

Al-Rummani said that *"in houses"* is connected to *yuqadu* (is kindled). Al-Hawfi said it is connected to an omitted verb that functions as an adjective of *mishkat* (niche). It was also said that it is an adjective of *misbah* (lamp), and it was said that it is an adjective of *zujaja* (glass). According to these four opinions, it restricts the thing used as the example, for the sake of emphasis on it. The nunation in the modified noun is for the category (*nau'iyya*), not for individuality (*fardiyya*), so that it does not contradict the plural of "houses."

It has been objected to what was mentioned that none of it is suitable to the dignity of the glorious revelation. How could it not be, since what follows Allah's words *"and had not fire touched it"* (24:35), according to the correct view, or what follows His words *"light upon light"* (24:35), according to what is said, up to His words *"of all things He is Knowing"* (24:35), is a statement connected to the example, definitely? Therefore, inserting it between the parts of the example, although it is of the type of separating the tree from its bark by a foreign element, leads to the mention of the condition of those who benefit from the example and are guided to His light by way of consequence and digression, while the explanation of the condition of their opposites is intended in itself. Such a thing is not known in human speech, let alone to be attributed to the inimitable speech.

Al-Khafaji criticized this, saying that it is an ornamental statement, since there is no separation in it, and what came before it up to here is part of the parable. In my view, the apparent meaning is that the parable was complete at His words *"and had not fire touched it."* It was said that *"in houses"* is connected to an omitted *sabbihu* or similar. That sentence, according to what is said, is consequent on what precedes it, and the omission of the particle *fa'* (then) is because it is known, as in *qum yad'uka* (stand, he calls you). They prohibited its being connected to *yadhkuru* (is mentioned), because it is part of the relative clause of *an* (that), so it does not govern what precedes it.

By "houses" is meant all the mosques, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and from Qatada and Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd that he said: "They are only four mosques, which none but a prophet built: the Ka'ba, which Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them, built; the Bayt al-Maqdis, which Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, built; the Mosque of Medina and the Mosque of Quba, which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ built." It was narrated from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is the Bayt al-Maqdis, and the plural is because it contains places that are distinguished from one another. This is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik and Buraydah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse, *'in houses'*, and a man stood up to him and said: 'What houses are these, O Messenger of Allah?' He ﷺ said: 'The houses of the prophets, peace be upon them.' Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this house among them, the house of 'Ali and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with them both?' He said: 'Yes, from among its best.'"

This, if it is authentic, should not be deviated from.

Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent meaning is that it is general, applying to the mosques and the houses in which prayer and knowledge take place." He permitted that it may mean the prayers of the believers or their bodies, since their prayers, which combine verbal and physical acts of worship, or their bodies surrounded by lights, resemble the mentioned houses, namely the mosques, and then their name is borrowed for that. He criticized this, saying that there is no beauty in what he mentioned, and I think you will not be satisfied with this degree of criticism.

By *"permitted to be raised"* is meant *commanded*, and by *"raised"* is meant *glorified*, that is, He, glorified be He, commanded that their status be glorified. This was narrated from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. It is not hidden that if the mosques are intended, glorifying their status is through various things, such as protecting them from entry by one in major ritual impurity (*junub*), a menstruating woman, or one in postnatal bleeding, even in passing, and they have stated the prohibition of this. It also includes bringing into them anything from which filth is feared. For this reason they said: "One who wishes to enter the mosque should check his sandal or shoe for impurity, and then enter, to avoid soiling the mosque." Also included is the prohibition of bringing a dead body into them, and the prohibition of bringing in children and insane persons. This is forbidden when their soiling is likely, and otherwise it is disliked. The command to keep them away from mosques has come in general terms.

Ibn Majah narrated from Wathila ibn al-Asqa', from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "Keep your children, your insane persons, your buying and selling, your disputes, the raising of your voices, the establishment of your legal punishments, and the drawing of your swords away from your mosques, and set up washing places at their doors, and gather them on the day of assembly." And he prohibited the reciting of lost property announcements and the reciting of poetry.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni, and Ibn Mandah narrated from Thawban, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever you see reciting poetry in the mosque, say: May Allah break your mouth, three times. And whoever you see announcing a lost item in the mosque, say: May you not find it, three times.'" The hadith continues.

The prohibition of reciting poetry should be restricted to when it contains something blameworthy, such as satirizing a Muslim, describing wine, mentioning women or beardless youths, or other things that are blameworthy according to the Sharia. As for when it includes praise of prophethood and Islam, or contains wisdom, or motivates noble character and asceticism and similar kinds of good, there is no harm in reciting it there.

Prohibited also is throwing a louse into it after killing it, and this is disliked as a matter of abstention (*tanzih*), according to what some later scholars have stated. It is recommended that a snake not be thrown into the mosque.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ahmad narrated from a man of the Ansar who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If one of you finds a louse in the mosque, let him place it in his garment until he takes it out."

He prohibited urinating in it, even into a vessel, and they have explicitly stated the prohibition of this. In *al-Ashbah* it is said: "As for bloodletting in the mosque into a vessel, I have not seen it." It should be that there is no difference, because both urine and blood are heavy impurities. He prohibited spitting in it.

In *al-Bada'i'* it is said: "Performing ablution in the mosque is disliked, because it is naturally disgusting, so it is obligatory to keep the mosque clean from it, just as it is obligatory to keep it clean of mucus and phlegm."

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from al-Sha'bi that the Prophet ﷺ saw in the direction of the mosque's qibla some phlegm, so he stood up to it and scraped it with his noble hand ﷺ, then called for perfume and smeared its place.

Al-Sha'bi said: "That is a sunna." They mentioned that placing phlegm on a mat is lighter than placing it beneath it. If one is compelled to do so, he should bury it.

In a hadith narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba from Anas, raised to the Prophet: "Spitting in the mosque is a sin, and its expiation is to cover it." Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* narrated similar from Ibn 'Abbas, also raised to the Prophet.

Prohibited also is sexual intercourse within it or on its roof, just like relieving oneself, and they have explicitly stated the prohibition of this. Prohibited also is entry by one who has eaten something with a foul smell, such as garlic, onions, or leeks, and one who has eaten radish and then belches similarly. In the time of the Prophet ﷺ, if a man was found to have the smell of garlic, he would be taken by the hand and led out to al-Baqi'. The apparent view is that one with bad breath, or one with persistent body odor, has the same ruling as one who has eaten garlic or onions. Likewise, one whose clothes have an offensive smell, such as the clothes of oil-sellers and tanners, is judged similarly. It is narrated from Malik that oil-sellers should hold back and not come forward to the first row, but sit at the back of the people.

Eating in it is prohibited, and so is eating garlic in it, except for one in seclusion (*mu'takif*). Sitting in it for mourning, or for talking about worldly matters, is prohibited. Making it a thoroughfare is prohibited, and this is either disliked or forbidden. The prohibition of this has come in a hadith narrated by Ibn Majah from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that making it a thoroughfare is one of the portents of the Hour. In *al-Qunya* it is said: "One who habitually does this is sinful and wicked. Yes, if there is an excuse, passing through is not disliked."

Among its honoring is sprinkling it with water and sweeping it. Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The mosque used to be sprinkled and swept in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He also narrated from Ya'qub ibn Zayd that "the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to follow the dust of the mosque with a palm branch." Likewise, hanging lamps in it and paving it with brick and mats.

In *Miftah al-Sa'ada* it is said: "The people of the mosque may pave the mosque with brick and mats and hang lamps. However, if the people of the mosque have funds, not the mosque's funds, that is only with the order of the ruler." Perhaps the place of this is where the founder (*waqif*) has not specified any part of the endowment's revenue for it.

It should be that kindling many lamps in it on certain nights of the year, such as the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan, which causes children and idle people to gather, play, raise their voices, and degrade the mosques, is an abominable innovation. Likewise, it should be that paving it with embroidered carpets which distract those who pray and remove their humility is similarly disliked.

Also among the honoring is to put the right foot forward when entering it and the left foot forward when leaving it. Also, the one entering should pray two rak'as before sitting, if his entry is not for prayer, according to what some have stated.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Abu Qatada that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the mosques their right." It was asked: "What is their right?" He said: "Two rak'as before you sit."

Among this also is building it high and lofty, unlike other houses. However, it should not be decorated with anything that distracts those who pray. In a hadith narrated by Ibn Majah and al-Tabarani from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, raised to the Prophet: "It should not be built with pictures, nor decorated with glass." Some interpreted "raising" as building it high, as in His words: *"And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il"* (2:127). In my view, it is better to interpret it according to what has preceded, and to include the building of it in this manner within the generality, which includes many matters other than what we have mentioned, which the jurists have mentioned at length.

Some exegetes claimed that attributing "raising" to it is metaphorical, and that the intended meaning is that the needs are raised in it to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: it raises voices by mentioning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in it. What is wrong with this is not hidden. In the expression "permitted" referring to the one who commands, there is an allusion that it is fitting for the one commanded to be turned toward what is commanded before the one who commands it, intending to fulfill it, as if he were seeking permission for it. So the command to it falls in the place of the command within it.

By mentioning His name, exalted be His glory, is meant what includes all of His remembrances. Among these are the scholarly discussions connected to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning is His unity, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the saying: "There is no god but Allah." Also from him: the intended meaning is the recitation of His Book, glorified be He.

[Page 177]

It has been said: the mention refers to His Most Beautiful Names. The apparent meaning, however, is what we have already stated. The mention (al-dhikr) is conjoined to "the raising" (al-raf', i.e., the raising of buildings) by way of ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm (the conjunction of the specific with the general), since the mention of His name in them is one of the forms of their glorification. It is not at all an ʿaṭf al-tafsīr (explicatory conjunction, where the second term explains the first), contrary to whoever imagined it. Al-tasbīḥ means declaring Allah transcendent and holy (al-tanzīh wa-al-taqdīs). It is used with the particle lām and without it, as in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1]. What is meant by it is either its apparent sense, or prayer, because prayer includes it. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Every tasbīḥ in the Qur'an is prayer." Confirming that prayer is meant here is the specification of the times by His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. Al-ghuduww is the plural of ghadāh, like fatan and fatāh, or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used for the time of morning. It is confirmed also by the fact that Abū Mujalliz recited "wal-īṣāl" as a verbal noun, meaning entering the time of the late afternoon (al-aṣīl). As al-Jawharī said, al-āṣāl is the plural of aṣīl, like sharīf and ashrāf. A group of scholars preferred this, although the plural of faʿīl on the pattern af'āl is not analogical.

Al-Zamakhsharī preferred that it is the plural of aṣl, like ʿunuq and aʿnāq. Al-aṣl is, like al-aṣīl, the evening, which runs from the decline of the sun to the morning. Thus it includes all the times other than al-ghadāh, which is from the beginning of the day until midday. Both terms are also applied to the beginning and end of the day. Their being mentioned separately is due to their nobility, and because they are the most common times in which people engage in their works and busy themselves with their affairs. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he took al-ghadāh to mean the time of the forenoon (al-ḍuḥā). This is what is implied by what Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Indeed the prayer of ḍuḥā is in the Qur'an, and the divers dive for it," and he recited the verse until he reached "al-āṣāl."

[Page 178]

Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr, al-Buḥturī from Ḥafṣ, Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr, al-Minhāl from Yaʿqūb, al-Mufaḍḍal and Abān recited "yusabbiḥu" with the yāʾ (third person masculine) and in the passive voice (al-binā' lil-maf'ūl). The deputy subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil) is ﴿lahu﴾ ("for Him") or ﴿fīhā﴾ ("in them"), if fī buyūtin is not connected to it, or ﴿bil-ghuduww﴾ ("in the mornings"). The first (lahu) takes precedence, because it is the one the verb is attached to, and the ascription to it is real, unlike the latter two. It has been permitted that the genitive phrase in what was mentioned is the deputy subject, with the prepositional phrase being redundant; but this involves a practice for which there is no need. The raising of "rijāl" (men) in this reading is either as the subject of an implied verb or as the predicate of an implied subject, according to what is in al-Baḥr: that is, "for Him glorifies men," or "men are the ones glorified for Him." The sentence is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), which came as an answer to a question arising from the preceding speech. This is like the saying:

"Let Yazīd weep, the one who has been struck down in a dispute, staggering from what the calamities cast down."

It is analogical according to many scholars, so it is permissible in their view to say: "Hind struck Zayd," with the meaning "her striking of him" or "his striker is Zayd." This is not like mentioning the agent as a specification (tamyīz) after a verb in the passive voice, such as "ḍuriba akhūka rajulan" (your brother was struck, a man), whose impermissibility Ibn Hishām declared explicitly in the fifth chapter of al-Mughnī, although the reasoning may suggest that it is similar. So consider this.

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Wathhāb recited "tusabbiḥu" with the tāʾ (feminine, i.e., the verb is agreeing with a feminine form) and in the active voice (al-binā' lil-fāʿil), and the subject is "rijālun" (men). The feminine form is because a plural of abundance (jamʿ al-takthīr) is very often treated as feminine. Abū Jaʿfar recited "tasbīḥun" with the tāʾ and in the passive voice, and the deputy subject is His saying ﴿bil-ghuduww wal-āṣāl﴾ ("in the mornings and the evenings"), with the bāʾ being redundant, and the ascription being metaphorical, by making the times in which their Lord is glorified "a means of glorification." Abū Ḥayyān permitted that the ascription is to the pronoun of tasbīḥah which is indicated by "tusabbiḥu," meaning "tusabbiḥu hiya" (it itself glorifies), i.e., the glorification itself. This is like what they said regarding His saying ﴿that He may recompense a people﴾ [al-Jāthiyah: 14] in the reading of one who put yajzī in the passive voice, meaning "li-yajziya huwa" (that it itself may recompense), i.e., the recompense. In Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm it says: "This is better than the first explanation, since there is no explicit object here." Some have weakened it here, on the grounds that unity (al-waḥdah) does not suit the context. It was answered by committing to the unity being generic (jinsiyyah).

Whatever the case, the raising of "rijāl" in this reading is either as the subject or the predicate, as you have just heard. The tanwīn on it, in all the readings, is for magnification (lil-tafkhīm). His saying: ﴿trade does not distract them﴾ is an attribute of it, emphasizing what the tanwīn conveyed of grandeur, and indicating the perfection of their devotion (tabattul) to Allah, without any diverting thing turning them aside, and without any sale that turns them back, however it may be. The specific mention of men is because they are the most deserving of the mosques.

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqī reported from Umm Salamah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The best of women's mosques is the innermost part of their houses."

The specification of trade, which is exchange in general, by this is because it is the strongest and most well-known distraction in their view. That is: no kind of trade distracts them, ﴿nor sale﴾, i.e., no single instance of sales, even if it is in its utmost profitability. The specific mention of sale, although it falls under trade, is to indicate its superiority over the other kinds of trade, because its profit is certain and immediate, while the profit of everything else is expected in the future at the time of sale. Therefore, the negation of distraction by other than it does not necessitate the negation of its distraction; and for this reason the word lā (not) was repeated, to emphasize and strengthen the negation.

It has also been permitted that by trade is meant profitable exchange, and by sale is meant exchange in general, so that its mention after it is by way of generalization after specification, for emphasis. It was transmitted from al-Wāqidī that what is meant by trade is purchasing, because it is its origin and beginning, so there is neither specification nor generalization. It was also said: what is meant by trade is importing (al-jalb), because it is the predominant element in it, so it is customarily necessary for it. From this one says: "tajurru fī kadhā," meaning he imports such-and-such. This is supported by what Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abū Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah

[Page 179]

(ﷺ), that he said concerning those described with what was mentioned: "They are the ones who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty."

al-Daylamī and others reported similarly from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, raised (marfūʿan). In this too is what implies that they were merchants, and this is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates, because one does not say "so-and-so is not distracted by trade" unless he is a merchant. This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "Indeed, by Allah, they were merchants, but their trade and their sale did not distract them from the remembrance of Allah."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also said this. It was said that they were not merchants, and the negation returns to the qualifier and the qualified together, as in the saying:

"On a faded road whose landmarks cannot be followed,"

as if it were said: they have no trade nor sale, so they are not distracted. For the verse was revealed concerning those who had withdrawn from the world, like the people of the Ṣuffah. You know that the verse according to the first view, supported by what you have heard, is more laudatory; and we have not found for its revelation concerning those who withdrew from the world any strong or weak chain of transmission (sanad). In this matter, mere possibility is not sufficient.

﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ by glorification, praise and the like. ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, i.e., establishing it at its appointed times without delay.

The original form is aqwām, and the vowel of the wāw was moved to the letter before it, so two unvocalized letters met and one was deleted, so it became "iqām." It is narrated from al-Zajjāj that the wāw was changed to an alif and then deleted because two alifs came together. It was objected to him that there is no reason to change it to an alif, since the condition is absent, which is that what follows it must not be unvocalized. al-Farrāʾ held that for the permissibility of this deletion there must be compensation with the tāʾ, so one says "iqāmah," or the genitive construction, as here. On this basis came His poet's saying:

"Indeed your companions hastened the parting and departed, and broke their promise to you, beyond the matter they had promised."

For he meant "ʿiddat al-amr" (the promise of the matter). Khālid ibn Kulthūm interpreted what is in the verse as: ʿadā is the plural of ʿadwah, meaning "side" (nāḥiyah), as if the poet meant the sides and the edges of the matter. The position of Sībawayh is that deletion without compensation by the tāʾ or the genitive construction is permissible. ﴿and the giving of zakāt﴾, i.e., the wealth whose giving to the entitled has been prescribed, as was narrated from al-Ḥasan. The indication that zakāt is explained this way rather than as an action is the apparent ascription of the giving (īrāʾ) to it.

It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the giving of zakāt was explained as sincerity in the obedience of Allah. This is far-fetched, as you see. The mention of this verb here, though it is not something done in houses, is because it is a companion that never separates from the establishment of prayer in most contexts, together with what it contains of an indication that the excellent deeds of these people are not restricted to what takes place in mosques. Likewise His saying: ﴿they fear﴾ to the end, for it is another attribute of "rijāl" (men), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of ﴿does not distract them﴾, or a resumed sentence preparing for the reason. Whichever it is, their fear is not confined to being in mosques.

His saying: ﴿a Day﴾ is an object of "yakhāfūna" (they fear), with an elided noun, meaning "the punishment of a Day," which is governed by it, or without the elision. It was also made an adverbial (ẓarf) of an elided object, which is a distant interpretation. As for making it an adverbial of "yakhāfūna" with the object elided, that is nothing at all, because the meaning is that they fear in this world a Day ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾, not that they fear something on that Day, which is described as one in which hearts and eyes are turned about, etc. What is meant by it is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes in it is their agitation and their alteration in themselves from the terror and dread, as in His saying: ﴿And when the eyes shall swerve, and the hearts reach the throats﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 10]. Or it is the change of their states, so that hearts comprehend what they did not comprehend, and eyes see what they did not see; or so that hearts expect salvation at one time and fear destruction at another, and eyes look to the right at one time and to the left at another, because most of the people of the gathering do not know from which direction they will be taken, nor from which quarter their books will be given to them.

It was said: what is meant is that hearts and eyes turn about on the embers of Jahannam, and this is nothing. Similar to it is the statement of al-Jubbāʾī: what is meant is that they move from state to state, so the fire scorches them, then ripens them, then burns them. Ibn Muḥaysin recited "tanqalibu" with the second tāʾ vowelless. And His saying, glorified is He:

**[Page 174]**

*"In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned. He is glorified therein morning and evening by men"* (24:36). The phrase **"men"** (*rijal*) begins a new, resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that explains the condition of those who were granted guidance to that light. It also mentions some of their inward and outward acts. The prepositional phrase, namely the phrase *"in houses"* (*fi buyut*) that is the complement of **"He is glorified"** (*yusabbihu*), is repeated with *"therein"* (*fiha*). This repetition was used for emphasis (*tawkid*) and to remind the reader of what came earlier in the sentence. It also signals that the fronting of the phrase is for emphasis, not for exclusivity. Similar examples of this repetition for emphasis include Allah's words: *"So in the mercy of Allah they abide therein forever"* (3:107), and your saying: "I passed by Zayd, by him." Some grammarians parsed such constructions as *badal* (substitution/apposition), as in the commentary on *Sharh al-Tashil*. In *al-Mughni*, it is said that it is an emphasis of the particle by repeating what it governs in pronominal form. The prepositional phrase is not an emphasis of the prepositional phrase, because the apparent (noun) is stronger and is not emphasized by a pronoun. Nor is the genitive noun a substitution by repeating the preposition, because a pronoun is not substituted by an apparent noun. Some grammarians permitted it only by analogy. You should know that what has been mentioned is not valid, because the whole is either a substitution or an emphasis. The apparent noun was used to avoid repetition. **"Men"** (*rijal*) is the subject (*fa'il*) of **"He is glorified"** (*yusabbihu*). It is placed after the adverbial phrases because its description has some length, and placing it first would disrupt the good arrangement of the sentence.

Al-Rummani said that *"in houses"* is connected to *yuqadu* (is kindled). Al-Hawfi said it is connected to an omitted verb that functions as an adjective of *mishkat* (niche). It was also said that it is an adjective of *misbah* (lamp), and it was said that it is an adjective of *zujaja* (glass). According to these four opinions, it restricts the thing used as the example, for the sake of emphasis on it. The nunation in the modified noun is for the category (*nau'iyya*), not for individuality (*fardiyya*), so that it does not contradict the plural of "houses."

It has been objected to what was mentioned that none of it is suitable to the dignity of the glorious revelation. How could it not be, since what follows Allah's words *"and had not fire touched it"* (24:35), according to the correct view, or what follows His words *"light upon light"* (24:35), according to what is said, up to His words *"of all things He is Knowing"* (24:35), is a statement connected to the example, definitely? Therefore, inserting it between the parts of the example, although it is of the type of separating the tree from its bark by a foreign element, leads to the mention of the condition of those who benefit from the example and are guided to His light by way of consequence and digression, while the explanation of the condition of their opposites is intended in itself. Such a thing is not known in human speech, let alone to be attributed to the inimitable speech.

Al-Khafaji criticized this, saying that it is an ornamental statement, since there is no separation in it, and what came before it up to here is part of the parable. In my view, the apparent meaning is that the parable was complete at His words *"and had not fire touched it."* It was said that *"in houses"* is connected to an omitted *sabbihu* or similar. That sentence, according to what is said, is consequent on what precedes it, and the omission of the particle *fa'* (then) is because it is known, as in *qum yad'uka* (stand, he calls you). They prohibited its being connected to *yadhkuru* (is mentioned), because it is part of the relative clause of *an* (that), so it does not govern what precedes it.

By "houses" is meant all the mosques, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and from Qatada and Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd that he said: "They are only four mosques, which none but a prophet built: the Ka'ba, which Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them, built; the Bayt al-Maqdis, which Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, built; the Mosque of Medina and the Mosque of Quba, which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ built." It was narrated from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is the Bayt al-Maqdis, and the plural is because it contains places that are distinguished from one another. This is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik and Buraydah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse, *'in houses'*, and a man stood up to him and said: 'What houses are these, O Messenger of Allah?' He ﷺ said: 'The houses of the prophets, peace be upon them.' Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this house among them, the house of 'Ali and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with them both?' He said: 'Yes, from among its best.'"

This, if it is authentic, should not be deviated from.

Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent meaning is that it is general, applying to the mosques and the houses in which prayer and knowledge take place." He permitted that it may mean the prayers of the believers or their bodies, since their prayers, which combine verbal and physical acts of worship, or their bodies surrounded by lights, resemble the mentioned houses, namely the mosques, and then their name is borrowed for that. He criticized this, saying that there is no beauty in what he mentioned, and I think you will not be satisfied with this degree of criticism.

By *"permitted to be raised"* is meant *commanded*, and by *"raised"* is meant *glorified*, that is, He, glorified be He, commanded that their status be glorified. This was narrated from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. It is not hidden that if the mosques are intended, glorifying their status is through various things, such as protecting them from entry by one in major ritual impurity (*junub*), a menstruating woman, or one in postnatal bleeding, even in passing, and they have stated the prohibition of this. It also includes bringing into them anything from which filth is feared. For this reason they said: "One who wishes to enter the mosque should check his sandal or shoe for impurity, and then enter, to avoid soiling the mosque." Also included is the prohibition of bringing a dead body into them, and the prohibition of bringing in children and insane persons. This is forbidden when their soiling is likely, and otherwise it is disliked. The command to keep them away from mosques has come in general terms.

Ibn Majah narrated from Wathila ibn al-Asqa', from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "Keep your children, your insane persons, your buying and selling, your disputes, the raising of your voices, the establishment of your legal punishments, and the drawing of your swords away from your mosques, and set up washing places at their doors, and gather them on the day of assembly." And he prohibited the reciting of lost property announcements and the reciting of poetry.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni, and Ibn Mandah narrated from Thawban, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever you see reciting poetry in the mosque, say: May Allah break your mouth, three times. And whoever you see announcing a lost item in the mosque, say: May you not find it, three times.'" The hadith continues.

The prohibition of reciting poetry should be restricted to when it contains something blameworthy, such as satirizing a Muslim, describing wine, mentioning women or beardless youths, or other things that are blameworthy according to the Sharia. As for when it includes praise of prophethood and Islam, or contains wisdom, or motivates noble character and asceticism and similar kinds of good, there is no harm in reciting it there.

Prohibited also is throwing a louse into it after killing it, and this is disliked as a matter of abstention (*tanzih*), according to what some later scholars have stated. It is recommended that a snake not be thrown into the mosque.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ahmad narrated from a man of the Ansar who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If one of you finds a louse in the mosque, let him place it in his garment until he takes it out."

He prohibited urinating in it, even into a vessel, and they have explicitly stated the prohibition of this. In *al-Ashbah* it is said: "As for bloodletting in the mosque into a vessel, I have not seen it." It should be that there is no difference, because both urine and blood are heavy impurities. He prohibited spitting in it.

In *al-Bada'i'* it is said: "Performing ablution in the mosque is disliked, because it is naturally disgusting, so it is obligatory to keep the mosque clean from it, just as it is obligatory to keep it clean of mucus and phlegm."

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from al-Sha'bi that the Prophet ﷺ saw in the direction of the mosque's qibla some phlegm, so he stood up to it and scraped it with his noble hand ﷺ, then called for perfume and smeared its place.

Al-Sha'bi said: "That is a sunna." They mentioned that placing phlegm on a mat is lighter than placing it beneath it. If one is compelled to do so, he should bury it.

In a hadith narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba from Anas, raised to the Prophet: "Spitting in the mosque is a sin, and its expiation is to cover it." Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* narrated similar from Ibn 'Abbas, also raised to the Prophet.

Prohibited also is sexual intercourse within it or on its roof, just like relieving oneself, and they have explicitly stated the prohibition of this. Prohibited also is entry by one who has eaten something with a foul smell, such as garlic, onions, or leeks, and one who has eaten radish and then belches similarly. In the time of the Prophet ﷺ, if a man was found to have the smell of garlic, he would be taken by the hand and led out to al-Baqi'. The apparent view is that one with bad breath, or one with persistent body odor, has the same ruling as one who has eaten garlic or onions. Likewise, one whose clothes have an offensive smell, such as the clothes of oil-sellers and tanners, is judged similarly. It is narrated from Malik that oil-sellers should hold back and not come forward to the first row, but sit at the back of the people.

Eating in it is prohibited, and so is eating garlic in it, except for one in seclusion (*mu'takif*). Sitting in it for mourning, or for talking about worldly matters, is prohibited. Making it a thoroughfare is prohibited, and this is either disliked or forbidden. The prohibition of this has come in a hadith narrated by Ibn Majah from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that making it a thoroughfare is one of the portents of the Hour. In *al-Qunya* it is said: "One who habitually does this is sinful and wicked. Yes, if there is an excuse, passing through is not disliked."

Among its honoring is sprinkling it with water and sweeping it. Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The mosque used to be sprinkled and swept in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He also narrated from Ya'qub ibn Zayd that "the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to follow the dust of the mosque with a palm branch." Likewise, hanging lamps in it and paving it with brick and mats.

In *Miftah al-Sa'ada* it is said: "The people of the mosque may pave the mosque with brick and mats and hang lamps. However, if the people of the mosque have funds, not the mosque's funds, that is only with the order of the ruler." Perhaps the place of this is where the founder (*waqif*) has not specified any part of the endowment's revenue for it.

It should be that kindling many lamps in it on certain nights of the year, such as the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan, which causes children and idle people to gather, play, raise their voices, and degrade the mosques, is an abominable innovation. Likewise, it should be that paving it with embroidered carpets which distract those who pray and remove their humility is similarly disliked.

Also among the honoring is to put the right foot forward when entering it and the left foot forward when leaving it. Also, the one entering should pray two rak'as before sitting, if his entry is not for prayer, according to what some have stated.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Abu Qatada that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Give the mosques their right." It was asked: "What is their right?" He said: "Two rak'as before you sit."

Among this also is building it high and lofty, unlike other houses. However, it should not be decorated with anything that distracts those who pray. In a hadith narrated by Ibn Majah and al-Tabarani from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, raised to the Prophet: "It should not be built with pictures, nor decorated with glass." Some interpreted "raising" as building it high, as in His words: *"And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il"* (2:127). In my view, it is better to interpret it according to what has preceded, and to include the building of it in this manner within the generality, which includes many matters other than what we have mentioned, which the jurists have mentioned at length.

Some exegetes claimed that attributing "raising" to it is metaphorical, and that the intended meaning is that the needs are raised in it to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: it raises voices by mentioning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in it. What is wrong with this is not hidden. In the expression "permitted" referring to the one who commands, there is an allusion that it is fitting for the one commanded to be turned toward what is commanded before the one who commands it, intending to fulfill it, as if he were seeking permission for it. So the command to it falls in the place of the command within it.

By mentioning His name, exalted be His glory, is meant what includes all of His remembrances. Among these are the scholarly discussions connected to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning is His unity, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the saying: "There is no god but Allah." Also from him: the intended meaning is the recitation of His Book, glorified be He.

[Page 177]

It has been said: the mention refers to His Most Beautiful Names. The apparent meaning, however, is what we have already stated. The mention (al-dhikr) is conjoined to "the raising" (al-raf', i.e., the raising of buildings) by way of ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm (the conjunction of the specific with the general), since the mention of His name in them is one of the forms of their glorification. It is not at all an ʿaṭf al-tafsīr (explicatory conjunction, where the second term explains the first), contrary to whoever imagined it. Al-tasbīḥ means declaring Allah transcendent and holy (al-tanzīh wa-al-taqdīs). It is used with the particle lām and without it, as in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1]. What is meant by it is either its apparent sense, or prayer, because prayer includes it. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Every tasbīḥ in the Qur'an is prayer." Confirming that prayer is meant here is the specification of the times by His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. Al-ghuduww is the plural of ghadāh, like fatan and fatāh, or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used for the time of morning. It is confirmed also by the fact that Abū Mujalliz recited "wal-īṣāl" as a verbal noun, meaning entering the time of the late afternoon (al-aṣīl). As al-Jawharī said, al-āṣāl is the plural of aṣīl, like sharīf and ashrāf. A group of scholars preferred this, although the plural of faʿīl on the pattern af'āl is not analogical.

Al-Zamakhsharī preferred that it is the plural of aṣl, like ʿunuq and aʿnāq. Al-aṣl is, like al-aṣīl, the evening, which runs from the decline of the sun to the morning. Thus it includes all the times other than al-ghadāh, which is from the beginning of the day until midday. Both terms are also applied to the beginning and end of the day. Their being mentioned separately is due to their nobility, and because they are the most common times in which people engage in their works and busy themselves with their affairs. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he took al-ghadāh to mean the time of the forenoon (al-ḍuḥā). This is what is implied by what Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Indeed the prayer of ḍuḥā is in the Qur'an, and the divers dive for it," and he recited the verse until he reached "al-āṣāl."

[Page 178]

Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr, al-Buḥturī from Ḥafṣ, Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr, al-Minhāl from Yaʿqūb, al-Mufaḍḍal and Abān recited "yusabbiḥu" with the yāʾ (third person masculine) and in the passive voice (al-binā' lil-maf'ūl). The deputy subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil) is ﴿lahu﴾ ("for Him") or ﴿fīhā﴾ ("in them"), if fī buyūtin is not connected to it, or ﴿bil-ghuduww﴾ ("in the mornings"). The first (lahu) takes precedence, because it is the one the verb is attached to, and the ascription to it is real, unlike the latter two. It has been permitted that the genitive phrase in what was mentioned is the deputy subject, with the prepositional phrase being redundant; but this involves a practice for which there is no need. The raising of "rijāl" (men) in this reading is either as the subject of an implied verb or as the predicate of an implied subject, according to what is in al-Baḥr: that is, "for Him glorifies men," or "men are the ones glorified for Him."
