The sentence is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), which came as an answer to a question arising from the preceding speech. This is like the saying:

"Let Yazīd weep, the one who has been struck down in a dispute, staggering from what the calamities cast down."

It is analogical according to many scholars, so it is permissible in their view to say: "Hind struck Zayd," with the meaning "her striking of him" or "his striker is Zayd." This is not like mentioning the agent as a specification (tamyīz) after a verb in the passive voice, such as "ḍuriba akhūka rajulan" (your brother was struck, a man), whose impermissibility Ibn Hishām declared explicitly in the fifth chapter of al-Mughnī, although the reasoning may suggest that it is similar. So consider this.

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Wathhāb recited "tusabbiḥu" with the tāʾ (feminine, i.e., the verb is agreeing with a feminine form) and in the active voice (al-binā' lil-fāʿil), and the subject is "rijālun" (men). The feminine form is because a plural of abundance (jamʿ al-takthīr) is very often treated as feminine. Abū Jaʿfar recited "tasbīḥun" with the tāʾ and in the passive voice, and the deputy subject is His saying ﴿bil-ghuduww wal-āṣāl﴾ ("in the mornings and the evenings"), with the bāʾ being redundant, and the ascription being metaphorical, by making the times in which their Lord is glorified "a means of glorification." Abū Ḥayyān permitted that the ascription is to the pronoun of tasbīḥah which is indicated by "tusabbiḥu," meaning "tusabbiḥu hiya" (it itself glorifies), i.e., the glorification itself. This is like what they said regarding His saying ﴿that He may recompense a people﴾ [al-Jāthiyah: 14] in the reading of one who put yajzī in the passive voice, meaning "li-yajziya huwa" (that it itself may recompense), i.e., the recompense. In Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm it says: "This is better than the first explanation, since there is no explicit object here." Some have weakened it here, on the grounds that unity (al-waḥdah) does not suit the context. It was answered by committing to the unity being generic (jinsiyyah).

Whatever the case, the raising of "rijāl" in this reading is either as the subject or the predicate, as you have just heard. The tanwīn on it, in all the readings, is for magnification (lil-tafkhīm). His saying: ﴿trade does not distract them﴾ is an attribute of it, emphasizing what the tanwīn conveyed of grandeur, and indicating the perfection of their devotion (tabattul) to Allah, without any diverting thing turning them aside, and without any sale that turns them back, however it may be. The specific mention of men is because they are the most deserving of the mosques.

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqī reported from Umm Salamah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The best of women's mosques is the innermost part of their houses."

The specification of trade, which is exchange in general, by this is because it is the strongest and most well-known distraction in their view. That is: no kind of trade distracts them, ﴿nor sale﴾, i.e., no single instance of sales, even if it is in its utmost profitability. The specific mention of sale, although it falls under trade, is to indicate its superiority over the other kinds of trade, because its profit is certain and immediate, while the profit of everything else is expected in the future at the time of sale. Therefore, the negation of distraction by other than it does not necessitate the negation of its distraction; and for this reason the word lā (not) was repeated, to emphasize and strengthen the negation.

It has also been permitted that by trade is meant profitable exchange, and by sale is meant exchange in general, so that its mention after it is by way of generalization after specification, for emphasis. It was transmitted from al-Wāqidī that what is meant by trade is purchasing, because it is its origin and beginning, so there is neither specification nor generalization. It was also said: what is meant by trade is importing (al-jalb), because it is the predominant element in it, so it is customarily necessary for it. From this one says: "tajurru fī kadhā," meaning he imports such-and-such. This is supported by what Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abū Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah

[Page 179]

(ﷺ), that he said concerning those described with what was mentioned: "They are the ones who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty."

al-Daylamī and others reported similarly from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, raised (marfūʿan). In this too is what implies that they were merchants, and this is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates, because one does not say "so-and-so is not distracted by trade" unless he is a merchant. This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "Indeed, by Allah, they were merchants, but their trade and their sale did not distract them from the remembrance of Allah."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also said this. It was said that they were not merchants, and the negation returns to the qualifier and the qualified together, as in the saying:

"On a faded road whose landmarks cannot be followed,"

as if it were said: they have no trade nor sale, so they are not distracted. For the verse was revealed concerning those who had withdrawn from the world, like the people of the Ṣuffah. You know that the verse according to the first view, supported by what you have heard, is more laudatory; and we have not found for its revelation concerning those who withdrew from the world any strong or weak chain of transmission (sanad). In this matter, mere possibility is not sufficient.

﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ by glorification, praise and the like. ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, i.e., establishing it at its appointed times without delay.

The original form is aqwām, and the vowel of the wāw was moved to the letter before it, so two unvocalized letters met and one was deleted, so it became "iqām." It is narrated from al-Zajjāj that the wāw was changed to an alif and then deleted because two alifs came together. It was objected to him that there is no reason to change it to an alif, since the condition is absent, which is that what follows it must not be unvocalized. al-Farrāʾ held that for the permissibility of this deletion there must be compensation with the tāʾ, so one says "iqāmah," or the genitive construction, as here. On this basis came His poet's saying:

"Indeed your companions hastened the parting and departed, and broke their promise to you, beyond the matter they had promised."

For he meant "ʿiddat al-amr" (the promise of the matter). Khālid ibn Kulthūm interpreted what is in the verse as: ʿadā is the plural of ʿadwah, meaning "side" (nāḥiyah), as if the poet meant the sides and the edges of the matter. The position of Sībawayh is that deletion without compensation by the tāʾ or the genitive construction is permissible. ﴿and the giving of zakāt﴾, i.e., the wealth whose giving to the entitled has been prescribed, as was narrated from al-Ḥasan. The indication that zakāt is explained this way rather than as an action is the apparent ascription of the giving (īrāʾ) to it.

It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the giving of zakāt was explained as sincerity in the obedience of Allah. This is far-fetched, as you see. The mention of this verb here, though it is not something done in houses, is because it is a companion that never separates from the establishment of prayer in most contexts, together with what it contains of an indication that the excellent deeds of these people are not restricted to what takes place in mosques. Likewise His saying: ﴿they fear﴾ to the end, for it is another attribute of "rijāl" (men), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of ﴿does not distract them﴾, or a resumed sentence preparing for the reason. Whichever it is, their fear is not confined to being in mosques.

His saying: ﴿a Day﴾ is an object of "yakhāfūna" (they fear), with an elided noun, meaning "the punishment of a Day," which is governed by it, or without the elision. It was also made an adverbial (ẓarf) of an elided object, which is a distant interpretation. As for making it an adverbial of "yakhāfūna" with the object elided, that is nothing at all, because the meaning is that they fear in this world a Day ﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾, not that they fear something on that Day, which is described as one in which hearts and eyes are turned about, etc. What is meant by it is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the turning of hearts and eyes in it is their agitation and their alteration in themselves from the terror and dread, as in His saying: ﴿And when the eyes shall swerve, and the hearts reach the throats﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 10]. Or it is the change of their states, so that hearts comprehend what they did not comprehend, and eyes see what they did not see; or so that hearts expect salvation at one time and fear destruction at another, and eyes look to the right at one time and to the left at another, because most of the people of the gathering do not know from which direction they will be taken, nor from which quarter their books will be given to them.

It was said: what is meant is that hearts and eyes turn about on the embers of Jahannam, and this is nothing. Similar to it is the statement of al-Jubbāʾī: what is meant is that they move from state to state, so the fire scorches them, then ripens them, then burns them. Ibn Muḥaysin recited "tanqalibu" with the second tāʾ vowelless. And His saying, glorified is He:

﴿So that Allah may reward them﴾ is connected, according to what Abu Hayyan preferred, with ﴿yusabbihu﴾ (He is glorified). Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be connected with ﴿la tulhihim﴾ (neither distracts them) or with ﴿yakhafuna﴾ (they fear). It is not hidden that connecting it to either of the mentioned verbs requires an interpretation. Perhaps connecting it to a deleted verb indicated by what is related about them is better than all of that, meaning: they do what they do of glorification, remembrance, paying zakat, and fearing, without anything diverting them from that, ﴿so that Allah may reward them the best of what they did﴾. The lam, in all the other possibilities, is the lam of purpose (ta'lil).

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is permissible for it to be the lam of result (lam al-sayrura, the lam indicating a consequence rather than an intention), like the one in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (Al-Qasas: 8). The clause would then be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning would be: they fear, inspired, so that Allah may reward them. This, as you see, is [weak].

Al-jaza' (recompense) is the requiting and repaying for what is praiseworthy. It takes the recipient with the preposition ''ʿan'' (from/for), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 48, 123). It takes what was done initially with ''ʿalā'' (upon), so you say: "I repaid him for his deed" (jazaytuhu ʿalā fiʿlihi). It may also take it with the bāʾ (with), so it is said: "jizītuhu bi-fiʿlihi." And it takes what was given in return with itself and with the bāʾ. Al-Raghib said: It is said "jizītuhu kadhā wa-bi-kadhā" (I rewarded him with such-and-such).

The apparent meaning is that ﴿ahsana﴾ (the best) is what was given in return, so the verb of recompense takes its object directly, and it requires the deletion of a noun modifying it, meaning: so that He may reward them with the best reward for their deed, or for what they did, according to what He promised them, for one good deed, ten like it, up to seven hundred times, so that the best is of the same kind as the reward.

He also permitted that the best ("ahsan") is the act for which one is rewarded, or the thing by which the person is rewarded, and there is no deleted noun. The speech is then on the deletion of the preposition: meaning, so that He may reward them for the best or with the best of what they did. The best of deeds is its least, the recommended (mandub), so one guards by it against the good (hasan), which is the permissible (mubah), since there is no reward for it. He preferred the first view for its freedom from deleting the preposition, which is not analogical (ghayr maqis) in cases like this, unlike deleting a noun modifier, which is common and analogical. He also permitted that the deleted noun modifier is before "ahsan," meaning: a reward, the best of what they did. The apparent meaning of "what they did" is more general than what preceded, though some of them explained it by that.

﴿And He increases them of His bounty﴾, meaning: He bestows favors upon them with things that were not promised to them in their particulars, nor in their measures, and their modes and quantities did not occur to their minds. Rather, they were promised only in general terms, as in His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best and an increase﴾ (Yunus: 26).

And the saying of (ﷺ), related from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived."

And other than that of the generous promises, among which is His saying, glorified is He:

﴿And Allah gives provision to whom He wills without reckoning﴾. This is a concluding clause confirming the increase, and a generous promise that He, exalted is He, will give them, beyond the recompense of their deeds, of good things that the reckoning cannot account for. The relative pronoun ("man") is an expression for those whose beautiful qualities were mentioned, as if it were said: "And Allah gives them provision without reckoning." He placed it in the position of their pronoun, to draw attention to what is in the relative clause, indicating that the basis of the mentioned provision is purely His will, exalted is He, and not their deeds described, just as the basis of what preceded, the guidance to His light, Mighty and Majestic is He. It also gives notice that they are among those whom Allah, exalted is He, willed to provide for, just as they are among those whom He, glorified is He, willed to guide to His light, according to what the good deeds they were detailed as doing make clear, for all of them are effects of that guidance.

[Page 180]

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, to the end of the verse, is a conjunction with what precedes it. It conjoins one account to another, or it is conjoined to an implied element that the preceding context leads to, as if it had been said: "Those who believe [have] their deeds [in terms of] state and outcome, just as He described those who disbelieve: ﴿their deeds are like a mirage﴾." That is, their deeds, which belong to the categories of righteousness, such as maintaining family ties (silat al-arham), freeing captives (fakk al-ʿanat), providing water to pilgrims (siqayat al-hajj), maintaining the House (ʿimarat al-bayt), aiding the distressed (ighathat al-malhufin), hospitality to guests (qura al-adyaf), and the like, according to what has been said. It has also been said that their deeds are those from which they expect benefit, whether they are of a kind for which faith is a condition, such as the Hajj, or of a kind for which it is not a condition, such as providing water to pilgrims and the rest of what has been mentioned. It has also been said that what is meant includes both good and bad deeds, so that the two comparisons may fit together. The discussion of this will come, God willing, in its place. The mirage (al-sarab) is a thin vapour that rises from the depressions of level ground (qaʿur al-qiʿan). When the light of the sun meets it, it resembles, from afar, flowing water (al-ma' al-sarib), i.e., running water. Al-Farra' stipulated that it must cling to the ground. It has also been said that it is what shimmers of the air at midday in the heat, in the wide open deserts. It has also been said that it is the ray that appears at midday when the heat is intense in the open country, which makes the onlooker imagine it to be flowing water. The poet says:

"When we restrained the war, your pledges were like the glitter of a mirage in the wilderness, shining."

Al-Tabarsi also took this view, and he interpreted al-ʿAla (the sheen) as a ray rising between heaven and earth, like water in the forenoon.

﴿in a level plain﴾ (biqiʿatin) is related to an omitted element which is an attribute of mirage: that is, "existing in a level plain," and the level plain (al-qiʿa) is the flat, even ground. It has also been said that qiʿa is the plural of qaʿin, like jirah for jar and nayyirah for nar. Muslima ibn Muharib read biqiʿatin with a long tāʾ, taking it as the plural of qiʿa, like dimat and qimat for dimah and qimah. It is also transmitted from him that he read biqiʿat with a round tāʾ, and he stopped on it with a hāʾ. It may be the plural of qiʿa, and he stopped with a hāʾ according to the dialect of Ṭayy, as they said al-buniha and al-ikhwaha. It may also, as the author of al-Lawāmiʿ said, be singular, its original form being qiʿah as in the recitation of the majority, but he prolonged the fatḥah so that an alif was produced from it.

﴿the thirsty one supposes it﴾ (yaḥsabuhu al-ẓamʾan) — water (māʾan) is another attribute of mirage.

It is also permitted that it be the attribute and that biqiʿah be an adverbial complement of what the kāf governs, which is the predicate. Al-ḥusbān (supposing) means conjecture according to the well-known view. Al-Raghib distinguished between them: ẓann is when two opposites occur to the mind and one of them prevails over the other, whereas ḥusbān is when one judges one of them without the other occurring to the mind, so that one holds the finger on it, and there is a chance that doubt will overtake it. Restricting ḥusbān to the thirsty one, although it includes everyone who sees it, whether the thirsty or the satiated, is to complete the comparison by establishing that both its parties share in the aspect of resemblance, which is the hope that appears and the despair that ends.

Shayba, Abu Jaʿfar and Nafiʿ, in one of the two transmissions from them, read al-ẓamʾān with the hamzah omitted and its vowel transferred to the mīm.

﴿until, when he comes to it﴾, that is, when the thirsty one comes to what he supposed to be water. It has also been said: when he comes to its place.

﴿he finds it not﴾, that is, he does not find what he supposed to be water. He made his hope depend on it.

﴿anything﴾, at all, neither verified nor presumed, although he used to see it before, let alone the aspect that it is water. The accusative of ﴿anything﴾ has been said to be the circumstantial (ḥāl). The matter of derivation is easy. It has also been said that it is the second object of wajada (to find), on the basis that it is among the sisters of ẓanna. It is also permitted that it be accusative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun. And it is permissible to substitute an indefinite noun for a definite one without a qualifier when it is meaningful, as al-Radi explicitly stated. Abu al-Baqāʾ preferred that it be accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as if it had been said: "he did not find it as a finding." And how you see that is [weak].

﴿and he finds God with him﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿he finds it not﴾, so it falls within the comparison: that is, the thirsty one finds the Exalted's power over his destruction beside the mirage mentioned. It has also been said: that is, he finds God calling him to account, the meaning of "with him" being reckoning, because the mention of full payment follows in His saying: ﴿so He pays him his reckoning in full﴾, that is, He gives him in full his account of his deeds and their recompense, or He completes his reckoning by presenting before him, through the scribes, what he sent forward.

﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, not occupied by one reckoning from another.

In Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim it is said that the description of the states of the disbelievers by way of the parable was complete with His saying ﴿he finds it not anything﴾, and His saying Exalted (and he finds) etc. is an explanation of the remaining states that befall them after that, by way of completion, lest one suppose that the utmost of their condition is only disappointment and despair, as is the case with the thirsty. It shows that there will come upon them after that, from evil states, what leaves no room for disappointment at all. So the sentence is not conjoined to ﴿he finds it not anything﴾, but to what is understood from it by way of the parable, from the disbelievers not finding their deeds, neither in substance nor in trace, as in His saying: ﴿And We turn to what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. How could it not be so, since the judgement that the deeds of the disbelievers are like a mirage which the thirsty supposes to be water, until when he comes to it he finds it not anything, is a judgement that they are of such a kind that they suppose them beneficial to them in the Hereafter, until when they come to them they find them not anything. It is as if it had been said: until when the disbelievers come on the Day of Resurrection to their deeds which they used to suppose beneficial to them in the Hereafter, they will not find them anything, and they will find God, that is, His judgement and decree, at the time of coming. It has been said: at the time of doing, so He pays them in full, that is, He gives them in full their reckoning, that is, the reckoning of the deeds mentioned and their recompense. For their belief in the benefit of them without faith, and their not acting according to its requirement, is disbelief upon disbelief which definitely entails punishment. The pronouns referring to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ are singular either because the genus is intended, like the thirsty one in the parable, or because each one of them is meant. Likewise the singular of what refers to their deeds. End. And what is in it of remoteness and of departing from the apparent meaning is not hidden.

Whichever it is, the thirsty one is meant in an absolute sense. It has been said that what is meant by the thirsty one is the disbeliever, and al-Zamakhshari took this view. He said: The Exalted likened what one who does not believe in faith does to a mirage which a disbeliever sees in the desert, while the thirst of the Resurrection has overcome him, so he supposes it to be water and comes to it, but finds it not, and finds the angels of God with him, seizing him and giving him to drink boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid. And it seems to be taken from what ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-Suddi in his Gharaʾib from the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the disbelievers will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as thirsty herds, and they will say: 'Where is the water?' Then the mirage will be presented to them, and they will suppose it to be water, so they will set out towards it, and they will find God with it, and He will pay them their reckoning in full, and God is swift in reckoning."

Al-ʿAllamah al-Tibi found this agreeable, saying: He only restricted the comparison to the seeing of the disbeliever and made his states what he meets on the Day of Resurrection, and he did not make absolute his saying Exalted: ﴿and he finds God with him﴾ etc., because it is part of the states of the one compared. This style is more eloquent, because the disappointment of the disbeliever is more penetrating, and his attainment of what is contrary to what he hopes for is more deeply rooted.

Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying: It follows from taking the thirsty one to be the disbeliever that a thing is likened to itself. He replied: the comparison, according to what Jar Allah mentioned, is a parable or restricted, not a separation, as he imagined. So it does not follow from the unity of some of the terms in the two sides that a thing is compared to itself, like the unity of the agent in: "I see you advancing one foot and delaying the other." In sum, this is better than what is in Irshad, as is not hidden from one whose mind is free of the dust of equipment.

The verse, according to what is transmitted from Muqatil, was revealed concerning ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa ibn Umayya, who worshipped, did not wear sackcloth, and sought the religion in the Jahiliyyah, then disbelieved in Islam. The saying Exalted ﴿and those who disbelieve﴾ does not preclude this, because it is not specific to the occasion of revelation, even though he entered it at the first stage. And it is not objected that the verse is Medinan, revealed after Badr, while ʿUtba was killed at Badr, for many verses were revealed concerning the dead, and there is no prohibition in that at all. Then it is not far that it applies to the ruling on these disbelievers, the philosophers and their followers among those who adorn themselves with the garb of Islam, for their belief and their deeds, since they do not conform to the Law, are like a mirage in a level plain.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 24, verse 40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or like darknesses﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with ﴿like a mirage﴾. Some scholars said that the word *aw* (or) is used for dividing the states of their good deeds. It is also permissible to take it as absolute, with regard to two times: in the Hereafter, the deeds are like the mirage in that they bring no benefit, and in this world they are like the darknesses in that they are empty of the light of truth. [The commentator] restricted this to the world on the basis of God's words: ﴿And whoever God does not give light, for him there is no light﴾, since this clearly refers to guidance and the specific divine success (*tawfiq*) that belongs to it. The first (the mirage) refers to the Hereafter, on the basis of God's words: ﴿and finds [God] there﴾, and so on. He placed the states of the Hereafter first, because they are greater and more important, and because this is connected to what relates to them in God's words: ﴿so that He may repay them﴾, and so on. Then He mentioned the states of this world to complete them.

[The commentator] also permitted reversing this, so that the first would refer to the comparison of their deeds with the mirage in this world at the time of death, and the second to their comparison with the darknesses on the Day of Resurrection, as in the hadith: "Injustices are darknesses on the Day of Resurrection." This would be an ascending order suited to the chronological sequence, but it is not as suitable as what you have heard. It was also said that *aw* is for variety. This is because the deeds they relied upon most strongly and boasted of in every valley and place are affected by the state of the mirage mentioned, while their evil deeds, which contain no trace of goodness, by which the deceived are deceived, are compared to the darknesses mentioned. Al-Jurjani claimed that what is intended here is only the comparison of their disbelief, but that is, as you see, not right. According to the variety interpretation, the most apparent meaning of "their deeds" in God's words ﴿their deeds﴾ is that it includes both kinds.

It was objected that this is contradicted by God's words: ﴿and finds God with him﴾, on the basis that the good deeds are included in the comparison. It was answered that even if it is granted that good deeds do not benefit disbelievers, there is no harm in their outcome, as God's words ﴿and finds﴾, and so on, indicate. The answer is that there is nothing indicating that the cause of punishment is good deeds. Rather, what is found is that the punishment is due to the evil of their deeds, but all of them are mentioned to show that some of them were made scattered dust and some are punished for. It was also permitted that the *aw* is for choice in the comparison, because their good deeds resemble the mirage, or in general the mirage, because they are vain and have no benefit, and the darknesses mentioned, because they are empty of the light of truth. Al-Kirmani chose this view.

It was objected that al-Radi, like others, mentioned that *aw* is used for choice only in the imperative. It was answered that although this is well known, many scholars held that it is not restricted to that, such as Ibn Malik and al-Zamakhshari, and its use in comparison is frequent. In any case, there is no omitted *mudaf* (an omitted possessive construction) in the sentence. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: there is an omitted *mudaf*, and the estimate is "or like [those of] one with darknesses," and this is indicated by God's words that come later: ﴿when he brings out his hand﴾. The comparison here may refer to the deeds according to the pattern of the earlier comparison, with the estimate "or like the deeds of one with darknesses." It may also refer to the disbelievers, with the estimate "or they are like one with darknesses." All of these are against the apparent meaning, and the matter of the pronoun will become clear to you, God willing.

Sufyan ibn Husayn read *"aw ka-zulumat"* with a fatha on the *waw*. In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) the explanation for this is that he took it as a *waw* of coordination (*waw al-'atf*) preceded by the interrogative particle *hamza*, which is for affirming the comparison and which is free of the pure sense of a question. It was also said that it is the *aw* of the reading of the majority, and the *waw* was given a fatha because of its proximity, just as the *dal* was given a kasra because of its neighbour in God's words ﴿al-hamdu lillah﴾ in some readings.

﴿in a deep sea﴾, that is, deep, abundant in water, attributed to *lujj*, which is the greater part of the sea's water. It was also said that *lujjah* is also its greater part, and it is an adjective of ﴿sea﴾. Likewise, the clause ﴿which is covered by﴾, that is, which covers that sea and completely conceals it, ﴿waves﴾. The first (the sea) was placed first because it is singular. It was also said that the clause is an adjective of the omitted *dhu* (the one with), and the pronoun refers to it, and you have known the state of that estimate. God's words ﴿above it are waves﴾ form a clause of subject and predicate, whose position is nominative as an adjective of "waves," or the prepositional phrase and what follows it is the subject of the adjective because it relies on the modified noun. The meaning is that it is covered by waves piled up and layered upon one another. God's words ﴿above it is a cloud﴾ are an adjective of the second "wave," according to one of the two previously mentioned views, that is, above that wave is a dark cloud that has hidden the light of the stars. In this there is an indication of the extreme piling up of the waves and their multiplication, to the point that they seem to have reached the cloud.

﴿darknesses﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, they are darknesses ﴿some of them upon others﴾, that is, densely and layeredly piled up. This is an explanation of the complete intensity of the darknesses, just as God's words ﴿light upon light﴾ explain the utmost strength of light. Except that this one relates to the compared item (the deeds or the disbelievers) and that one relates to the thing to which it is compared, as what follows indicates.

Al-Hawfi permitted that ﴿darknesses﴾ be the subject, with the predicate God's words ﴿some of them upon others﴾. Abu Hayyan criticised this, and Ibn Hisham followed him, saying that the apparent view is that it is not permitted, because it involves beginning with an indefinite noun without a justifying reason, unless one estimates an adjective for it, which the nunation indicates, that is, "darknesses many or great," and this is a strain. He also permitted that ﴿some of it﴾ be an appositive (*badal*) of ﴿darknesses﴾. This was criticised on the grounds that it is not permitted in terms of meaning, because what is intended, and God knows best, is the report that they are darknesses and that some of those darknesses are upon others, that is, they are piled-up darknesses, not the report that some darknesses are upon others without reporting that those earlier darknesses are piled up.

Qanbal read *"darknesses"* in the genitive, as an appositive of the first ﴿darknesses﴾, with no emphasis on it. The clause ﴿some of it upon some﴾ is in the position of an adjective for it. Al-Bazzi read *"cloud darknesses"* with the construction of "cloud" to "darknesses." This construction is like the construction in *luj-ayn al-ma'* (the silver of water), or it is to show that this cloud is not a cloud of rain and mercy.

﴿when he brings out﴾, that is, from the one tested by them. Its omission without mention is clearly indicated by the meaning. Likewise the estimate of a pronoun referring to ﴿darknesses﴾, which is needed because the clause ﴿when he brings out﴾, and so on, is in the position of an adjective for "darknesses," and it must have a connecting pronoun, and what we have pointed to is not the only possibility. It was said: the pronoun of the subject refers to the active participle understood from the verb, following the pattern of the saying "he does not drink wine while he is a believer," that is, when the one who brings out, in it, brings out ﴿his hand﴾ and places it close to his eyes in front of him so that he may look at it, ﴿he almost does not see it﴾, that is, he does not come close to seeing it, though it is the closest thing to him, let alone that he should see it. Ibn al-Anbari claimed that *yakad* (almost) is an addition. Al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad claimed that the meaning is: he did not see it except after great effort, because the custom is to say "he hardly did such-and-such" and "he did not almost do such-and-such" for an action that was done with difficulty and with the expectation that it would be hard to do. On this basis came God's words: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they almost did not do it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:71). From here Ibn Shubrumah erred when he (speaking of) Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Other than the separation of the lovers, the trace of love for Mayya does not almost cease."*

Dhu al-Rummah accepted this, and when someone called him "O Abu Ghaylan, I see that it has ceased," he corrected his verse to: *"other than the separation of the lovers, the trace of love for Mayya does not cease."* Yet the correct view is that *lam yakad* and *ma kada yaf'alu* mean: the act never existed in the first place, nor did it come close to occurring in one's opinion, and there is no doubt about this.

It is known that *kada* is used for the extreme closeness of an action to occurring and its approach to it. So it is impossible for its negation to establish the existence of the action, because that would lead to the conclusion that what came close is also not so. Thus, when the meaning is not that there was a state in which the action was far from occurring but then changed, as in God's words ﴿so they slaughtered it﴾ and so on, one keeps the apparent sense and takes the meaning to be that the action did not come close to occurring, let alone occurred. The verse is so, and so is the line of verse. It has been mentioned that *lam yakad* in both of them is the answer to *idha* (when), so it is future. When I say "when she went out, I did not go out," I have negated going out in the future, so it is impossible for the meaning in both to be that the action had happened.

This verification is the essence of what al-Shaykh (Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani) verified in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (*Proofs of Inimitability*). From it you can know the error of those who claim that negating *kada* is affirmation and affirming it is negation.

In *al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyya* it is stated that the negation of *kada*, according to the verification mentioned, is more emphatic than the negation of the verb it enters upon, because negating its approach indicates its negation by a demonstrative method, except that when it occurs in the past it does not contradict its affirmation in the future, and perhaps it suggests that it occurred after despair of it, as in the verse of al-Baqarah. When it occurs in the future it does not contradict its occurrence in the past. If there is a clear indication of its affirmation in the past, it suggests that it has ceased and that hope has been lost after it had not been so, as in this verse, because due to the intensity of the darkness he cannot see his hand, which was right before his eyes. Then he derived from this that you may say: what is meant by the one who said that its negation is affirmation and its affirmation is negation is that its negation in the past suggests affirmation in the future, and the reverse, as you have heard. This is the reason for the criticism of Ibn Shubrumah and the alteration of Dhu al-Rummah, because his intention was that the old state of his love had not come close to ceasing at any time, and its negation in the future gives the impression that it was affirmed in the past. It cannot be said that they were both among the eloquent Arabs whose speech is cited as evidence, so how could that have been hidden from them? For this reason, [al-Zamakhshari] found it improbable in *al-Kashshaf* and held that their story is fabricated, and he urged keeping this, saying: "Keep it, for it is an elegant verification and a precise success that came by pure kindness and divine assistance." End of quote.

By my life, what the speaker interpreted is extremely far-fetched, and I do not think it would be accepted by him. The negation of any verb in the past does not contradict its affirmation in the future, and its negation in the future does not contradict its occurrence in the past. Nor is *kada* exclusively for this. So I wonder whether what Dhu al-Rummah changed his verse to removed the misleading impression. So reflect on this, and may God, the Exalted, guide you.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of the verse requires that what prevents the seeing is the intensity of the darkness, and that is so, because the condition of sight in this world, according to custom, is light. This is so whether it is by pure creation of God, as the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*, the orthodox theologians) held, or by the emission of a ray from the eye in the shape of a solid cone or one composed of lines gathered at the end near the head, or without a cone shape but in a straight line, while its end near the eye remains fixed and connected to the seen object, or by the ray in the eye taking on the quality of air, and the whole becoming an instrument of sight, as the mathematicians (*al-Riyadiyyin*) held, or by the impression of the image of the seen object in a part of the glacial humour, which resembles cold and ice, as the naturalists (*al-Tabi'iyyun*) held. These two views are the best known among the philosophers, and it is attributed to the Illuminationists (*al-Ishraqiyyun*) among them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 40 (part 2 of 2):

Shihab al-Din al-Maqtul (Suhrawardi) preferred the view that sight occurs through the facing of an illuminated object to the seeing organ, which contains the moisture of the crystalline lens (*siqlliyya*). When these conditions are present and the obstacle is removed, the soul acquires an illuminative (*ishraqi*) knowledge by presence (*huduri*) of the one who sees, so the soul perceives it as a direct, manifest, clear witnessing, without any ray or impression.

Mulla Sadra preferred the view that sight is by the creation of a form similar to the object seen, by the power of God Most High, from the world of the psychic dominion (*malakut*), abstracted from external matter, present to the perceiving soul and subsisting in it as an act subsists in its agent, not as a received thing subsists in its recipient. The verification of this, with what is for and against it, is in the extended books of philosophy.

It may be thought that darkness, whether it is an existent thing or a privation of a capacity, is a condition of sight, like light; but this holds only with respect to some bodies, such as things that shine at night.

Ibn Sina denied this and said: "Darkness cannot be a condition for the existence of luminous things being seen. This is because a luminous body is seen whether the viewer is in darkness or in light, as with fire, which we see absolutely. As for the sun, we cannot see it in darkness because, whenever it rises, darkness does not remain. As for the stars and shining bodies, they are seen only in darkness and not in daytime, because the light of the sun dominates their light. When the sense is affected by a strong light, it is naturally not affected by a weak one. At night, however, there is no dominant light over their light, so they are seen. In sum, their not being visible is not because seeing depends on darkness, but because of the presence of an obstacle to seeing, namely the dominant light." End of quotation.

It may be said: the light of the sun, as mentioned, is an obstacle to seeing the stars, and removing the obstacle to seeing is a condition for it; and the removal of the light is darkness. So darkness is a condition for seeing the stars at night, which is what is sought. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

*Page 185*

And God Most High knows best the realities of things.

﴿And whoever God does not give light, for him there is no light﴾ is a closing addition (*i'tiradh tadhyili*), brought to confirm what the parable has conveyed, namely that the deeds of the unbelievers are as described. The verification is that this is because God has not guided them to His light. The use of the relative pronoun indicates, by what it contains in its clause, the cause of the ruling, and that they are among those whom God has not willed to guide. That is: whoever God has not willed to guide to light in this world, for him there is no guidance at all in it.

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that whoever has no light in this world, there is no light for him in the Hereafter. It has also been said: both matters refer to the Hereafter, and the meaning is that whoever God does not illumine with His pardon and does not have mercy on with His mercy on the Day of Resurrection, there is no mercy for him from anyone on that day. The reliance is on what was mentioned earlier.

The apparent meaning is that the intention is to liken the deeds of the disbelievers to dense darkness, without considering parts in the two sides of the comparison, so that one would consider the comparison of some parts to others. Some have considered parts and said: "The darknesses are the corrupt deeds and false beliefs; the deep sea is the breast and heart of the disbeliever; the wave is misguidance and ignorance that has overwhelmed his heart; the second wave is crooked thinking; the cloud is his desire for disbelief and his turning away from faith." It has been said: "The darknesses are the deeds of the disbeliever; the sea is his desire, deep in its bottom, abundant, so that the drowning person is in danger in it; the wave is what covers his heart of ignorance and heedlessness. The second wave is what covers him of doubt and suspicion, and the cloud is what covers him of polytheism and bewilderment, which prevents him from being guided." All of this, as you see, is so; but if it were taken as a matter of allusion (*ishara*), the matter would be easier.

* * *

Among the matters of allusion is what has been said: that in the words of God Most High, ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾, there is an indication that when a shaykh wishes to discipline a disciple (*murid*) and break his commanding self (*nafs ammara*), he should discipline him in the presence of a group of disciples who do not need discipline.

From here Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: "None attends the places of discipline except one who does not deserve discipline, and they are a group of the believers, not all believers." For them, adultery is an allusion to inclination toward this world and its desires. In the words of God Most High, ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress﴾ etc., and His words ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men﴾ etc., is an allusion to the fact that it is not proper for the righteous to associate with the wicked, for birds of a feather flock together. In the words of God Most High, ﴿Do not reckon it an evil for you; rather it is good for you﴾, there is an allusion that one whom the deniers among the shaykhs disparage should not grieve over that and think it an evil for him, for it is good for him, causing his advancement.

In the words of God Most High, ﴿And let not the people of virtue swear﴾ etc., there is an allusion that shaykhs and the great should not abandon the companions of slips and the people of lapses among the disciples, nor cut off their kindness and divine overflowings from them. In the words of God Most High, ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their people﴾, there is an allusion that one who wishes to enter upon the saints (*awliya*) should not enter until he finds the spirit of acceptance and permission, through the outpouring of spiritual support upon his heart, which is indicated by the seeking of intimacy. For the saint may have a state which is not fitting for the entrant to witness, and this may harm him.

Some Sufis have extended this to one who wishes to enter to visit the graves of the saints, may God sanctify their secrets. He said: "Whoever wishes that should stand at the door with the most complete courtesy, gather his senses, rely in his heart seeking permission, and make his shaykh an intermediary between himself and the saint being visited. If he obtains an expansion of breast, spiritual support and inner overflow, let him enter; otherwise let him return." This is what is meant by the courtesy of visitation among them. We have not found this from any of the righteous predecessors (*salaf*). The Shi'a, when visiting the imams, may God be pleased with them, one of them calls out: "May I enter, O Commander of the Faithful?" or "O son of the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)" or something like that, and they claim that the sign of permission is the arising of tenderness of heart and tears of the eye. This too is something we do not know from any of the predecessors, nor did our jurists mention it. I do not consider it except an innovation (*bid'a*), and its doer is regarded only as a laughing-stock by the wise. That the one visited is alive in his grave does not require seeking permission to enter to visit him, and likewise what some jurists mentioned, that the visitor should observe courtesy with the one visited as he would with him while alive, as is not hidden.

After writing this, I saw in *al-Jawhar al-Muntazam fi Ziyarat al-Qabr al-Mu'azzam* (may God bless its occupant and grant him peace) by Ibn Hajar al-Makki the following text: "Some of them said: the visitor should stop at the door, a gentle standing, like one who seeks permission to enter upon the great." End of quotation.

And in it: "There is no basis for that, nor any state, nor any courtesy that requires it." End of quotation. From this it is known that if this is not prescribed in visiting his grave (ﷺ), then its non-prescription in visiting others is by even greater reason. So remember this, and may God protect us from innovations, and protect you.

It has been said regarding the words of God Most High, ﴿Say to the believers that they lower their gaze﴾ etc., that in it is a command to lower the gaze of the self from its desired worldly things, the gaze of the heart from seeing deeds and the bliss of the Hereafter, the gaze of the secret from ranks and nearnesses, the gaze of the spirit from turning toward anything other than God Most High, and the gaze of resolve from seeing oneself as worthy of witnessing the Truth, glorifying and exalting Him. It is also a command to guard the inner private part from the dispositions of the two worlds in it. The indication in the command to women not to display their adornment except to those excepted is that one who adorns himself with the adornment of secrets should not display it to other than the unmarriageable kin (*mahram*), and one who does not conceal it from strangers [should not display it].

By the words of God Most High, ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ etc., there is a reference to the spiritual marriage, which is that the perfect shaykh deposits in the womb of the heart, from the loins of guardianship (*wilaya*), a drop of readiness to receive the divine overflow. This readiness is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty﴾. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And let those who do not find [a shaykh] at present be chaste﴾, that is, let be guarded those ﴿who do not find﴾ a shaykh at the moment, the wombs of their hearts from the dispositions of this world, the desire and the devil, ﴿until God enriches them﴾ by providing them with a perfect shaykh, or by specially favouring them, glorified is He, with one of His attractions.

By His words, ﴿And those who seek the Book﴾ etc., there is an indication that when a disciple seeks release from the bond of spiritual discipline, it is obligatory to respond to him if good is known in him, which is tawhid, knowledge, trust in God (*tawakkul*), contentment, sincerity of deed, and fulfilling of the covenant; and it is obligatory to give him some of the gifts which God Most High has specially bestowed upon the shaykh.

By His words, ﴿And do not compel﴾ etc., there is an indication that when the self is not inclined to act in this world, it is not compelled to it.

They have a long and broad discourse on the words of God Most High, ﴿God is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾. What we have mentioned earlier may be considered of this category. It is mentioned that the words of God Most High, ﴿men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God﴾, are among what includes in its generality the people of the exalted Naqshbandi path, who attained the inner remembrance, which took root in their hearts such that they are never heedless of Him, glorified is He, in any state. Although this is established for others among the adherents of the paths as well, it is established only in the ultimate stages and not in the beginnings, as it is established for the people of that path.

In the *Maktubat* of the Divine Imam (Ahmad Sirhindi), may God sanctify his secret, there is what suffices to avoid lengthy explanation of the states of these people and the explanation of their rank in remembrance and presence among the other groups. May God gather us and them under the banner of the Prophet (ﷺ).

It has been said that the words of God Most High, ﴿And whoever God does not give light, for him there is no light﴾, are an allusion to what has come in the hadith: "God Most High created creation in darkness, then sprinkled upon them of His light. Whoever is reached by some of it is guided, and whoever misses it goes astray."

And God Most High is the One who grants success for righteous deeds.

[p. 187]

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate/glorify Him all who are in the heavens and the earth﴾ and so on: this is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), addressed to the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ),

[p. 187 cont.]

to give notice, as in *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), that Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon him the highest and most manifest degrees of light, and has made clear to him the most subtle and most hidden of the secrets of the dominion (*al-mulk*) and the realm of the unseen (*al-malakut*). Al-Tabrisi said: it is an explanation of the signs that He made a light, and the address is to him (ﷺ), but what is meant is all the accountable people (*al-mukallafun*). The interrogative *hamza* is for affirmation (*taqrir*), and the verb "to see" (*ru'yah*) here means knowledge ('*ilm*). The apparent view is that its use for this is literal (*haqiqah*). It has been said that it is literal for sight, and its use for knowledge is a metaphor (*isti'arah* or *majaz*) based on the relation of necessity (*'alaqat al-luzum*). Whichever is the case, the meaning is: "Do you not know, through revelation, or through unveiling (*mukashafah*), or through reasoning (*istidlal*), that Allah the Exalted glorifies Him moment by moment, in His essence, His attributes and His acts, from everything unfitting to His majestic station, of deficiency or defect, in a figurative sense of glorification (*tanzih ma'nawi*) which sound minds understand, all who are in the heavens and the earth, of the rational and others, whatever they may be? For every existent among the possible existents, whether composite or simple, is, by its very essence, its existence and its changing states, a proof of a Creator who is necessarily existent (*wajib al-wujud*), characterized by the attributes of perfection, exalted above everything unfitting to His majestic affairs." He, glorified is He, has alerted to the perfect strength of that proof and the utmost clarity of it, in that He expressed it by what pertains to the rational beings, namely glorification (*tasbih*), which is the strongest and clearest degree of glorification, making the state's tongue (*lisan al-hal*) stand in the place of the tongue of speech (*lisan al-maqal*). The specification of glorification by mention, though the two (heavens and earth) indicate His being described with the attributes of perfection too, is because the context of the discourse is to condemn the condition of the unbelievers in their violation of glorification by making the inanimate objects partners with Him, glorified is He, in divinity, and attributing to Him, Mighty and Majestic, the taking of a son and the like, from which Allah is exalted far above.

The use of *man* (who) for rational and non-rational beings is by way of predominance (*taghlib*). Neither consideration of this, nor of a metaphor like it, is dispensed with by attributing glorification, which is specific to the rational, in its apparent sense, as some eminent scholars imagined. Some scholars took glorification to a metaphorical meaning encompassing the glorification of rational and non-rational beings, and called this a general metaphor (*'umum al-majaz*). It has been refuted that some of the rational beings, namely the unbelievers among the two groups (humans and jinn), definitely do not glorify Him in that sense; rather their glorification is only the indication mentioned, in which non-rational beings also share with them. There is in that a rebuke and a dismissal of them, as is evident. The claim that the unbelievers glorify just like the believers, but without awareness (*min haythu la yash'uruna*), as al-Hallaj said: "My denial of You is a sanctification that rational minds do not accept, and it is worthy that it not be accepted." Some said: if *man* is for predominance, it includes the obedient rational beings, the disobedient rational beings, and non-rational beings absolutely; so glorification is taken to a metaphorical meaning that can be attributed to all that has been mentioned. What prevents that? And this, as you see, is weak.

Abu Hayyan preferred keeping glorification in its apparent sense and restricting *man* to the obedient rational beings, and what was mentioned first is better.

﴿And the birds﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), as a conjunction upon *man* (who). Their specific mention, though they are included in what is on the earth, is because they do not permanently remain on the earth and because of their independence through a masterful craft and a splendid creation. Their glorification is intended to be explained from that aspect, because their reports clearly show the perfection of the power of their Maker and the subtlety of the management of their Originator, as indicated by the restriction in His words, exalted is He: ﴿in ranks﴾, meaning, their glorifying, i.e. being in a state of spreading their wings. For His giving the heavy bodies what enables them to stand in the air and to move as He wills, from wings and light tails, and His guiding them to the way of using them by folding, spreading, and moving them right and left and the like, is a proof clearly indicating the perfect power of the Skilled Maker and the utmost wisdom of the Originator and Restorer.

The conjunction upon what Abu Hayyan preferred is also upon *man*, and he stated this. It is reported from the majority (*al-jumhur*) that their glorification is real, and its apparent sense is that it is in the manner of the glorification of the rational beings of the two groups. Perhaps one who holds this does not commit to the obligation that the real glorification must be by words familiar to us, otherwise it would not be possible to say that their glorification is real with this obligation, since the words familiar to us from them are lacking. It is permissible to say that

[p. 188]

He, exalted is He, inspired the birds a specific glorification suitable to them, which is other than the state glorification which is the earlier indication. He estimates a verb raising them (*fi'l raf'*), meaning by it that inspired meaning: "and the birds glorify." The specification of their glorification by that meaning is mentioned because their voices are more manifest in existence and closer to being carried to glorification. But the restriction by the state, on this view, is in the beauty of its position, not as it was before.

Al-A'raj read *wa al-tayr* with *nasb* (accusative), as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*). Al-Hasan and Kharijah from Nafi' read *wa al-tayru saffatin* with both in *raf'*, as an inchoative and predicate. The apparent sense on this reading is that His words, exalted is He, ﴿each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ is a predicate after a predicate. On the majority's reading, it is a resumptive sentence brought to explain the perfect firmness of each one of those mentioned among the birds and those included in the generality of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ in glorification, and the firmness of its foot in it, by depicting its state with the state of one who knows what proceeds from him of actions, so he does them by intent and purpose, not by chance without thought. He, glorified is He, has embedded within it the indication that each of the things mentioned, together with what was mentioned of glorification, has an essential need for Him, the Exalted, and an overflow from Him, Mighty and Majestic, for what concerns it, by the tongue of its readiness. Its verification is that each of the possible existents in itself is far from deserving existence, but it is prepared to receive from Him, exalted is He, what suits His majesty of existence and what follows it of perfections, initially and continuously. So it receives overflow from Him, exalted is He, continually, and He overflows upon it at every moment from the varieties of overflows related to His essence and attributes, that speech cannot encompass, such that if the connection between what He has explained and the divine care were severed, it would cease entirely. He has expressed that spiritual overflow by prayer, which is supplication and entreaty, to complete the depiction. Its placement before glorification in mention is because it precedes it in rank. So says *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*. The discourse on it is a depictive metaphor (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*). The *mudaf ilayh* (the genitive element) that the *tanwin* in ﴿each﴾ replaces includes what is mentioned explicitly and what is included under the generality, even inanimate things. The pronoun in ﴿knew﴾ and likewise the two pronouns in ﴿its prayer and its glorification﴾ refer to each one. Al-Zajjaj went to this.

Some claimed that on this reading there is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*) in ﴿knew﴾, and he said in explaining it: it likens the indication of each of those mentioned upon the Truth by the tongue of the truth and the speech, and the inclination of each of them to benefit, whether by choice or by nature, to knowledge of glorification and prayer. So it applies the name "knowledge" to each of those indications and inclinations by way of metaphor, and derives the word "knowing" from it. Whoever has any taste does not accept this. He also permitted that prayer be a metaphor for inclination and glorification a metaphor for indication. Despite this, it was said that although it is valid, it is not suitable for the depiction. Some claimed that it is better to make the *mudaf ilayh* not include inanimate things, and this is not so. He permitted that the two pronouns in ﴿its prayer and its glorification﴾ refer to God, exalted is He, with the genitive being in the sense of the object. He permitted that they refer to each one of what is in the heavens and the earth, and the pronoun in ﴿knew﴾ refers to God, Mighty and Majestic. Many others said: it is permissible that there is no metaphor there, and "knowledge" is in its literal sense, meaning by it absolute perception, and by what the *tanwin* replaces are the kinds of birds or their individuals, and by prayer and glorification what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inspired each one of them, the specific supplication and glorification belonging to it. There is no remoteness in this inspiration, for He, glorified is He, inspired every kind of animal with subtle knowledge which the wisest of rational beings can hardly reach. This is something that cannot at all be denied. How not, when the hedgehog, though being the most distant of animals from perception, is said to sense the north and south winds before they blow, so it changes the entrance to its burrow. The sentence on this view is to explain the perfect firmness in the two matters, and that their issuing from the birds is not by chance without thought, but by knowledge and mastery, similar to what has passed, but not in the manner of depiction. A verb raising the birds was estimated

[p. 189]

over them, meaning: "and the birds glorify," as was mentioned before. It was not made conjunctive upon *man* and raised by its raiser. It was said that this leads to the glorification indicated by the mentioned verb meaning a metaphorical sense that includes the spoken and the state glorification of rational and non-rational beings, and what is in this has been mentioned before. It permitted that what the *tanwin* replaces be something that includes the birds and others from what is included in the earlier generality. But it has the problem that the inanimate, which is included in the generality, cannot be attributed knowledge, even if by the meaning of absolute perception, and it requires that it has knowledge and that He inspired it with prayer and glorification suitable to it, which many people do not accept. What relates to this station has been mentioned to you in Surat al-Isra', so remember it.

Some permitted, on the assumption of taking knowledge in its literal sense, that the conjunction of glorification upon prayer be an explanatory conjunction (*'atf al-tafsir*). You know that if this is accepted on that assumption, what prevents accepting it on the earlier assumption of making the metaphor depictive? Yes, on that, the inclusion that was pointed out earlier is lost, but this is not a hindrance. The truth is that the probability of the explanatory reading is remote, there is no need to commit to it, and rather it forfeits what it forfeits, as is not hidden.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning "of that which they do," is a closing parenthetical statement (*i'tiradh tadhyili*) confirming the content of what precedes. The *ma* (what) is either an expression for the indication that comprises all existents, rational and non-rational, and its expression by the verb attributed to the pronoun of the rational beings is as we indicated at the beginning of the discourse. Or it is an expression for it and for the specific glorification of the birds together, or for the glorification of the birds alone; then the verb is literal and its attribution to the pronoun of rational beings is as has passed, and the parenthetical statement on this confirms the glorification of the birds alone, and on the first two (readings) confirms the glorification of all. Or it is an expression for what is more general than prayer and glorification and other actions issuing from those in the heavens and the earth, and the states that befall them; then the parenthetical statement confirms the content of ﴿each has known﴾, meaning Allah, exalted is He, knows its prayer and its glorification. The matter of the expression by the verb and its attribution to the pronoun of rational beings is not hidden. And since the aspects in what passed are numerous, the possibilities here are multiplied, so reflect and do not be heedless.

Al-Hasan, 'Isa, Sallam and Harun from Abu 'Amr read *ta'alun* (you do) with the second-person *ta* (of address). In this, as it has been said, is a warning and intimidation. Apparently the address in it is to the unbelievers. Perhaps it is also permissible that the plural pronoun in the majority's reading refers to them too, with the meaning of the sentence being to frighten them for their turning away from glorifying Him, exalted is He, after He informed about those He informed about, that He knows their prayer and glorification. This, though remote, has in the mentioned reading a kind of support for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 42:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, not to other than Him, exalted is He, either independently or jointly, because He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of both and of what is in them, of the essences and the attributes, and He is the One who disposes of all of them by bringing into existence and annihilating, originating and restoring. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾, meaning: to Him, mighty and majestic, exclusively, not to anything else at all. ﴿The final return﴾, meaning the return of all things through annihilation and resurrection, is an explanation of the exclusivity of sovereignty to Him, exalted is He, in the end, following the explanation of His exclusivity in the beginning. It has been said that the sentence serves to clarify that what is seen of the manifestation of some effects at the hands of created beings does not contradict the preceding restriction, by conveying that the ending is toward Him, exalted is He, and not toward other than Him, and that this suffices for the restriction. But the first (view) is perhaps better. The mention of the Majestic Name in the place of the pronoun serves to inspire awe and to indicate the reason for the ruling. His, exalted is He, saying:

[Page 190]

*Ruh al-Ma'ani* of al-Alusi, on surah 24, verse 43:

﴿Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds gently﴾, etc. This is like an emphasis on what came before it. Al-ʾIzjaʾ (driving gently, from the root *z-j-w*) for something means to drive it gently and easily. It was said: he drove the heavy thing gently. It is also used, as some of the great scholars mentioned, for driving something small or insignificant. From this comes *al-biḍaʿa al-muzjāh* (the meagre merchandise), meaning goods driven along one piece after another, in small quantity and weakness. It was also said: *muzjāh* means "that which is driven," i.e., "pushed away" because one has no desire for it. The expression *yuzjī* (drives), as mentioned, hints that the cloud, in relation to God's power, is something of no account. *Saḥāb* (clouds) is a collective noun (*ism jins jamʿī*), whose singular is *saḥāba*. The meaning, as in the sea, is that He drives one cloud towards another. ﴿Then He joins it together﴾, by connecting one cloud with another. Many have said:

*"The cloud is one, like the 'ʿamāʾ' (a thing of unity)."*

The meaning is that He joins its parts and pieces together. This is because *bayn* (between) cannot be attached to something that is not plural. By this interpretation plurality is obtained, as it was said in the line: *bayn al-dukhūl fa-ḥawmal* (between Dukhūl and Ḥawmal). Some have dispensed with this by making *saḥāb* a collective noun, as you have heard.

Warsh, from Nafiʿ, read *yūlifu* without hamza. ﴿Then He makes it into a heap﴾, i.e., piled up, some of it upon the other. ﴿Then you see the rain﴾ (*al-wadq*), i.e., the rain, whether heavy or light, following its piling up and thickening. Ibn Abi Ḥatim transmitted from Abu Bajīla, from his father, that he explained *al-wadq* as lightning, but we have not seen this from anyone else. What we have found in most of the tafsirs and lexicons is that it means rain. ﴿It comes out from within it﴾, i.e., from its openings and exits which came about through piling up and compression. *Khilāl* is the plural of *khalal*, like *jibāl* of *jabal*. It was said that it is singular, like *ḥijāb* and *ḥijāz*. This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Zayd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muʿādh al-ʿAnbarī, from Abu ʿAmr and al-Zaʿfarānī, of *khallalahu* (with a doubled *l*). The intended meaning then is the category. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) from *al-wadq*, because the seeing is visual. In the mention of the making (*al-jaʿl*) being followed by seeing it coming out, rather than its emerging, there is an exaggeration of the speed of its emergence, in the manner of His words: *Then We said, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it split* (al-Shuʿarāʾ 63). There is also in it, in emphasising the seeing, what is not hidden.

﴿And He sends down from the sky﴾, i.e., from the clouds, for everything above you is a sky. The shifting from the cloud to the sky seems to hint that elevation has a part in what descends, according to the well-known opinion about the cause of hail's formation. It is also permitted that by "sky" is meant the direction of height, and the mention is made together with the sending down for this hint. ﴿Mountains﴾, i.e., pieces of great size resembling mountains in their bulk, as an eloquent simile (*tashbīh balīgh*), as in His words: *until, when He made it fire* (al-Kahf 96). By "mountains" are meant pieces of cloud. Among the strange things which language does not support, as in *al-Durar wal-Gharar al-Riḍawiyya*, is the statement of al-Iṣfahānī that "mountains" are what Allah created (*jabalahu*), i.e., made from hail. ﴿In them﴾, i.e., in the sky. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a qualifier for *jibāl* (mountains). His words, ﴿of hail﴾, and it is well known. It was named *barad* (hail) because it cools (*yubarridu*) the face of the earth, i.e., it strips it, from *barradtu al-shayʾa bil-mibrad* (I cooled the thing with the file). It is the object of *yunazzilu* (sends down), on the basis that *min* (from) is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*). It was said that it is redundant according to al-Akhfash's opinion. The first two *min*s are for the starting point (*ibtidāʾiyya*), and the second prepositional phrase is a substitute (*badal*) for the first, a substitute of inclusion or of part, i.e., "He sends down, starting from the sky, from mountains existing in it, some hail," or "hail."

Al-Ḥawfī claimed that the second *min* is partitive, like the third, together with his saying that it is a substitute, and this is a clear error. It was said: the first *min* is for the starting point, the second is partitive and stands in the position of the object. It was said: it is redundant according to al-Akhfash's opinion too, and the third is explanatory (*bayān*), i.e., "He sends down, starting from the sky, some mountains, or mountains existing in it which are hail," so what descends is hail. From al-Akhfash: the second *min* and the third *min* are both redundant, and each of the two prepositional phrases is in the position of an accusative: the first, as the object of *yunazzilu*, and the second as a substitute for it, i.e., "He sends down from the sky mountains, not hail," and its result is "He sends down hail from the sky."

Al-Farrāʾ said: they are both redundant, except that the noun with the first is in the position of the accusative (object), and the noun with the second is in the position of the nominative, either as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) with *fīhā* (in them) as its predicate, and the pronoun in *fīhā* refers to the mountains, i.e., "He sends down from the sky mountains; in those mountains is hail, and nothing else of pebbles or other things." Or it is the agent of *fīhā*, because it relies on the qualified noun, namely *jibāl*, and a pronoun referring to it too.

The intended meaning of *jibāl* (mountains), other than the position of the majority, is a metaphor, and its use in this sense has come in the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

*If I die, away from the remembrance of the rhymes, you will not find for them a poet from me, seeking and composing.*

*And the most abundant verse of a poet for whom the bellies of the mountains of poetry were struck, until it was made easy.*

It is said: he has a mountain of gold, and a mountain of knowledge. According to Mujāhid, al-Kalbī and most of the exegetes, the "sky" means the canopy, and "mountains" means their literal sense. They said: Allah created in the sky mountains of hail, just as He created in the earth mountains of stone. There is nothing in reason that negates this by any decisive proof, so it is permissible to keep the verse on its outward meaning, as has been said.

The well-known view among the people of philosophy (*ahl al-ḥikma*) is that the emanation of the powers of the heavenly bodies and their rays may cause the elevation of subtle bodies above the water, mixed with the air, and these are what are called vapour (*bukhār*). Because of its weight in relation to smoke, owing to its moisture, and the dryness of smoke, it stands in the region of the air in such a way that the heat coming from the ray reflected from the body of the earth does not reach it, and it remains far from what is heated by the heat of fire. So it remains in the cold layer of the air, and it cools and thickens gradually by rising, and a cloud is piled up from it, which then drips rain, either all of it or some of it, and some of it disperses, remaining in its airy form, and what has been dripped is changed back to its watery form. If its distance is long, it joins together, so its drops become larger. If the cold is intense upon them, they become hail, or they descend as snow. The rising of the vapour is then prevented, the surface of the earth cools along with the coldness of the atmosphere, and from this comes intense hail. If it meets wind, the hail intensifies, because the wind removes the earthly vapour. If it does not meet wind, the vapour melts the snow and the surface of the earth warms.

They mention that whenever the distance becomes long until they join, and the drops grow large, and cold meets them, the hail is greater in quantity. Sometimes rain freezes into hail inside the cloud and then descends. This happens in spring when it is touched by heat from outside, so the coldness within is concealed while it dissolves into drops, and then it freezes. Sometimes the vapour is too dense, so it cannot rise, and it cools quickly by what reaches it from the cold of the night, because there is no ray, and it does not become a cloud. From it comes the shade (*ẓill*). Sometimes it freezes in the heights before it piles up, and from it comes the frost (*ṣaqīʿ*). Sometimes the air is thickened by extreme cold, so it solidifies into a cloud and rains in its own state.

The truth is that all of this depends on the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His purpose, glory be to Him, which is founded upon wisdoms, benefits and causes, which were mentioned as customary (*ʿādiyya*). I see no harm in saying this. And considering that the first of the causes are the heavenly powers and their rays, it is correct to say that the descent begins from the sky, as the Allama al-Bayḍāwī indicated in his discussion of surah al-Baqara. Taking the verse according to what agrees with the well-known view does not impair its eloquence; rather it is more eloquent on this basis, and further from the doubts of the common people, especially the people of the mountains, who sometimes receive rain, and hail descends upon their land while they are above the mountains in the sun.

﴿So He strikes with it whom He wills﴾, i.e., with what descends of the hail, He strikes it upon whom He wills, so he suffers what harm he suffers to his property and person. ﴿And averts it from whom He wills﴾, that He turns it away from him, so he escapes its calamity. The return of the two pronouns to the hail is the apparent meaning.

In *al-Baḥr* it is permitted that the two pronouns return to *al-wadq* (rain) and the hail, and they are treated as the demonstrative: as if it were said, "He strikes with that, and averts that," and the rain is more prevalent in striking and averting, and more eloquent in benefit and kindness. End of quote. There is in it distance and clear prevention.

﴿The brightness of its lightning almost takes away the sight﴾, i.e., the light of the lightning of the cloud, described by what has passed of driving, joining, and other things. The attribution of the lightning to it before the statement of its existence in it is to announce the manifestness of its matter and its being independent of explicit mention. According to what you have heard from Abu Bajīla, there is no need for this. The return of the pronoun to the hail, i.e., the lightning of the hail which accompanies it, is nothing. The discussion of the reality of lightning has already passed, so recall it.

Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read *sanāʾan* (with a long *a*), *barquhu* with a *ḍamma* on the *bāʾ* and a *fatḥa* on the *rāʾ*, the plural of *barqa* with a *ḍamma* on the *bāʾ*, which is an amount of lightning, like *ghurfa* and *luqma*. From him also: he read *barqahu* with a *ḍamma* on the *bāʾ* and the *rāʾ*, making the vowel of the *rāʾ* follow that of the *bāʾ*, as it was said, a parallel to *ẓulumāt* (darknesses). *Sanāʾ* with the long vowel means height and elevation of rank, and here it is a metaphor for the strength of the light. It was read *yakādu sanā* with the *dāl* assimilated into the *sīn*. ﴿It almost takes away the sight﴾, i.e., snatches it away because of the extreme brightness and the speed of its arrival. The unrestricted mention of "sights" adds magnitude to its terror and a statement of the intensity of its effect upon them, as if it almost takes them away even at closing the eyes. This is among the strongest evidences of complete power, in that it brings forth an opposite from an opposite.

Abu Jaʿfar read *yadhhabu* with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a *kasra* on the *hāʾ*. Al-Akhfash and Abu Ḥātim held that this reading is an error. They said: because the *bāʾ* replaces the *hamza* (of causation), and it is not permitted for two transitivising particles to combine. They were wrong in this, because he would not have read except what was transmitted, and he took the reading from the leaders of the Successors, who took it from the great Companions, such as Ubayy and others, may Allah be pleased with them. He did not stand alone in it, as al-Zajjāj claimed; rather Shayba also read thus. It is explained as the addition of the *bāʾ*, meaning "it takes away the sights," and as the *bāʾ* being in the sense of *min* (from), as in the verse:
