*So she kissed a mouth holding back with its hardness, the drinking of one intoxicated, with the cold water of al-Ḥashraj.*

The object is omitted, i.e., "the light is taken from the sights." Al-Ḥarīrī, as transmitted from him by al-Ṭībī, permitted the combination of two transitivising particles.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 44:

﴿Allah alternates the night and the day﴾ by bringing one of them after the other, or by the decrease of one and the increase of the other, or by changing their states with heat and cold and other things that occur in them, among which is what was mentioned of driving the clouds and what follows from it. It seems that, according to this, the sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the wisdom behind what has passed. According to the first two views, it is a resumptive clause explaining that the Mighty and Majestic is not hindered by what precedes it, namely the driving (of the clouds), and what follows it. It has also been said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with what precedes it and falls within the scope of the seeing (al-ru'yah), and the conjunctive particle was dropped for the purpose of enumeration. But this, as you see, is weak.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ is a reference to what was detailed just before. The sense of distance in it, despite the nearness of what is referred to, serves to signal the elevation of its rank and the remoteness of its station. ﴿is surely a lesson (la-'ibrah)﴾: a clear indication of the existence of the eternal Creator, His oneness, the perfection of His power, the all-encompassing extent of His knowledge of all things, the penetration of His will, and His transcendence above what is not fitting for His exalted dignity. The indication of His oneness is through the proof of mutual exclusion (burhan al-tamanu'), since otherwise there would be obscurity in it; whereas its indication of the other matters is clear. ﴿for those endowed with sight (li-ulil-absar)﴾, i.e., for everyone who has insight (basirah) which he reflects upon and comprehends. Thus al-absar here is the plural of basar in the sense of insight (basirah), unlike its usage in what preceded. It has also been said that it means the outward sight (al-basar al-zahir), as is the immediate understanding of the word, and the expression with this, rather than basa'ir (insights), is to signal the clarity of the indication.

It has been objected that this implies the loss of the elegance of paronomasia (husn al-tajnis) and the commission of what is akin to iyta' (repetition of a word in close proximity). It is well known that there is no perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm) in the Qur'an other than in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And on the day the Hour will be established, the criminals will swear that they remained not but an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55]. There is a discussion of this which al-Suyuti transmitted in al-Itqan, arising from a lack of precision for one who examines it closely. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani identified another instance, namely this noble verse, and it holds only according to what we have said. Al-Baydawi and others also pointed to it. Perhaps whoever chose the immediate sense considered that the excellence of that indication exceeds the excellence of paronomasia, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 45:

﴿And Allah created every creature (dabbah)﴾, that is, every animal that crawls upon the earth. They included birds and fish in this. The apparent sense of the words of some of the imams of tafsir (exegesis) is that angels and jinn enter into the generality of "dabbah." Perhaps in his view it refers to everything that crawls and moves, without restriction, while most of the lexicographers explain it as I have heard. The ta' in it is for transfer to the category of nouns (ism), not for feminine marking. It has also been said that dabbah is a singular whose plural is dabb, like kha'inah and kha'in.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabbath and al-A'mash read "khaliq" as an active participle, with "kulli dabbah" in the genitive through the construction (idafah): ﴿from water﴾. It is the constituent part of its material. He singled it out for mention because of the evident greater need of living beings for it after the perfection of their composition, and because the mixing of the earthy parts with it, and for other reasons; or [the water is] a particular water, which is the nutfah (seminal fluid). So the indefinite form (in "ma'") is for the generic singularity according to the first view, and for the individual singularity according to the second.

It is permitted that it may be for both of these, and the word "kull" according to the second view is for multiplication, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to which the fruits of every (kull) thing are brought﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], because among the animals there are those that come into being not from a nutfah. Some claimed that it is also for this according to the first view, on the basis that dabbah includes the angels created from light and the jinn created from fire. He also claimed that among mankind there are those who were not created from water either, namely Adam and Jesus, peace be upon them both: the first was created from earth, and the second was created from the Spirit. But what is wrong with this is not hidden. It is permitted that the generality be considered in "kull" and that by dabbah be meant what is created by procreation, with the indication "min ma'" meaning nutfah. There is discussion in this. It has also been said: there is nothing, whether a dabbah or otherwise, except that it is created from water, so it is the origin of all created things, because of what has been narrated: "The first thing Allah, exalted is He, created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air and light, and from them He created the creation." Whichever is the case, "min" is related to "khalq" (creating).

Al-Qaffal said, and al-Imam approved it: it is related to a deleted element that occurs as a qualifier of dabbah. The meaning is the information that He, exalted is He, created every dabbah existing or generated from water. So the generality of dabbah in his view is specified by the qualifier, and the generality of "kull" is on its apparent sense.

The apparent view is that it is related to "khalq," and this is more suited to the context, as is not hidden from those of understanding. The indefiniteness of "ma'" here and its definiteness in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30] is because the intention here is the meaning of individuality, whether individual or kind, while the intention there is the meaning of the genus, and that the true nature of water is the origin of every living thing. ﴿So among them is one that walks on its belly﴾, like snakes and fish. Calling their movement "walking" despite it being crawling is a metaphor for the sake of emphasis in showing power, and that they crawl without an instrument, like walking and more powerful. What adds beauty to this is the correspondence (mushakalah) with the mention of the crawler alongside those who walk. The parallel here, in one view, to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10] ... ﴿and among them is one that walks on two legs﴾, like humans and birds, ﴿and among them is one that walks on four﴾, like cattle and wild animals.

The apparent view is that what is meant is four legs, so this gives the application of "leg" to what preceded of the limbs of beings with four limbs. The application of "hand" to it has come, and the omission of mention of what walks on more than four, like spiders, the mother of forty-four, and other insects, is because they are not counted, along with the indication to them in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah creates what He wills﴾, that is, of what is mentioned and what is not mentioned, simple or compound, in whatever forms, limbs, movements, natures, powers and actions He wills. The philosophers claimed that the support of an animal having more than four is only on four, and they have no proof for that. In the codex of Ubayy: "and among them is one that walks on more," and this is clear against what they claim, but it was not established as Qur'an. The masculine form of the pronoun in "minhum" is for giving precedence to rational beings, and the expression "man" applied to what does not reason is built upon this precedence in the pronoun, as stated by al-Radi. The wording of some expressions suggests that precedence is considered in ﴿every dabbah﴾, but this is not intended; rather, the meaning is that since this included rational beings and others by way of mixing, it required considering that in the pronoun returning to it, and giving precedence to rational beings within it. It is understood from the words of some verifiers that there is no precedence in the first and third "min," but it is only in the second. It may be said: there is no precedence in the three after considering it in the pronoun, so reflect.

The arrangement of the categories is as they are ordered, to put first what is more evident in power. This does not contradict that walking on the belly in the sense of crawling is a metaphor, as was supposed. The displaying of the noble Name in place of the pronoun is to magnify the status of the mentioned creation and to announce that it is among the rulings of divinity. The display in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾, that is, He does what He wills as He wills, also for this, with emphasis on the independence of the explanatory resumption.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 46:

﴿Indeed We have sent down clear verses﴾ That is, clarifying everything whose clarification is fitting, of the religious rulings (al-ahkam al-diniyya) and the cosmic secrets (al-asrar al-takwiniyya); or, clear in themselves. This is like an introduction to what follows, and for this reason no conjunction (al-'atif) is used in it, unlike what He, glory be to Him, used in what preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses and an example from those who passed away before you﴾ [al-Nur: 34], and from the difference in context the reason for mentioning "to you" (ilaykum) there and not mentioning it here becomes known.

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills﴾ His guidance is by His granting success (tawfiq) to the correct consideration of them and to reflection upon their meanings, ﴿to a straight path﴾ that leads to the reality of the truth and to success in Paradise.

﴿And they say, "We believe in Allah and in the Messenger"﴾. This begins an account of the condition of some who were not guided by Allah the Exalted to the straight path. They are a category of disbelievers whose deeds were described earlier.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Qatadah that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and similar was narrated from al-Hasan.

It was also said that it was revealed "concerning Bishr the hypocrite. A Jew called him in a dispute between them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he called the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Then they went to the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and he ruled in favour of the Jew, but the hypocrite was not pleased with his judgment (peace and blessings be upon him) and said, 'Let us go to judgment before Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).' When they both went to him, the Jew said to him, 'The Prophet (ﷺ) ruled for me, but he did not accept his judgment.' So Umar said to the hypocrite, 'Is that so?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Stay where you are until I come out to you.' He (may Allah be pleased with him) entered his house and came out with his sword, struck the neck of that hypocrite until he was cold, and said, 'This is how I judge for whoever is not pleased with the judgment of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).' Then it was revealed." Jibril (peace be upon him) said, "Umar distinguished between truth and falsehood," and for that he was named al-Faruq (the Distinguisher). This was narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them).

Al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il. There was a dispute between him and Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) over land. They divided it, and Ali received a portion that water could reach only with difficulty. Al-Mughirah said, "Sell me your land," so he sold it to him, and they exchanged. It was said to al-Mughirah, "You have taken a salt marsh (sabkhah) that water cannot reach." Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said to him, "Take back your land, for I only sold it to you if you were pleased with it, and you were not pleased with it, since water does not reach it." Ali said, "You bought it, you were pleased with it, you took possession of it, and you know its condition. I will not accept it back from you." He invited him to bring the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he said, "As for Muhammad, I will not go to him, for he bears enmity towards me, and I fear that he will be unjust to me." Then it was revealed.

According to this and what precedes it, the pronoun in the plural (يَقُولُونَ, "they say") is used either because the ruling is general, or because the speaker has a group who support him and agree with him in that statement, as in the saying "The sons of so-and-so killed a man," while the killer is only one of them.

The repetition of the preposition (ب, "in/by") in ﴿بِالرَّسُولِ﴾ serves to emphasise the claim of faith. Likewise, referring to him (ﷺ) by the title "the Messenger" (الرَّسُولِ) does the same. And their saying, along with that, ﴿وأطَعْنا﴾ ("and we obeyed"), means: and we obeyed Allah the Exalted and the Messenger (ﷺ) in command and prohibition. ﴿ثُمَّ يَتَوَلّى﴾ ("then turns away") means: turns away from what this statement requires, namely accepting the legal ruling imposed upon them. ﴿فَرِيقٌ مِنهم مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("a party of them after that") means: after what proceeded from them of claiming faith in Allah the Exalted and in the Messenger (ﷺ) and obedience to both of them. The sense of distance in ذَلِكَ ("that") is to indicate that this is a matter that is significant and must be observed. ﴿وما أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("and those are not") refers to the speakers of ﴿آمَنّا﴾ ("we believed"), etc., and they are the hypocrites, all of them, not only the party that turns away from among them. The sense of distance in أُولَئِكَ indicates the remoteness of their rank in disbelief and corruption. That is: and those are not the ones who claim faith and obedience, then some of them turn away, those who associate with them in the creed and the deed. ﴿بِالمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("believers") means: truly believers, as the ل (lam) in الْمُؤْمِنِينَ indicates, i.e., they are not the believers known for sincerity and steadfastness upon it. Negating faith in this sense of them necessitates negating it from the party in the most emphatic and forceful way, and therefore it was chosen that the demonstrative refers to them. It is also permitted that it refers to the party, with the meaning that those intended are a party of hypocrites, and the pronoun in ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ ("they say") refers to believers in general. The judgment against that party, negating faith from them, is due to the manifest sign of denial, which is the turning away from them. And ثُمَّ ("then") on this reading, as established by al-Tibi, is for remoteness, as if it were said: how do they enter among the company of the believers who say, "We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey," then turn away, and deviate from the believing party, and turn away from that statement? This is far from any sound, discerning person. On the first reading, as he also established, ثُمَّ is for delay in rank, indicating that the elevation of the level of disbelief of the party that turns away from them is the lowering of the level of those others.

In al-Kashf: the speech, on the assumption that the demonstrative refers to the speakers and not to the party that turns away alone, is like an exceptional addition, and in it is an indication of the deep immersion of those who turn away in disbelief, while the root of disbelief includes both groups. As for the assumption that the demonstrative is restricted to those who turn away, the benefit of ثُمَّ is to express the remoteness of turning away after that statement, and the benefit of the report is to show that they did not remain steadfast in their saying, as if it were said: they say this, then there is found among them what contradicts it, so there is no implication in its indication that others are believers. End of quote. Accordingly, the pronoun in ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ refers to the hypocrites, including the party that turns away, not to the believers in general, on both readings. So reflect.

﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾, i.e., between them and their adversaries. The pronoun in (yahkuma, "he may judge") refers to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to what is understood from the context, namely "the one called to," which includes Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, though the one who actually carries out the judgment is the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah mentions Himself alongside him under both interpretations, to magnify him, upon him be blessings and peace, to indicate the exalted status of his position with Allah the Exalted, and that his judgment is in reality the judgment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For they have said: when two connected nouns are mentioned and the ruling applies to only one of them, as in His saying, ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9], this conveys the strength of the connection between the conjoined term (al-ma'tuf) and the term it is conjoined to (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi), and that the two are as one thing, such that the attributes and conditions of one may be attributed to the other. The pronoun in ﴿da'u﴾ ("they are called") refers to the same thing that the pronoun in (yaqulun, "they say") refers to. That is: when the hypocrites, or the believers in general, are called, ﴿behold, a party of them turn away﴾, i.e., a party of them suddenly turns away from submitting to the judgment of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, because the right is against them, and because they know that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, judges only by the truth. The conditional clause (al-jumla al-shartiyya) explains the turning away and intensifies it, since it conveys that they abruptly turn away immediately upon being called, not merely upon being judged against, together with what the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) serving as the response (jaza', "apodosis") conveys of establishment and continuity, according to the well-known view. The expression ﴿between them﴾ is used rather than ﴿against them﴾, because it is customary for one of two disputants to say to the other: "Come with me to so-and-so, that he may judge between us, not against you," and this is the fair manner. It was also said: this turning away occurs when the matter is unclear to them. For this reason He, glorified is He, said ﴿between them﴾ and not ﴿against them﴾. In this there is additional intensification in censuring them. However, there is a point of discussion in this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 49:

﴿And if the right is theirs﴾, i.e., not against them, as the fronting of the predicate (al-khabar) indicates, ﴿they come to him﴾, i.e., to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ﴿submissively﴾, i.e., compliant, knowing that he, upon him be blessing and peace, will judge in their favour.

Page 196

The apparent reading is that ilā (to) is connected to ya'tū (they come). It has also been permitted to connect ilā to mudh'inīn (submissively), taking it to mean the lām (to/for), or by taking idhān (submission) to imply the sense of hastening. Al-Zajjaj explained it as hastening together with obedience. The fronting of the object (ta'dim al-ma'mul) is for exclusivity (ikhtisas), or for the sake of the closing rhyme (fasila), or for both. The use of idhā (when) earlier indicates the realisation of the condition, while the use of inna (indeed/if) here indicates its non-realisation. In this too there is a censure of them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 50:

And His saying, ﴿Is there a sickness in their hearts, or have they become doubtful, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust toward them?﴾ is a division (taqsim) of the cause of the aversion mentioned. The axis of the interrogation is what is understood from the speech, as if it were said: Is the cause of their aversion from being judged by him (ﷺ) that they are sick at heart due to their disbelief and hypocrisy, or is its cause that they have become doubtful and have doubted the matter of his prophethood (peace be upon him) despite the clarity of its truth, or is its cause that they fear that Allah, exalted is His majesty, and His Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) will act unjustly and oppress them?

This is like your saying: "Is there sickness in him, or has he gone away from the town, or does he fear the informer?" after saying, for example, "The beloved has abandoned (me)." For the meaning that the cause of his abandonment is that he has a sickness, or that its cause is that he has gone away from the town, or that its cause is that he fears the informer, is very clear, and it is common in conversation. However, the interrogation in the verse is denunciatory (inkari), and it is for the denial of causality (sababiyya).

And His saying, ﴿Rather, those are the wrongdoers﴾ is a specification of the cause after the negation of the causality of all that preceded. Thus it contains an emphasis on what the interrogation implies, as if it were said: None of what was mentioned is a cause for that aversion. As for the first two, if either of them were a cause for it, they would have turned away from being judged by him (peace be upon him) when the right was on their side, and when they came to him (peace be upon him) submitting to his judgment, since their hypocrisy and doubt would then also be established. As for the third, it is negated altogether, since they did not fear injustice at all, because they knew the details of his (peace be upon him) circumstances in trustworthiness and firmness upon the truth. Rather, the cause of that is that they themselves are the wrongdoers, who wish to wrong (others) regarding the right that he has over them, and their aim cannot be achieved while submitting to being judged by him (peace be upon him). So they turn away from it, because he (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) judges with the truth against them. Thus, the core of the negation derived from the denunciatory interrogation and the transitional idrab (bal, "rather," which turns from one point to another) in the first two is the attribute of their being causes of the aversion only, while those two are themselves established in reality. In the third, the negation concerns both the root and the attribute together.

If one restricts doubt (irtiyab) to what has some valid basis for arising in them in general, as some have done when they made the meaning "or they have become doubtful, by seeing from him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) an accusation, so their trust and certainty in him (peace be upon him) were removed," then the negation in the second is the same as in the third. This is how one of the eminent scholars established it.

(And "am") in it is connected (muttasilah). Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also held that it is connected, since they took what preceded as a division of the cause of the aversion. However, the former made the idrab from the last of the three matters, and justified it by saying that it is more indicative of what they were upon and more emphatic in denial, inasmuch as it contradicts their hastening to him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) when the right was on their side against others. The latter made it an idrab from the last two of them in order to confirm the first division, and said: The aspect of the division is that their refusal to be judged by him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) is either due to a defect in them or in the judge, and the latter is either certain or anticipated. He interpreted doubt as seeing an accusation that removes their certainty. Then he said: Both are invalid, so the first is determined. As for the first, it is obvious. As for the second, the station of prophethood and his (peace be upon him) extreme trustworthiness prevent it, and their wrongdoing encompasses the defect of their belief and the inclination of their souls toward injustice.

The Allamah al-Tibi said: The truth is that "bal" is an idrab from the division itself, and it is a transitional idrab, as if it were said: Leave the division, for they are the complete wrongdoers, who combine all those attributes, and therefore they turn away from your judgment. This is indicated by the use of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah).

The address, the definiteness of the predicate by the generic lam (lam al-jins), and the placement of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) all support this. What is related from the Imam also indicates that "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah). He said: I establish them upon each of these attributes, so there was in their hearts a sickness, which is hypocrisy, and so there was in them doubt, so they feared injustice. The aspect of the idrab is that each causes the other, and the knowledge of its existence is an addition. It was objected that causation is not necessarily required unless one claims it specifically for this material.

Abu Hayyan explicitly said that it is disjunctive, and that the interrogation is for reproach and rebuke, so that they acknowledge one of these aspects which are upon them, and what is upon them in acknowledging it. It is used in blame and in praise, as in the saying of the poet:

"Are you not of the people who pledged together to (commit) baseness and abomination in the bygone age?"

And his saying:

"Are you not the best of those who mounted the mounts, and the most generous of all people in offering wine?"

It is not hidden that the more apparent view is that it is connected. The mutual implication among the three matters is disputed, but even so it does no harm, and the meaning of the verse is what we mentioned at first. The placing of ﴿upon them﴾ before "the Messenger" is for emphasis that his (peace be upon him) judgment is the judgment of Allah, exalted is He. The reason for the variation in the styles of the sentences becomes apparent upon slight reflection.

[Page 197]

The saying of the Most High: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ follows His usual practice of mentioning the one who is right and the one who is wrong, and of drawing attention to what is fitting after denouncing what is not.

The accusative ﴿qawla﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of kana, and "an" with what follows it is, in interpretation, the verbal noun (masdar) standing as its subject (ism). Sibawayh explicitly permitted the reverse in such constructions: ﴿qawlu﴾ is put in the nominative as the subject, and the masdar formed from the "an" clause is put in the accusative as the predicate.

Ali, may Allah honor his face, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read ﴿qawlun﴾ in the nominative on this basis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The accusative is stronger, because what is more appropriate to serve as the subject is what is more definite, and that is the masdar interpreted from 'an yaqulu'. It cannot be indefinite, unlike ﴿qawla al-mu'minin﴾, which admits indefiniteness, as when the genitive is dropped from it." It has been said regarding its being more definite that it cannot take an adjective, like a pronoun. It is not hidden that this has no bearing on definiteness. Furthermore, you know that the masdar formed from "anna" and the verb does not have to be annexed (idafa) in every position. Do you not see that they said regarding the saying of the Most High: ﴿And it was not for this Qur'an to be invented﴾ [Yunus: 37] that it means "this Qur'an was not an invention"?

He mentioned that permitting its indefiniteness is the view of al-Farisi, and that it is required in examples such as "an yaqumu rajul" (that a man should stand), since it is definitively interpreted as "qiyam rajul" (the standing of a man), which is certainly indefinite.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim it is stated that the accusative is stronger in terms of grammatical construction, but the nominative is more firmly grounded in meaning and more fully suited to the context, since the locus of benefit and the point of clarification in sentences is the predicate. Therefore what is more informative, more clearly indicative of occurrence, and more inclusive of specific relations that are remote from occurrence in external reality and in the hearer's mind, is more deserving of being the predicate. There is no doubt that this is most complete and perfect here in "an" with what follows it. So it is more deserving of being the predicate. As for what the annexation conveys of a general, unspecified relation, since it is of little use and easy to attain both externally and mentally, it is appropriate that it be considered in a general way and made the heading of the subject. The meaning is: "Only the general saying issued by the believers, when they are called to Allah the Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) so that he may judge between them and their opponents, is that they say, 'We hear,' etc.," meaning the particular nature of this saying related about them, not any other saying at all. As for the accusative, the meaning according to it is: "It was only a saying of the believers, the particular nature of their saying 'We hear,' etc." In this there is one who made the more specific and more remote of the two relations, in occurrence and in presence in minds, and the more deserving of explanation, taken as already settled, the heading of the subject, while bringing forward what is contrary to them in the context of the primary intention is not hidden. End of quotation. Some of them examined this and said: the flow of the verse requires that the saying of the believers, "We hear and we obey," stand in contrast to the turning away of the hypocrites. Since that was condemned in the most complete way, it is appropriate that this be praised. There is no doubt that the most fitting way to praise it is to report it as a fact rather than to report it as something predicated. So ﴿an yaqulu sami'na wa atana﴾ should be made the subject of kana and ﴿qawla al-mu'minin﴾ its predicate. In this there is praise for their saying "We hear and we obey", since the meaning of it being "the saying of the believers" is that it is a saying fitting for them and characteristic of them. Moreover, what is more important to convey is that this particular saying is their saying ﴿when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that he may judge between them﴾, meaning their saying restricted by what was mentioned, so that the contrast between their saying "We hear and we obey" and the saying of the hypocrites, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger and we obey", may appear in the fullest clarity. So reflect on this, for it is not free of some unease.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended by "atana" (we obeyed) here is other than what is intended in what came before. It is as though they meant: "We hear your speech and we obey your command to go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that he may judge between you and us." It has been said that the meaning is: "We accept your word, submit to it, and respond to the judgment of Allah the Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ)." It is also related from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil that the meaning is: "We hear the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) and we obey his command." It has been said that what is meant by obedience is steadfastness or sincerity, because it differs from what came before. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

Al-Jahdari and Khalid ibn al-Ilyas read ﴿liyuhkama﴾ in the passive voice, responding to ﴿da'u﴾ (they were called). Abu Ja'far likewise read it here and in the earlier instance. The deputy of the subject is the pronoun for the verbal noun, meaning "that it (the judgment) may be judged," that is, "that the judgment may take place," as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿and a barrier will be placed between them﴾ [Saba: 54].

﴿And those﴾ is a reference to the believers in view of the utterance of the aforementioned saying from them, and the sense of distance in it is to signal the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence, meaning: "And those described with what has been mentioned of the sublime attribute, ﴿they are the successful﴾," that is, they are the ones who attain every desired goal and are saved from every dreaded thing.

[Page 198]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 52:**

﴿Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that begins afresh), brought to confirm the content of what precedes it regarding the good state of the believers, and to encourage others to join their ranks. That is: whoever obeys Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger (ﷺ), whoever he may be, in what he has commanded of the obligatory and the recommended rulings. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger in the obligatory duties and the sunnah." This allows for *al-laff wa al-nashr* (a rhetorical device of wrapping and unfolding, where two items are mentioned and each is matched with its corresponding counterpart without explicit specification), and al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan) followed this interpretation. ﴿And fears Allah﴾ for what has passed of his sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what is yet to come. ﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with what was mentioned of obedience, fear, and taqwa (God-consciousness), ﴿they are the triumphant﴾ with everlasting bliss, not by reason of their number.

Abu Ja'far, Qalun on the authority of Nafi', and Ya'qub read «wa-yattaqihi» with a kasra on the qaf and a kasra on the ha', without ishba' (lengthening of the vowel). Abu 'Amr, Hamzah in the narration of al-'Ijli, Khallad, Abu Bakr in the narration of Hammad, and Yahya read it with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ha'. Hafs read it with a sukun on the qaf and a kasra on the ha', not lengthened. The rest read it with a kasra on the qaf and a kasra on the ha', lengthened such that a yā' is produced.

The justification for this was given by Abu 'Ali: the principle regarding the ha' of the pronoun, when the letter before it is vowelled, is that its vowel is lengthened, as in «yu'tihi» and «yu'addihi». The justification for not lengthening is that the letter before the pronoun is, in effect, quiescent, and lengthening is not applied to its vowel when the preceding letter is quiescent, as in «kaffayhi» and «minhu». The justification for the sukun on the ha' is that it is the ha' of pause (*ha' al-sakt*), which is quiescent in their speech; it was also said that it is the ha' of the pronoun, but it was treated as the ha' of pause and so became quiescent, and the connected state is often treated as the pausal state. It is related from Sibawayh that he heard someone say: "Hadhihi ummatu Allah" in both connection and pause.

The justification for Hafs's reading is that he gave «yattaqihi» the status of «katif» because it follows its pattern, so he lightened its middle with a sukun, treating it as a single word, just as he lightened «yalida» in the saying: "And one with a child whom two parents did not beget" (*yalid*).

It is related from Ibn al-Anbari that this is a dialect of some Arabs regarding every defective verb whose final letter has been elided: they say "lam ara Zaydan" (I did not see Zayd), dropping the letter for the jussive and then making the preceding letter quiescent. On this is the saying of the poet:

"And whoever keeps his duty, then Allah is with him,
and the provision of Allah is brought morning and evening."

And his saying:

"Sulayma said: 'Buy us some sawiq (a kind of porridge),
and bring bread of wheat or flour.'"

The ha' is either the ha' of pause, moved because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, or a pronoun. The analogy would have been to vowel it with a damma in that case, as in «minhu», but the sukun, being incidental, was not taken into account, and so that it would not shift from a kasra to a damma by estimation. The first view was deemed weak because it requires moving the ha' of pause and retaining it in connection. Thus it was said, so consider this carefully.

[Page 199]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 53:**

﴿And they swore by Allah﴾

This is a report of another of the lies of the disbelieving hypocrites, emphasized with false oaths. It is a return to the beginning of the topic. The *qasam* (oath) means swearing. Its root is from *qasamah* (the procedure of oaths imposed on those accused of murder, as explained in the books of jurisprudence), and then the word became the name for every oath.

Allah's words, ﴿with the utmost of their oaths﴾, are in the accusative (*nasb*) as a *masdar* (verbal noun) emphasizing its omitted verb. The clause of that verb with its subject is in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial accusative). Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase, meaning: they swore by Him, the Exalted, exerting their oaths to the utmost, or striving in their oaths. The meaning of *juhd al-yamin* (the utmost of an oath) is reaching its end, by way of *isti'arah* (metaphor), from the saying "juhd nafsihi" when someone reaches the limit of his capacity and strength. The intended meaning is that they swore with the strongest degree of oath in intensity and firmness. It is also permitted that it be a *masdar* emphasizing ﴿they swore﴾, meaning: they swore with the swearing of striving in the oath. Muqatil said: whoever swears by Allah, the Exalted, has exerted himself in the oath.

Apparently here, they intensified and strengthened the oaths and did not suffice with saying "By Allah" ﴿If you were to order them﴾, that is, to go forth, as His words indicate: ﴿they would surely go forth﴾.

The intended meaning of this going forth is going out for jihad, as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, what indicates that the intended meaning is going out from wealth.

Whichever it is, the clause is the answer to ﴿they swore﴾, and the answer of the condition is omitted, because this clause indicates it. The clause is a report in meaning, and the original is ﴿we would surely go forth﴾ in the first person plural form. It was said that the original is ﴿we went forth﴾, but what is intended is reporting the past situation, so it was expressed in that way. It was objected that the criterion is the time of the ruling, which is future.

﴿Say﴾, that is, as a reply to them and a rebuke to them for uttering those oaths, and to show that they are not accepted, because they are liars in them:

﴿Do not swear﴾ about what your speech indicates of obedience. ﴿Reasonable obedience﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: your obedience is reasonable obedience. The sentence is a causal explanation (*ta'lil*) of the prohibition, as if it were said: do not swear about what you claim of obedience, because your obedience is well-known obedience, in that it occurs only by the tongue without agreement of the heart, which none of the people fail to know. It was said that the intended estimate is: what is required from you is well-known, recognized obedience, which no one doubts, like the obedience of the sincere believers. It was said that ﴿obedience﴾ (*ta'ah*) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: a reasonable obedience, moderate according to capacity, is better and more fitting for you than your oath. Al-Zajjaj chose this. It was also said: it is in the nominative by a verb estimated, meaning: let there be reasonable obedience from you. All were weakened: the first because the context does not support it, and the last because it involves omitting the verb in a place where omission does not belong.

Al-Baqa'i said: there is no estimate in the sentence. ﴿And obedience﴾ is a subject whose predicate is ﴿reasonable﴾.

What justifies beginning with an indefinite noun is that it is intended as the reality, so it is general, and generality is one of the justifications. It was not made definite, lest it be thought that its definiteness is for a specific reference. The sentence is a causal explanation of the prohibition, meaning: do not swear, for obedience is known from you and from others, not hidden. The custom of Allah, the Exalted, is that the servant, even if he strives to hide his obedience, his signs must appear on his character. Likewise disobedience. So there is no benefit in displaying what contradicts reality. The hadiths bear witness to what has been mentioned.

Al-Tabarani transmitted from Jundub: "No servant conceals a secret but Allah clothes him in its garment."

Al-Hakim transmitted, and said it is of sound chain, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "If one of you were to work inside a solid rock that has no door or window, his work would come out for people, whoever they might be."

This meaning, as has been said, is good, but it contradicts the apparent sense.

Zayd ibn Ali and al-Yazidi read ﴿reasonable obedience﴾ in the accusative, as an estimate of "you obey with reasonable hypocritical obedience". It was also said: "obey with reasonable genuine obedience". And *ta'ah* is in the sense of *ita'ah* (obedience), as in His words: ﴿He brought you forth from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17].

﴿Indeed, Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, of the apparent and hidden actions, among which are what you show of the lies emphasized by false oaths, and what you conceal of disbelief, hypocrisy, the determination to deceive the believers, and other kinds of evil and corruption. The intended meaning is a warning that He, the Exalted, will requite them for all their evil deeds, among which is their hypocrisy. In *al-Irshad* it is said that the sentence is a causal explanation of the ruling that their obedience is hypocritical obedience, indicating that the basis of the fame of its matter among the believers is His, the Exalted, informing about that, and a warning to them of requital.

[Page 200]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 54:

﴿Say: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger."﴾ The command to "say" is repeated to show the utmost concern with it and to signal the difference between the two statements: the first statement is a prohibition by way of rebuttal and rebuke, while the second is a command by way of obligation and legislation. In the repetition of the verb of obedience, and in the shift from "obey me" (aṭīʿūnī) to "obey the Messenger" (aṭīʿū al-Rasūl), there is an evident encouragement to obedience. Its absolute form, free of any qualifier such as soundness or sincerity, comes after their obedience was described in the preceding verse, to draw attention to the fact that what they offered was not obedience at all.

Allah's words, ﴿But if they turn away﴾, are addressed to the hypocrites, to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say what he had heard from his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. This is not included within the scope of "Say," according to what Ṣāḥib al-Taqrīb and others have chosen. It contains an emphasis on the preceding command, an intensification in making compliance with it obligatory, and an urging toward it through both warning and encouragement, because changing the wording of a speech that has been directed toward a certain meaning, and diverting it from its established course, indicates a new concern on the part of the speaker with its matter and draws greater desire for it from the listener, especially when this is done by shifting the address to a direct intermediary, as here. The particle "fa" (then) denotes that what follows is the consequence of the Prophet's (ﷺ) conveying to them what he was commanded to convey. The non-explicit mention signifies his (ﷺ) utmost haste in conveying what he was commanded, and that mention is unnecessary. That is: if you turn away from obedience after the Messenger (ﷺ) has commanded you to it, ﴿then upon him﴾, that is, upon the Messenger (ﷺ), is only ﴿what he was charged with﴾, that is, what he was commanded to convey, which you have witnessed when he said: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger." ﴿And upon you is what you are charged with﴾, that is, what you were commanded to obey. Perhaps the expression "charged" (ḥummila) is used first to indicate the weight of revelation in itself, and second to indicate the weight of the command upon them. It has been said that perhaps this expression is used with regard to them to indicate its weight and that its burdens remain upon them afterward, as if it were said: since you have turned away from that, you remain under that heavy burden. The expression is used regarding him (ﷺ) for the sake of parallelism. The "fa" falls in the response of the condition, and what follows stands in place of the response, or is a response in the manner of the expression in Allah's words: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Naḥl: 53], as if it were said: "If you turn away, then know that upon him is..." etc.

That said, some have chosen to include the conditional clause within the scope of "say." Al-Ṭībī said: The apparent meaning is that Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger," and not to fear their harm. So the original statement was: "Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger; but if they turn away, then upon you is what you are charged with, and upon them is what they are charged with," meaning: "they cannot harm you at all, and they only harm themselves." He shifted the speech from the past tense, since the third-person form in ﴿tawallaw﴾ was past, to the present, and the address in "tatawallaw" is with one of the two tā' elided, meaning: "they did not harm you, and they only harmed themselves," so that the direct address would be more forceful in rebuking them. Others regarded this as a shift (iltifāt) in a loose sense, while others regarded it as a true iltifāt, in that they were first made the subject of third-person address when the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to address them with "say to them," and then they were addressed directly, by Allah, with "if you turn away," independently and not through His Messenger (ﷺ). It is not hidden that reading the verse as an independent direct address, not included within "say," adds to the rebuke.

It is reported in al-Aḥkām that this verse has been cited as evidence that the command (amr) denotes obligation, because Allah commanded obedience and then threatened, with His words ﴿But if they turn away﴾ and so on, and a threat for opposing something is evidence of obligation. This has been objected to: we do not concede that this is a threat but rather a statement of fact; and even if we concede that it is a threat, it is evidence of obligation only for the commands whose opposition is threatened, and there is nothing in it indicating that every command whose opposition is threatened is obligatory, on account of the command of recommendation (amr al-nadb), for the recommended act is commanded yet is not threatened for opposing it. When commands are divided into those threatened upon and those not threatened upon, it becomes necessary to believe in obligation only where a threat is attached, and not otherwise. By this, the answer is resolved for every form of command upon whose opposition a threat has been made and against which warning has been given, and whose opponent has been described as disobedient. By this, most of what the proponents of obligation have mentioned in arguing for their claim is also repelled, so reflect.

﴿And if you obey him﴾ in what he has commanded you of obedience, upon him be peace and blessings, ﴿you will be guided﴾ to the truth, which is the primary aim, leading to every good and delivering from every evil. Perhaps in placing the first part (turning away) before this one, and delaying this, there is an indication that warning is more fitting for them and that they are engaged in what it requires. In al-Irshād, the statement of the ruling on obedience is delayed relative to the statement of the ruling on turning away, because placing warning first emphasizes encouragement and brings it close to what belongs to its own category, namely the gracious promise.

Allah's words, ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾, form an concluding parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī) confirming what precedes, namely that the peril of turning away and the benefit of obedience are confined to those addressed. The article "al" (in al-Balāgh) is either for the genus, which includes him (ﷺ) in an initial sense, or for a specific reference, meaning: upon the genus of messengers, whoever they may be, or upon our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), is only the conveyance that makes clear everything that needs clarification, or that is clear in itself. The word "mubīn" is taken from abāna, which is transitive, in the sense of bāna, which is intransitive. You know that he (ﷺ) has indeed fulfilled this in a manner beyond which nothing more is required, and only what is upon you remains.

[Page 202]

The words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾, are addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to those who believe with him. In the verse there is a variation of address (*tanwi' al-khitab*): He, glorified is He, addressed those who turned away, assuming they had turned away, and then turned the address from them to the steadfast believers. This is like a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*), based on what will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, that ﴿And establish prayer﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Obey Allah﴾. Its benefit is that, since the preceding speech implied that He should command them to obedience face to face and not fear their harm, He emphasized that he (peace be upon him) is the victor, and those with him as well, so there is no room for fear. If you wish, you may make it a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), brought for the emphasis of
[Page 203]
what the speech implies of the negation of harm in the most eloquent manner, without considering it a parenthetical insertion, for in the coordination mentioned there is what you will hear, if Allah the Exalted wills. The *min* is explanatory (*bayaniyya*). The prepositional phrase has been placed between the clause ﴿who believed﴾ and the clause coordinated with it, which falls within the same scope as the relative clause (*ṣila*), that is, His words, the Exalted: ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾. The order is reversed in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds, among them, forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. It has been said that this is to indicate that the basis for the establishment of succession (*istikhlaf*) is faith, and for this reason the more correct view is that a ruler is not deposed by a subsequent sinfulness, and this is indicated by the sound hadiths, and by the involvement of righteousness at the beginning of the pledge of allegiance (*bay'a*). As for forgiveness and the great reward, both are fundamental, so the appropriate arrangement was to delay. It may also be said that this is to hasten the joy of the addressees, since the verse was brought for that purpose. It has also been said: the address is to those who turned away, and the speech is a completion (*tatmim*) of His words: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾, by explaining what they will have in this world of succession and what follows from it, and in the next world what cannot be measured, by way of what is incorporated (*idmaj*) in His words, glorified is He: ﴿so that you may be shown mercy﴾. The preposition is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the matter of the placement of the intervening phrase remains as it is. Some eminent scholars did not approve of this, because if ﴿believed﴾ is in the past tense in its literal sense, it does not fit, since there were none among them who had believed at the time of address. If it is taken to mean the present tense, in accordance with the customary use in reports from Allah the Exalted, then, despite its remoteness from this context, it would not be evidence for the validity of the caliphs' authority, and it would not correspond to reality either, because those eminent ones were not among those who believed from among those addressees, nor was there among those who were turned away anyone who attained the caliphate. End of quote, and there is something in it.
Perhaps this does not harm the purpose. Abu al-Su'ud approved of linking the speech to this, and claimed that it is a resumptive sentence establishing what is in His words, the Exalted: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾ and so on, of the gracious promise, expressed explicitly, and explaining the details of what was summarized in it of the kinds of religious and worldly felicities which are among the effects of guidance, and including what is meant by obedience to which guidance was attached. And that by ﴿those who believed﴾ is meant everyone who has been characterized by faith after disbelief, absolutely, from whatever group and at whatever time, not only those of the group of hypocrites, nor only those who believed after the revelation of this noble verse, by necessity of the generality of the gracious promise; and that the address is not to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and those with him of sincere believers, or whoever includes them and others of the community, nor to the hypocrites specifically, but it is to the general body of disbelievers. And that *min* is partitive. He said, regarding the wisdom of the intervening placement, that it is to manifest the originality and nobility of faith in bringing about its effects and rulings, and to announce that it is what is demanded of them and the most important of what is obligatory upon them. As for the delay in the verse of Surat al-Fath, the *min* there is explanatory, and the pronoun refers to those with him (peace be upon him) from the purest of the believers, and there is no doubt that they combined faith with righteous deeds, persevering in them, so there must be an explanation of them after mentioning their noble attributes in full. End of quote.
You know that the address being to the general body of disbelievers is contrary to the apparent meaning, and that interpreting the past-tense verb as encompassing both past and future in the same way is also remote; and what he mentioned is also distant from the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*). Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* have related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: «When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs shot at them from one bow. They did not spend the night except armed, nor did they rise in the morning except armed. They said: Do you think we will live until we spend the night secure and tranquil, fearing none but Allah the Exalted? Then there was revealed: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾, the verse». And with this, it is not possible to derive evidence from the verse for the validity of the caliphs' authority at all. Perhaps he does not hold this view and dispenses with it in favor of what is clearer in indication. And from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it is general, concerning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). They both used the word "community" (*ummah*), and it is applied to the community of response and the community of call, but
[Page 204]
the more prevalent usage is the first application, so do not be heedless. And if the *min* is explanatory, the meaning is: Allah has promised those who believed, who are you, ﴿that He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾, that is, that He will make them successors who dispose of it as kings dispose of their slaves, or successors from among those whom the disbelievers used to fear, by granting them victory over them and making them inherit their land. The "earth" is, as has been said, the Arabian Peninsula. It has also been said that it is the realm of the Prophet (peace be upon him) from the eastern and western parts of the earth.
In the authentic collection: «The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it».
The *lam* is the response of an omitted oath, and the second object of "promised" is omitted, indicated by the response; that is, Allah promised those who believed their succession, and swore that He would surely make them successors. It is also permissible that His promise, exalted is He, be treated, because its fulfilment is certain without doubt, as if it were in the position of an oath, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj; and ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ would then occupy the place of the object, so there is no omission.
The *ma* in His words ﴿as He made successors﴾ is verbal-masdarian (*mașdariyya*), and the prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element that stands as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: that He make them successors with a succession like His succession of ﴿those before them﴾. These were the Children of Israel, whom Allah, mighty and majestic, made successors in Syria after the destruction of the tyrants, and likewise in Egypt, as has been said, since it came under their control after the destruction of Pharaoh, even though they did not return to it. They and those before them of the believing nations, whom Allah the Exalted settled on the earth after the destruction of their enemies, the disbelieving wrongdoers.
It has been read ﴿as He made successors﴾ in the passive form, so the meaning would be: He will make them successors on the earth, and they will be made successors in it, a succession like the succession of ﴿those before them﴾. ﴿And He will surely establish for them their religion﴾ is coordinated with ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾, and what applies there applies here. Its placement after it, although it is the most desirable and greatest of the promised objects, is because it is like a result of the mentioned succession.
It has been said: since souls incline more toward immediate advantages, beginning the promises with them is more effective in winning hearts. Establishment (*tamkin*) originally means placing a thing in a place, then it was used for its necessary consequence, which is firm establishment. The meaning is: that He will surely make their religion firm and settled, by exalting His own station, strengthening its pillars by His support, and magnifying its adherents in the eyes of their enemies, who spend day and night planning to extinguish its lights, and rouse men and horses to reach the erasing of its traces. So they will be such that they despair of gathering against it, since He disperses them from it, so that it departs from the midst, and they scarcely entertain in their souls the thought of coming between them and it, so that it returns as a trace after being a visible thing.
It has been said: the meaning is that He will make it established such that they continue to act according to its rulings and refer to it in everything they do and leave undone. The original sense of *tamkin* is making a thing a place for another, and the expression of this by it is to indicate the full stability of the religion, the solidity of its rulings, and its safety from alteration and change, because it is founded on likening it to the earth in stability and firmness, together with what it involves of observing the correspondence between it and succession on the earth. End of quote, and there is discussion in it. The placement of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is to hasten to show that the promised thing is one of their benefits, with suspense toward the delayed element; and because placing it between it and its description, namely His words, the Exalted: ﴿which He has approved for them﴾, and delaying it after the description would disrupt the eloquence of the noble arrangement in ways that are not hidden. In attributing the religion, which is the religion of Islam, to them, and then describing it as what He has approved for them, there is additional encouragement toward it and firmness upon it.
﴿And He will surely change them﴾ is with the doubled (*tashdid*) form. Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin read it with the light (*takhfif*) form, from *ibdal* (substitution), and Abd ibn Humayd related this from 'Asim. It is coordinated with ("He will surely make them successors" and "He will surely establish") ﴿after their fear﴾, according to the requirement of human nature, in this world, ﴿from their enemies in religion﴾, ﴿security﴾ beyond measure. It has been said that the fear is in this world of the punishment of the Hereafter and the security is in the Hereafter, and this was preferred on the ground that the speech on it is further from admitting emphasis in any way, unlike the first view.
You know that the first view is more suitable to the context, and the reports about the occasion of revelation require it, and the matter of admitting emphasis is easy.
﴿They worship Me﴾: It is permitted that the clause be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), either from the first ﴿those who﴾, to restrict the promise to steadfastness upon monotheism, because what falls within the relative clause, namely faith and righteous deeds, is in the past tense, indicating the basic attribution of it, so what is mentioned has been brought as a circumstantial clause in the present tense, indicating continuous renewed habit; or from the pronoun referring back to it in ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ or in ("He will surely change them"). It is also permitted that it be a resumptive sentence, either merely as praise of those believers, meaning: they worship Me; or to explain the reason for the succession and what is united with it in the thread of the promise. His words, the Exalted: ﴿They do not associate anything with Me﴾ are a circumstantial clause from the *waw* in ﴿they worship Me﴾, or from ﴿those who﴾, or a substitute for the circumstantial clause, or a resumptive sentence. ﴿Anything﴾ is in the accusative as a direct object, that is, anything of what they associate with Him; or as an absolute object, that is, anything of association. The meanings of worship and non-association are evident.
Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said regarding His words, glorified is He, ﴿They worship Me, they do not associate anything with Me﴾: they do not fear anyone other than Me. He and a group related similar from Mujahid. Perhaps both intended by this an explanation of ﴿they do not associate anything with Me﴾, and it seems they considered fear of other than Allah a kind of association. On this view, the clause is preferred as a circumstantial clause from the *waw*, as if it were said: they worship Me, not fearing anyone other than Me. It is also permitted that they intended to explain the meaning of the whole ﴿they worship Me, they do not associate﴾ and so on, and it seems they claimed that not fearing anyone other than Him, glorified is He, is one of the necessary consequences of worship and monotheism, and that the clause ﴿they worship Me﴾ and so on is a resumptive sentence explaining what they attain in security, as if it were said: they will be secure in Me, since they do not fear anyone other than Allah the Exalted. The delicacy of using the first-person singular pronoun alone in ﴿they worship Me, they do not associate with Me﴾, rather than the third-person pronoun or the pronoun of majesty, is not hidden.

[Page 205]

﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ means whoever apostatizes from among the believers, ﴿after that﴾ meaning after the promised thing has come about, ﴿those﴾ apostates, who are far from the truth, ﴿they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ meaning those who are complete in defiant disobedience and in going beyond the bounds of disbelief and transgression, since they have no excuse at that point, not even the weight of a gnat's wing. It has also been said that the disbelief here means ingratitude (kufran) and not disbelief (kufr) as the opposite of faith, and this was narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah. Their completeness in defiant disobedience is due to the greatness of the blessing they denied. It has also been said that it refers to the promise mentioned earlier itself. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud) it is stated that the meaning is: whoever is characterized by disbelief, by being firmly established and persisting in it, and is not affected by the encouragement and warning mentioned earlier, after that gracious promise and the lofty demands detailed, which warrant the utmost concern in attaining them, then those are the complete in defiant disobedience. That the intended sense of disbelief in what was mentioned is more fitting to the context than that it means apostasy or denying blessings is the end of the quotation. In my view, however, what came before is preferable, for it is the apparent meaning. In reading it this way there is also a magnification of the worth of the promised thing, in that after it has come about it leaves no excuse for anyone who apostatizes. The strength of its suitability to the context is not hidden. This is also the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Sha'tha' that he said: "I was sitting with Hudhayfah and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, when Hudhayfah said: 'Hypocrisy has gone. Hypocrisy was only in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what remains is only disbelief after faith.' Ibn Mas'ud laughed, then said: 'On what basis do you say this?' He said: 'By this verse: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds…﴾' to the end of the verse." Ibn Mas'ud's laughter was probably out of astonishment at this, and his silence after the argument is clear evidence of his approval of what the source of the secret of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ understood from the verse.

(﴿And whoever﴾) may be a relative pronoun, and it may be a conditional. The clause ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ and so on has been said to be coordinated with the clause ﴿Allah has promised﴾ and so on, or with an omitted clause, as if it were said: "Whoever believes, they are the successful, and whoever disbelieves…" This clause, and likewise the clause ﴿they worship Me﴾, is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani). As for the first, the question arises from the words ﴿Allah has promised﴾ and so on, as if it were said: "What then befits the believers after this gracious promise, or after its fulfillment?" And so it was said: ﴿they worship Me, not associating anything with Me.﴾ As for the second, the question arises from the answer just mentioned, as if it were said: "But if they do not do this, then what?" And so it was said: ﴿and whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, and their recompense is known; and it is as you see.

This is what has been said. Many have used this verse as evidence for the validity of the caliphate of the Four, may Allah be pleased with them all, because Allah, exalted is He, promised in it those among the believers present in the presence of the Message the istikhlaf (installation as successors), the establishment of the religion, and great security from their enemies. What was promised must come to pass, since it is impossible for Allah, exalted is He, to break His promise, and that entire collection did not come to pass except in their time. So each of them was a true caliph, by Allah's installing him as such, just as He promised, glorious and exalted is He. It does not follow that the installation applies to all those addressed who were present; rather it occurred among them, as in the expression "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," which does not contradict the generality of the address to all. The word min here is explanatory (bayaniyya). Likewise, the trials that occurred during the caliphates of 'Uthman and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, do not contradict this, because the intended security is from the enemies of the religion, who are the disbelievers, as was mentioned earlier.

Some of the Ahl al-Sunna used this as an argument against the Shi'a in their belief that the caliphates of the three caliphs were invalid. They did not use it to prove the validity of the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, because it is accepted by the Shi'a. The evidences for it among both groups are numerous against those who deny it from the Nawasib (those who hate 'Ali), on whom be from Allah what they deserve. The argument runs: Allah, exalted is He, promised in it a group of righteous believers present at the time of its revelation the istikhlaf and what accompanies it, and His promise, glorified is He, is true; this was not fulfilled except in the time of the three; and the Imam al-Mahdi was certainly not in existence at the time of revelation, by consensus (ijma'), so it is impossible to interpret the verse as a promise to him. As for the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, although he was in existence at that time, the religion that was pleased with them did not flourish as it should have in his time, may Allah be pleased with him, according to the claim of the Shi'a. Rather, by their claim, his situation became worse than it had been in the time of the disbelievers, as al-Murtada explicitly stated in Tanzih al-Anbiya' wa al-A'imma (The Purification of the Prophets and Imams), peace be upon them. Indeed, all the books of the Shi'a explicitly state that the Commander of the Faithful and his followers used to conceal their religion and display the religion of their opponents out of taqiyya (dissimulation). Complete security was not present at all in his time, may Allah be pleased with him. The people of Syria, Egypt and the Maghrib denied the very basis of his imamate and did not accept his rulings, and by the claim of the Shi'a they were disbelievers, and most of the Commander's army feared them and took the utmost precaution against them. Furthermore, it is possible that a single individual is intended by "those who believe," so that he, may Allah be pleased with him, would be the referent of the verse, as they claim. For interpreting a plural word as referring to one person contradicts their principles, since the least plural in their view is three individuals. As for the other imams, who were born later, there is no possibility of their being intended by the verse, since they were not in existence at the time of its revelation, did not attain authority on earth, their pleasing religion did not flourish, and they were not secure but rather were afraid of the enemies of the religion from among them, as the Shi'a unanimously agree. Therefore it follows that the three caliphs are the referents of the verse, so their caliphate is true, and that is what was to be proven.

[Page 206]

Al-Tabarsi claimed that the address is to the Prophet and his Household ﷺ, so they are the ones promised the istikhlaf and what accompanies it, and it suffices for this that the promise was realized in the time of al-Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him. This does not conflict with the fact that he did not exist at the time of revelation, because oral address (al-khitab al-shifahi) does not restrict itself to those present; likewise it does not conflict with the fact that it was not realized for all of them, because the matter is like the expression "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so." He supported this with what al-'Ayyashi narrated with his chain of transmission from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited the verse and said: "By Allah, they are our Shi'a, the People of the House. Allah will do this to them at the hands of a man from us, and he is the Mahdi of this Ummah, and he is the one about whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Were there to remain of the world only one day, Allah would prolong that day until a man from my family (itrati), whose name is my name, governs, filling the earth with justice and equity as it was filled with injustice and oppression.'"

He also claimed that the like of this was narrated from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both. But this, despite what is in it, is contrary to the context and to the authentic reports concerning the occasion of revelation, and the state of the reports of the Shi'a is not hidden, especially for one who has consulted the Twelver Tuhfa (the Tuhfa Ithna 'Ashariyya). Yes, there is a report from our side that they may take comfort in in this matter, but it too is not relied upon, like their reports. It is what 'Abd ibn Hamid narrated from 'Atiyyah that the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him recited the verse and said: "The People of the House are here," and he pointed with his hand toward the qibla. Some others claimed something similar to what you have heard from al-Tabarsi, except that he said: it concerns all of the People of the House, 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and the other twelve Imams, and it will be realized in them during the Return (raj'a) when the Qa'im (the Riser) arises, may Allah be pleased with him. He claimed that it is one of the evidences for the Return, and this has added a new note to the tambour (a proverbial expression for adding an unwelcome element to an already troubled matter). 

The learned 'Abd Allah al-Mashhadi said in his book Izhar al-Haqq (The Manifestation of the Truth), refuting the use of this verse as evidence for the validity of the caliphate of the three caliphs: "It is possible that the istikhlaf is in the linguistic sense, which is the bringing of one person after (khalf) another, i.e., after him, as in His saying, exalted is He, concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors (yastakhlifakum) in the land﴾ [al-A'raf: 129]. So at most what is established is that they were successors in the linguistic sense, and that is not the point of contention. Rather, the dispute concerns the technical sense (al-ma'na al-istilahi), which is a meaning that came into being after the departure of the Prophet ﷺ." End of quotation.

It is answered that even if this were established, it would not then be complete for them to use it as evidence for the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, in the technical sense, by the hadith: "You are to me as Harun was to Musa"; by what He, exalted is He, related of Musa, peace be upon him, saying to Harun: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]; and by what they narrate of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "O 'Ali, you are my successor (khalifati) after me."

Likewise it is not complete for them to use as evidence for the imamate of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, what is contained in the word imam, because it was not used in the Glorious Book at all in the technical sense; it was used only in the sense of prophet, guide, one who directs, and one who is followed in a matter, whether good or bad. If they claim that the technical sense is understood from it by necessary implication, then let them claim that the technical sense of khalifa is understood in the same way. Perhaps they will claim that their understanding of it is stronger, because it occurs in the Mighty Book in association with the word "in the earth," which indicates general authority, which is the characteristic of the caliph in that sense. Moreover, the basis of the argument for the caliphate of the three from this verse is not merely the word istikhlaf, such that the objector's purpose would be achieved; rather it is that together with considering its ascription to Allah, exalted is He. When the linguistic istikhlaf is ascribed to Allah, glorious and exalted is He, it becomes a legal istikhlaf. This question may be put to the scholars of the Shi'a, who may be told: The Children of Israel were placed in the position of the people of Pharaoh and the Amalekites and made to rule in the land of Egypt and Syria; was this true or not? I do not think they would say anything but that it was true. Then it is incumbent on them to say the same about the verse, since there is no difference. By this the point is established. This is the summary of what has been said on this matter.

[Page 207]

What I incline toward is that the verse clearly demonstrates the innocence of the three caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, from what the Shi'a attribute to them of injustice, oppression, and disposing of the land without right, because the establishment of the religion and complete security from its enemies is manifest in their time. Praising someone with a false disposition, whose punishment is severe torment, would hardly be fitting. Likewise, it would hardly be fitting to praise the people of their age with what the verse contains, given that they were the leaders who held the reins of binding and loosing, if they were as the Shi'a claim about them, and far be it from them. And once their innocence from what they are accused of is established, we are content with that. This depends only on their being characterized by faith and righteous deeds at the time the verse was revealed, and the Shi'a's denial of this is a denial of what is necessary (al-darurriyyat). That the verse refers to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, or to al-Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, and the Ahl al-Bayt in an unqualified sense, is something no fair-minded person would say.

In the words of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, there is something that, by its context, contradicts what the Shi'a hold. In Nahj al-Balagha it is reported that when 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, consulted the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, about setting out to fight the people of Persia when they gathered for war, he said to him:

This is the third and final part of al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 24, verse 55.

This matter (of the caliphate and the religion) was not victorious or defeated by numbers, whether many or few. It is the religion of God Most High, which He made manifest, and His army, which He strengthened and supported, until it reached what it reached and rose where it rose.
