We are upon a promise from God Most High, when He, may His name be exalted, said: ﴿God has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, as He made successors those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely replace their fear with security﴾. God Most High fulfils His promise and supports His army. The standing of the pillars (al-qiyam) in Islam is like the standing of the string (al-nizam) among the beads: if the string is cut, the beads scatter, and many a scattered thing never gathers again. The Arabs today, although they are few, are many through Islam and mighty through unity. So be a pivot (qutb) and let the millstone (al-rahā) turn by means of the Arabs, and let the fire of war be kindled by them behind you. For if you depart from this land, the Arabs will rise against you from its edges and its regions, until what you leave behind you of the frontiers (al-awarith) becomes more important to you than what lies before you. It was already time for the non-Arabs (al-a'ajim) to look at you and say tomorrow: "This is the root of the Arabs; if we cut it off, we will be at rest." That would make their dog-like snarling against you fiercer and their greed for you stronger. As for what you mentioned of their number, we did not fight in the past by means of multitude, but we fight by means of victory and divine assistance.

End of quotation. Ponder this, and may God Most High guide you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 56:

﴿And establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and obey the Messenger﴾. It is permissible that this be coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿obey God﴾, included together with it within the scope of the speech and with an intervening element, and it is not entirely alien in any respect, for it is a promise regarding what is commanded, and part of it is a completion of it. In al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary): it is not far-fetched that an intervening element may occur between the coordinated element and that to which it is coordinated, even if it is long, because the coordinated element ought to be other than that to which it is coordinated, and the intervening element emphasizes the difference and reinforces it, since proximity is a presumption of connection and unity. Thus the repetition of the command to obey the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, is for emphasis. It was emphasized, rather than the command to obey God Most High, because in people's souls, especially the souls of the Arabs, there is a difficulty in submitting to humans that is not present in them regarding submission to God Most High. And [it is for] attaching mercy to them, or to what they are included in, which is the sentences falling within the scope of the speech, by His saying, Most High: ﴿so that you may be shown mercy﴾, just as He attached guidance to obedience in His saying, Most High: ﴿and if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. The fair assessment is that this coordination is remote; rather, some have said that it is among the things that do not befit the eloquence (jazala) of the noble composition.

It is also permissible that it be coordinated with ﴿they worship Me﴾, and in it there is specification after generalization. The apparent wording would have been: "they worship Me, do not associate anything with Me, establish the prayer, give the zakat, and obey the Messenger, so that they may be shown mercy." But He turned away from that to what He mentioned, by way of shifting to address (iltifat) for greater attention, and the address in (minkum) [in "from among you"] made it good here. It was objected that this is something without basis, because even after granting the shift of address and the permissibility of coordinating an imperative with a declarative, it is not appropriate, and that the preceding sentence being a circumstantial clause (hal) or an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnaf bayani) [is also not appropriate]. What he preferred is that it is coordinated with an implied element which the speech extends over and which the structure requires; for when He, glorified be He, mentioned ﴿and whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiantly disobedient (fasiqun)﴾, the prohibition against disbelief was implied, as if it were said: "So do not disbelieve, and establish the prayer, etc."

It is also permissible that the implied element be understood from the whole of what preceded, namely His saying, Most High: ﴿Say: obey God﴾ etc., since it necessitates the command to faith and righteous deeds, so it is as if it were said: "So believe, and do righteous deeds, and establish etc." And it is permissible, regarding ﴿obey﴾, that it be a command to obey him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, in all the legislated rulings that comprise the pleasing etiquettes, and that it be a command to obedience in what is other than the two preceding commands, so that its mention is for completing those two, as if it were said: "And obey the Messenger in all that he commands you." His saying, Most High: ﴿so that you may﴾ etc., is connected to the three commands, and on the first [view] it is connected to the last one.

The Almighty's words, ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve will escape [Allah] in the earth﴾, etc., explain the fate of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, after explaining how far they have gone in wickedness and the success of their opposites through the absolute mercy that brings the happiness of both abodes. This also removes the improbability of the fulfilment of the previous promise, given the great number of the disbelievers. The address is to everyone who is capable of supposing, similar to the Almighty's words, ﴿If only you could see when the guilty will bow their heads before their Lord﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

It is also permitted that the address be to the Messenger (ﷺ) by way of allusion to whoever has done this, like the saying, "I mean you, but listen, neighbour," or as an indication that the supposition mentioned has become so ugly and dangerous that one forbids someone who cannot possibly do it. This is similar to what has been said about the Almighty's words, ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14; Yunus: 105; al-Qasas: 87]. Therefore, the statement of Abu Hayyan, that making the address to the Messenger (ﷺ) is not good because such a supposition cannot be imagined from him, peace and blessings be upon him, is not sound, because it involves neglect of what has been mentioned.

The relative clause (al-mawsul) is in the accusative, as the first object (maf'ul awwal) of "yahsabanna" (think). The Almighty's words, ﴿mu'jizin﴾ (escaping), are the second object. The Almighty's words, ﴿fi al-ard﴾ (in the earth), are an adverbial complement (zarf) modifying ﴿mu'jizin﴾, but not to convey that the escape being negated is in the earth and not elsewhere, for that is clear without explanation. Rather, it conveys that the non-escape extends to all parts of it. That is: do not think they can escape Allah, the Exalted, from their apprehension and destruction in any region of the earth, however wide it is, even if they flee from it in every direction.

Hamzah and Ibn Amir read ﴿yahsabanna﴾ with a *ya'* (third person), so that the subject is anyone at all, as if it were said: let no one who thinks of the disbelievers think that they can escape Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in the earth. The pronoun referring to Him, ﷺ, is due to the previous mention of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in the Almighty's words, ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) took this view.

Abu Hayyan's claim that this is not good, for the reason already mentioned, is not sound. Or [the pronoun refers to] the disbelievers, meaning: let not the disbelievers, those who disbelieved, think that they are escaping. This was reported from Ali ibn Sulayman. Or the relative clause and the first object are omitted, as if it were said: let not those who disbelieved think themselves to be escapers in the earth. He mentioned that the original form on this reading is "let not those who disbelieved think them to be escapers," then the pronoun which is the first object was deleted. What permitted this is that the subject and the two objects, being like one thing, are sufficient with two mentions instead of the third. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr, criticised this, saying that this pronoun is not one of those pronouns explained by what follows, so the original form cannot be "let not those who disbelieved think him [such that]..." any more than one may say "I think him Zayd standing."

The Kufans said: ﴿mu'jizin﴾ is the first object and ﴿fi al-ard﴾ is the second object, and the meaning is: let not those who disbelieved think that anyone can thwart Allah, the Exalted, in the earth, so that they hope for the like of that. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a strong and good meaning. It was criticised on the ground that it does not fit the context, since the locus of the benefit is the second object and there is no benefit in stating that the escapers are in the earth. It was answered that although the locus of benefit is the second object, it is treated as already settled, and what is intended is the explanation of the place: that they cannot thwart Him, glorified be He, in the earth. The truth is that what has been mentioned goes against the apparent meaning, and the apparent meaning is that ﴿fi al-ard﴾ is connected to ﴿mu'jizin﴾. In any case, the reading mentioned is sound, though its interpretations vary in strength and weakness. From this one knows what is wrong with the statement of al-Nuhas: "I have not known any of the grammarians, Basran or Kufan, but that he errs in Hamzah's reading." Some of them say it is a solecism (lahn), because it has only one object for yahsabanna. Others, such as Abu Hatim, said the same. This is the end of [al-Nuhas's words], which show lack of understanding, excessive babbling, and audacity in attacking a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) part of the Qur'an. By my life, if the reading were based on opinion, then whoever did not understand the basis of Hamzah's reading should have refrained from such speech, blamed himself, and held back from attacking that imam.

The Almighty's words, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾, are conjoined to the prohibitive clause, interpreting it as a declarative clause, because the intention of the prohibition against supposing is to affirm firmly the negation of that supposition, as if it were said: the disbelievers are not escapers, and their refuge is the Fire.

It is also permitted that it be conjoined to an implied element, since the first clause is a threat of this world, as if it were said: they are overpowered in this world by annihilation, and disgraced in the Hereafter by the torment of the Fire. From the author of al-Nazm (Sahib al-Nazm), the implied element is: rather, they are subject to power and reckoning, and their refuge is the Fire.

In al-Kashf: he made it a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense that supposing is not fitting for one whose refuge is the Fire, as if it were said: how can the disbeliever have this supposition when the Fire has been prepared for him? The turn to ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ is for emphasis on the certainty of this, and that it is known to them without doubt, which is a good aspect, free from the strain that afflicted some of the imams. It is not hidden that in its apparent meaning there is an inclination towards some of the interpretations of the reading "yahsabanna" with the third-person ya'.

In al-Bahr, the interpretation of the prohibitive clause, so as to make it correct to conjoin to it, was criticised with the statement: the correct view is that it is permissible to conjoin clauses that differ from one another even when they are not of the same type. This is the view of Sibawayh. "Al-ma'wa" is a noun of place, and it has been permitted to be a verbal noun (masdar), but the first is more apparent.

The Almighty's words, ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, are the answer to an implied oath, and the thing praised or blamed (al-makhsus bi al-dhamm) is omitted, meaning: and by Allah, wretched is the destination, which is the Fire. The clause is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiradh tadhyili), confirming what precedes it. In the presentation of the Fire under the description of being their refuge and destination, there is a trace of the negation of their escape by fleeing in every direction in the earth, of such eloquence that there is no limit beyond it. So, by Allah, how excellent is the art of the revelation!

[p. 209]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 58 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed﴾, etc. This is, according to most scholars, a return to explaining the completion of the previous rulings, after preparing what necessitates compliance with the commands and prohibitions contained in them and in the following rulings, through examples, encouragement and warning, promise and threat. In verification, it is possible to say that this is among the things in which Allah the Exalted and His Messenger are obeyed, and its specific mention is because its inclusion in obedience, in terms of it being among the etiquettes (adab), is more remote than others. The address is either to men exclusively, with women included in the ruling by indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), or to both groups by way of predominance (taghlib). The first view is objected to on the basis that the verse was revealed because of women,

for it is narrated that "Asma' bint Abi Marthad had a grown male servant of hers enter upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Our servants and our young boys enter upon us at times we dislike,' so this was revealed." Al-Itqan (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an) mentions that the inclusion of the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) within the ruling is definitive.

It is answered that there is nothing preventing the ruling being known regarding the occasion through indication and clear analogy (qiyas jali), and that this would be within the ruling of entry. It is reported from al-Subki that it is speculative (zanni), so it is permissible to exclude it, and the full discussion of this is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Furthermore, what is mentioned regarding the occasion of revelation is not unanimously agreed upon,

for it is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent at midday to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, a young man from the Ansar called Mudlij, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was sleeping. He knocked on the door and entered, so he (Umar) woke up and sat up, and something of him became uncovered. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I wish that Allah had forbidden our fathers, our sons and our servants from entering upon us at this hour except with permission.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went with him and found that this verse had been revealed, and he fell down in prostration.'" This is one of the instances of his correct opinion, may Allah be pleased with him, agreeing with revelation.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) liked to have intercourse with their wives at these hours, then they would bathe and go out to prayer. So Allah commanded them to instruct the slaves and the boys not to enter upon them during those hours except with permission," by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. From this it is known that the command in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Let those whom your right hands possess and those of you who have not reached puberty ask permission of you﴾, although apparently it is addressed to the slaves and the children, in reality it is addressed to the adults, so it is as though they were commanded to instruct the aforementioned to ask permission. By this, what is said is resolved: "How does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, command one who has not reached puberty to ask permission, when it is an obligation (taklif) and there is no obligation before puberty?" Its summary is that Allah the Exalted did not command him directly, but rather commanded the adult to instruct him in this, just as He commanded him to instruct him in prayer.

For it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Command your children to pray when they are seven years old, and strike them for it when they are ten years old." His commanding of what was mentioned and similar things is a matter of discipline (ta'dib) and teaching, and there is no difficulty in it. It was also said: the command is directed at the adult among those mentioned in the literal sense, and at others by way of discipline. It was said: it is for all in the literal sense, and obligation depends on discernment (tamyiz) and does not depend on puberty, so what is meant by "those who have not reached puberty" are the discerning among the young; and this, as you see, is weak. This command has been disputed: some scholars held that it is for obligation, while the majority held that it is for recommendation (nadb). On both views it is muhkam (definitive in its ruling), according to the correct view, and the full discussion of this will come.

The majority hold that ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is general in covering male and female slaves, adult and young. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid

that it is specific to males, as is the apparent sense of the wording, and this was narrated from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Al-Sulami said that it is specific to females, and this is a strange view on which no reliance is placed. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it is restricted to the young, and this is very contrary to the apparent meaning. What is meant by "those who have not reached puberty" is the young children, male and female, according to what the earlier statement from the majority requires, and some restricted it to those approaching puberty (al-murahiqin) among them. The phrase ﴿of you﴾ is for restricting them to the free, and the contrast also indicates this.

In al-Bahr: it is general in covering children, whether slaves or free. Puberty being lacking is alluded to by the mentioned phrase, because the wet dream (ihtilam) is its strongest sign. The jurists have agreed that when a boy has a wet dream, he has reached puberty. They differed regarding one who reaches fifteen years and has not had a wet dream. Abu Hanifa said, according to the well-known position: he is not adult until he completes eighteen years. Likewise, a girl who has not had a wet dream, has not menstruated, or has not become pregnant, is not adult in his view until she completes seventeen years. His evidence is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. The maturity (ashudd) of the child, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and followed by al-Qutaybi, is eighteen years, and this is the least of what has been said regarding it, so the ruling is built upon it for certainty. However, girls' growth and maturing is faster, so one year is subtracted in their case, because it includes the four seasons, one of which necessarily suits the temperament. His two companions, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: when a boy or a girl reaches fifteen years, they have reached puberty. This is also a narration from the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, and on it the fatwa is based.

Their evidence is that the widespread custom is that puberty in both does not come later than this period. The custom was qualified as widespread because a boy may reach puberty at twelve years, and a girl may reach it at nine years. Some of them used as evidence for what precedes what was narrated by "Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he was presented to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the day of Uhud when he was fourteen years old, and he did not permit him; and he was presented to him, peace and blessings be upon him, on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq) when he was fifteen years old, and he permitted him."

Abu Bakr al-Razi objected to this, saying that Uhud was in the third year (of Hijra) and the Trench was in the fifth year, so how is what was mentioned in the report correct? Furthermore, there is no proof in it for the claim, because permission in fighting has no connection with puberty; one who has reached puberty may not be permitted due to weakness, and one who has not reached puberty may be permitted due to his strength and ability to carry weapons.

Perhaps the reason for his not being permitted at first, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was Ibn 'Umar's weakness, and this is indicated by the fact that he (ﷺ) did not ask him about the wet dream and the age.

Among what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, uniquely held, according to what has been said, is taking the growth of pubic hair as evidence of puberty, and he argued for it by what 'Atiyya al-Qurazi narrated: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the killing of whoever among Qurayza had grown hair, and the sparing of whoever had not grown it. He said: They looked at me and I had not grown it, so they spared me." Abu Bakr al-Razi criticised this by saying: a report of this kind is not permissible for establishing the Shari'a, for this 'Atiyya is unknown and is known only through this report. Furthermore, its wordings differ, for in one narration: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the killing of whoever had the pubic hair pass over him (jarat 'alayhi al-mawasi)." Furthermore, it is possible that the order to kill whoever had grown hair was not because he was adult, but because he was strong, for growth indicates physical strength. Al-Shafi'i was defended by saying that the possibility is refuted by what was narrated from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked about a boy, and he said: "Has his waist-wrap turned green?" This indicates that this was like a matter agreed upon among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Then, the well-known position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that he made this a sign of puberty regarding the children of unbelievers. The Shafi'is' exertion in defending it, and the reproach directed at it, are not hidden from one who has examined them.

Among what is strange is what was narrated from some of the predecessors (salaf), that they considered for puberty that a person reach five spans (ashbar) in height.

It was narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "When a boy reaches five spans, the hudud punishments apply to him; he is retaliated for and retaliated against." And from Ibn Sirin, from Anas, who said: "A boy who had stolen was brought to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, so he ordered him to be measured, and he was a span, minus a fingertip, so he released him." And al-Farazdaq adopted this view in his saying praising Yazid ibn al-Muhallab:

He has not ceased since his hands tied his waist-wrap, and he rose and reached the five spans,
He brings near the battalions to battalions that meet, in spear-thrusting on the day of tumult and confusion.

Most jurists do not hold this, because a person may be below puberty yet tall, and above puberty yet short, so there is no significance in that. Perhaps the preceding reports are not sound. What is attributed to al-Farazdaq does not necessarily mean puberty. Some people said that he meant by "five spans" the grave, as another said:

How strange: four cubits in five, in its interior a great, lofty mountain!

Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in a narration, read ﴿al-halm﴾ with a sukun on the lam, and this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Raghib mentioned that al-hulm with a damma and al-hulm with a sukun are both verbal nouns of halama in his sleep with such-and-such, when he sees it in a dream, yahlamu with a damma, and he did not restrict that to one dialect over another. It is also said from some that 'uddu halaman with a fatha is a verbal noun for that too. In al-Sihah: al-hulm with a damma is what the sleeper sees; you say from it: halama with a fatha and ihtalama, and you say halimtu bi-kadha and halamtuhu also, so it is transitive with the preposition "bi" and directly, as he said:

So I dreamed of her, while the Banu Rufayda were between her and me, they do not remove the dreamt-of image of her.

Al-hulm with a kasra on the ha' is patience; you say from it: hulma al-rajulu with a damma when he becomes forbearing. In al-Qamus: al-hilm with a kasra, and with two dammas, is a vision, its plural ahlam. Then he said: halama bihi and 'anhu saw a vision of him or saw him in sleep, and al-hulm with a damma and al-ihtilam is intercourse in sleep, and the noun is al-hulm like 'unuq, and al-hulm with a kasra is patience and intellect, and its plural is ahlam and hulum. End quote. The apparent meaning is that what we are dealing with here is the sense of intercourse in sleep, which is the well-known wet dream, and the reason for the earlier metaphor regarding it is clear.

Al-Raghib said: al-hulm is the time of puberty, and it was called al-hulm because it makes its possessor worthy of al-hilm, meaning patience and self-control against the flaring up of anger, and there is something of it in the soul. ﴿three times﴾, that is, three times in the day and night. The expression of them as "times" (marrat) is to indicate that the basis of seeking permission is the coincidence of those times with the passing of the seekers upon those addressed, not the times themselves. So the accusative of ﴿three times﴾ is adverbial of time for "seeking permission", and this is what the majority held. What indicates what has been mentioned is His saying: ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾, etc., for the apparent sense is that it is in a position of accusative or genitive, as it was said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿three﴾ or for ﴿times﴾: a detailed substitute (badal mufassal) from a general one (mujmal).

[Page 210]

I'd be glad to translate this, but I should note the passage contains a very large amount of text across these pages. Here is the faithful translation of the passage as given:

It was also permitted that it be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are three occasions before [the dawn prayer]," etc. This also indicates what we have mentioned. Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr) preferred that the meaning is "three occasions of seeking permission," as is apparent, for if you say, "I struck three times," it is understood only as three strikes. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Seeking permission is three [times]." On this reading, ﴿three times﴾ is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "seeking permission," and "before" (min qabli) etc. is an adverbial complement of it. The legislation of seeking permission before the dawn prayer is because it is evident that it is the time of rising from beds, removing sleeping clothes, and putting on clothes for waking, and all of this is a likely occasion for the exposure of nakedness. Also, a person often becomes ritually impure at night, so he bathes at that time and is shy of being seen in that state, even if his nakedness is covered. ﴿And when you put off your clothes﴾, i.e., when you take off the clothes you wear in the day and set them down from yourselves, ﴿at midday﴾ is an explanation of the time. Al-Raghib said that "midday" (zahirah) is the time of noon, and in al-Qamus it is the limit of the middle of the day, and that is only in the summer heat.

It was also permitted that "min" is causal, and the statement is elliptical of a noun, meaning: "and when you put off your clothes because of the heat of midday." Some explained "midday" as the intensity of heat at the middle of the day, so there is no need for the omission. ("And when") is coordinated with ("before"), which is clear if it is in the accusative position. As for the other two readings, one must hold that "when" (hina) is indeclinable with a fatha vowel, even if it is followed by a present-tense verb, as was said regarding His saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119], according to the reading with a fatha on the mim of "yawm." The explicit mention of the basis of the matter, namely the putting off of clothes at this time and not what was said and what follows, is because undressing at this time is for the sake of the noon rest, due to its brief duration, as is indicated by the use of "time" as a noun qualified by a temporary, passing verb, and because it occurs in the day, which is a sign of frequent occurrence and passing, and a likely occasion for the manifestation of conditions and the emergence of matters. It is not, in certainty and regularity, on the level of what is in the two stated times, for the certainty of the basis in those two is a known matter that needs no explicit mention.

﴿And after the night prayer﴾: it is necessarily the time of stripping off waking clothes and wrapping oneself in sleeping clothes, and often sexual preliminaries are engaged in at it; although it is better to delay it for one who does not bathe immediately until the end of the night. It is understood from what was mentioned in the context of explaining the wisdom of legislating seeking permission at the first time and the last time that what is meant by the two stated prior and subsequent times is not their absolute sense, which is realized in the extended period between the dawn prayer and the night prayer, but rather the two ends of that extended period, which are connected customarily with the two stated prayers. The non-mention of the command to seek permission in the rest of that extended period is either because it is understood after the command to seek permission in the stated times, by way of a fortiori reasoning, or because the reports about it are very rare, as was said. It was also said that the reason is the customary practice that whoever enters at that time does not return until he informs the household, since entering the house at that time without informing its people involves the suspicion that is not hidden.

﴿Three occasions of nakedness﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject. The phrase ﴿for you﴾ is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of it, meaning: "They are three occasions of nakedness belonging to you." "Nakedness" (awrah) is a flaw; from it comes "one-eyed" (a'war) of a horseman and a place when its condition is defective, and "a'war" means one whose eye is defective. The nakedness of a person is his private part, and its origin, as al-Raghib said, is from "shame" (ar), because of the disgrace that attaches to its exposure. The omitted pronoun ("them") refers to the three times, and the statement is elliptical of a noun, meaning: "they are three times in which concealment is customarily defective." Abu al-Baqa' supposed the omitted noun before "three," saying: "i.e., they are times, three occasions of nakedness," or there is no omission in it. The use of "nakedness" for the stated times containing it is for emphasis, as if they were themselves the nakedness. The sentence is a resumptive clause given to explain the reason for requiring permission at those times.

Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "three" in the accusative, as a substitute for "three times." Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it be a substitute for the stated times, or that it be accusative by an implied "I mean." al-A'mash read "'awarat" with a fatha on the waw, which is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah and Banu Tamim.

﴿There is no blame on you or on them﴾, i.e., upon those whom your right hands possess and those of you who have not reached puberty, ﴿in entering without permission﴾ ﴿after them﴾, i.e., after each one of those three occasions of nakedness, which are the times intervening between each two of them. Presenting them under the heading of "after" although each time before each nakedness is also after another of them, is to fulfill the right of obligation and dispensation, which is an expression for lifting it, since dispensation is only conceivable in an act occurring after the time of the act of the obligated person, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim. Its apparent meaning is that there is no sin in entering without permission in the time intervening between what is after the night prayer and what is before the dawn prayer, in the earlier sense of "after" and "before"; and what we previously stated requires that there is sin in that, so it would be like an exception from what was mentioned.

It would have been expected to say: "There is no blame on them after them," and the non-mention of negating blame upon the addressees is because those ordered apparently in what preceded regarding seeking permission at the three occasions of nakedness are only the slaves and the adolescent free persons. If those ordered in reality are considered in what passed, the apparent expression here would be: "There is no blame on you after them," restricted to it. Perhaps the choice of what is in the sublime text is to observe emphasis in permitting omission of permission in what is other than those three, where blame is negated for those ordered regarding them apparently and in reality.

The apparent meaning of "blame" (junah) is sin in the legal sense. It is objected that it is understood from the verse that this applies to the addressees if the slaves and those who have not reached puberty enter upon them without permission in those occasions of nakedness, although "no bearer bears the burden of another" [al-An'am: 164], and that it applies to the slaves and children in the same way, although children are not obligated, so legal sin cannot be conceived for them.

It is answered that this application to those mentioned is through implication (mafhum), and implication is not considered by us; and on the view that it is considered, it is possible that it applies to the addressees at that time for their neglecting to teach them and enabling them to enter upon them. The difficulty of its application to children remains, and there is no resolution for it except by holding that obligation depends on discernment and does not depend on puberty, which is contrary to what the majority of the imams hold.

An objection to the view that this application to those mentioned is through implication is a matter that is not hidden. He adopted in the answer that what is meant by "blame" is customary sin, whose return is leaving the better course; otherwise, it would be created from the standpoint of manliness and courtesy. The possibility of this applying to the obligated and the non-obligated is not in dispute. So it is as if the meaning is: "There is no blame upon you, O believers, in their entering upon you after them, because you neglect to teach them and enable them to do so, which leads to exposure to what manliness and jealousy find unbearable to be exposed to. And there is no blame upon them in that, because of their violation of courtesy, which leads to exposure to what people of sound natures dislike to be exposed to and are affected by." The previous command does not preclude this, nor does what the Irshad mentions about the reason for presenting the three occasions of nakedness under the heading of "after," as you have heard. So reflect, for it is subtle.

Some scholars held that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], is abrogated by this verse, since it indicates permission to enter without permission after the three occasions, and that indicates the opposite. Whoever does not hold this said: it applies to children and the slaves of the one entered upon, and the verse of seeking permission applies to free adult persons; and the slaves of others are in the same ruling as them, so there is no contradiction requiring abrogation.

Then know that the negation of blame after them upon those mentioned is not general, for whenever it is established or suspected that the people of the house are in a state that they dislike the slaves and adolescent free persons seeing them in it, such as the exposure of one's nakedness or his intimacy with his wife or his female slave, or otherwise, it is not appropriate to enter upon them without permission, whether that is in one of the three occasions or in others. The command to seek permission in them and the negation of blame after them is based on the customary general practice that the people of the house during the stated three times are in a state that requires permission, and that they are in a state that does not require it at other times.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation of the verse mentioned by Abu Hayyan, and his practice apparently indicates that he prefers it, and Abu al-Baqa' limited himself to it: that the implied meaning is "There is no blame on you or on them after their seeking permission in them," so the agent and the prepositional particle were omitted, leaving "after their seeking permission in them," then the verbal noun was omitted, so it became "after them." By this the burden of discourse in the verse is lightened, except that it is very contrary to the apparent meaning. The majority hold what you have heard first as its meaning. The apparent meaning is that the sentence, on the two previously mentioned readings for "three," is resumptive, given to affirm what precedes it. In the Kashshaf it is said that if "three" is nominative, the sentence is in the nominative position as a description. The meaning is: "They are three occasions specified for seeking permission." If it is accusative, it has no position, and it is a statement confirming the seeking of permission in those circumstances only.

The author of al-Taqrib said: If the lifting of blame beyond the three occasions is intended in itself, then when it is described by "three occasions of nakedness" in the accusative, being a substitute for "three times," the meaning would be: "Let these ask your permission in three specified occasions of nakedness requiring permission." This is rejected by several considerations derived from the science of meanings. The first is that the condition of prior knowledge of the hearer of the description is not met, since he does not know except from this. The second is making the intended ruling a description of the time-frame, so it becomes unintended. The third is that the command to seek permission in the three times is already established, whether or not it is described as having no blame beyond them, so the description would be pointless. But if the nominative is described, the objections disappear, because it is the beginning of instruction: "They are three occasions specified for seeking permission," as a description of the intended predicate, and the command to seek permission is not restricted to it. So consider this, for it is subtle and sublime. End.

It was objected that the last two considerations are baseless and of no value, and the first is the valid one. If it is said: it shares the same implication, it is answered that what preceded in His saying: ﴿that they may ask your permission﴾ already guides to knowledge of this, and the final sentence is not part of its parts, as it is in the case if it is made a description of the substitute. With this, there is no need for the discussion that lifting blame beyond the three occasions is intended in itself. Rather it is said that it is in itself nothing, for al-Tibi said: the intended matter first is seeking permission in the specified times, and lifting blame in other times [is secondary].

Following on from this, in line with the statement of the narrator of the hadith, may Allah be pleased with him: "I wished that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had forbidden our fathers and our servants from entering upon us at this hour except with permission." Then he set off to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse had been revealed.

In al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary), it is said that the statement indicating the lifting of hardship was brought, namely ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ and so on, with ﴿three﴾ placed in the nominative, as a confirmation of what precedes, by way of *tard wa-'aks* (the direct and inverse arrangement). The same applies if it is put in the accusative and taken as a resumption (*isti'naf*). But if it is taken as a qualifier (*wasf*), this meaning is lost. This too is among the supporting considerations, end of quotation. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

And His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿They are attendants upon you (*tawwafun 'alaykum*)﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are attendants," and the clause is a resumption (*isti'naf*) explaining the excuse that permits leaving off seeking permission, which is the necessary mingling and frequent coming and going. In this there is evidence that the legal rulings have reasons (*ta'lil al-ahkam*), and likewise in distinguishing these three times from others, on the basis that they are times of nakedness (*'awrat*).

As for His, the Majestic's, statement: ﴿some of you upon others (*ba'duhum 'ala ba'd*)﴾, it is permitted that it be a subject and predicate, with the complement of the preposition being a general verb (*kawn 'amm*) omitted because the preceding context indicates it, i.e., "some of you circulate among others." It is also permitted that it be governed by an omitted verb, i.e., "some of you circulate upon others." Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Ba'dukum﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿tawwafun﴾. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) objected to this: if he means it is a substitute for ﴿tawwafun﴾ itself, it is not permissible, because the sense becomes "they are some of you upon others," which is an unsound meaning. If he means it is a substitute for the pronoun within it, it is also not sound if the pronoun is taken as a third-person pronoun, since the sense becomes "they circulate, some of you upon others." If the sense is taken as "you circulate upon you, some of you upon others," this is refuted by the fact that ﴿upon you﴾ indicates that they are the ones circulated upon, while ﴿you are attendants﴾ indicates that they are the ones circulating, so the two contradict each other. It has also been said that the phrase is taken as "you are attendants," with "you" referring to the addressees, and the absent (third person) referring to the slaves and children. But this, as you see, is weak. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the clause be a substitute for the one before it, or that it be explanatory and emphatic. Nothing is hidden from you of what this contains by way of consoling the hearts of the slaves by counting them among the addressees, and by this the matter of the reason (*'illiyyah*) is strengthened.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿tawwafina﴾ in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿'alayhim﴾.

﴿Thus﴾ refers to the verbal noun (*masdar*) of the verb that has preceded, its detailed explanation having passed in the commentary on His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and also elsewhere. That is, like this clarification, ﴿Allah makes the verses clear to you﴾, those that indicate what is beneficial and good for you. That is, He sends them down clear and manifestly indicative, not that He, glorified is He, clarifies them after they were not so. The placement of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for the reason already given more than once. It has also been said: He clarifies the reasons of the rulings. This was objected to as not evident, and as leading to restricting the verses to what is mentioned here.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾: an intensive form regarding knowledge of all known things, so He knows your conditions. ﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His acts, so He legislates for you what is good for you in this life and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 59:

﴿When the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission, as those before them asked permission.﴾ Having previously stated the ruling regarding children, that they do not need to seek permission outside the three times, He, Exalted is He, then followed it with an explanation of their condition once they reach puberty, to repel what might be suspected: that although they are strangers, they are not like the other strangers because of their habit of entering. So the lam in ﴿al-atfal﴾ (the children) is for specification (al-'ahd), referring to those who have not reached puberty, who are placed as a counterpart to the slaves. That is, when the free children who are strangers reach puberty, ﴿then let them ask permission﴾ when they wish to enter upon you, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾, i.e., those who were mentioned before them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. It is also permitted that the precedence (al-qabaliyyah) be by way of the attribute and not by way of mention in the sublime composition, by the indication of the mention of puberty and the ruling of childhood, i.e., those who reached puberty before them. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Muqatil, and some claimed that it is more apparent.

Page 216
It was objected that the purpose of the comparison is to explain the manner of the permission-seeking of these and to increase its clarity, and this cannot be achieved except by comparing it to the permission-seeking of those known to the listener. There is no doubt that their reaching puberty before these is something that does not occur to anyone's mind, even if that is the case in reality. Rather, what is known and familiar is their being mentioned before them. So the meaning is: ﴿let them ask permission﴾ with a permission-seeking like the permission-seeking of those mentioned before them, by asking permission at all times and returning if they are told "return," as was detailed earlier. That the intended meaning of "children" is free foreign children has been held by more than one scholar. Some eminent scholars said: what is intended by them is what includes both free persons and slaves, so permission is obligatory upon whoever among both groups has reached puberty. This verse led some to make it obligatory for a mature slave to seek permission from his mistress. In al-Bahr, it is said: ﴿among you﴾ means among your children and relatives.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar to this interpretation from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. He also transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that he said: "A man seeks permission to enter upon his mother; the verse ﴿When the children among you reach puberty, the children⦆ was revealed concerning that." Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ata' that he asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Should I seek permission to enter upon my sister?" He said: "Yes." I said: "She is in my care, and I spend on her, and she is with me in the house. Should I seek permission to enter upon her?" He said: "Yes. Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Let those whom your right hands possess and those of you who have not reached puberty ask your permission⦆ [al-Nur: 58], the verse... so He did not command these to seek permission except at the three times of nakedness (al-'awrat al-thalath). And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿When the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission.﴾ So seeking permission is obligatory upon all of Allah's creation." It was also reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A verse which most people do not believe in is the verse of seeking permission. Indeed, I order my neighbor, meaning his wife, to seek permission from me." And from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission from your fathers, your mothers and your sisters."

It is reported from some of them that the obligation of seeking permission derived from the command indicated in the verse is abrogated (mansukh). Sa'id ibn Jubayr denied this, and it is reported from him: "They say it is abrogated. No, by Allah, it is not abrogated, but people have been negligent regarding it." From al-Sha'bi: "It is not abrogated." It was said to him: "People do not act upon it," and he said: "Allah is the One sought for help." It was also said that this is restricted to the absence of consent and the absence of a door that is closed, as was the case in the first era.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ The discussion regarding it is like what preceded. The repetition is for emphasis and for intensifying the demand for seeking permission. Attributing the verses to the Divine Name (damir al-jalalah) is to honor them, and this is among what strengthens the matter of emphasis and intensification.

[p. 217]

﴿And women past child-bearing﴾, that is, the aged women. It is the plural of *qa'id*, like *ha'id* and *tamith*, so it is not made feminine because the word is specific to them. For this reason it takes the plural pattern *fawa'il*, because the *ta'* in it is like the one mentioned earlier (i.e., the feminine marker is treated as the one in the root word), or it is an irregular form. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "A woman *qa'id* is one who has ceased from menstruation." Ibn Qutaybah said: "The aged women were called *qawa'id* because they sit a great deal due to their advanced age." Ibn Rabi'ah said: "It is because they sit apart from enjoying intimacy, since they have despaired and no hope remains for them of husbands." So His statement, exalted is He, ﴿who do not hope for marriage﴾, that is, they do not aspire to it because of their old age, is a descriptive (*sifah kashifah*) qualifier. ﴿there is no blame upon them if they lay aside their garments﴾, that is, the outer garments whose removal does not lead to the exposure of nakedness, such as the *jilbab*, the *rida'* (cloak), and the veil that is over the *khimar* (head covering).

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "In the *mushaf* of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and in the *mushaf* of Ibn Mas'ud, it reads: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they lay aside their *jalabib*﴾." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they used to recite it in this way. Perhaps for this reason some have restricted the interpretation of *thiyab* (garments) to the *jilbab*. The sentence is the predicate (*khabar*) of *al-qawa'id*, and the *fa'* (in *fa-laysa*) is either because the *lam* in *al-qawa'id* is a relative pronoun meaning *allati* (those who), or because it is described by a relative clause.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿without displaying adornment﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The root meaning of *tabarruj* is the deliberate effort to display what is hidden, from the saying of the Arabs: "a *safinah* *barij*" (a ship with no covering over it). The *burj* is the width of the eye such that its whiteness is seen surrounding all of its blackness, with nothing of it hidden. It is said that its origin is manifestation from the *burj* (tower), meaning a palace; then it was specialized to mean that a woman exposes herself to men by displaying her adornment and showing her beauties. Adornment is not included in its concept, so that it could be said that mentioning adornment is a case of *tajrid* (abstraction, i.e., emphasizing a component). The apparent view is that the *ba'* is for transitivity, though it is said that it is redundant in the object, because they interpret *tabarruj* as a transitive verb. Thus in the *Qamus* (dictionary): "*tabarrajat*: she displayed her adornment to men." But there is consideration in this. The intended meaning of "adornment" here is the hidden adornment, due to the prior knowledge that the ruling is specific to it, and because of the implication contained in the word *tabarruj*. The indefinite form (*tankir*) serves to convey generality, and that any adornment, however subtle, is included in the ruling, that is, not displaying any adornment of the kind which they were commanded to conceal in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and not display their adornment﴾ [al-Nur: 31].

﴿And that they refrain (from it)﴾, by not laying aside (their garments) and remaining covered, like the young women, ﴿is better for them﴾ than laying them aside, because it is further from suspicion. Thus, ﴿for every fallen (one) there is a picker-up﴾. Ibn al-Munir mentioned an interpretation of the verse which al-Tayyibi found good. He said: "It appears to me, and Allah knows best, that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿without displaying adornment﴾ is of the type of the poet's line: 'Upon a love with no beacon by which one is guided.' That is, there is no beacon in it by which one is guided. Likewise the meaning is: 'And the aged women, who have no adornment, so they do not display it,' because the discussion concerns those who are in this condition. It seems that the purpose of this is that if their refraining from laying aside their garments is better for them, then what is your opinion about those possessing adornment among the young women? The most eloquent aspect of this is that He made not laying aside garments with regard to the aged women a form of chastity, as a notification that laying aside garments has no bearing on chastity. This is regarding the aged women, so how about the young women (*kawa'ib*)?"

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾, an intensive form emphasizing the hearing of all that is heard, so He hears what passes between them and men of conversation. ﴿All-Knowing﴾, so He, glorified is He, knows their intentions. There is in this a warning that is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves﴾ [the Qur'anic phrase in the text is: "There is no blame on the blind, no blame on the lame, and no blame on the sick."]. In the Kitab al-Zahrawi, it is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that these groups used to refrain from eating with the healthy, out of fear of the healthy finding them repulsive and fear of being harmed by their actions and conditions, so this verse was revealed. It is also said: they would enter upon a man seeking food, and if he did not have anything to feed them, they would take them to the houses of their fathers and mothers, or to some of those whom Allah the Exalted named in the noble verse. They would refrain from this and say: "He has taken us to someone else's house, and perhaps its people dislike that." Likewise, they used to refrain from eating from the wealth of those who, when they went out to fight, left these weak ones in their homes, handed them their keys, and permitted them to eat from what was in them, for fear that their permission was not given with full willingness on their part. Others besides these also refrained from eating in the houses of others. It is narrated from Ikrimah that "the Ansar were, in themselves, of a scrupulous nature (qazazah), so they would not eat from the houses that Allah the Exalted mentioned." Al-Suddi said: a man would enter the house of his father, his brother, or his sister, and the woman would offer him some food, but he would refrain because the master of the house was not present.

As for linguistic meaning, al-Zajjaj said that "haraj" (blame, narrowness) is, linguistically, the narrow [place], from "al-harajah," which is a tree whose branches are intertwined with one another, due to the narrowness of its paths. Al-Raghib said: it is originally the gathering of a thing, then it was applied to narrowness and to sin. The meaning according to the first narration is: there is no blame upon these people for eating with the healthy. For the other narrations, what is appropriate to them is to be understood, which is not hidden. ("Ala," "upon") is in its own meaning in all of that.

[p. 218]

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when the verse ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] was revealed, the Muslims refrained from eating with the blind, because he cannot see the place of good food; and [they refrained from eating with] the lame, because he cannot compete for food; and [they refrained from eating with] the sick, because he cannot take his full share of the food. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. It is also said: the Arabs and those in Medina before the Mission (al-Ba'th) avoided eating with the people of these disabilities, because of the free movement of the blind man's hand, the spreading out of the lame man's sitting, and the sick man not being free of a bad odor, an oozing wound, or a running nose. So this verse was revealed. Whoever holds this view takes "ala" to mean "fi" (in), i.e., there is no blame in eating with the blind man, and so on for the rest. Otherwise, the correct construction would have been: "There is no blame upon you that you eat with the blind man." The same is said regarding what follows, and this has a distance that is not hidden.

It is also said: there is no need to posit an omitted element after His words "blame" (haraj), as indicated, since the meaning is: there is no blame upon the listed groups, ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾ [there is] blame ﴿that you eat﴾, you and those with you ﴿from your houses﴾, etc. Our master, Shaykh al-Islam, held that the meaning is like this. Then he said: generalizing the address to include the mentioned groups as well is contradicted by what precedes it and what follows it, for the address in both is definitively to others than those groups. Perhaps what came earlier is preferable. As for generalizing the address, I do not hold it at all.

It is also narrated from Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan, and al-Jubba'i held it. Abu Hayyan said: the apparent view is that the blame negated from the people of excuse is the blame in staying behind from jihad and other things for which they were granted dispensation, and the blame negated for those after them is the blame in eating from the houses mentioned. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the discourse on it is correct, because the two groups converge in that each is negated of blame. An example of this: a traveler asks about breaking the fast in Ramadan, and a solitary pilgrim asks about putting the shaving (halq) before the sacrifice (nahr). You say: "There is no blame upon the traveler for breaking his fast, nor upon you, O pilgrim, for putting the shaving before the sacrifice." This is a clarification of the matter of the conjunction (al-'atf). That is because it had a strangeness at first sight, due to the distance of the common element (al-jami'), so he removed it by saying: since the purpose was to explain the ruling for occurring events, two events, even if they are completely different, when they occur together and are both in need of explanation, the common element between them is close. This is not so when the speech is not in the context of issuing rulings and explanation. This statement is not based on the idea that sufficiency in conceiving something is enough for a common element, as he supposed. By this the answer becomes clear to what was raised against this narration: that the discourse according to it does not fit what precedes it or what follows it. Its fit with what follows has been explained. As for its fit with what precedes, it is not necessary, since it is not conjoined to it. It may be said regarding mentioning the negation of blame from the people of excuse with regard to abandoning jihad and similar things for which they were granted dispensation, in the midst of explaining seeking permission and the like: the negation of blame from them implies that seeking permission from him (ﷺ) is not obligatory for them, so they may remain behind from jihad and the like without seeking permission or leave. Just as for slaves and children there is the right to enter houses, outside the three times of privacy (al-'awrat al-thalath), without seeking permission or leave from the people of the house. A matter like this suffices as a reason for inserting a clause in the midst of clauses that are clearly related. There is an objection to this that may be resolved on reflection.

As for why blame was not mentioned in His words ﴿nor upon yourselves﴾, saying "nor upon yourselves is blame," it is because of relying on its mention earlier, and the latter parts are places for omission. And he did not suffice with one [mention of] blame, saying: "There is no blame upon the blind, the lame, the sick, and yourselves that you eat," to prevent the suspicion of a meaning contrary to what is intended. It was also said that the omission of "blame" at the end is to indicate that it is different from what was mentioned, and does not detract from its indication of it, especially if we say that what indicates it is not restricted to it. This is as you see. The meaning of ﴿upon yourselves﴾, as in al-Kashshaf, is "upon you and upon those in a situation like yours among the believers." In it, as in al-Kashf, there is an indication of the benefit of inserting "yourselves," and that what results is

[p. 219]

that there is no blame upon the weak who are fed, nor upon those who go to the houses of relatives and those in a situation like theirs, who are friends. It was also said: the benefit of inserting it is to indicate that the mentioned eating, although it involves no blame, does not diminish the dignity of one who has a station. This is a fine, subtle point, which does not require using the expression in both its literal and figurative senses at once. Its source is the frequent insertion of "yourselves" concerning people of standing. Among this is His words: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed upon Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54], and He did not say, "Your Lord has prescribed upon Him mercy." And His words, mighty and majestic is He, in the hadith qudsi: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice upon Myself," rather than saying, "I have forbidden injustice upon Me," and other examples known to the diligent and fair researcher. As for what was said, that the benefit of the insertion is to indicate that avoiding the mentioned eating is not free from preserving one's own share, although that is hidden, it fits only some of the earlier narrations about the occasion of revelation. Similar to what was said, that it was inserted to indicate that the negation of blame concerning the addressees eating from the mentioned houses is for their own persons, unlike the negation of blame from the people of excuses eating from them, since they are together with the addressees and go with them there. And mentioning the negation of blame from them in eating from their own houses, although the negation of that is evident, is to show equality between this and their companions, as in His words: ﴿and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ [Al 'Imran: 46]. But that is in what we are discussing from the outset. He did not mention the houses of their children, because it is evident that they are like their own houses. A group has mentioned that they are included in the houses of the addressees. For Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated: "You and your wealth belong to your father," and in a hadith narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others: "Indeed the best thing a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed his child is from his earnings."

Some have said: the intended meaning of "the houses of the addressees" is the houses of their children, and it was attributed to them to emphasize its special connection to them, as both the Shari'ah and custom indicate. It was also said: the meaning is that you eat from your houses from the wealth of your children and your wives who are in your houses and among your dependents. This, as you see, is [weak]. ﴿or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers﴾. Hamzah read with a kasrah on the hamzah and the mim, and al-Kisa'i and Talhah with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the mim. ﴿or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or what you possess the keys to﴾; that is, or [what is] under your hands and disposal, from an orchard, livestock, a trusteeship (wikalah), or safekeeping. This is what the words of Ibn Abbas require. Many narrated from him that he said: "That is the agent of a man and his steward over his estate and his livestock, so there is no harm in his eating from the fruit of his garden and drinking from the milk of his livestock, but he should not carry it away or store it."

Al-Suddi said: it is the man who manages the food of another and looks after it, so there is no harm in his eating from it.

Ibn Jarir said: it is the one who has been handed the key to the house and permitted to dispose of it. It was also said: it is the guardian of an orphan who has the right to dispose of his property, for it is permitted for him to eat from it in a reasonable manner. The "possession of the key" in all of these is a metonymy for a thing being under the control and disposal of a person. The conjunction (the 'atf) is upon what we pointed to, upon what comes after "from." It is narrated from Qatadah that what is meant by "what you possess the keys to" is slaves, so the conjunction is upon what comes after "houses," and the implied phrase is: "or the houses of those whose keys you possess." Possession of the key, because it was commonly used, was a metonymy, and one does not consider that the one who disposes of it is someone who gains access to it by means of the key first. Many similar examples exist. Or it is a complement (tarshih) to the way slaves are treated like inanimate property, indicated by the use of the word for what is among them. It is not hidden from you, after this statement, that the houses of slaves are included in His words ﴿your houses﴾, because the slave has no ownership, and that the intended meaning is freed slaves, by the context of "you possessed" in the past tense, is not something worth paying attention to. Ibn Jubayr read "mullikatim" with a dammah on the mim and a kasrah on the lam, shaddah, and "wa-mafatihuhu" with a ya' after the ta', the plural of miftah (key). Qatadah and Harun, from Abu 'Amr, read "miftahahu" in the singular, which is the instrument of opening. Likewise al-mufatah, as in al-Qamus. Al-Raghib said: al-mufattah and al-miftah are that with which something is opened, and its plural is mafatih and mafatih. In some books it is said that the plural of mufattah is mafatih, and the plural of miftah is mafatih.

﴿or your friend﴾, that is, or the houses of your friend, who is one who is sincere in his affection toward you and whom you are sincere toward in his affection. The word applies to singular and plural, and what is meant here is the plural. It was also said that it is singular. The secret of using the singular rather than "your friends" is to indicate the scarcity of friends, to the point that it was said:

The saad of "sadiq" (friend) and the kaf of "kimya" (alchemy) do not exist together, so leave off your hope for them.

It is reported from Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik that he said: "I attained what I attained, even the caliphate, but I lacked a friend from whom I would feel no shame." It was also said: it is an indication that the nature of friendship is the removal of duality, and the removal of blame in eating from a friend's house, because he is more pleased with the familiarity, and more delighted by it, than many relatives. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "A friend is greater than the parents," for the people of Hell, when they cried out for help, did not seek it from fathers and mothers, but said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100-101].

It is narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "Of the greatness of the sanctity of a friend is that Allah the Exalted placed him, in intimacy, trust, ease, and the removal of formality, in the position of one's own self, father, and brother."

It was said to Aflatun (Plato): "Who is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He said: "I do not love my brother except when he is my friend." The predecessors used to be at ease eating from the houses of their friends, even when they were absent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 61 (part 2 of 2):

It is related on the authority of al-Hasan that he entered his house and found a circle of his friends who had pulled out baskets from beneath his bed, containing khabis (a sweet dish) and choice foods, and they were bent over them, eating. His face lit up with joy, and he laughed and said: "This is how we found them, this is how we found them," meaning the senior Companions and those among the People of Badr whom he had met. A man among them would enter the house of his friend while he was absent, ask his slave-girl for his purse, and take whatever he wished. When the owner arrived and was informed, he would free her out of joy at that. And this was a thing that once existed.

"When people were people and the time was time." As for today, its carpet has been folded up, to my knowledge, and it has vanished. God Most High has taken down its tent, its traces have been effaced, and its moons have set. A friend has become a name for an enemy who hides his enmity and awaits for you the calamities and raids of the times. So: alas, then alas, and there is no power and no strength except in God.

From the wretchedness of this world for the free man is that he sees
An enemy of his, from whose friendship there is no escape.

Then, the lifting of blame regarding the eating mentioned is conditional upon the eater knowing the owner's consent, either by explicit permission or by an indication. It may be objected that if consent is found, eating from the property of a stranger or an enemy would also be permitted, so there would be no point in the specification. The answer: the specification of these (relatives and friends) is due to the habit of informality among them, so there is no implication (mafhum) in it. Abu Muslim said: "This applies to the disbelieving peoples. In this verse God permits what He forbade in His saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]." But this is not right. It has also been said:

That was in the early period of Islam, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the good pleasure of his soul."

And his peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both: "No one shall milk another's livestock except with his permission." And the saying of God Most High: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their people﴾ [al-Nur: 27], and the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission to a meal, not waiting for its preparation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. For if they were prohibited from the Prophet's house except on the mentioned condition, and he, upon him be blessings and peace, was the most generous of people and the least in veiling himself, then others, may God bless him and grant him peace, are all the more so.

You know that there is no need to say abrogation, based on what we said at first. Some of the imams of the Hanafis argued from this verse that there is no amputation for theft of the property of mahram relatives (those with whom marriage is forbidden) in any case, with no distinction in this between parents and children and others, because it indicates the permissibility of entering their houses without their permission, so their property is not protected (muhraz). The mere possibility that the apparent meaning is intended, and the absence of abrogation, suffices for doubt that averts the hadd (prescribed punishment). This was objected to, on the ground that averting the hudud (prescribed punishments) by doubts is not absolute among them, as is known from their principles. It was also objected that this would imply that the hand of one who steals from a close friend should not be cut off. This was answered: a close friend, once he intends to steal from his friend's property, becomes an enemy. This was challenged: the Shari'ah looks at the outward, not at inner secrets.

It was read as "ṣadīqukum" with a kasra on the ṣād, following the vowel of the dal; Hamid al-Khazzaz transmitted this. ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together﴾, meaning gathered together. "Jamī'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of "ta'kulu" (you eat). Originally it means "all," and it does not by itself imply gathering, contrary to al-Farra'. Here it does imply gathering, because it is contrasted with the saying of God Most High: ﴿or in separate groups﴾ (ashtatan), for the latter is coordinated with it, and is included in its ruling. Ashtat is the plural of shatt, used as an adjective like haqq; one says amr shatt, meaning a scattered matter. Or it is originally a verbal noun described by it for emphasis. The verse, according to the view of most exegetes, is a new independent statement, given to explain another ruling of the same kind as what precedes it. It was revealed, as is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah, concerning the tribe of Layth ibn Amr ibn Kinanah, who were scrupulous about eating their food alone. A man among them would not eat and would remain all day until he found a guest to eat with him; if he found no one to eat with, he would eat nothing. Sometimes a man among them would sit with food before him, not touching it from morning until evening; and sometimes he had camels with milk and would not drink from it until he found someone to drink with him. When evening came and he had found no one, he would eat. It is said: this scrupulousness was an inherited custom from the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), upon him be blessings and peace. Hatim has said:

When you prepare food, seek for it
A companion, for I do not eat it alone.

And in a hadith: "The worst of people is he who eats alone, beats his servant, and withholds his gift." This condemnation is for the habit of stinginess in hospitality. The negation of blame for its occasional occurrence is an explanation that there is no sin in it and that it is not condemned by the Shari'ah as the Jahiliyyah condemned it. So there is no need to say that the threat in the hadith applies only to one in whom the three traits are combined, not to eating alone by itself, for that would imply that each of them on its own is not forbidden, which is not the case. And the saying that they were people of eloquence to whom the like would not be hidden, but that because the particle "wa" (and) comes with the meaning of "aw" (or), they left each one of them out of caution, has no basis, because these scrupulous people did not hold to the hadith. And that "wa" means "awtu-hum" (they were given) is of no account. There is no doubt that gathering of hands over food is a sunnah, so abandoning it without a reason is blameworthy, ended.

It is related from Ikrimah and Abu Salih that it was revealed concerning a people of the Ansar who, whenever a guest came to them, would not eat except with him. So God permitted them to eat however they wished. It is said: the wealthy man would enter upon a poor relative or friend and invite him to his food, and he would say: "I am scrupulous about eating with you while I am rich and you are poor." This is related from Ibn Abbas. Al-Kalbi said: when they gathered to eat food, they would set aside food separately for the blind and the like. So God Most High explained that this was not obligatory.

It has also been said: they used to eat alone, out of fear that one of them would eat more than the other, or that the gathering would produce something repugnant or harmful. So it was revealed to negate the obligation of this. Whichever is the case, the lesson is by the generality of the wording, not by the specific cause. It has also been said: the verse is a continuation of what precedes it, in the sense that it came as an answer to a question arising from it, as if a questioner asked: "Has blame been negated for eating from the houses of ... [the specific list]?" Is that only when eating with the people of those houses or not? It is answered by the saying of God Most High: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together﴾, meaning gathered with the people of those houses in eating, ﴿or in separate groups﴾, meaning scattered, each of you eating alone without the owner of the house with him. How delicate is the negation of blame in what has a wide scope, and the negation of "junah" (blame) in what is related between two matters. Nuances need not be consistently applied, so it is said; so reflect.

﴿So when you enter houses﴾: a beginning of explaining the etiquette that should be observed when engaging in what has been permitted, after explaining the permission for it. ﴿Houses﴾, meaning from the houses mentioned, as the "fa" indicates.

﴿then greet one another﴾, meaning greet the people of them, as Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn Abbas. Close to this is what Abd al-Razzaq and a group reported from al-Hasan, that the meaning is: "let some of you greet others," like the saying of God Most High: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. Referring to the people of those houses as "yourselves" is to place them in the position of the selves due to the closeness of the connection. In the Intisaf it is said that describing them with this points to the secret that required the permissibility of eating from those mentioned houses: that these houses, relative to the one entering, are like his own house, due to kinship and the like. It has also been said:

The intended meaning is greeting the people of the houses in the most complete manner, because when a Muslim returns his greeting upon himself, it is as if he greeted himself, just as the killer, because he deserves death by his act, is as if he killed himself. Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and others reported from Ibn Abbas that he said concerning the verse: "It is the mosque: when you enter it, say: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God.'" So he took "houses" in it to mean mosques, and "greeting upon yourselves" in its apparent sense. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the houses of the addressees and their families. It is mentioned that when a man enters upon his family, it is recommended for him to say: "Peace be upon you, a blessing from God, good and pure." If he finds no one, let him say: "Peace be upon us from our Lord." This is related from Ata.
