It has also been said: greeting upon the selves in its apparent sense, and the intended houses are the houses of the disbelievers. It is mentioned that whoever enters them, and likewise empty houses, says what I just heard from Ibn Abbas. It has also been said: he says upon the disbelievers: "Peace be upon those who follow the guidance," which is not hidden as suitable for the context. "Salam" (peace) here means safety from calamities. It has also been said that it is one of the names of God, Mighty and Majestic. The discussion of this has passed in its fullest form, so recall it.

﴿a greeting from God﴾, meaning established by His command, legislated from His presence, Mighty and Majestic. So the prepositional phrase is related to a omitted word that occurs as an adjective to "greeting." It is also permitted that it relates to "greeting," for it is a request for life, and that is from Him, Mighty and Majestic. The original meaning of it is that you say: "May God give you life," that is, may He, glory be to Him, give you life. Then it was generalized to every supplication. Its accusative is as a verbal noun, as if it were said: "so greet with a greeting," or "so greet with a greeting," ﴿blessed﴾, one in which blessing is sought for its reward, as is related from Muqatil. al-Dahhak said: "In the salam there are ten good deeds; with the mercy twenty; with the blessings thirty."

﴿good﴾, by which the listener's soul is made content. The apparent meaning is that the Muslim adds to his greeting what has been mentioned. It is related from some of the early scholars that he adds to it, as has just passed. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "I did not take the tashahhud except from the Book of God. I heard God Most High say: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet your selves with a greeting from God, blessed and good﴾. So the tashahhud in prayer is: 'All the greetings, the blessed, the good, are for God.'"

﴿Thus God makes clear to you the verses﴾: a repetition for further emphasis, and in it is a grand glorification of the rulings with which it concludes. ﴿so that you may reason﴾, meaning what is within its folds of legislations and rulings, and that you may act according to what they require, and attain thereby the happiness of both abodes.

In this explanation with this utmost goal, after concluding the former verses with what requires it, there is an eloquence that is not hidden. Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that God, glory be to Him, began the surah with His saying: ﴿And We have sent down in it clear signs﴾ [al-Nur: 1], and concluded it with His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs.﴾ Then He, Blessed and Exalted, made the seal of the seal His saying, glory be to Him:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 24, verse 62:

﴿Truly, the believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger﴾, etc. This indicates that the criterion of all of that, and the one who benefits from those verses, is the group who have surrendered themselves to the Lawgiver, may the blessings and peace of Allah the Exalted be upon him, like a corpse between the hands of the washer, who neither holds back nor advances without his signal (ﷺ). For this subtle point, Shihab al-Haqq wa'l-Din Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi, may Allah sanctify his secret, cited this verse in the chapter on the disciple's conduct with the shaykh, and by this he alerted that everything he lays down of the matters of religion is a comprehensive matter.

Shaykh al-Islam said: This is a resumptive clause, brought at the end of the preceding rulings, to confirm them, to affirm the obligation of observing them, and to complete them by clarifying another part of their kind. The mention of belief in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) as a relative clause for the relative pronoun which is the predicate of the subject, despite its definitely implying it, is to confirm what precedes it, to prepare for what follows it, and to announce that he is worthy of being made a companion of the aforementioned belief, arranged in its thread. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾, etc., is conjoined to (believed) and falls within the scope of the relative clause with it, and by this the reading is correct. The restriction is in terms of perfection, i.e., the ones who are perfect in faith are only those who have believed in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) from the sincerity of their hearts, and have obeyed in all the rulings, among which is what was detailed before of the rulings concerning the general affairs of their conditions that are constantly occurring, and their conditions that occur by chance, such as when they are with him, upon him be prayer and peace, on a matter of importance that requires their gathering concerning it, such as Friday prayer, the festivals, wars, and other matters that call to gathering for some purpose. It is related from Ibn Zayd that the common matter is jihad. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Salam said it is every prayer in which there is a sermon, such as Friday, the two festivals, and the prayer for rain. It is related from Ibn Jubayr that it is jihad and the Friday and two festivals prayer. It is not hidden that generality is preferable, even though the verse was revealed concerning the digging of the trench, and perhaps what was mentioned is by way of example. The matter is described as "common" although it is its cause, for emphasis, and the apparent view is that this is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli). It is also permitted that there be a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyyah) there.

Al-Yamani read "on a matter that is gathered (jami')" and it means "comprehensive" or "gathered for it," by ellipsis and conveying. ﴿They do not go away﴾ from him (ﷺ) ﴿until they ask his permission﴾, upon him be prayer and peace, to leave; so he grants them permission to go, and they go. The limit is the permission obtained after asking permission. The restriction to asking permission is because it is what is completed on their part, and it is the criterion for the perfection of faith, not the permission nor the going that follows from it. Its consideration in this is because it is like the proof of its validity and the distinguisher of the sincere from the hypocrite, for the hypocrite's habit is to slip away to flee. And to magnify what there is in leaving without his permission, upon him be prayer and peace, of offense; and to alert to this, Exalted and Glorified is He followed with His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission, they are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. So He made those who ask permission the believers, the reverse of the first, indicating that the two are mutually reciprocal, equal to equal. From this it follows that it is like the proof of the validity of the two faiths. Likewise, with the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara), because it indicates that the deserving of the two faiths is for this. ﴿So when they ask your permission﴾ is an explanation of what is his duty, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, in this matter, after the explanation of what is the duty of the believers. The fa' is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes it, i.e., after it has been established that the perfect in faith are those who ask permission, so when they ask your permission ﴿for some of their affair﴾, i.e., for some of their important matter and pressing concern.

﴿So grant permission to whom you will of them﴾: a delegation of the matter to his opinion (ﷺ). It has been used as evidence that some rulings are delegated to his opinion, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. This is the issue of delegation (tafwid), whose permissibility is disputed among the scholars of usul, namely that the ruling is delegated to the mujtahid, so it is said to him: "Judge as you will, for it is correct." Some permitted this, but they differed. Musa ibn 'Imran said: its permissibility is absolute, for the Prophet and for other scholars. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: its permissibility is for the Prophet alone, in one of his two opinions. It has been reported from Imam al-Shafi'i, may mercy be upon him, in al-Risalah, what indicates hesitation between permissibility and prohibition. The rest prohibited it. Those who permit it differed on whether it occurred. Al-Amidi said: the preferred view is permissibility, not occurrence. He has extended discussion on this point, so let it be consulted. What I incline to is the permissibility of delegating the ruling to the mujtahid when it is known that he judges with deliberation, not caprice, and the delegation then is like a command to exercise ijtihad. The most fitting thing for the majesty of Allah the Exalted and the majesty of His Messenger (ﷺ) is to interpret what is here in this way, and the will is restricted by knowledge of the benefit. Some eminent scholars mentioned that there is no disagreement on the permissibility of saying: "Judge as you will" with deliberation; rather the disagreement is on the permissibility of saying: "Judge as you will" with caprice, however it happens. You know that after this restriction, what we are dealing with is not a point of dispute. Among the strange things said is that the intended one among them is Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, and what is in it is not hidden. ﴿And ask forgiveness for them from Allah﴾, for asking permission, even if for a strong excuse, is not free of a trace of preferring worldly affairs over the affair of the Hereafter. The fronting of "for them" (lahum) is for the immediate understanding that the seeking of forgiveness is for those asking permission, not for the granting of permission.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾: intensive in forgiving the lapses of the servants; ﴿Merciful﴾: intensive in pouring down the showers of mercy upon them. The clause is a reason for the forgiveness promised within the seeking of forgiveness for them. He, may His majesty be exalted, has exceeded in honoring His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah the Exalted be upon him, so He made asking permission to leave him a sin in need of seeking forgiveness, let alone leaving without permission; and He tied the granting of permission to asking permission for some of their affairs, not to asking permission in general, nor to asking permission for any matter whatsoever or for an unimportant one; and yet He made the granting of permission contingent on will. If you consider the aspects of exaggeration in His saying, ﴿Truly, the believers are only...﴾ up to here, you will find them to exceed ten.

In Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, it is that in the verse there is evidence for the obligation of asking his permission, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, before departing from him, upon him be prayer and peace, in every matter they gather over. Al-Hasan said: other than the Messenger, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, of the imams is similar to him in that, for in it is the courtesy of religion and the courtesy of the self. Ibn al-Furs said: there is no disagreement that in military campaign one asks permission of his commander if he has an excuse that calls him to depart. There is disagreement concerning Friday prayer if he has an excuse such as a nosebleed or other; it is said he is obliged to ask permission whether the commander is present or someone else, taking it from the verse. This was narrated from Makhul and al-Zuhri.

[Page 224]

Her "lā taj'alū du'ā'a al-Rasūli baynakum ka-du'ā'i ba'ḍikum ba'ḍan" (﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like the summoning of some of you by others﴾) is a resumptive sentence (*istif'nāf*, a new clause that reinforces what precedes it), and the shift to the third person (*iltifāt*, a change of grammatical person) serves to highlight the greater importance of his status. The meaning is: do not compare his summoning of you, upon him be blessings and peace, with the summoning of some of you by others, in any state or matter, among which is being lax about it and withdrawing from his assembly, upon him be blessings and peace, without seeking permission. For that is among the forbidden acts. This is the view of Abu Muslim, which al-Mubarrad and al-Qaffal also chose. It has also been said: the meaning is, do not think that his summoning you, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is like the summoning of some of you upon others, so that you expose yourselves to his displeasure and to his supplication against you, upon him be blessings and peace, by opposing his command and withdrawing from his assembly without permission, and the like. This is derived from what has come in some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and is reported from al-Sha'bi. Ibn 'Atiyya criticised this, saying that the wording of the verse rejects this meaning. It seems that he meant that the apparent sense is "upon some of you." It has also been said that the word "baynakum" (among you) contradicts it, and it is within the scope of prohibition. It has also been said: the meaning is, do not make his supplication, upon him be blessings and peace, to his Lord, mighty and majestic, like the supplication of the young among you to the old, the poor to the rich, who asks him for his need: sometimes He answers him and sometimes He rejects him. For his supplication, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is answered, and there is no turning it back before Allah, mighty and majestic. So do not expose yourselves to his supplication for you by obeying his command and seeking his permission when you depart from him while you are with him on a matter of common concern, and seek to make sure his prayer for forgiveness for you is accepted, and do not expose yourselves to his supplication against you by the opposite of that.

There is no obscurity about how this sentence reinforces what precedes it according to these two views. However, there is a discussion regarding the claim that all of his supplications, upon him be blessings and peace, are answered: it is established that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked Allah concerning his community that some of them should not taste the violence of others, and He refused him. This clearly indicates that he may reject some of his supplications, upon him be blessings and peace. It has been objected: how could He reject them when Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [40:60]?

And in a ḥadīth: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, does not reject the supplication of a believer, even if it is delayed."

Imam al-Suhayli said in *al-Rawḍ*: Responses (to supplication) are of kinds: either the hastening of what was asked, or He stores up for him something better than what he requested, or He averts from him a calamity equal to the good he asked for. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was given, in place of not having the violence of some of his community tasting the violence of others, the intercession.

And he said: "This community of mine is a merciful community; in the Hereafter there is no punishment for it; its punishment in this world is earthquakes and trials," as in Abu Dawud. So if trials became a cause for averting the punishment of the Hereafter from the community, it cannot be said that his supplication, upon him be blessings, was not answered, because not being answered would mean not being given what he asked for, or not being compensated with something better than it. The meaning of "refusal" in the ḥadīth is the refusal of that particular matter, not the non-answering of supplication in the sense mentioned. The full discussion of this issue is to be sought in its proper place.

It has also been said: the meaning is, do not make his calling, upon him be blessings and peace, and naming him, like the calling of some of you to others by name, and raising the voice with it, and calling from behind the apartments; rather (call him) by his honoured title, such as "O Prophet of Allah" and "O Messenger of Allah," with reverence, humility and lowering the voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dalā'il* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: They used to say, "O Muhammad, O Abu al-Qasim," so Allah, the Exalted, forbade them from that by His saying, ﴿Do not make﴾ [the verse], in honour of His Prophet ﷺ. So they said, "O Prophet of Allah, O Messenger of Allah." A similar report is transmitted from Qatada, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. In *Aḥkām al-Qur'ān* of al-Suyuti, it is stated that this prohibition includes the prohibition of calling the Prophet ﷺ by his name.

The apparent meaning is that this continues after his death until now. Al-Tabarsi mentioned that among what is prohibited is calling out "O son of 'Abd Allah," for this is what the Arabs call one another. This view has been criticised on the grounds that the verse, according to it, does not fit the preceding and following context.

Some said: the connection with what precedes it is that it guides to the fact that seeking permission should be by saying, "O Messenger of Allah, we seek your permission," or the like. Likewise, addressing him, ﷺ, by one who is with him on a matter of common concern should be with something like "O Messenger of Allah," not with "O Muhammad." This degree of connection with what came before is sufficient, and there is no need to explain the relevance by saying that each of the two (matters) contains something that contradicts the reverence befitting his great station, ﷺ. Yes, the more evident meaning of the verse is what we mentioned first, as is not hidden.

Al-Hasan and Ya'qub, in one narration, read "nabiyyakum" (your Prophet) with an open nūn, a kasrah on the bā', and a shaddah on the yā', instead of "baynakum" (among you), which is the adverbial form in the reading of the majority. It is taken as a substitute (*badal*) for "al-Rasūl" (the Messenger), and it was not made an attributive adjective (*na't*) to it, because it is annexed to a pronoun, and the annexed noun is at the level of a proper noun, and it is more definite than what is defined by "al," and an attributive adjective must be less definite than the noun it qualifies or equal to it in definiteness. Abu Hayyan said: It should be permissible to make it an attributive adjective, because "al-Rasūl" has become a proper noun by predominance, like "al-Bayt" for the Ka'ba, so they are equal in definiteness.

﴿Allah certainly knows those among you who slip away﴾: this is a threat to those who are the opposite of those believers who did not leave until they had asked his permission, upon him be blessings and peace. *Al-tasallul* is leaving from among the gathering gradually and secretly. *Qad* is for emphasis (*taḥqīq*). It is permitted that it be for lessening the number of those who slip away in comparison with what Allah knows, and that it be for amplification, either literally or as an oppositional metaphor (*isti'āra didiyya*). Abu Hayyan said: the statement of some grammarians that *qad*, when it enters upon the present tense, indicates amplification is not correct; rather, amplification is understood from the context of speech, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"A trustworthy brother, wine does not destroy his wealth, but wealth may indeed destroy his generosity."

For the context of the speech is praise, and this is understood from it. That is, Allah certainly knows those who go out from the congregation little by little, secretly.

﴿Lewādhan﴾ means by concealing themselves behind one another until one goes out. Abu Dawud reported in his *Marāsīl* from Muqatil, who said: No one would leave because of a nosebleed or a breach of wind until he had asked permission from the Prophet ﷺ, pointing to him with the finger next to the thumb, and the Prophet ﷺ would permit him by signalling with his hand. Among the hypocrites were those who found the sermon and sitting in the mosque burdensome; so when a man among the Muslims sought permission, a hypocrite would stand beside him, hiding behind him until he went out. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Allah certainly knows﴾ [the verse]. It is said that he would cling to him, showing that he was one of his followers.

*Lewādhan* is in the accusative either as an infinitive of manner (*maṣdariyya*) or as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāliyya*), with the interpretation "those concealing themselves." It is the verbal noun of *lāwadha*, its *wāw* not being changed to a *yā'* because it follows the verb form, and if it were the verbal noun of *lādha*, it would have been said *liyādhan*, like *qiyāman*.

Yazid ibn Qutayb read "lawdhan" with a fatḥah on the lām. This could be the verbal noun of *lādha*, whose *wāw* was not changed to *yā'* because there is no kasrah before it, so it is like *ṭawāfan*, the verbal noun of *ṭāfa*. It could also be the verbal noun of *lāwadha*, with the fatḥah on the lām because of the fatḥah on the wāw.

The *fā'* in His saying, ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾, is for the ordering of caution (or the command to be cautious) upon what precedes it, namely His knowledge of their conditions, for this necessarily requires caution. *Mukhālafa* (opposition), as al-Raghib said, is that each one takes a path different from the path of the other in his state or action. Its most common usage is without *'an*, so one says "Zayd opposed 'Amr" (*khālafa Zaydun 'Amran*). When it is used with *'an*, that is on the basis of implying the meaning of turning away.

It has been said that the meaning is "going out," i.e., "those who oppose, turning away or going out from his command." Ibn al-Hajib said: "yukhālifūna" is transitive with *'an* because opposition contains the sense of distance and deviation, as if it were said: "those who deviate from his command by opposing," which is more eloquent than saying "those who oppose his command."

It has been said that it is on the basis of implying the meaning of *ṣadd* (turning away, obstructing). It has also been said that when it is transitive with *'an*, the meaning intended is *ṣadd* without implication, and it may be transitive directly to an object, as one says: "khālafa Zaydan 'an al-amr," meaning he turned him away from it. The object here is omitted, i.e., "the believers oppose them," meaning they turn them away from his command. The object was omitted because the purpose is to disparage the state of the opponent and to magnify the matter they oppose; so the more important is mentioned and what is of no concern is left out. It may also be transitive with *ilā*, as one says "khālafa ilayhi" when he approaches him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'an" here has the meaning of distance; the meaning is that their opposition occurs after his command, just as you say: "the rain was after wind" (*kāna al-maṭaru 'an rīḥin*) and "I fed him after hunger" (*aṭ'amtuhu 'an jū'in*). Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: it is superfluous, i.e., "they oppose his command." The pronoun in "amrihi" refers to Allah, the Exalted, for the command truly belongs to Him, or to the Messenger ﷺ, for he is the one intended by the mention. The "command" here has been said to mean the request, or the matter, or what includes both. It is not hidden that there is some difficulty in permitting each of the two possibilities regarding the pronoun, so do not be heedless.

"Yukhalliqūna" with shaddah has also been read, meaning they leave themselves behind from his command.

[Page 227]

﴿Lest a trial afflict them﴾: that is, a calamity and a tribulation in this world, as is reported from Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted "trial" as killing. From Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, it is interpreted as the empowerment of an unjust ruler. From al-Suddi and Muqatil, it is interpreted as disbelief. The first interpretation is preferable.

﴿Or a painful punishment strike them﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. It has been said that it is in this world; and that the painful punishment means killing, while the trial is what is less than that, but this is not correct. The particle *aw* (or) is for preventing the absence of both, not for combining them. Repeating the verb explicitly is for the sake of attending to the threat and warning. It is widely cited as evidence that the command is for obligation (*wujūb*): for He, the Exalted, made it obligatory in this verse for the one who opposes the command to be wary of punishment, and this is a threat for opposing the command, and it is evidence that the command is for obligation, since there is no threat for leaving what is not obligatory. Also, attaching the ruling of caution against punishment to the one who opposes requires that his caution against it be on account of the opposition, and that occurs only if it leads to punishment, as in your saying: "let the one who insults the emir beware lest he strike him," and there is no such leading to punishment in leaving what is not obligatory.

This command, namely ﴿let him beware﴾, specifically, is used for obligation, since there is no sense in recommending caution against punishment or permitting it. Also, the implication of the verse for the obligation of caution is not hidden, given the context in which it occurs, the warning of the coming of a punishment. Moreover, even if the aforementioned command were taken to be for recommendation, the aim would be achieved, because being cautious against what one does not know or does not suspect will occur, and against what does not lead to its occurrence in any way, is foolish and contrary to wisdom, and for this reason one who warns against the collapse of a sound wall that is not leaning is blamed. In any case, the following objection is refuted: we do not accept that His saying, ﴿let him beware﴾, is for obligation, because that is the very point in dispute. For according to what we have established, it suffices for the purpose that it is used for recommendation too. And the claim that the meaning of opposing a command is not believing in its truth, or interpreting it as other than what it is, such as taking it to be obligatory or recommended while it is otherwise, is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning that comes to mind is that one abandoned compliance and doing what was commanded, so one does not turn from that except by evidence. It was objected that after all this discussion, it does not prove that all commands are literally for obligation, because the command is unqualified (*li-ițlāq al-amr*).

I answer that ﴿amrihi﴾ ("his command") is a genitive-construct verbal noun (maṣdar mudāf), and it conveys generality when the indicator of a specific reference ('ahd) is absent. The unrestricted sense suffices for the intended point, namely that an unqualified command (amr muṭlaq) is for obligation (wujūb) specifically. For if it were a true (ḥaqīqah) meaning for something else as well, the threat would not follow from opposing an unqualified command.

Some of the eminent scholars said: there is no one who makes a distinction among forms of command, holding that some are for obligation and others for something else. Some claimed that the argument does not hold if by "command" is meant a request (ṭalab); and that if it were interpreted as "affair" (sha'n), with the pronoun referring to the Messenger ﷺ, then from the view that its forms indicate obligation it would follow that everything he ﷺ does is obligatory upon us, and no one holds this. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as religion and obedience.

The author of al-Kashf said: the argument from the verse that command indicates obligation is well known, whether it is interpreted in the manner mentioned, because obedience is compliance with a spoken command, or it is interpreted literally. As for when it is taken as a reference back to the previously mentioned collective command (al-amr al-jāmi'), and the meaning of ﴿yukhalifūna 'an amrihi﴾ is "they turn away from it," then no; and this is not the preferred view, even though a group adopted it, because it loses the intensification (mubālagha), the first sense of inclusion, and the departure from the literal meaning in the word "command," and then opposition without necessity. The end of his words. This which a group preferred was mentioned by al-Tibi from al-Baghawi, and then he said: this is the interpretation on which reliance is placed, and the context and the interpretive reasoning support it, because the command then means "affair" and the singular of "affairs." Its explanation is that what precedes it is a discussion of the collective command, which is the matter that people gather over, and it praises those who remain in the assembly of the Messenger of God ﷺ and do not leave from it, and blames those who depart from him without permission, and it commands seeking forgiveness regarding those who depart with permission, because
Page 228
the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So grant permission to whom you will of them﴾ indicates that the people are of three groups: the one permitted to leave after asking leave; the one who stays behind from that; and then the one who stays behind either remains in his assembly, peace be upon him, and does not leave, and these are the sincere believers; or he slips away furtively, and these are the hypocrites. And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then let those beware﴾ and so on is consequent upon the third category, in the manner of a warning, and the present-tense verb conveys the sense of habit and custom, and the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun as the reason for their deserving the trial of both abodes. The end of his words. Al-Kashf has already uncovered some of what is in it.

Yes, it was said against this: the loss of intensification and inclusion does not outweigh the reference (al-'ahd), and there is no departure from the literal meaning, because the command is literal in the event, and likewise the opposition in what was mentioned. And even if it is granted, it carries equal implication, for the command is not literal in the general command. And his saying "without necessity" is disputed, for the annexation of the reference is a diverting indicator. It was responded that this is obstinacy and a bare denial that is not heard, for there is no doubt about the intensification, since threatening one who does not comply with his command ﷺ is more severe than leaving without permission; and that the command being literal for request is the most correct view in the principles of jurisprudence; and that opposition accompanying a command, its literal meaning is undoubtedly non-compliance. The equal implication is not complete, because if his command is general, it also includes the collective command in the sense of request; and the reference of annexation is not definite so as to be counted as a diverting indicator, so it is said. But there is discussion in this, so consider. It may be said, based on the matter mentioned being a reference to the collective command, that the phrase ﴿that a trial befall them or a painful punishment befall them﴾ was brought as an alternative, because the collective command is either a worldly matter, such as consultation and matters of war, so departing from it is the likely cause of worldly affliction for those who depart; or it is a religious matter, such as the establishment of Friday prayer in which there is the glorification of the rites of Islam, so departing from it is the likely cause of the punishment of the Hereafter.

In sum, there is no argument from the verse for the consideration of the reference. As for when it is not considered, then it has been used as an argument, and you have heard some discussion on this, and its full treatment, both in terms of impugning and vouching, and other matters, is in the books of usul.

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, of all existing things, entirely, in creation, dominion and disposal: bringing into being and annihilating, originating and returning, with no partner to anyone else and no independent power of anyone else. ﴿He knows well the state you are in﴾, O (you) who are responsible (for the law), of conditions and circumstances, among which are agreement and opposition, sincerity and hypocrisy, and the entry of the hypocrites. Although the address in what precedes was to the believers, by way of *taghlib* (the rhetorical device of giving precedence to one group within a broader address). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Day they are returned to Him﴾ is specific to the hypocrites. It is an object governed by the verb, coordinated with what is in ﴿you are﴾, meaning: He knows on the Day when the hypocrites, who oppose the command, are returned to Him, mighty and majestic is He, for reward and punishment.

Linking His knowledge to the Day of their return rather than to their return itself serves to strengthen the affirmation of His knowledge, glorified is He, of that matter and to give the utmost confirmation to it, because knowledge of the time of an event's occurrence entails knowledge of its occurrence in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It also implies that His knowledge, exalted and high is He, has made their return so manifest in itself that it needs no explanation at all. It is possible that the preceding address is also specific to them, so that there are two *iltifat* (shifts): a shift from the third person to the second person in ﴿you are﴾, and a shift from the second person to the third person in ﴿they are returned﴾, while the coordination remains as it is. It has also been allowed that it be governed by an implied element, meaning: what you are upon now, and the Day etc., since the nominal sentence indicates the present state within continuity and stability. It has been said: "Yawm" (Day) may be an adverb governed by an implied verb coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: and He will call them to account on a Day, or something similar. But I do not see its being specific to the second of these interpretations in the address.

In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), after mentioning the two possibilities in it, and that the more apparent view is that "Yawm" is coordinated with ﴿what you are upon﴾, it says: Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that the implied element is: "and knowledge will become evident to you," or something similar, on a Day; so "Yawm" is in the accusative as an adverb governed by an implied verb, and *qad* (indeed) serves for emphasis. Both of the aforementioned possibilities are in it. The sense of such a sentence as regards threat or promise has been mentioned more than once before. What fits each of the possibilities in ﴿you are﴾ and ﴿they are returned﴾ is not hidden.

Ibn Ya'mar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu 'Amr read ﴿they are returned﴾ in the passive voice. ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾, that is, of their deed, or of what they did of the evil deeds, among which is opposition to the command; so He, glorified is He, metes out to it what is fitting for Him of rebuke and recompense. Or: He will inform them of what they did, good or evil, and then He metes out to that what is fitting for Him: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. ﴿And God is Knower of all things﴾, nothing among things is hidden from Him. The sentence is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) confirming what precedes it. The mention of the Glorious Name in a place where a pronoun would be expected serves to emphasize the independence of the sentence and to indicate the reason for the ruling, and the fronting of the adverbial phrase serves the rhyme of the verses. It has been said, and there is an investigation in this: it is for restriction, meaning: God is Knower of every thing, not of only some things, as some ignorant philosophers and those who follow their path claim. May God, exalted is He, protect us and the Muslims from the errors they are in; may He make for us a light by which we are guided when the night of ignorance leads them astray. This is (the end of the matter).

* * *

From the gate of *al-ishara* (allusive or esoteric interpretation) in the verses is what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that God drives clouds﴾ to the end of the verse: that it is an allusion to the gathering of the four elements and the composition of the human being from them; then the emergence of the rain of sensation from his two eyes and two ears, for example; and it descends from the sky of the overflowing intellect with the return of the realities of knowledge, so that it strikes whomever He wills, and its effects appear on him, and He turns it away from whomever He wills, as the divine wisdom requires. ﴿The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sights﴾: the light of its manifestation, ﴿takes away the sights﴾ by disabling them from seeing and annihilating their possessors from them, since perception by its light is above perception by the light of sight. ﴿God alternates the night and the day﴾: an allusion to the night of effacement and the day of sobriety, or the night of contraction and the day of expansion, or the night of majesty and the day of beauty, or something similar.

It has been said: He drives the cloud of sins until it accumulates, so you see the rain of repentance coming out from within it, as the rain came out of the cloud of ﴿And Adam disobeyed﴾ — the rain ﴿then his Lord chose him﴾ — and it descends from the sky of hearts, from mountains of hardness in them, from the cold of subjugation. God alternates the night of disobedience for whomever He wills into the day of obedience, and vice versa. ﴿God created every moving creature from water﴾: the discussion about water has already passed. ﴿Among them are those who walk on their bellies﴾: they rely in their walking on the inner dimension, and they are the people of attraction, immersed in the seas of love. ﴿Among them are those who walk on two legs﴾: they rely in their walking on the Sharia and the Tariqa (the spiritual path), but only in what pertains specifically to them of the two; and they are a class of the perfected who have dwelt in the corners of obscurity, did not mix with people, and did not occupy themselves with guidance. ﴿Among them are those who walk on four﴾: they rely in their walking on the Sharia and the Tariqa in what pertains to them and to others of them; and they are another class of the perfected who came forth to the people, mixed with them, occupied themselves with guidance, acted within themselves according to what the Sharia and the Tariqa require, and dealt with people and seekers likewise. ﴿God creates what He wills﴾: so it is not unlikely that among His creation there are those who walk on more (than four), like the perfected whom God, exalted is He, has made to stand upon the secrets of the dominion and the malakut (the unseen realm), and what He has set as a limit for each nation among the nations and each kind among the kinds of created beings; so they dealt, after acting within themselves in a manner fitting for them, each nation and each kind with what has been set for it. ﴿Each one knows its prayer and its glorification﴾.

In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: We believe in God and in the Messenger﴾ and the verses that follow: an allusion to the states of those who deny in the heart the shaykhs, and the states of those who affirm them, in heart and in outward form. In His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾: an allusion to the fact that obedience to the Messenger is a cause of the attainment of unveilings (*mukashafat*) and the like. Abu 'Uthman said: Whoever puts the Sunna over his self in word and deed speaks wisdom, and whoever puts his desire over his self speaks innovation, because God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾. In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter that calls for gathering, they do not depart until they ask his permission﴾: an allusion to the fact that it is not proper for the disciple (*murid*) to act independently in anything. 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Some people among the companions of Abu 'Uthman said to Abu 'Uthman: Advise us. He said: Stand together in religion, beware of opposing the elders, and do not enter into any act of obedience except with their permission and counsel; and console the needy with what you are able to. When you do this, I hope that God, exalted is He, will not lose your effort. ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾: in it is what it contains of the magnification of the command of the Messenger (ﷺ). He mentioned that the shaykh in his community is like the Prophet in his nation, so one should show respect in addressing him and give him precedence over others. ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them﴾. Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz said: The trial is the lavishing of blessings together with gradual deception (*istidraj*). Al-Junayd, may God sanctify his secret, said: It is hardness of the heart concerning the knowledge of the good and the evil. Some of them said: It is a seal upon the hearts; and the painful punishment is the punishment of distance and the veil from the Presence. We seek refuge in God, exalted is He, from that, and we ask Him, glorified is He, for success toward the most upright paths; there is no lord but Him, and none is hoped for except His good.
